works.title: The soil microbiome in an era of global change
A viral replication level-dependent continuum of transcriptional and microRNA reprogramming in HIV-1-infected microglia links productive infection to neurocognitive-associated gene networks
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Microglia are major targets of HIV-1 in the brain. Despite effective antiviral therapy, infected microglia, including those containing a replication-defective provirus, can express viral products that contribute to neuroinflammation, yet how productive infection shapes the host response remains poorly defined. Using single-cell RNA-seq of HIV-1-infected C20 microglia, we stratified cells by HIV-1 splice junction-supporting reads into low- and high-infection groups, resolving a graded rather than binary host transcriptional response. The computational pipeline developed for this quantification is made publicly available. A core set of immune and cell cycle pathways was induced, regardless of infection level, but several programs reversed direction with increasing viral burden: interferon-α/γ and EMT /hypoxia signatures peaked at low infection, while high infection featured suppression of these signatures alongside induction of mTORC1 / MYC signaling, ribosome biogenesis, RNA processing, and mitotic activity, with progressive loss of cytoskeletal, motility, and developmental programs. This pattern, except for cell cycle/mitotic signatures, was reproduced in iPSC-derived microglia, supporting its generalizability beyond an immortalized cell line. To identify potential regulatory mechanisms underlying these transcriptional programs, we integrated differentially expressed miRNAs and genes from the low- and high-infection groups, filtered for the canonical inverse miRNA-target relationship, revealing miRNA/mRNA networks enriched for miRNAs previously implicated in HIV-1 replication (e.g., miR-33a-5p and miR-3065-3p ) and in neurodegenerative and psychiatric disease (e.g., miR-107 and let-7c-5p ). These findings define a productive infection-level continuum in microglial transcription and miRNA reprogramming and identify candidate miRNA-mediated mechanisms, complementary to the canonical Env / Nef / Tat pathway by which HIV-1-infected microglia may contribute to neuroinflammation and neurocognitive impairment in people with HIV-1. IMPORTANCE HIV-1 persists in the brain despite antiviral therapy in part because infected microglia continue to express viral RNA and proteins that promote neuroinflammation, contributing to the cognitive impairment seen in many people with HIV-1. How the level of active viral replication within a microglial cell shapes its response has been unclear since most infection models capture only an averaged, post-replication snapshot rather than the transition from low to advanced infection. By ranking microglia by HIV-1 splice junction-supporting reads, we show that the host transcriptional response is graded rather than binary, and that several pathways, including interferon and growth/proliferative signaling, reverse direction as viral load increases. We further identify a network of HIV-1-dysregulated miRNAs, several previously linked to viral replication or to neurodegenerative and neurocognitive disease, pointing to a mechanism by which infected microglia may influence neuronal health, complementary to the well-studied viral Env , Nef , and Tat proteins.

works.title: Host-mediated SUMOylation of pE248R promotes African swine fever virus replication and virulence
works.abstract: ABSTRACT SUMOylation, the covalent conjugation of small ubiquitin-like modifier (SUMO) proteins to lysine residues in target substrates, is an essential post-translational modification in eukaryotes. Recently, microbial manipulation of SUMOylation has emerged as an important virulence strategy for viruses. Here, we demonstrate that African swine fever virus CN/GS/2018 (ASFV CN/GS/2018) pE248R can be conjugated to SUMO1 and provide evidence that prevention of pE248R SUMOylation can block ASFV CN/GS/2018 infection. The E3 SUMO ligase PIAS4 interacts with pE248R via its SUMO interaction motifs (SIMs) and promotes pE248R SUMOylation at its lysine residues at positions 103 and 240. Additionally, PIAS4 can increase the stability of pE248R. Importantly, studies on ASFV CN/GS/2018 pE248R with mutations have shown that the SUMOylation sites, the SIMs, or both are essential for the viral replication cycle in vitro and that mutations in these regions attenuate the virus in swine. Collectively, these findings indicate that ASFV CN/GS/2018 pE248R SUMOylation is critical for ASFV CN/GS/2018 pathogenesis and virulence, thereby providing a potential strategy for ASF vaccine development. IMPORTANCE African swine fever virus (ASFV) poses a devastating threat to the global swine industry, yet effective vaccines and antiviral strategies remain unavailable. While microbial manipulation of host post-translational modifications is a common virulence strategy, how ASFV exploits the host SUMOylation machinery has remained elusive. Here, we demonstrate that ASFV CN/GS/2018 pE248R undergoes SUMO1 conjugation mediated by the E3 SUMO ligase PIAS4 via specific SUMO-interacting motifs, which enhances pE248R stability and is essential for the viral replication cycle and virulence in swine. Blocking pE248R SUMOylation at lysine residues 103 and 240 inhibits viral infection, revealing that ASFV CN/GS/2018 hijacks the host SUMOylation system as a critical pathogenesis mechanism. These findings identify a druggable virus-host interaction node and provide a rational target for developing next-generation attenuated ASFV vaccines.

works.title: Community science uncovers environmental azole resistance in Aspergillus fumigatus across Norway, including a novel tandem repeat variant (TR 62 )
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Azole-resistant Aspergillus fumigatus (AR Af ) is an emerging global health concern, mainly driven by environmental selection caused by azole fungicide use. Despite reports of environmental resistance across Europe, data from northern regions remain scarce. Here, we conducted the first nationwide investigation of environmental AR Af in Norway using a community science-based air sampling approach. Volunteers across the country collected airborne fungal spores using passive sticky-seal traps during three sampling periods between 2022 and 2023. In total, 2,332 air samples from 398 locations were analyzed, yielding 1,583 A. fumigatus isolates. Azole resistance screening identified 15 resistant isolates (0.95%) from 14 locations across four out of five Norwegian regions. Minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) confirmed resistance to medical azoles and elevated MICs toward azole fungicides. Whole-genome sequencing revealed known environmentally associated resistance mechanisms, including TR 34 /L98H ( n = 11) and TR 46 /Y121F/T289A ( n = 2), as well as a TR 46 /Y121F/T289A/S363P/I364V/G448S variant ( n = 1). In addition, a previously undescribed promoter tandem repeat variant (TR 62 ) was identified in one isolate that exhibited multi-azole resistance. Population genomic analyses indicated that resistant isolates were genetically diverse and not restricted to a single clonal lineage, suggesting both local expansion and recombination within a structured population. Although the observed resistance frequency was low, the presence of globally disseminated resistance mechanisms in airborne spores across Norway demonstrates that environmental azole resistance is established in the region. This study provides baseline data on the frequency and distribution of environmental AR Af in Norway and contributes to international efforts to strengthen monitoring of antifungal resistance. IMPORTANCE Azole-resistant Aspergillus fumigatus (ARAf) is an emerging public health concern, yet data from northern Europe remain limited. This study provides the first nationwide investigation of the frequency, distribution, and genetic diversity of environmental ARAf in Norway. By combining community-based environmental sampling with whole-genome sequencing, we demonstrate that resistance-associated genotypes of international concern are established in the Norwegian environment and occur across multiple regions. These findings provide important baseline data for future surveillance and contribute to global efforts to monitor and understand the emergence and spread of antifungal resistance.

works.title: Spatiotemporal recurrence and dissemination of Salmonella subpopulations in surface waters of central Chile
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Agricultural waters have been identified as one of the primary sources of Salmonella contamination, which has resulted in numerous outbreaks associated with the consumption of contaminated produce. Consequently, an improved understanding of Salmonella contamination of agricultural waters could facilitate the development of control strategies to prevent food contamination. The objective of this study was to examine the diversity and spatiotemporal recurrence of Salmonella isolates in surface water related to agricultural activities. Water samples ( n = 2,690) were collected between 2019 and 2024 in central Chile using modified Moore swabs, and whole-genome sequencing was carried out for 1 to 10 Salmonella isolates per sample. Non-clonal genomes from each sample ( n = 1,034) were analyzed, showing that the most frequently identified serovars were Infantis (14.6%), Typhimurium (10.8%), Newport (8.5%), and Enteritidis (5.8%). The highest antimicrobial resistance burden was shown by Salmonella Infantis, which carried up to 11 antimicrobial resistance genes simultaneously. Importantly, phylogenomic analyses revealed a highly clonal population structure among the most prevalent serovars and identified recurrent subpopulations that were repeatedly detected across multiple watersheds and consecutive years, including lineages associated with human infections. These findings provide genomic evidence that agricultural surface waters may serve as reservoirs and dissemination routes for recurrent Salmonella subpopulations in central Chile, including multidrug-resistant strains. Our work underscores the critical importance of continuous environmental surveillance and the integration of environmental and clinical genomic surveillance data to improve our understanding of the Salmonella ecology and inform evidence-based mitigation strategies aiming to protect public health. IMPORTANCE Salmonella enterica is a leading cause of foodborne illness worldwide, and contaminated irrigation water is an important pathway by which this pathogen can reach fresh produce. By analyzing more than 1,000 Salmonella genomes collected from agricultural waters in central Chile over 5 years, we found that specific bacterial lineages persisted across multiple watersheds and years, including multidrug-resistant strains linked to human infections. These findings indicate that agricultural surface waters in Chile can serve as reservoirs and dissemination routes for recurrent Salmonella subpopulations. Our study highlights the value of continuous environmental surveillance and the need to integrate data from environmental and human sources to identify potential contamination sources and reduce the risk of foodborne disease.

works.title: Correction: Nucleocapsid-like cryo-EM structure of influenza B virus
Singapore grouper iridovirus VP018 exploits FTR86 to promote viral replication through Tollip-mediated degradation of the STING-TBK1 axis
works.abstract: Members of the tripartite motif (TRIM) family have been demonstrated to exert crucial roles in immune defense against pathogens. However, functions of the fish-specific TRIM subfamily (FTR), which lacks mammalian orthologues, remains poorly understood. In the current study, we investigated the potential roles of grouper FTR86 (EcFTR86) on innate immune response and its actions during fish virus infection. EcFTR86 was found to localize to lysosomes, and its transcription was significantly up-regulated in grouper spleen cells upon Singapore grouper iridovirus (SGIV) infection. Notably, the exogenous expression of EcFTR86 markedly enhanced SGIV replication, whereas knockdown of endogenous EcFTR86 significantly attenuated viral infection, demonstrating that EcFTR86 functions as a pro-viral factor against virus infection. EcFTR86 negatively regulated type I interferon signaling triggered by STING-TBK1 and interacted with the key molecules of STING-TBKl axis. Mechanistically, EcFTR86 degraded STING or TBK1 via an autophagy-lysosome-dependent pathway. Moreover, autophagic cargo receptor Tollip was identified to interact with EcFTR86, and was involved in EcFTR86-mediated degradation of STING or TBK1. In addition, EcFTR86 was verified to interact with SGIV viral proteins, including VP018 and VP075, whereas only VP018 exploited EcFTR86 to accelerate the degradation effects on STING and TBK1, thereby abrogating the interferon response. Collectively, our findings firstly showed that FTR86 functioned as a negative regulator of interferon response, and was exploited by fish iridoviral proteins to promote viral replication via Tollip-mediated autophagic degradation of the STING-TBK1 axis.

works.title: StIA is a novel nucleoid-associated protein of Streptococcus pneumoniae that activates DNA topoisomerase I
works.abstract: Topoisomerases are essential enzymes that maintain DNA topology. The activity of some of these enzymes is regulated by protein cofactors. Here, we identify a previously uncharacterized nucleoid-associated protein from the human pathogen Streptococcus pneumoniae that binds double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) in a sequence-independent manner both in vitro and in vivo and activates topoisomerase I (Topo I). This protein was named StIA (Streptococcal Topoisomerase I Activator). In vivo analyses showed that deletion of stIA impairs bacterial growth in the presence of the Topo I inhibitor seconeolitsine, whereas its overproduction decreases susceptibility to this compound. Consistent with these observations, StIA specifically stimulates Topo I activity without affecting DNA gyrase. StIA forms oligomers and assembles into higher-order nucleoprotein complexes upon DNA-binding. Mechanistic analyses revealed that StIA does not alter DNA cleavage by Topo I but specifically enhances the DNA religation step of its catalytic cycle. This activation is likely mediated through a direct protein-protein interaction, as StIA and Topo I physically associate in vitro . Structural modeling further supports the formation of a StIA-Topo I complex and identifies putative contact residues involved in the interaction. Collectively, these findings establish StIA as a novel nucleoid-associated protein with a dual function: promoting the assembly of nucleoprotein complexes and stimulating Topo I activity through direct interaction with the enzyme. More broadly, our results suggest that the regulation of topoisomerase activity by accessory proteins may represent an important mechanism for fine-tuning DNA topological homeostasis and could provide new opportunities for the development of antibacterial therapies.

works.title: Effects of gelatin/chitosan/Zanthoxylum bungeanum essential oil composite coating on microbial composition and metabolite profiles in refrigerated mandarin fish (Siniperca chuatsi)
works.abstract: Our previous study demonstrated that a gelatin/chitosan/ Zanthoxylum bungeanum essential oil (GE/CS/ZEO) composite film effectively delayed spoilage in refrigerated mandarin fish ( Siniperca chuatsi ). However, the underlying microbial and metabolic mechanisms responsible for its preservative efficacy remain unclear. In this study, high-throughput sequencing coupled with untargeted metabolomics was employed to characterize the core microbiota and metabolic profiles of mandarin fish treated with the GE/CS/ZEO composite film during refrigerated storage. The results showed that the GE/CS/ZEO composite film significantly suppressed the relative abundances of Acinetobacter and Pseudomonas in mandarin fish fillets. At the later stage of refrigerated storage, the predominant genera in the TM-15 group were Acinetobacter , Aeromonas , Vagococcus , and Shewanella . Untargeted metabolomic analysis yielded 2,449 metabolic features, among which the differential metabolites were predominantly glycerophospholipids, bitter-tasting amino acids and their derivatives, amines, nucleotides, and coenzymes. These differential metabolites were significantly enriched in 17 metabolic pathways ( p < 0.05), with purine, phenylalanine, tryptophan, and tyrosine metabolism emerging as key metabolic pathways associated with quality deterioration in mandarin fish during refrigerated storage. Correlation analysis further revealed that Acinetobacter and Chryseobacterium were closely associated with tryptophan metabolism, whereas treatment with the GE/CS/ZEO composite film markedly reshaped the metabolic associations of Aeromonas , resulting in significant correlations with nicotinamide and inosine. Collectively, these findings provide mechanistic insights into the preservative action of the GE/CS/ZEO composite film and highlight the critical roles of microbiota–metabolite interactions in regulating spoilage-related metabolic changes, thereby providing a theoretical basis for the development and application of edible active films for the preservation of refrigerated fish.

works.title: Carvacrol with ARO1 repression synergistically alters Candida albicans mitochondrial integrity, energy metabolism, membrane ultrastructure, and function
works.abstract: Among Candida species, Candida albicans is the leading cause of candidemia and invasive candidiasis, which can cause morbidity and mortality in immunocompromised patients. Fungi have developed resistance to the few existing antifungal drugs, which are limited in efficacy and mechanistic diversity, emphasizing the urgent need for novel antifungals and combination therapies. Developing novel antifungals is more challenging than developing antibacterial agents, since eukaryotic fungi share components and metabolism with human cells, making the discovery of compounds with low cytotoxicity difficult. Phenolic compounds from plant-based essential oils with broad-spectrum antifungal activity and minimal cytotoxicity to humans, such as carvacrol, are regaining interest as antifungals. This study investigates the combined impact of carvacrol treatment and conditional repression of ARO1 , a key enzyme of the shikimate pathway, which synergistically disrupts metabolic activity, mitochondrial function, intracellular adenosine triphosphate levels, causes oxidative stress, and perturbs mitochondrial and plasma membrane potentials, as visualized by altered cell membrane and wall ultrastructure in Candida albicans . These findings indicate a potential strategy for combination therapy to address antifungal resistance.

works.title: Bacterial endophytes in Arctium lappa seeds were found to play an important role in the metabolism of Arctium lappa lignans
works.abstract: Objective Bacterial endophytes in plant seeds provide multifaceted benefits, such as nutrient acquisition, growth promotion, and pathogen suppression. This study aimed to explore the diversity, functional roles, and metabolic impacts of bacterial endophytes in Arctium lappa L. Methods The diversity of bacterial endophytes in different tissues of A. lappa was analyzed using 16S rRNA sequencing, followed by an isolation and functional characterization of key endophytic strains from A. lappa seeds. Genomic analysis of these key strains was performed to identify β-glucosidase genes involved in arctiin metabolism. Gene expression was validated by quantitative reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR), and the metabolic effects of endophytes on A. lappa at different developmental stages were assessed by liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry (LC–MS). Results The analysis of bacterial endophyte diversity revealed the highest richness in root tissues, followed by stem and fruit tissues. Two key endophytic strains, DI4 and ISX2, were successfully isolated from A. lappa seeds. Functional characterization demonstrated their capabilities in nitrogen fixation, phosphate solubilization, siderophore production, and IAA biosynthesis. Genomic analysis indicated a high level of conservation between these two strains and identified β-glucosidase genes (BglX1 and BglX3) involved in the biosynthesis and metabolic pathways of the lignan compound arctiin. qRT-PCR analysis showed significant stage-specific expression differences of BglX1 and BglX3 during A. lappa development. Subsequent ultra-performance liquid chromatography –mass spectrometry (UPLC–MS) analysis further confirmed the different effects of DI4 and ISX2 strains on lignan metabolism during seed germination. Conclusion This study underscores the significant role of endophytes in the growth and development of A. lappa , elucidating the collaborative and adaptive relationship between endophytes and A. lappa in response to environmental conditions. It also suggests potential applications for enhancing the bioactive compounds in medicinal plants.

works.title: Soil reclamation induced salinity decline is associated with shifts in bacterial, fungal and protistan communities and higher wheat yield in saline-alkali fields
works.abstract: Soil reclamation is widely practiced in saline–alkali land areas. However, limited research has focused on how reclamation duration regulates soil microbial communities and crop yield via modifying soil environmental conditions. In this study, high-throughput sequencing, ecological network analysis, and soil physicochemical characterization were integrated to investigate variations in soil properties, microbial community composition, and crop yield across saline–alkali fields with different reclamation durations (1, 5, and 10 years). The results showed that prolonged reclamation significantly reduced soil salinity and increased soil nutrient contents as well as wheat yield. The richness of fungi and protists increased with the extension of reclamation durations, whereas bacterial richness exhibited an opposite trend. Network-associated key taxa of bacteria, fungi and protists were significantly correlated with wheat yield, soil salinity, soil organic matter (SOM), total nitrogen (TN), as well as the activities of leucine aminopeptidase (LAP) and β-glucosidase (Glu). Structural equation modeling (SEM) further revealed that soil salinity was associated with soil physicochemical traits, network-associated key taxa and enzyme activities, altered the soil microecological environment, and ultimately affected wheat yield. In conclusion, reclamation durations mitigated soil salinity, which drove the screening of microbial taxa by soil microhabitats and reconstructed the overall microbial community structure, thereby influencing wheat productivity. These findings provide theoretical and technical support for the sustainable reclamation of saline–alkali land, health management of farmland soil, and stable improvement of grain productivity.

works.title: Antifungal activity of pyrrolnitrin produced by Burkholderia seminalis strain R456 against Alternaria brassicicola in broccoli
works.abstract: Introduction Black spot disease, caused by Alternaria brassicicola , significantly reduces the yield and quality of broccoli. Growing concerns about environmental pollution and fungicide resistance have increased interest in beneficial microorganisms as sustainable biological control agents for plant disease management. Methods This study evaluated the in vitro and in planta antifungal activity of cell-free culture filtrates (CFFs) produced by the rice rhizosphere bacterium Burkholderia seminalis R456 against A. brassicicola and investigated candidate bioactive metabolites associated with the observed antifungal effects. Results and discussion R456 CFF suppressed mycelial growth in a fermentation-time- and concentration-dependent manner; the filtrate obtained after 5 days of fermentation showed the best activity, and 50% CFF caused complete or near-complete inhibition under the plate-assay conditions. The filtrate reduced conidial germination to 3.87%. Microscopic observations showed that CFF treatment was associated with pronounced morphological abnormalities in A. brassicicola , including hyphal and conidial deformation, shrinkage, collapse, and surface irregularities. In planta assays under controlled conditions showed that R456 CFF suppressed black spot disease, achieving control efficacies of 71.56% on detached leaves and 70.72% on whole plants. The 100% ethanol-eluted fraction showed the best activity among the fractions tested, and LC-MS/MS comparison with an authentic standard supported pyrrolnitrin as an important candidate antifungal metabolite. Functional validation with the pyrrolnitrin standard further showed concentration-dependent disease suppression, with control efficacies at 50 mg/L of 100% on detached leaves and 96.50% on whole plants. Overall, these findings support R456-derived extracellular metabolites as a potential antifungal resource and provide direct evidence that pyrrolnitrin is biologically active in the A. brassicicola -broccoli pathosystem; however, the quantitative contribution of

works.title: Editorial: Biophysics and molecular biology of antimicrobial resistance: toward new targets and strategies
works.abstract: analysis and genetic distance calculations supported the clustering of KLUS-1 through KLUS-4 as a distinct lineage. KLUS-1-3 conferred high-level resistance to ampicillin and ceftriaxone, whereas KLUS-4 showed greater ceftazidime resistance and a reduced phenotypic response to clavulanic acid. Structural modeling revealed a conserved catalytic cavity alongside 23 unique substitutions and a V77I substitution near the Ωloop relative to CTX-M-2, highlighting the continuous evolutionary diversification of □□-lactamases. Integrating computation with structural biophysics, Pang et al. targeted penicillin-binding protein 2a (PBP2A) in methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA) using ensemble molecular dynamics simulations and deep generative modeling.By sampling dynamic cryptic pockets, they identified a promising candidate compound, designated Compound 1, which demonstrated robust conformational stability and favorable binding free energy across dynamic states, ultimately translating to concentration-and timedependent growth inhibition and cell envelope perturbation in MRSA.Mechanistic studies of bacterial motility, a crucial virulence factor, extend its framework to the insight into protein exporting, which is associated with toxin secretion in some pathogens. The studies compiled in this Research Topic collectively demonstrate that combating AMR requires an intimate convergence of physical principles and molecular genetics. They also highlight the need to connect structural predictions and biochemical observations with activity in intact cells and infection models. Integrating biophysics, structural biology, nanotechnology, and genetic engineering would provide a powerful paradigm to discover vulnerable targets and formulate enduring therapeutic strategies capable of outracing microbial evolution.

works.title: Amplicon-based microbiome profiling of honey bee drones and dandelions—the role in contributing to microbial diversity and carrying antimicrobial resistance
works.abstract: Introduction The microbiota of honey bees forms a complex community, whose composition changes throughout the life cycle and varies between castes and hives. Bee-inhabiting microorganisms can be transmitted through direct contact with nestmates, interactions with the hive environment, and while collecting food. Honey bees may act as reservoirs and disseminators of pathogenic microorganisms and antimicrobial resistance. While not involved in economically important pollination services, honey bee males are increasingly recognized as important for overall hive health. This study aimed to characterize bacterial communities associated with western honey bee ( Apis mellifera L.) drones at different developmental stages and dandelions ( Taraxacum officinale F. H. Wigg), located in the hives’ surrounding area, and to assess their role in maintaining microbial diversity and carrying antimicrobial resistance. Methods The microbial DNA was extracted from different stages of honey bee drones and dandelion flowers, and bacterial communities were revealed by Next Generation Sequencing of the PCR-amplified V3-V4 region of the 16S rRNA gene. The distribution of genes conferring resistance to aminoglycosides, β-lactams, tetracyclines, sulfonamides, and tylosins was analyzed by target-specific PCR. Results The results show that prokaryotic community structure differed significantly among sampled groups, including honey bee drones at different stages of life and dandelion flowers, although pairwise comparisons were not significant. Host-health-supporting beneficial microorganisms were detected across all developmental stages of drones, with higher diversity at the larval stage. The bacterial microbiota of dandelion flowers formed a separate cluster and contained taxa previously associated with plant-beneficial or phytopathogenic traits. Taxa shared between honey bee males and dandelion flowers included those that play a vital role in bee health or cause their diseases. The microbiota of honey bee drones and dandelions accumulate various ARGs, with the highest prevalence of genes encoding resistance to tetracycline and sulfonamide. Discussion Our research provides insights into the contribution of honey bee males to microbial diversity, highlights the importance of drones and dandelions as reservoirs for both beneficial and pathogenic bacteria, and identifies them as carriers of antimicrobial resistance genes.

works.title: Antifungal and antibiofilm activity of the protease-resistant peptides NET1 and NET3 against Candida reference strains, with exploratory analysis of mitochondrial and membrane-associated changes
works.abstract: The global rise of drug-resistant fungal pathogens, particularly non- albicans Candida species, necessitates the development of novel therapeutic strategies. In this study, we investigated the antifungal, antibiofilm, and mitochondrial/membrane-disruptive activities of NET1 and NET3, two novel, protease-resistant synthetic antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) composed of D- and L-amino acid combinations, against reference strains of Candida albicans , Candida krusei ( Pichia kudriavzevii ), Candida lusitaniae ( Clavispora lusitaniae ), and Candida parapsilosis . Minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) values for both peptides ranged from 8 to 16 μg/mL across all tested strains. Notably, both peptides inhibited initial biofilm formation at sub-MIC levels in C. albicans (MBICs of 2 μg/mL for NET1 and 1 μg/mL for NET3; 8- to 16-fold below their MICs). To elucidate the cellular mechanisms accompanying fungal growth inhibition, key mitochondrial and membrane-associated changes and membrane hallmarks were evaluated following peptide exposure. At 0.5 × MIC, JC-1 fluorescent staining revealed that both NET1 and NET3 induced widespread collapse of the mitochondrial membrane potential. At 1 × MIC, subcellular fractionation and spectrophotometric analysis at 550 nm showed a marked shift of Cytochrome c from the mitochondrial to the cytosolic fraction, consistent with outer mitochondrial membrane permeabilization. Furthermore, CF®488A Annexin V and Propidium Iodide (PI) dual-staining at 0.5 × MIC revealed phosphatidylserine externalization with intact membranes (predominantly early apoptotic-like Annexin V + /PI − cells) in C. albicans and C. parapsilosis , and dual-positive staining (Annexin V + /PI + , consistent with late apoptosis-like progression or secondary membrane permeabilization) in peptide-treated C. krusei and C. lusitaniae ; primary necrotic (Annexin V − /PI + ) cells were rarely detected at sub-MIC levels. These results suggest that the antifungal activity of NET1 and NET3 involves a mitochondria-associated, apoptosis-like response alongside membrane disruption rather than primary necrosis alone. Overall, these protease-resistant AMPs represent promising therapeutic candidates for combating opportunistic Candida infections.

works.title: Broad use of feline APN by alphacoronaviruses implicates cats in cross-species transmission
works.abstract: Coronaviruses continue to pose a global public health threat, and the increasing frequency of zoonotic spillover events highlights the crucial role of animal hosts in cross-species transmission. As companion animals, cats warrant attention for their potential involvement in coronavirus cross-species spread. Here, we show that feline aminopeptidase N (fAPN) functions as a shared receptor utilized by multiple alphacoronaviruses (α-CoVs), including human coronavirus 229E (HCoV-229E), transmissible gastroenteritis virus, and type-II feline infectious peritonitis virus, to mediate entry into feline cells. Structural and functional analyses reveal that distinct viruses engage fAPN through alternative binding sites, enabling multimodal receptor recognition, and demonstrating notable receptor compatibility. Animal challenge experiments further indicate that HCoV-229E showed detectable viral RNA and infectious virus in the feline respiratory tract, with no apparent clinical signs. Together, these findings establish fAPN as a shared receptor for diverse α-CoVs and reveal a molecular basis for receptor compatibility across viral lineages, providing insight into the determinants of coronavirus host range and cross-species transmission.IMPORTANCEZoonotic coronaviruses repeatedly threaten human health, yet the rules governing their ability to cross species remain incompletely understood. Cats live in close contact with humans and may act as hidden hosts for coronaviruses, but the molecular basis supporting cross-species infection in these animals is unclear. This study demonstrates that feline aminopeptidase N (fAPN) serves as a common receptor for several alphacoronaviruses (α-CoVs), including human coronavirus 229E (HCoV-229E), transmissible gastroenteritis virus, and type-II feline infectious peritonitis virus. These viruses recognize fAPN through distinct binding sites, highlighting the flexibility of receptor recognition. Additionally, HCoV-229E inoculation resulted in detectable viral RNA in the respiratory tract of cats, without apparent clinical signs. These results help explain why α-CoVs can move across host barriers and suggest that cats should be considered when assessing coronavirus spillover risks at the human-animal interface.

works.title: Targeting sterylglucosidase 1 attenuates virulence and enables immune protection against Candida albicans
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Sterylglucosidases are fungus-specific enzymes that regulate ergosterol 3-β-D-glucoside (Erg-SG) homeostasis and represent promising targets for antifungal intervention. Previous studies demonstrated that sterylglucosidases from Cryptococcus neoformans and Aspergillus fumigatus contribute to fungal virulence, and that deletion of these enzymes elicits protective immunity. However, whether sterylglucosidase-mediated pathways similarly influence Candida albicans pathogenicity remains unknown. Here, we identified C. albicans Sgl1 as a bona fide sterylglucosidase that selectively hydrolyzes Erg-SG but not fungal glucosylceramide. Deletion of SGL1 resulted in marked Erg-SG accumulation without altering glucosylceramide levels, confirming its conserved role in sterylglucoside homeostasis. Although the Δ sgl 1 mutant displayed largely preserved growth, morphogenesis, and stress adaptation, it exhibited impaired biofilm formation. Biochemical characterization, inhibitor profiling, and structural analyses revealed marked species-specific inhibitor susceptibility among fungal sterylglucosidases despite highly conserved overall architecture and catalytic machinery. Structural modeling and docking studies identified differences in ligand positioning and active-site interactions that likely contribute to these divergent pharmacological responses. Functionally, loss of SGL1 significantly attenuated virulence in a murine model of systemic candidiasis. Importantly, vaccination with heat-killed Δ sgl 1 cells conferred 70% protection against lethal systemic challenge and markedly reduced kidney fungal burden, providing the first evidence that sterylglucosidase-dependent vaccination can induce protective immunity against a non-pulmonary fungal infection. Collectively, these findings establish C. albicans Sgl1 as a conserved regulator of sterylglucoside homeostasis, fungal pathogenicity, and host protection, and identify fungal sterylglucosidases as promising targets for antifungal drug and immunotherapy development. IMPORTANCE Fungal infections are associated with substantial morbidity and mortality, yet effective immunotherapies and novel antifungal targets remain limited. Candida albicans is a major cause of invasive and mucosal fungal disease, highlighting the need for new therapeutic strategies. Here, we identify the fungus-specific sterylglucosidase Sgl1 as a conserved regulator of ergosterol 3-β-D-glucoside homeostasis and a critical determinant of C. albicans pathogenicity. We further demonstrate that fungal sterylglucosidases exhibit distinct species-specific pharmacological responses despite conserved structural frameworks, revealing opportunities for rational antifungal drug design. Importantly, deletion of SGL1 attenuated virulence and enabled protective vaccination against lethal systemic candidiasis, providing the first evidence that targeting sterylglucoside metabolism can elicit protective immunity against a non-pulmonary fungal pathogen. Together, these findings identify Candida albicans Sgl1 as a promising target for antifungal drug and immunotherapy development.

works.title: The BspC surface adhesin and gastrointestinal fungal colonization enhance group B streptococcal neonatal infection
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Group B Streptococcus (GBS) colonizes the gastrointestinal (GI) and female reproductive tracts of up to 30% of healthy adults, but during pregnancy can be transmitted to the newborn, causing neonatal sepsis, pneumonia, and meningitis. Neonatal GI colonization is an important precursor to invasive disease, yet the mechanisms governing GBS intestinal persistence and dissemination are still being elucidated. Given the predominance of hypervirulent sequence type 17 (ST-17) strains in neonatal invasive disease, we hypothesized that the ST-17-associated surface adhesin BspC contributes to gastrointestinal colonization and infection. Using a neonatal mouse model, we found that pups infected with wild-type GBS exhibited increased mortality and significantly higher bacterial burdens in the intestine, blood, spleen, and brain compared with pups infected with a Δ bspC mutant. We also observed that BspC promoted adherence to a 2D organoid model of the human infant colon and Caco-2 intestinal epithelial cells through its variable domain. Building on previous findings that Candida albicans interacts with BspC, we found that C. albicans enhanced GBS intestinal epithelial adherence in a BspC-dependent manner, and coinfection increased intestinal GBS burden and brain dissemination in neonatal mice. Finally, analysis of published human neonatal fecal microbiome data sets revealed higher GBS abundance in infants colonized with C. albicans or other Candida species. Together, these findings identify BspC as a key mediator of GBS intestinal colonization and invasive disease and suggest that fungal colonization of the neonatal GI promotes GBS pathogenesis. IMPORTANCE Group B Streptococcus (GBS) is a leading cause of neonatal infection, which can result in fatality or long-term neurological morbidity in survivors. Intestinal colonization is an important precursor to invasive disease, yet the factors that promote GBS persistence in the neonatal gastrointestinal tract remain incompletely understood. Here, we identify the GBS surface adhesin BspC as a mediator of intestinal epithelial adherence, gastrointestinal colonization, and systemic dissemination. We further demonstrate that the common fungal pathobiont Candida albicans enhances GBS intestinal adherence and infection. Consistent with our experimental findings, analysis of human infant microbiome data sets revealed greater GBS abundance in infants colonized with Candida species. These findings identify BspC as a key mediator of this process and suggest that fungal colonization can enhance GBS disease.

works.title: Ehrlichia chaffeensis and its retropepsin-type protease engage the complement inhibitor C4b-binding protein
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Ehrlichia chaffeensis is a tick-borne obligate intracellular bacterium that causes human monocytic ehrlichiosis. Significant advances have been made in understanding immune evasion strategies in Ehrlichia ; however, the role of the complement system has been largely overlooked. This study provides evidence for a novel interaction between E. chaffeensis and the complement inhibitor C4b-binding protein (C4BP). We confirmed that E. chaffeensis recruits and binds C4BP at its surface, demonstrating binding of C4BP in human serum. This interaction is concentration-dependent, and C4BP retains its regulatory cofactor activity when bound to the bacteria. Furthermore, we identified the ehrlichial retropepsin-type protease—named APEhc—as a new C4BP ligand. We show that the soluble domain of APEhc targets multiple serum components, directly binding factor H, forming complexes with C4BP, and cleaving two major complement components, C3b and C4b. Quantitative binding analysis reveals a strong interaction between APEhc and C4BP, with apparent dissociation constants in the nanomolar range. Analysis of C4BP CCP deletion mutants supports a contribution of CCP3, CCP6, and CCP7 to APEhc-C4BP binding. Additionally, we demonstrate that C4BP retains its factor I cofactor activity in the presence of APEhc, and that APEhc independently cleaves C4b. Consistent with the targeting and modulation of serum components, our results show that APEhc significantly inhibits activation of the classical, lectin, and alternative pathways. Our findings reveal the unprecedented interaction between E. chaffeensis , its retropepsin protease, and complement inhibitors, raising intriguing questions regarding complement targeting by E. chaffeensis and its role in immune evasion. IMPORTANCE Human monocytic ehrlichiosis is a tick-borne disease caused by Ehrlichia chaffeensis , which can be severe or fatal if untreated. Understanding how E. chaffeensis evades the immune system is crucial for identifying new virulence factors and developing new treatments. The complement system, an essential part of the body’s first line of defense, is often targeted by pathogens to avoid immune attacks. We show that E. chaffeensis binds to C4b-binding protein (C4BP), a major inhibitor of the classical pathway (CP) and lectin pathway (LP), and identify the ehrlichial retropepsin-type protease, APEhc, as a novel C4BP ligand. Additionally, we demonstrate that APEhc targets other serum components, inhibiting complement CP, LP, and AP activation, suggesting an unprecedented dual-inhibitory activity for APEhc through complex formation with C4BP (and factor H) and cleavage of C3b and C4b. Our findings reveal a multifunctional role for APEhc in immune evasion, raising intriguing questions about the mechanisms used by intracellular pathogens like E. chaffeensis to bypass host defenses.

works.title: Decoding the cefazolin inoculum effect: phenotypic and genotypic insights beyond the MIC
works.abstract: ABSTRACT The cefazolin inoculum effect (CzIE) is a clinically relevant in vitro phenomenon that may compromise cefazolin efficacy in high-inoculum methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA) infections such as bacteremia and infective endocarditis. We aimed to define mechanisms underlying CzIE beyond BlaZ-dependent enzymatic pathways. We evaluated CzIE in 198 MSSA isolates (single center) by comparing minimum inhibitory concentrations at standard and high inoculum. The inoculum effect index was used as a quantitative measure of the CzIE to validate the operational definition and assess its concordance with the classical definition of CzIE. Whole-genome sequencing was used to define β-lactamase gene ( blaZ ) allotypes, accessory gene regulator ( agr) genotypes (I–IV), and clonal lineages. CzIE was observed in 16.16% of isolates, with Type A (71.9%) and Type C (28.1%) blaZ allotypes predominating among CzIE-positive strains. These isolates were enriched within clonal complex CC8 and CC30. Twenty-four-hour time-kill experiments combining cefazolin with BlaZ inhibitor (sulbactam) demonstrated initial killing followed by regrowth in CzIE-positive isolates, while complete eradication was observed in CzIE-negative isolates. Population analysis profiles (PAP) revealed the expansion of cefazolin–non-susceptible subpopulations at high inoculum, consistent with phenotypic heterogeneity. agr typing identified agr III as the predominant genotype among CzIE-positive isolates, and agr dysfunction was significantly associated with CzIE-positive phenotype. Together, these findings suggest that CzIE is driven not only by BlaZ-mediated activity but also by agr -dependent regulatory pathways. These observations highlight the potential clinical importance of CzIE and support further investigation into its implications for therapeutic optimization and improved patient outcomes. IMPORTANCE Cefazolin inoculum effect (CzIE) represents an underrecognized potential determinant of therapeutic failure in methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA) infections, yet it remains absent from routine susceptibility testing frameworks. We demonstrate that CzIE is not solely driven by blaZ-mediated activity but is strongly associated with agr-dependent regulation and population heterogeneity. Our findings suggest that standard MIC testing can underestimate cefazolin failure under high-inoculum conditions commonly encountered in invasive diseases. Importantly, identification of CzIE-positive isolates could inform therapeutic decision-making, including selection of alternative β-lactams or adjunctive strategies to suppress tolerant subpopulations. Integration of CzIE assessment with genomic markers such as blaZ allotype and agr genotype may enable more precise prediction of treatment response. These data provide a framework for incorporating CzIE into diagnostic workflows and guide future studies evaluating its clinical utility. Ultimately, recognizing CzIE as a multifactorial phenotype may improve antibiotic selection, reduce treatment failure, and enhance outcomes in serious MSSA infections across patient populations.

works.title: Integrated physiological and multiomic analyses reveal the multilayered aluminum tolerance mechanisms of acidophilic alga Coccomyxa sp. A2
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Acid mine drainage (AMD) is a pervasive global environmental challenge, and algal-based bioremediation represents one of the most robust strategies for its treatment. However, the mechanisms by which algae survive in metal-rich AMD remain largely unclear. Here, we integrated physiological, transcriptomic, and proteomic analyses to explore the tolerance mechanisms of the acidophilic alga Coccomyxa sp. A2 to aluminum (Al), a metal prevalent in AMD. The results demonstrated that A2 exhibited substantially higher Al tolerance than the model alga Chlamydomonas reinhardtii under their respective optimal pH conditions. Upon Al exposure, A2 significantly increased the extracellular levels of three strong organic acids (oxalic, citric, and tartaric acids), thereby facilitating chelation of free Al 3+ present in the acidic environment. In the near-neutral cytosol, A2 accumulated a broader array of organic acids at higher concentrations to sequester Al despite severe extracellular H + stress. To restrict Al influx, A2 enhanced the synthesis of cellulose, hemicellulose, and proteins across the distinct layers of its cell wall, increasing cell wall dry weight by 66%. This remodeling was probably supported by starch degradation, enhanced gluconeogenesis, and Calvin cycle activation, which together supplied sufficient monosaccharide precursors for polysaccharide synthesis. Concurrently, the upregulation of glycosyltransferases facilitated rapid polysaccharide chain elongation. To scavenge ROS, the alga likely initiated a temporally coordinated, biphasic antioxidant response, in which non-enzymatic ascorbic acid pools compensated for lagging superoxide dismutase activity during the early acute phase of stress. Calcium, abscisic acid, and jasmonic acid coordinated these defense mechanisms, with calcium serving as the primary signaling hub. IMPORTANCE The conventional treatment method for acid mine drainage (AMD) involves neutralization with lime, which is costly and generates large amounts of sludge that is difficult to manage. The application of sulfate-reducing bacteria (SRB) presents a promising alternative by eliminating secondary pollution and enabling metal sulfide recovery. However, a key challenge of this approach is ensuring an affordable and sustainable organic carbon source for SRB since AMD is oligotrophic. A potential solution is the in-situ cultivation of acidophilic algae. Given the high metal concentrations in AMD, investigating the metal tolerance mechanisms of acidophilic algae is vital for producing sufficient biomass to support SRB. Meanwhile, about 40% of the world’s arable soils are acidic, and these soils typically contain high concentrations of aluminum (Al), which is a major factor limiting crop production. Therefore, research on the exceptional Al tolerance mechanisms of acidophilic algae can provide insights into improving crop metal resistance through genetic engineering techniques.

works.title: Temperature defines metabolic states that lead to seasonal adaptation of the soil nitrite oxidizer Nitrobacter vulgaris strain CN101
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Nitrite-oxidizing bacteria (NOB) play a central role in nitrification, yet their temperature-dependent ecophysiology remains poorly understood, particularly in terrestrial environments. In this study, the physiological and transcriptomic responses of Nitrobacter vulgaris strain CN101, isolated from forest soil in Japan, were investigated across different culture temperatures. Temperature-dependent kinetics revealed two distinct activation energies below and above 20°C, suggesting a shift in metabolic state. At lower temperatures, nitrite oxidation rates declined, and transcriptomic analysis showed reduced expression of genes involved in electron transport and protein synthesis, whereas genes related to carbon and nitrogen assimilation remained relatively unchanged. Electron microscopy revealed smaller cell size and simplified membrane structures under low-temperature conditions. Together, these findings indicate that metabolic activity is maintained while biomass production is constrained below 20°C. At higher temperatures, efficient electron transport, increased translational capacity, and enlarged cell morphology were restored, consistent with a growth-promoting state. These coordinated metabolic and structural changes suggest that strain CN101 adopts a temperature-dependent strategy that balances survival and proliferation in seasonally fluctuating forest soils. By integrating physiological, ultrastructural, and transcriptomic analyses, this study provides a concrete example of how temperature influences the ecophysiological adaptation of terrestrial NOB. IMPORTANCE Nitrification is a key microbial process in the global nitrogen cycle, yet how nitrifying microorganisms remain active under fluctuating environmental conditions remains poorly understood. In temperate soils, seasonal temperature variation strongly influences nitrification, but the physiological responses of nitrite-oxidizing bacteria (NOB) remain largely unexplored. In this study, we show that the soil nitrite oxidizer Nitrobacter vulgaris strain CN101 exhibits temperature-dependent physiological states, shifting from a metabolically active but growth-limited state at low temperatures to a state of active growth at higher temperatures. These findings demonstrate how temperature restructures NOB metabolism and physiology. This study provides a representative example of the seasonal ecophysiology of soil nitrifiers and highlights temperature-driven physiological restructuring as a key mechanism shaping nitrification dynamics in terrestrial ecosystems.

works.title: The pore-forming protein APOL7C ruptures Leishmania major-containing parasitophorous vacuoles in dendritic cells to promote IL-12 production and the induction of T helper type 1 immunity
works.abstract: Classical dendritic cells (cDCs) are required for the efficient priming of T helper type 1 (Th1) immunity against Leishmania major infections in mice. They do so by producing large quantities of IL-12 in response to L. major infection. IL-12 in turn supports the generation of protective CD4+ Th1 cells. However, the mechanism(s) by which L. major instigates robust IL-12 production by cDCs has not been addressed. Here we show that expression of a pore-forming protein called APOL7C is induced in cDCs by L. major infection. APOL7C is expressed in the cytosol of host cells and, remarkably, upon infection is recruited to L. major parasitophorous vacuoles (PVs) where it induces PV rupture. PV rupture leads to the exposure of L. major-derived pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) to cytosolic pattern recognition receptors (PRRs). Cytosolic PRR signaling then drives IL-12 production by cDCs. Consequently, L. major challenge of APOL7C-deficient mice results in reduced numbers of IL-12 producing cDCs as well as a diminished Th1 response. In sum, our data indicate the presence of pore-forming proteins in the cytosol of cDCs that interfere with the intracellular niche of Leishmania to modulate immunity to these parasites.

works.title: Swimming motility and type IV pili modulate phagocytosis by shaping physical interactions between Pseudomonas aeruginosa and macrophages
works.abstract: During chronic lung infections, Pseudomonas aeruginosa diversifies under selection from antibiotics, metabolic constraints, and host defenses. Macrophages are key sentinels of the innate immune system and play a central role in clearing airway pathogens. Yet, how they process heterogeneous bacterial populations remains poorly understood. Here, we investigate how P. aeruginosa evades phagocytosis under conditions that resemble chronic infection. We use an attenuated mutant lacking a functional type III secretion system (T3SS), which reduces macrophage killing, allowing us to isolate determinants of bacterial susceptibility to phagocytosis. Using transposon insertion sequencing (Tn-seq), we identify bacterial fitness factors under phagocytic selection. Our screen reveals that disruption of genes involved in swimming and twitching motility reduces uptake by macrophages. We find that defects in flagellar and type IV pili (T4P) function interfere with the physical interactions between bacteria and macrophages. Live-cell imaging shows that motility-deficient bacteria exhibit reduced surface accumulation and unstable attachment to macrophages, limiting their internalization. Clinical isolates with reduced swimming or twitching motility display similarly impaired uptake. We also test the influence of bacterial motility on macrophage survival by restoring T3SS activity in flagellar and T4P mutants. In the PAO1 background, most motility mutants retained the ability to kill macrophages indicating that cytotoxicity dominates bacteria-macrophage competition in the presence of a functional T3SS. However, the non-flagellated, hyper-piliated Δ fliC Δ pilT mutant showed a surprisingly attenuated killing, which may reflect reduced bacterial encounters with macrophages, impaired engagement of cytotoxic effectors, or both. Together, our results show that swimming motility and type IV pili shape physical interactions between P. aeruginosa and macrophages, thereby influencing phagocytic uptake.

works.title: Baloxavir and molnupiravir protect against severe influenza A(H5N1) infection in immunosuppressed hamsters
works.abstract: Highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) viruses continue to expand their geographic and host range, raising concerns about zoonotic transmission and pandemic preparedness. Immunocompromised individuals often develop severe and prolonged disease, yet evidence guiding antiviral therapy remains limited. Here, we characterized the pathogenesis and assessed direct-contact transmission of an influenza A(H5N1) clade 2.3.4.4b genotype D1.1 virus recently isolated from a human case in British Columbia, Canada, in cyclophosphamide-immunosuppressed hamsters, with normal hamsters included for comparison of infection outcomes and viral shedding kinetics. We also evaluated the antiviral efficacy of oseltamivir (20 mg/kg twice daily for 5 days), baloxavir (50 mg/kg, 2 doses), and molnupiravir (50 or 200 mg/kg twice daily) as monotherapies or in combination (oseltamivir with low-dose molnupiravir) in immunosuppressed hamsters. While normal hamsters showed no mortality and achieved viral clearance, infection in immunosuppressed hamsters caused severe disease characterized by prolonged viral replication, neuroinvasion, and 75% mortality, with no direct-contact transmission detected. In the antiviral efficacy experiment, placebo-treated hamsters exhibited 50% mortality. Baloxavir resulted in 100% survival, shortened viral shedding, reduced viral replication and pulmonary inflammatory responses, and prevented neuroinvasion. High-dose molnupiravir also prevented mortality and achieved viral clearance in lung and brain tissues. Combination therapy resulted in 75% survival and similarly achieved viral clearance in both tissues, with reduced morbidity compared with oseltamivir and low-dose molnupiravir monotherapies. Oseltamivir resulted in 75% survival but failed to prevent severe clinical signs or reduce tissue viral titers, whereas low-dose molnupiravir showed outcomes comparable to placebo. These findings demonstrate the high pathogenicity of a human A(H5N1) isolate in immunosuppressed hamsters, support baloxavir as an effective therapeutic option, and identify molnupiravir-based regimens as promising strategies for severe influenza A(H5N1) infection.

works.title: Nuclear egress complex promotes capsid nuclear egress during Kaposi’s Sarcoma-associated herpesvirus reactivation
works.abstract: During herpesvirus replication, newly assembled capsids exit the nucleus by nuclear egress, in which capsids bud at the inner nuclear membrane forming perinuclear enveloped virions that then fuse with the outer nuclear membrane, releasing capsids into the cytoplasm. This process is mediated by the nuclear egress complex (NEC), a conserved viral heterodimer of UL31 and UL34 homologs. Although prior studies demonstrated that overexpression of the NEC from Kaposi's Sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV) induces nuclear membrane vesiculation and proliferation in uninfected cells, its role during lytic replication remained undefined. Here, we examined nuclear egress in two models of lytic KSHV replication, reactivated iSLK-BAC16 and TREx-BCBL1-RTA cell lines, using transmission electron microscopy (TEM). In iSLK-BAC16 cells, loss of the NEC caused capsid accumulation at the nuclear periphery and abolished infectious virion production, demonstrating that the NEC is required for efficient nuclear egress. In both cell lines, we observed capsid egress and virion assembly, but the associated phenotypes differed considerably. KSHV reactivation in iSLK-BAC16 cells induced extensive nuclear membrane remodeling, including membrane proliferations and invaginations, whereas these features were largely reduced or absent in reactivated TREx-BCBL1-RTA cells. Moreover, KSHV nuclear egress proceeded more rapidly in TREx-BCBL1-RTA than in the iSLK-BAC16 cell line, demonstrating that KSHV lytic replication can vary across biological systems. Collectively, our data demonstrate the critical role of the KSHV NEC and show that nuclear egress can vary substantially across biological systems, underscoring the importance of the cellular context and the need to study KSHV replication in multiple model systems.

works.title: A quantitative microbial risk assessment of Escherichia coli O157:H7 in sheep meat in Saudi Arabia
works.abstract: Background Escherichia coli O157:H7 is an important foodborne pathogen associated with severe clinical outcomes. It has been detected in sheep and sheep meat in Saudi Arabia. However, quantitative estimates of exposure and illness risk under the Saudi food-supply context remain limited. Methods A probabilistic quantitative microbial risk assessment model was developed for sheep meat. Seven fixed initial contamination levels were evaluated, ranging from −3 to 3 log 10 CFU/g. Each level was simulated under two storage scenarios: recommended refrigeration (1–5 °C) and a plausible temperature distribution. Saudi consumption and supply patterns were maintained across scenarios. Results Across the seven contamination levels, both the probability of illness and modeled annual incidence increased with initial concentration. At 3 log 10 CFU/g, the median probability of illness was 1.50 × 10 −9 under recommended storage and 3.40 × 10 −9 under plausible storage. Median annual incidence was zero cases per 100,000 under both scenarios when rounded to the nearest whole case. Factor-fixing sensitivity analysis identified the probability of illness from a single organism as the most influential parameter, followed by internal cooking temperature. Conclusion The modeled results suggest that population-level risk is associated with a subset of high-exposure scenarios observed within the simulation. Variation across storage and cooking conditions is reflected in the distribution of outcomes.

works.title: Marine particles as underexplored hotspots for antimicrobial peptide discovery: an ecology-guided frontier in marine natural product bioprospecting
works.abstract: The increasing global antibiotic resistance has created a pressing need for new antimicrobial drugs. Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) come into the spotlight for their antibacterial properties, particularly against multidrug-resistant pathogens. Because AMPs typically mediate localized interference competition, we hypothesize that spatially confined, highly competitive microbiomes create ecological conditions that favor the evolution, expression, and diversification of AMPs, although spatial structure may equally promote niche partitioning, cooperative interactions, and producer–resistant coexistence. We therefore propose, as a working hypothesis, that marine particles represent promising yet underexplored reservoirs of untapped marine AMPs. Marine particles are ubiquitous throughout the ocean, ranging from the sunlit surface waters to the deepest hadal environments. They are densely colonized microhabitats where nutrient gradients, spatial proximity, chemical signaling, and interspecies competition among microorganisms converge—unique characteristics that position marine particles as natural laboratories for the evolution of novel AMPs. However, most marine microorganisms are challenging to cultivate. Fortunately, metagenomics is greatly expanding the scope of marine AMP discovery by enabling researchers to screen for elusive peptide-encoding genes and complex biosynthetic gene clusters in uncultivated microbial communities. Additionally, advancements in artificial intelligence are further transforming marine AMP bioprospecting by moving from passive exploration to active molecular understanding and navigation. This review synthesizes our current understanding of the microbial ecology and emerging technologies that drive marine AMP discovery, and explores the application potentials of marine AMPs in human medicine, agriculture, and mariculture.

works.title: Cistanche deserticola exosome-like nanoparticles alleviate constipation through PINK1-dependent mitophagy and gut microbiota remodeling
works.abstract: Introduction Constipation is a prevalent gastrointestinal disorder with limited long-term treatment options. This study investigates the therapeutic potential and mechanisms of Cistanche deserticola exosome-like nanoparticles (CELNs) in alleviating constipation, focusing on mitochondrial quality control and gut microbiota regulation. Methods CELNs were isolated and characterized using ultracentrifugation, transmission electron microscopy, and nanoparticle tracking analysis. Using a loperamide-induced mouse model, constipation parameters, histopathology, inflammation, and gut microbiota were assessed after CELNs treatment. The role of PTEN-induced kinase 1 (PINK1) was investigated with knockout mice, and mechanisms were analyzed via molecular and sequencing approaches. Results CELNs treatment significantly improved defecation, moisture content, and intestinal transit in constipated mice, reduced colonic inflammation, and restored gut morphology. Transcriptomic analysis revealed CELNs enriched pathways related to mitophagy and apoptosis. Crucially, CELNs activated PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy, enhanced mitochondrial function, and inhibited apoptosis of interstitial cells of Cajal. These benefits were abolished in PINK1 −/− mice. Furthermore, CELNs reversed constipation-associated gut microbiota dysbiosis, specifically enriching genera like Alistipes and Bacteroides . This microbial restoration was also PINK1-dependent. Discussion In summary, this study demonstrates that CELNs effectively alleviate constipation through a dual-pathway mechanism centered on PINK1. CELNs activate PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy to clear damaged mitochondria, thereby restoring energy homeostasis and suppressing ICC apoptosis. Simultaneously, CELNs remodel the gut microbiota in a PINK1-dependent manner, which may reinforce mitophagy activation. These findings elucidate a novel exosome-PINK1-mitophagy axis essential for restoring intestinal motility and highlight CELNs as a promising multi-target therapeutic strategy for functional gastrointestinal disorders.

works.title: Distinct associations of rhizoid-sphere and endophytic bacteria with dominant moss traits along an elevational gradient on Segrila Mountain
works.abstract: Microbial communities associated with alpine mosses remain poorly characterized in southeastern Tibet, particularly the distinction between bacteria at the rhizoid-soil interface and those inside moss tissues. We used 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing to characterize 36 rhizoid-sphere and 12 endophytic samples from three dominant mosses ( Actinothuidium hookeri , Ptilium crista-castrensis , and Dicranum fuscescens ) across four elevations (3,700–4,300 m) on Segrila Mountain. We combined community analysis, SPIEC-EASI networks, random forests, and path modeling to examine how habitat, elevation, soil properties, and bacterial community attributes were related to moss traits. The endophytic network showed higher clustering (0.665) and modularity (0.84) and a larger proportion of positive partial correlations (94.71%) than rhizoid-sphere’s (0.305, 0.79, and 83.48%). Elevation uniquely explained 25.9% of the variation in rhizoid-sphere bacterial composition ( p = 0.0001), compared with 7.9% for moss species ( p = 0.0093), while neither factor significantly explained endophytic composition (both p > 0.05). Soil properties explained rhizoid-sphere community variation (adjusted R 2 = 0.199, p = 0.001), whereas the endophytic model was nonsignificant (adjusted R 2 = 0.029, p = 0.239). Random-forest models most strongly predicted moss tissue K (LOOCV R 2 = 0.58) and N (LOOCV R 2 = 0.48). In path modeling, rhizoid-sphere Shannon diversity was positively associated with morphology ( β = 0.500, p = 0.0005) and negatively associated with nutrient ( β = −0.263, p = 0.0036). These findings highlight the rhizoid-sphere as an interface linking elevation, soil conditions, bacterial community variation, and moss traits.

works.title: Long-term fertilizer-derived chloride inputs suppress nitrification and alter nitrogen supply patterns in a temperate agricultural brown soil
works.abstract: Chloride-containing fertilizers, especially those used as accompanying components in nitrogen fertilizers, are widely applied into the soil for agricultural production. However, the long-term impacts of this chloride input on nitrification and inorganic nitrogen supply remain poorly understood. Here, in order to determine whether long-term chloride-containing fertilization is associated with soil acidification, suppressed potential nitrification rate, altered ammonia-oxidizing microbial communities, and a shift in inorganic nitrogen supply patterns, we used a 35-year field experiment in Northeast China to compare chloride-free, low chloride, and high chloride fertilization regimes under equal total N, P, and K inputs. The results showed that High chloride treatments were associated with lower soil pH, although the direct effect of chloride on pH was not statistically significant in the path model, suggesting that ammonium-based fertilization itself is a major contributor to acidification in this system. Linear mixed models (LMM) further verified the significant effects of chloride addition and soil pH on PNR and the abundance of ammonia-oxidizing microorganisms. Our results suggest chloride may suppress soil nitrification via two hypothesized pathways: putative direct inhibitory effects of chloride, and an indirect pathway mediated by chloride-associated shifts in soil pH that may suppress ammonia-oxidizing microorganisms. Together, these two pathways facilitate the accumulation of ammonium-N relative to nitrate-N. High chloride treatments suppressed ammonia-oxidizing archaea (AOA) and ammonia-oxidizing bacteria (AOB), and the abundance of AOA decreased by up to 72%. Amplicon sequencing of harvest-stage soil samples demonstrated that high chloride input altered the diversity and community composition of ammonia-oxidizing microorganisms, and reduced maize grain yield. Our findings reveal that combined application of potassium chloride and chloride-containing nitrogen fertilizers exacerbates soil acidification and substantially disturbs soil nitrification as well as ammonia-oxidizing microbial communities. Such disturbances reshape soil inorganic nitrogen supply patterns within this long-term brown-soil agroecosystem.

works.title: Expression, purification and broad-spectrum antibacterial characterization of Pseudomonas aeruginosa phage PPAT endolysin
works.abstract: The prevalence of multidrug-resistant Gram-negative bacteria poses a serious threat to clinical anti-infective therapy, and bacteriophage-encoded endolysins have emerged as promising alternatives to conventional antibiotics due to their high efficiency and low risk of resistance development. In this study, the endolysin gene lysPPAT from Pseudomonas aeruginosa bacteriophage PPAT was cloned and heterologously expressed in Escherichia coli , and the recombinant protein was successfully purified. Bioinformatic analysis revealed that LysPPAT contains a conserved phage lysozyme domain without transmembrane regions or signal peptides, consistent with typical endolysin characteristics. In vitro assays demonstrated that LysPPAT exhibits broad-spectrum antibacterial activity against a subset of tested Gram-negative and Gram-positive pathogens, including clinically resistant strains of P. aeruginosa , Klebsiella pneumoniae , Acinetobacter baumannii , Escherichia coli , and Staphylococcus aureus , even in the absence of outer membrane permeabilizers. The optimal enzymatic activity was observed at 37 °C and pH 8.0. Scanning electron microscopy and peptidoglycan degradation assays confirmed that LysPPAT directly disrupts bacterial cell walls, with degradation activity against P. aeruginosa peptidoglycan comparable to that of lysozyme. Molecular docking revealed stable hydrogen bond interactions between LysPPAT and peptidoglycan, with a docking score of −4.56 kcal·mmol −1 . Amphipathic α-helices were predicted to be the structural basis for outer membrane penetration. Additionally, LysPPAT significantly reduced mature P. aeruginosa and S. aureus biofilms biomass. Collectively, LysPPAT represents a novel broad-spectrum endolysin with great potential for combating multidrug-resistant bacterial infections.

works.title: Correction: Controlling bacterial biofilm formation by native and methylated lupine 11S globulins
works.abstract: The correct MIC values for M11S against Proteus mirabilis and Pseudomonas aeruginosa are 0.3 µg/mL and 0.5 µg/mL, respec:vely, as reported in Table 2 and confirmed by the original raw data. The higher values appearing in Figure 3 (approximately 1 and 2 µg/mL, respec:vely) resulted from a transcrip:on error when transferring the original data into the Excel worksheet used to prepare the figure. These incorrect values were inadvertently introduced into Figure 3, whereas the corresponding values in Table 2 and the text were correct. We acknowledge this inconsistency and clarify that the values in Table 2, supported by the original raw data, are the correct ones. The error is confined to the graphical presenta:on of these MIC values.The concern raised regarding Supplementary Figure 1 in Enan et al. (2023, Fron2ers in Microbiology) and Figure 6 in Abdel-Shafi et al. (2023, Molecules) relates to the apparent similarity of certain diffusion-assay photographs and the different treatment labels assigned to the K. oxytoca images (BS in Molecules and 11S in Fron2ers). This discrepancy resulted from an inadvertent figure-assembly error in the Molecules ar:cle, whereby images corresponding to the 11S and BS treatments were inadvertently interchanged. Both studies originated from the same thesis project and used the same purified 11S protein batch. The error concerned the selec:on and labeling of images during figure prepara:on, rather than manipula:on of the underlying experimental data. The original data and experiments presented in Fron:ers ar:cle are sound and accurate.

works.title: Seed development shapes the diversity, succession, and functional potential of endophytic bacterial communities in Camellia oleifera
works.abstract: Camellia oleifera is a significant woody oil crop with considerable commercial, nutritional, and ecological importance. The developmental processes of seed endophytic bacterial populations are inadequately understood. This study used 16S rRNA high-throughput sequencing to analyze the diversity, community structure, and predicted functions of endophytic bacteria in C. oleifera seeds across four developmental stages: early fruit-set (YC1), young fruit (YC2), early mature (YC3), and late mature (YC4). A total of 907,440 raw reads were obtained, and 874,097 effective sequences were retained across 12 sequencing samples, which were taxonomically assigned to 41 phyla, 112 classes, 258 orders, 448 families, 994 genera, and 1,602 putative species-level ASVs. The predominant phyla were Proteobacteria, Firmicutes, Actinobacteriota, and Bacteroidota, with Pseudomonas , Methylobacterium-Methylorubrum , and the uncultured lineage 1174-901-12 as the prevalent taxa. Alpha- and beta-diversity analyses showed distinct stage-specific community succession: YC1-YC3 exhibited greater richness and diversity, whereas YC4 showed a decline in both. PICRUSt2-based prediction of COG functional categories showed that functions related to energy production and conversion (C), amino acid transport and metabolism (E), inorganic ion transport and metabolism (P), translation, ribosomal structure and biogenesis (J), and cell wall/membrane/envelope biogenesis (M) were relatively abundant. These results provide a microbiological foundation for comprehending seed development and identifying functional strains in C. oleifera .

works.title: Therapeutic effects of a potential probiotic product (Ogi-Pro) on gut microbiota and diarrhea alleviation: a preliminary in vivo evaluation in a murine model
works.abstract: Background Probiotics have shown promise in improving gut health and alleviating diarrheal diseases; however, evidence supporting non-dairy probiotic formulations remains limited. This study evaluated the safety, gastrointestinal persistence, immunomodulatory activity, and anti-diarrheal efficacy of Ogi-Pro, a cereal-based probiotic formulation containing indigenous Lactiplantibacillus pentosus 15ST2 and Lacticaseibacillus casei KN3, in a castor oil-induced murine model of acute diarrhoea. Methods Swiss albino mice received Ogi-Pro (1 × 10 9 CFU/mouse/day) by oral gavage for 14 days before induction of diarrhoea. Safety was assessed through general health observations, bacterial translocation, and histopathology. Therapeutic efficacy was evaluated by fecal bacterial enumeration, diarrhoea frequency, intestinal histology, and cytokine expression using RT-qPCR and ELISA. Results Ogi-Pro was well tolerated, with no evidence of bacterial translocation or treatment-related toxicity. Probiotic administration increased intestinal lactobacilli while suppressing coliform populations and reduced diarrhoea severity to a level comparable with the commercial probiotic control. Total lactobacilli count (TLC) in both groups were higher than total coliform counts (TCC) by 3 log cfu/mL, only the standard control group showed competitive growth between TLC and TCC. Histopathological examination showed preservation of intestinal architecture with only mild inflammatory changes as compared to the standard group. The expression of the anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-10, in the treatment group was significantly ( p < 0.05) elevated; while modulating IL-8 and TNF-α responses, indicating an immunomodulatory effect associated with improved intestinal homeostasis. Conclusion These findings demonstrated that Ogi-Pro is a safe cereal-based probiotic formulation with promising anti-diarrheal and immunomodulatory properties in a murine model. The study supported the potential of traditional fermented cereal foods as non-dairy probiotic delivery systems while highlighting the need for mechanistic investigations and well-designed human clinical trials to establish clinical efficacy.

works.title: Gut microbiome dysbiosis in premature ovarian insufficiency and polycystic ovary syndrome: a prospective cohort observational study
works.abstract: Background Premature ovarian insufficiency (POI) and polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) are two major reproductive endocrine disorders associated with impaired ovarian function and infertility. Although gut microbiota dysbiosis has been implicated in both conditions, direct comparisons of their microbial and functional characteristics remain limited. Methods In this prospective cohort study, 102 women of reproductive age, including patients with PCOS and POI as well as healthy controls (NG), were recruited between March 2024 and March 2025. Gut microbial profiles were initially characterized by 16S rDNA amplicon sequencing in 101 fecal samples, and 90 fecal samples (30 per group) were subsequently subjected to metagenomics sequencing for comprehensive taxonomic and functional analyses.
