Differential taxa, microbial functions, and their associations with baseline characteristics were evaluated. Results Both PCOS and POI exhibited gut microbial dysbiosis characterized by reduced abundances of Bacteroides compared with healthy controls. Distinct disease-specific microbial signatures were identified. The PCOS microbiome was enriched in Escherichia coli , together with functional pathways associated with energy metabolism, lipopolysaccharide biosynthesis, biofilm formation, antimicrobial resistance, and environmental adaptation. In contrast, the POI microbiome was characterized by enrichment of Gemmiger , Subdoligranulum , and Clostridiales -related taxa, accompanied by enhanced aminoacyl-tRNA biosynthesis, fatty acid biosynthesis, glucuronate metabolism, and carbohydrate utilization pathways. Correlation analyses further demonstrated close associations between disease-specific microbial taxa, microbial functions, and host metabolic and reproductive hormone profiles. Conclusion PCOS and POI share common features of gut microbial dysbiosis but exhibit distinct taxonomic and functional signatures. These findings provide new insights into microbiome-associated mechanisms underlying female reproductive endocrine disorders.

works.title: Butyricimonas virosa AM16-14 attenuates dextran sulfate sodium-induced colitis and shifts mouse fecal metabolomic trajectories
works.abstract: Ulcerative colitis (UC) involves epithelial injury, inflammation, and microbiota-linked metabolism. We evaluated Butyricimonas virosa AM16-14 in an acute dextran sulfate sodium (DSS) colitis mouse experiment, resolved its complete genome, analyzed human UC microbiome data as ecological context, and examined fecal liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC–MS) profiles in positive- and negative-ion modes. AM16-14 carried a 5.00 Mb circular genome with 42.95% GC content and 4,126 predicted coding sequences. Compared with DSS alone, AM16-14-treated mice showed higher final body weight, a lower disease activity index (DAI), longer colons, reduced histological injury, stronger Alcian blue mucin staining, and lower tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-alpha) and interleukin-6 (IL-6); interleukin-1beta (IL-1beta) and interleukin-10 (IL-10) did not change significantly. The human analysis associated B. virosa with lower focal network connectivity in UC. Positive-ion profiles identified recovery-oriented feature shifts and two dominant recovery trajectories. Complementary negative-ion analysis retained 1,079 features. Complementary genomic screens yielded nine loci associated with antimicrobial resistance (AMR), virulence-associated reference homologies, and one final predicted provirus. A cluster of four AMR-associated loci occurred near transposase annotations. These findings support AM16-14 as a complete-genome-resolved microbiota-directed candidate strain that attenuates multiple acute mouse colitis readouts.

works.title: The ulvanolytic capacity of the seaweed associated bacterium Aliiglaciecola sp. SL4
works.abstract: Polysaccharide utilization loci (PULs) enable marine heterotrophic bacteria to access the complex carbohydrates that constitute a major reservoir of fixed carbon in seaweed biomass. Here, we identify and characterize two enzymes from a novel ulvan utilization locus (uPUL) from the genome of Aliiglaciecola sp. SL4 ( Gla SL4), an epiphytic bacterium isolated from an Ulva species of green macroalgae. Genome analysis revealed a dedicated ulvan degradation system encoding a suite of carbohydrate-active enzymes (CAZymes) and auxiliary enzymes predicted to carry out ulvan depolymerisation and downstream oligosaccharide processing. Biochemical validation of the polysaccharide lyase Gla PL25a and the unsaturated glycoside hydrolase Gla GH105 confirmed their activities and broader roles as key initiating enzymes in the ulvan utilization pathway. These findings provide experimental evidence linking a previously uncharacterized uPUL to ulvan degradation, advancing our understanding of marine carbon cycling and expanding the repertoire of enzymes available for algal biomass conversion and the generation of value-added ulvan oligosaccharides.

works.title: Contrasting microbial and environmental associations link water availability to soil multifunctionality in the rhizosheath and bulk soil of Eremopyrum distans
works.abstract: Introduction Changes in water availability can alter soil resources and microbial communities, but whether association structures linking water availability to soil multifunctionality (SMF) differ between the root–soil interface and bulk soil remains unclear. Methods We subjected Eremopyrum distans to five water treatments over one growing season and assessed dimension-weighted and threshold-based SMF, together with bacterial, fungal and protistan community attributes, in the rhizosheath and bulk soil. Results Dimension-weighted SMF generally increased across the imposed water-treatment gradient. At higher functional thresholds, W + 25 supported more functions at high levels, particularly in bulk soil. After accounting for water treatment, microhabitat and their interaction, C- and N-related functions were associated mainly with microbial diversity, whereas P-related functions and high-threshold SMF were more closely associated with network complexity and the community-stability proxy. Piecewise structural equation models indicated that, in the rhizosheath, soil moisture was associated with SMF primarily through modeled indirect associations involving integrated microbial diversity, network complexity and the community-stability proxy. In bulk soil, the positive direct association of soil moisture and the negative direct association of soil pH with SMF were more prominent. Formal paired-bootstrap comparisons showed that most corresponding paths did not differ between microhabitats, although selected path differences were detected across SMF thresholds. Conclusion Water availability was associated with SMF through microhabitat-dependent association structures. Microbial community organization was more closely associated with SMF in the rhizosheath, whereas local environmental conditions retained stronger direct associations with SMF in bulk soil. These findings highlight the importance of distinguishing rhizosheath and bulk-soil microhabitats when evaluating soil functional responses to changing water availability.

works.title: ST-26 serotype V Group B Streptococcus: an unexpected lineage among maternal carriage strains and neonatal infection in Gabon
works.abstract: Background To investigate the burden of neonatal Group B Streptococcus (GBS) infection, we conducted a prospective study at a regional hospital in Gabon. Methods Consecutive parturients and their newborns were enrolled in this study. Vaginal swabs were collected and cultured to test for GBS colonization. Blood cultures were obtained from newborns presenting clinical signs suggestive of infection during the first 28 days of life. All GBS strains underwent whole-genome sequencing. Results A total of 203 newborns and 197 mothers were enrolled. One newborn developed GBS disease, corresponding to an incidence of 4.93 cases per 1,000 live births. Vaginal GBS colonization was detected in 28 parturients (14.2%). Seven colonizing strains (25.0%) and the neonatal strain belonged to clonal complex CC26. Conclusion These initial data on the molecular epidemiology of maternal GBS colonization and neonatal infection in Gabon reveal an unexpected contribution of CC26 strains, a lineage that has been rarely reported in this context.

works.title: Lineage-aware evaluation of machine learning for observed cross-genus occurrence of IncC plasmids in public databases
works.abstract: Introduction IncC plasmids contribute to the dissemination of antimicrobial resistance across bacterial hosts. We developed an IncC-specific model to classify plasmids belonging to highly similar cross-genus pairs observed in public databases and evaluated its performance when related lineages were kept together during validation. Methods The development cohort comprised 988 PLSDB plasmids (266 label-positive), and a separately sourced RefSeq cohort contained 250 plasmids. The operational label denotes occurrence in databases rather than experimentally measured transfer. Among five standalone learners, LightGBM with 100 foldwise-selected 4-mers (LightGBM-100) was retained, with a fixed threshold of 0.306 derived via nested random-CV Youden-index selection. Results Under random five-fold cross-validation, pooled out-of-fold AUROC and average precision (AP) were 0.960 and 0.928, respectively, but fell to 0.742 and 0.498 with primary Mash-component blocking and to 0.712 and 0.412 with more permissive blocking. At the random-CV-derived threshold, blocked sensitivity was 0.259 and 0.162, respectively. In RefSeq, LightGBM-100 achieved an AUROC of 0.937 and an AP of 0.894, although 81 of 84 positives lay within Mash distance d < 0.00124 of the development cohort and the labels partly relied on pair evidence from both databases. Biological features did not reproducibly improve the 4-mer model after lineage blocking, and family- and order-crossing outcomes showed similar limitations. Discussion This study establishes an IncC-specific, lineage-aware benchmark for predicting database-observed cross-genus occurrence and demonstrates how lineage relatedness and database representation shape predictive performance. The model may help prioritize plasmids within represented sequence backgrounds for follow-up, while the integrated biological analyses provide a basis for targeted experimental investigation.

works.title: From microbial dysbiosis to immune evasion: evidence and emerging mechanisms of gut microbiota-mediated modulation of PD-1/PD-L1 efficacy in genitourinary malignancies
works.abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitors targeting the PD-1/PD-L1 axis have transformed the treatment landscape for genitourinary malignancies, yet primary and acquired resistance remains a substantial clinical obstacle. The gut microbiome has emerged as a critical determinant of immunotherapy efficacy, with dysbiosis driving immune evasion through disruption of metabolite-mediated signaling, impairment of intestinal barrier function, and systemic immunosuppression. This review synthesizes current mechanistic understanding of how gut microbial metabolites, including short-chain fatty acids, tryptophan catabolites, and bile acids, modulate PD-1/PD-L1 expression via epigenetic reprogramming, aryl hydrocarbon receptor activation, and T cell functional modulation. Specific bacterial taxa such as Akkermansia muciniphila and Blautia coccoides enhance antitumor immunity through distinct molecular pathways, while the genitourinary microbiome exerts local immunomodulatory effects. Clinical evidence supporting microbiome-based candidate biomarkers associated with ICIs outcomes and emerging therapeutic strategies including fecal microbiota transplantation, probiotics, and dietary interventions are critically evaluated. This review distinguishes direct genitourinary-specific evidence from cross-cancer mechanistic evidence and provides a unified framework for understanding the microbiome-immunity axis and its translational potential in genitourinary oncology.

works.title: Long-read metagenomic characterization of the resistome and mobilome in heavy-metal-contaminated soils
works.abstract: Introduction Heavy-metal contamination is widely proposed to co-select for antibiotic resistance by placing metal- and antibiotic-resistance genes on the same mobile elements, yet the evidence for this rests largely on short-read co-occurrence rather than on direct observation of physical linkage. Methods We applied Nanopore long-read metagenomics to four soils from the Ridder polymetallic mining and metallurgical district of East Kazakhstan, where zinc, cadmium and lead exceed a single local reference site by up to two orders of magnitude. Physical linkage between antibiotic- and metal-resistance genes was tested at the contig, read, genome and community levels against chance expectation. Results Ensemble binning of two complementary assemblies produced 261 metagenome-assembled genomes, 97% of them lacking a GTDB species assignment and dominated by Actinomycetota, together with 73 closed circular elements including complete phages and plasmids. Screening this catalogue recovered 991 antibiotic-resistance and 395 metal-resistance loci. In these metal-enriched soils, the two classes were rarely physically linked. Only four contigs carried both, against 28.9 expected under a degree-preserving null model, a 0.14-fold depletion that was robust to catalogue thresholds; co-carriage on single reads was likewise rare. At the genome level the classes were independent, and in 22 of 24 dual-carrier genomes they occupied different contigs. The mobilome nonetheless carried metal resistance preferentially: contigs called as plasmids were enriched for metal genes relative to the catalogue base rate, and a 142-kb plasmid predicted to be conjugative encoded copper, cadmium/zinc, mercury and silver efflux systems, a complete type-IV secretion system and a CBASS anti-phage defense system, but no antibiotic-resistance gene. No genome belonged to an ESKAPE or WHO-priority pathogen genus. Discussion These soils are therefore a large environmental resistance reservoir, but no direct clinical-risk linkage was demonstrated in the present dataset. Community co-occurrence should not be read as evidence of physical linkage. Co-selection through cross-resistance or co-regulation was not excluded.

works.title: Genotypic drug resistance characteristics and their clinical guiding value in people living with HIV
works.abstract: Objective Genotypic drug resistance testing plays a critical role in guiding antiretroviral therapy (ART) for people living with HIV (PLWH). However, current studies lack a stratified quantitative framework to evaluate its clinical utility, which hinders the precise translation of resistance data into routine practice. Methods In this study, 274 PLWH who underwent HIV genotypic drug resistance testing were enrolled to characterize drug resistance profiles, subtype-specific resistance heterogeneity, resistance transmission clusters, and metabolic features, with particular emphasis on grading the clinical utility of genotypic resistance. Results The overall drug resistance rate was 24.09%, predominantly involving non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs) and nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs). The three major locally circulating recombinant subtypes showed distinct resistance spectra and active transmission of resistant strains, whereas subtype-specific metabolic variations were confounded by demographic and immunological factors rather than resistance mutations. Notably, graded genotypic resistance guidance values were closely associated with clinical outcomes: stronger guidance values corresponded to better virological suppression and CD4 recovery, whereas weaker guidance values were associated with poorer prognosis. Conclusions This stratified evaluation framework improves the interpretation of genotype-phenotype discordance in resistance assessment, helps refine standardized resistance evaluation criteria, supports individualized ART decision-making, and provides real-world evidence for optimizing clinical management strategies and targeted HIV treatment policies.

works.title: Karst wetland reclamation increases the proportion of inorganic sulfur in total sulfur: associations with sulfate-reducing bacteria abundance and soil enzyme activity
works.abstract: Karst wetlands are fragile and critical ecosystems for soil sulfur biogeochemical cycling. In this study, six typical land-use types in the Huixian karst wetland of Guilin, southern China, were selected to investigate the variations in soil physicochemical properties, four inorganic sulfur fractions, soil enzyme activities, and sulfate-reducing bacteria (SRB) abundance across 0–40 cm soil profiles. The results showed that wetland reclamation significantly reduced soil pH, soil organic carbon (SOC), silt content, total nitrogen, and total sulfur, while increasing soil bulk density, electrical conductivity (EC), and redox potential (Eh). Reclamation reduced the content of total inorganic sulfur, while elevating its proportion in total sulfur; water-soluble sulfur dominated the inorganic sulfur pool. The composition of inorganic sulfur fractions differed markedly across land-use types. Reclamation increased SRB abundance but inhibited soil enzyme activities. Correlation analysis indicated that soil enzyme activities were negatively correlated with inorganic sulfur contents in abandoned land, whereas positive correlations were observed in other land-use types. Close internal correlations existed among different inorganic sulfur fractions. Soil pH and SOC were associated with greater inorganic sulfur accumulation, while Eh showed an inhibitory association. SOC, Eh, EC, pH, and silt content were the key environmental factors associated with SRB abundance and soil enzyme activities. Collectively, wetland reclamation reduced absolute concentrations of both total inorganic sulfur (TIS) and total organic sulfur (TOS), and preferential loss of TOS increased the TIS/TS ratio, altered sulfur transformation processes, and were accompanied by higher SRB abundance and lower soil enzyme activity. This study reveals the responses of soil sulfur biogeochemical processes to land-use conversion in subtropical karst wetlands and provides insights into sulfur cycle regulation under wetland disturbance.

works.title: Environmental drivers of microbial community dynamics in a cool-water aquaponics system
works.abstract: Aquaponic systems represent an integrated water-efficient approach to food production by combining recirculating aquaculture with hydroponic plant cultivation. Performance and stability of these systems depend not only on fish and plant interactions but also on the structure and function of associated microbial communities, which regulate nutrient cycling and water quality. Microbial communities play a central role in the stability and performance of aquaponic systems, yet the relative importance of temporal dynamics, spatial heterogeneity, and environmental drivers remains poorly understood. In this study, we evaluated microbial consortia and production characteristics in six replicate aquaponic systems with cool/cold water fishes, including rainbow trout ( Oncorhynchus mykiss ) and yellow perch ( Perca flavescens , all female) to cultivate lettuce ( Lactuca sativa ) and kale ( Brassica oleracea ), and investigated microbial community structure across production cycles and system compartments using high-throughput sequencing of 16S rRNA gene and multivariate ecological analyses. DNA samples were collected from fish tank water during the initial control cycle and from key aquaponic compartments, including circulating water, rhizosphere, biodeposits, and biofilters, during three subsequent harvesting cycles. Across all four cycles, a core microbiome was observed, with 136 shared taxa. Microbial communities were consistently structured at the system level where each system supported a distinct microbial assemblage. Permutational multivariate analysis of variance revealed that microbial community composition was significantly influenced by both production cycle and compartment with temporal effects emerging as a dominant driver of variation. Observed shifts in microbial communities were closely associated with temperature and pH gradients. Significant but comparatively weaker differences were observed among individual AP systems, fish species, and plant species. These results indicate that microbial community structure was shaped primarily by temporal succession across production cycles, with additional contributions from spatial structuring and biotic factors. These findings provide insight into ecological processes governing aquaponic microbiomes and highlight the importance of managing environmental conditions to promote system stability and performance.

works.title: Commentary: Antimicrobial resistance trends of ESKAPEE pathogens isolated from intensive care unit patients at a tertiary care hospital in Mogadishu, Somalia: a retrospective study (2020–2024)
works.abstract: We read with interest the retrospective study by Ibrahim and colleagues describing ESKAPEE resistance patterns among intensive care unit patients in Mogadishu, Somalia [1]. The study contributes valuable local microbiological evidence. Its implications for empirical treatment and surveillance would be strengthened by clarification of laboratory validation, reconciliation of the multidrug resistance (MDR) estimates, and more explicit reporting of uncertainty in annual resistance proportions. These issues concern how the findings should be interpreted rather than whether local surveillance is needed.First, the methods describe Kirby-Bauer disk diffusion, including vancomycin and colistin disks, but do not clearly describe organism-antibiotic-specific minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) confirmation [1]. CDC guidance does not recommend disk diffusion for vancomycin susceptibility testing in Staphylococcus aureus and advises verification of suspected intermediate or resistant results through repeat identification and a validated MIC method [2]. For colistin, the joint CLSI-EUCAST recommendations identify broth microdilution as the reference method and do not recommend disk diffusion [3]. The authors acknowledge that vancomycin-resistant S. aureus was not systematically assessed, yet report approximately 6% vancomycin resistance in 2024. They also report low colistin resistance in Klebsiella pneumoniae [1]. Were these results obtained or confirmed using appropriate MIC methods? Reporting the methods, MIC values, and interpretive criteria would help readers assess whether these findings represent validated resistance phenotypes. CLSI M100 and EUCAST breakpoint tables provide organism-antibiotic-specific interpretive criteria [4,5]. The authors should specify the standard and version applied in each study year and whether historical results were reinterpreted using a common version. Screening results alone should not be presented as MIC-confirmed vancomycin-intermediate or vancomycin-resistant S. aureus (VISA or VRSA).Second, the MDR estimates require reconciliation. The abstract reports MDR in 85% of Acinetobacter baumannii and 78% of K. pneumoniae isolates, whereas Table 4 reports 150/194 (77.3%) and 70/144 (48.6%), respectively [1]. It remains unclear whether different analytical populations or denominators explain these differences. Magiorakos and colleagues define MDR by acquired non-susceptibility affecting at least one drug within each of three or more antimicrobial categories [6]. Clarifying how the study's stated definition was operationalized, including the categories assessed and handling of intermediate results and incomplete testing, would aid interpretation. Because these estimates underpin the characterization of the MDR burden, clarification of the applicable denominators and consistency between the abstract and detailed results are important. The authors could also explain how missing MDR classifications were handled and state the number of isolates included in each analysis.Third, annual percentages need explicit testing denominators and uncertainty estimates. The authors appropriately acknowledge sparse samples and missing organism-year observations [1]. Nevertheless, Table 3 reports 100% Enterobacter resistance in 2023 for several agents, each based on one resistant isolate, implying one tested isolate. Such a proportion provides limited evidence of a population-level temporal shift. Reporting resistant/tested counts and appropriate 95% confidence intervals for each organism-antibiotic-year combination would make this uncertainty visible. Clarification of repeat-isolate handling is also needed: was analysis restricted to the first isolate per patient and organism, or were repeat episodes included? CLSI M39 distinguishes routine antibiogram preparation from analyses intended to detect emerging resistance; the chosen approach should match the surveillance objective [7]. In addition, the October 2024 endpoint limits direct comparison of annual isolate counts, although an incomplete year does not inherently bias resistance proportions. Changes in testing coverage, breakpoints, and specimen mix should be considered when interpreting annual differences.These clarifications would strengthen confidence in the study's interpretation and support its use in locally informed stewardship. We encourage the authors to reconcile the MDR estimates, document appropriate confirmation of the relevant susceptibility results, and provide transparent denominators and uncertainty estimates. This would help clinicians distinguish preliminary surveillance signals from findings sufficiently supported to inform empirical treatment protocols.

works.title: Global research landscape and emerging trends in intervertebral disc degeneration and the gut microbiota: a multi-database bibliometric and knowledge mapping analysis
works.abstract: Objective To characterize the global research landscape and thematic evolution of intervertebral disc degeneration (IDD) and gut microbiota using multi-database bibliometric analysis and knowledge mapping, and to identify major research hotspots and emerging trends. Methods This study employed a bibliometric and knowledge-mapping design. We searched the Web of Science Core Collection (WoSCC) and Scopus for relevant English-language original articles and reviews from database inception to July 31, 2026. We merged records retrieved from the two databases. After removing duplicates, screening for relevance, and standardizing data, we performed bibliometric and knowledge mapping analyses using VOSviewer, CiteSpace, and bibliometrix. We analyzed research output, collaboration networks, co-citation relationships, and keyword evolution. Results We included 385 publications from 58 countries and 224 journals. The annual number of publications showed an overall upward trend, with more rapid growth after 2020. China and the United States led contributions, while the United States played a central role in the international collaboration network. European Spine Journal published the most articles. Co-citation and keyword analyses showed that research interest gradually shifted from local disc infection, clinical phenotypes, and inflammatory mechanisms toward gut microbiota dysbiosis, the gut–disc axis, and potential causal relationships. “Gut microbiota” and “Mendelian randomization” showed the two strongest keyword bursts, both during 2024–2026. The “gut–disc axis” emerged as a burst keyword in 2025. Recent studies have also drawn increasing attention to the NLRP3 inflammasome and pyroptosis. Conclusion Research on IDD and the gut microbiota is increasingly integrating local pathological mechanisms with the gut microbial ecosystem. The gut–disc axis, inflammation-related cell death, and causal inference have emerged as important research priorities requiring further validation. However, bibliometric trends alone cannot establish biological causality or therapeutic effectiveness. Future studies should integrate longitudinal population studies, genetic causal inference, and functional experiments to clarify potential causal relationships and evaluate the therapeutic relevance of microbiome-targeted interventions.

works.title: Study on the nutrient spatiotemporal changes and multi-habitat microbial succession in a decoupled largemouth bass–garlic chive aquaponics system
works.abstract: The decoupled aquaponics system was an important model of circular agriculture and represents a mature circular agricultural framework, yet integrated studies simultaneously tracking nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium and microbial communities in water, sediment, substrate and fish gut remain scarce. To address this gap, we conducted a three-month continuous monitoring (July to September 2024) of a triplicate indoor decoupled aquaponics system combining largemouth bass ( Micropterus salmoides ) and garlic chives ( Allium tuberosum ) in northern Chinese greenhouses. Nutrient dynamics (total nitrogen, TN; total phosphorus, TP; total potassium, TK) were quantified monthly in aquaculture water, sedimentation tank mud and cultivation substrate, while microbial community structure, succession and putative functions were characterized via 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing, canonical correspondence analysis (CCA), variance partitioning analysis (VPA) and PICRUSt2 functional prediction. The results were as follows: (1) The three modules formed a characteristic “water transport → mud accumulated → substrate consumption” nutrient cascade, with nutrient reserves ordered as mud > substrate > water. (2) TN in water increased by 237.60% over the cultivation period, indicating a latent risk of eutrophication. Microbial communities exhibited strong habitat partitioning, with Proteobacteria as the shared dominant phylum across environmental media, while fish gut harbored a temporally dynamic assemblage shifting from Fusobacteriota (83.11% in July) to Firmicutes (73.31% in September), forming a distinct “environmental versus host” bistable zonation. (3) VPA revealed that TN and TP synergistically regulated mud microbiota (27.70% interaction), whereas TK independently structured substrate communities (19.95% independent contribution), ranking as the strongest single-nutrient driver (K > N > P). (4) PICRUSt2-based functional prediction indicated metabolism as the core function across all habitats, with complementary profiles—sediment for nutrient sensing, substrate for stable transformation, water for temporal adaptation, and gut for host-specific nutrition. These provide species-specific nutrient–microbe linkage data, synchronous four-habitat temporal dynamics, and quantitative partitioning of N/P/K effects, offering actionable baselines for structural optimization, seasonal nutrient regulation and targeted microbial modification in decoupled aquaponics facilities.

works.title: Genomic characterization and early macrophage inflammatory responses to an emerging Mycobacterium wolinskyi isolate
works.abstract: Mycobacterium wolinskyi is an emerging rapidly growing nontuberculous mycobacterium increasingly recognized as a cause of skin, soft-tissue, and device-associated infections, including infections in immunocompetent individuals. However, its genomic characteristics and interactions with host immune cells remain poorly understood. In this study, we characterized a clinical M. wolinskyi isolate, designated QL01, recovered from a facial skin infection in an 11-year-old child, by combining antimicrobial susceptibility testing, whole-genome sequencing, comparative genomic analysis, and macrophage infection assays with transcriptomic profiling. QL01 was resistant to clarithromycin, imipenem, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, while remaining susceptible to amikacin, linezolid, moxifloxacin, minocycline, and doxycycline. Whole-genome sequencing generated a complete circular chromosome and identified antimicrobial resistance-associated homologs and host interaction-associated homologs. Comparative analysis revealed variable conservation of type VII secretion system (T7SS)- and Mce-associated loci among representative rapidly growing mycobacteria. Following uptake by mouse bone marrow-derived macrophages, viable intracellular QL01 remained recoverable after 24 h. RNA sequencing revealed an early innate immune and pro-inflammatory transcriptional response, with enrichment of TNF, NF-κB, Toll-like receptor, and C-type lectin receptor signaling pathways. RT-qPCR further confirmed increased expression of Ccl2 , Tnf , Il1b , Tlr2 , Clec4e , and Tnfaip3 . ELISA confirmed increased secretion of TNF-α, IL-1β, and IFN-β. Inhibition of IKK/NF-κB signaling attenuated QL01-induced phosphorylation of p65 and IκBα and reduced inflammatory cytokine secretion. These findings characterize the genomic features of a clinical M. wolinskyi isolate and describe the early macrophage response to this emerging nontuberculous mycobacterial species.

works.title: The small intestine microbiome: composition, host interactions and therapeutic potential
S-layer expansion is mediated by hoop-like cracks in the paracrystalline lattice during Bacillus anthracis growth
works.abstract: Surface layers (S-layers) are paracrystalline protein monolayers that envelop archaea and some bacteria, including Bacillus anthracis. S-layer subunits in B. anthracis are tethered to the underlying cell wall through glycopolymers that are covalently attached to the peptidoglycan (PG) meshwork. Cell growth in this rod-shaped organism occurs by dispersed PG synthesis throughout the cell cylinder. How the crystalline lattice expands in lockstep with the cell wall has remained unclear. Here, using fluorescently labelled S-layer subunits and high-resolution imaging, we show that S-layer expansion during B. anthracis growth is mediated by pervasive hoop-like cracks in the lattice. Pulse-chase experiments reveal two modes of S-layer assembly at these cracks: dispersed and focused. Our data suggest that local pulling forces on the S-layer array generated by dispersed cell wall synthesis and expansion of the underlying PG cause crack formation, with ensuing dispersed and focused synthesis enabling S-layer expansion with bacterial growth.

works.title: Env-specific antibodies promote post-treatment control in SIV-infected macaques
works.abstract: Abstract Viral latency reversal was observed in simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV)-infected rhesus macaques receiving antiretroviral therapy (ART), CD8α lymphocyte depletion and N-803 immunotherapy. However, this therapeutic approach did not reduce the viral reservoir size and treatment interruption resulted in rapid virus rebound. Here, to address this shortfall, we used four anti-SIV Env-specific rhesus IgG1 monoclonal antibodies (RhmAbs) that recognize unique targets on the SIV envelope. SIV mac239 -infected macaques were treated with ART only (group 1); ART + RhmAbs (group 2); or ART + RhmAbs + CD8α-depletion + N-803 (group 3). Robust latency reversal was only achieved in group 3. Viraemia rebounded in all macaques with similar kinetics after treatment interruption. However, compared with pre-ART viral loads, a greater fold reduction in rebound viraemia was seen in groups 2 and 3 and post-treatment control (PTC) required SIV RhmAbs. CD4 + T cells from macaques with PTC maintained low levels of intact SIV proviruses off ART and expressed increased interferon and decreased TGF-β signalling genes. This antiviral gene expression profile was also observed in CD4 + T cells with lower human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)-DNA content from ART-treated people with HIV. These results suggest that reduced virus production may contribute to PTC following ART interruption and provide a target for immune-based strategies to achieve durable viral control.

works.title: A convergent proline biosynthetic step couples cell wall integrity to virulence in Cryptococcus neoformans
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Metabolic adaptation is essential for the pathogenicity of the opportunistic fungus Cryptococcus neoformans . Although amino acid biosynthesis pathways are critical fitness determinants in fungal pathogens, the physiological contributions of proline biosynthesis remain incompletely understood, with most studies focusing on proline catabolism. Here, we characterized the proline biosynthetic enzymes Pro1, Pro2, and Pro3 in C. neoformans . Proline is produced by two routes that converge on Δ 1 -pyrroline-5-carboxylate (P5C): a de novo pathway from glutamate via Pro1 and Pro2, and an arginine-derived bypass via Car1 and Car2—both requiring Pro3 for the final reduction of P5C to proline. Although all biosynthetic mutants were strictly auxotrophic for proline, their requirements for virulence differed markedly: in a murine infection model, pro1 Δ and pro2 Δ mutants retained full virulence, whereas pro3 Δ exhibited significantly attenuated virulence accompanied by growth defects and impaired cell wall integrity. Genetic disruption of P5C-generating routes partially restored distinct pro3 Δ phenotypes, with PRO2 deletion alleviating delayed growth, and combined PRO2 and CAR2 deletion partially restoring cell size, while cell wall defects remained unresolved. This dissociation indicates that growth requires proper balance of P5C-generating metabolic flux, whereas cell wall integrity depends on a distinct mechanism that is not resolved by blocking P5C production. Together, these findings identify Pro3 as a metabolic gatekeeper coupling proline biosynthesis to cell wall homeostasis, establishing the biosynthetic branch of proline metabolism as a previously unappreciated determinant of fungal pathobiology. IMPORTANCE Cryptococcus neoformans is a leading cause of fungal meningitis worldwide, causing life-threatening infections primarily in immunocompromised individuals. To survive within the human host, this pathogen must synthesize essential nutrients through de novo biosynthesis when host-derived supplies are limited. Although proline catabolism has been studied extensively in fungal pathogens, the physiological roles of individual proline biosynthetic enzymes in human fungal pathogens remain incompletely understood. Here, we show that the terminal enzyme Pro3, but not the upstream enzymes Pro1 and Pro2, is selectively required for full virulence in a murine model. Pro3 supports pathobiological fitness by promoting growth under host-relevant conditions and maintaining cell wall integrity. These findings highlight the importance of proline biosynthesis beyond nutrient production and link this pathway to growth, cell wall integrity, and virulence in C. neoformans .

works.title: Intraspecies competition reveals branched-chain amino acid homeostasis as a targetable metabolic vulnerability in uropathogenic E. coli
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Urinary tract infections (UTIs) are among the most prevalent bacterial infections worldwide, with ~50% of women experiencing at least one UTI in their lifetime. Uropathogenic Escherichia coli (UPEC) is the causative agent of ~80% of UTIs. In contrast, asymptomatic bacteriuria E. coli 83972 (ABU 83972) colonizes the human urinary bladder without causing symptoms and inflammation. Deliberate colonization with ABU 83972 reduced UTI incidence in patients with voiding disorders. However, the mechanisms by which ABU 83972 outcompetes uropathogens in the urinary tract remain poorly understood and are the focus of this report. We performed comparative metabolomics to identify metabolites that promoted the fitness of ABU 83972 in human urine compared to UPEC strain CFT073. Competition assays were conducted between ABU 83972 and UPEC CFT073 in human urine supplemented with select metabolites that were differentially abundant in metabolome profiling. There was a significant reduction in the fitness of ABU 83972 when supplemented with branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs) such as leucine and isoleucine in a dose-dependent manner. Further, we identified that BrnQ, a low-affinity BCAA importer, is the main determinant of fitness advantage of ABU 83972 over UPEC. Using isogenic mutants, genetic complementation, amino acid analysis, cell culture, chemical inhibition of BCAA biosynthesis, and mouse models of UTI, we demonstrate that BCAA homeostasis represents a unique nutritional vulnerability in UPEC that could be targeted with chemical inhibitors. In summary, our study highlights that intraspecies competition between commensal and pathogenic strains could be used to detect novel fitness mechanisms and metabolic bottlenecks. IMPORTANCE Millions of people suffer from urinary tract infection (UTI) globally, and uropathogenic E. coli is the main cause of UTI. A urinary probiotic strain of E. coli has been used clinically to prevent UTI in some high-risk groups for recurrent UTI for more than 25 years. However, the mechanism of competition between the probiotic and pathogenic strains is not clear. We demonstrate that competition for specific amino acids is critical for the probiotic to compete against the pathogen. Our study identifies specific amino acid import and biosynthetic processes as targets for controlling UPEC growth during UTI.

works.title: Bacterial extracellular vesicles as carriers of genetic and regulatory messages
works.abstract: Although bacterial extracellular vesicles (BEVs) are increasingly recognized as mediators of communication, the contribution of their nucleic acid cargo remains poorly understood. Providing an overview of BEV-nucleic acid content and their roles, this review first examines their true significance. In particular, it highlights why they should not be treated as bulk cargo, given that DNA and RNA contents exhibit various sub-vesicular localizations that may define their ecological roles. We propose that this heterogeneity allows viewing BEVs as distinct subpopulations. Furthermore, recent studies increasingly propose the involvement of DNA associated with BEVs in horizontal gene transfer between bacteria and that of vesicular small RNA (sRNA) during host-bacteria interactions. Overall, this review offers insights into considering BEVs in an ecological context based on notable recent studies.

works.title: A conserved CusR-dependent regulatory pathway couples copper homeostasis with oxidative stress resistance in Klebsiella pneumoniae
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Host-derived copper toxicity is a central antimicrobial strategy that restricts bacterial survival during infection, yet how pathogens integrate copper detoxification with oxidative stress resistance remains incompletely understood. Here, we identify the response regulator CusR as a pivotal coordinator of copper homeostasis and oxidative stress defense in Klebsiella pneumoniae . Loss of cusR results in profound defects in copper tolerance, marked intracellular copper accumulation, and hypersensitivity to hydrogen peroxide, accompanied by elevated intracellular reactive oxygen species. Mechanistically, CusR directly activates the cusCFBA copper efflux operon through promoter binding, whereas regulation of the copA transporter occurs independently of CusR. Importantly, a conserved aspartate residue (D56) within CusR is essential for its activity; both plasmid-based and chromosomal substitution of this residue abolish copper efflux regulation, disrupt copper homeostasis, and exacerbate oxidative stress susceptibility. Comparative sequence analysis further demonstrates that this residue is highly conserved across diverse bacterial species, underscoring its evolutionary importance in copper-responsive signaling. Collectively, our findings reveal a conserved Asp-dependent CusR-CusCFBA regulatory axis that couples copper detoxification to oxidative stress resistance, enabling bacterial adaptation to host-imposed copper stress. IMPORTANCE Copper intoxication is an important host-mediated antimicrobial strategy that challenges bacterial pathogens during infection. Although copper resistance systems have been extensively studied, how bacteria coordinate copper detoxification with protection against oxidative stress remains poorly understood. In this study, we identify the response regulator CusR as a key factor linking copper homeostasis and oxidative stress resistance in Klebsiella pneumoniae . We demonstrate that CusR directly controls the cusCFBA copper efflux system through promoter binding and that a conserved aspartate residue is essential for this regulatory function. Loss of CusR disrupts copper balance, increases reactive oxygen species accumulation, and reduces bacterial resistance to oxidative stress. These findings reveal a conserved regulatory mechanism that integrates metal stress adaptation with oxidative stress defense, providing new insights into how bacterial pathogens survive under host-imposed environmental pressures.

works.title: Elevated ozone reshapes wheat root-associated microbiomes through coordinated plant responses and rhizosphere environmental filtering
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Elevated tropospheric ozone (O 3 ) threatens crop productivity, but how O 3 -induced changes in plant responses influence root-associated microbiomes remains unclear. We investigated the responses of microbial communities inhabiting the rhizosphere and root endosphere to elevated O 3 using four cultivars grown under ambient and 1.5-fold ambient O 3 in a field-based free-air O 3 -concentration enrichment (FACE) system. Plant traits, root-released organic carbon (ROC), rhizosphere properties, extracellular enzyme activities, and bacterial and fungal communities were jointly analyzed. Elevated O 3 reduced yield and root biomass, with cultivar-dependent changes in ROC. Elevated O 3 consistently increased rhizosphere pH and altered microbial resource allocation, increasing ecoenzymatic vector length by 4.1% and decreasing vector angle by 4.6%. Bacterial communities showed a stronger response than fungal taxonomic communities, particularly in the rhizosphere. However, variation partitioning indicated that soil properties, especially pH, rather than O 3 treatment alone, provided the strongest independent explanation for bacterial community variation. Fungal communities showed limited taxonomic turnover but exhibited shifts in predicted trophic guilds, including increased pathotroph- and saprotroph-associated groups and decreased symbiotroph-containing guilds under elevated O 3 . These results demonstrate that elevated O 3 reshapes the wheat root-associated microbiome through coordinated changes in plant performance, rhizosphere environmental filtering, and microbial functional strategies, highlighting the importance of plant-mediated processes in regulating belowground responses to atmospheric change. IMPORTANCE Elevated tropospheric O 3 is an increasing threat to crop production, but its effects on belowground microbial processes remain poorly understood. This study demonstrates that O 3 -induced root-associated microbiome changes are closely linked with altered plant carbon allocation and rhizosphere environmental conditions rather than O 3 exposure also. By integrating plant traits, soil properties, extracellular enzyme allocation, and microbial community analyses, we reveal a compartment-specific plant-soil-microbiome response to elevated O 3 . These findings improve our understanding of how atmospheric pollution may reshape crop-associated microbial functions and soil ecological processes under future climate change.

works.title: Hybrid genome assemblies of Bacteroidota isolates uncover mobile genetic elements, antimicrobial resistance genes, and novel antimicrobial peptides
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Members of the phylum Bacteroidota dominate the mammalian gut microbiota and represent promising candidates for next-generation probiotics. However, the resolution of complete Bacteroidota genomes is often hindered by extensive repetitive sequences and mobile genetic elements, a technical challenge further exacerbated by high intraspecies diversity and strain-level variants that drive assembly fragmentation and preclude the recovery of contiguous scaffolds. We recently isolated 18 strains that belonged to the Bacteroidales order of Bacteroidota from mouse ceca, human feces, and tortoise stool, which we now sequenced using both Illumina and Oxford Nanopore platforms. We developed a specialized assembly workflow to reconstruct high-resolution genomes and characterize their extrachromosomal landscapes. The hybrid pipeline yielded 2 fully closed, single-contig chromosomes, 10 almost closed genomes, and 6 draft assemblies. Genomic integrity was exceptionally high, with completeness scores ranging from 99.6% to 100% and contamination levels below 2%. A total of 12 circular plasmids were detected across 10 isolates; eight isolates harbored a single plasmid, while two isolates (241163E and 241171E) each carried two distinct circular plasmids. Seven of these plasmids were experimentally confirmed through isolation and sequencing, and five were classified as viral contigs. Functional annotation revealed a diverse repertoire of antimicrobial resistance genes and identified several predicted antimicrobial peptides in the assemblies through machine-learning analysis, of which two selected ones were experimentally verified. Overall, the resulting assemblies provide a reliable foundation for tracking mobile genetic elements, assessing resistance potential, and mining bioactive peptides in Bacteroidota species intended for therapeutic development. IMPORTANCE Bacteria in the phylum Bacteroidota are essential to mammalian gut health and are currently being developed as advanced probiotics. However, their complex DNA often prevents scientists from mapping their complete genetic blueprints, which can leave hidden traits like antibiotic resistance undetected. In this study, we combined two advanced DNA sequencing methods to create highly accurate and complete genetic maps for 18 Bacteroidota isolates from humans, mice, and tortoise. We successfully uncovered small, elusive DNA rings (potential plasmids) and confirmed their physical presence in the laboratory. Furthermore, we identified genes responsible for antibiotic resistance and used artificial intelligence to discover new antimicrobial peptides. This research provides a crucial foundation for the scientific community to accurately track mobile genes, rigorously evaluate the safety of potential gut therapeutics, and discover novel molecules for medical applications.

works.title: Heterogeneous transfusion risk linked to variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease in a non-human primate model
works.abstract: Among the 178 cases of variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (v-CJD) in the UK, three were reported between 2003 and 2007 to be linked to a probable transmission through blood transfusion. With no further primary or iatrogenic cases observed worldwide since 2016, several countries are lifting - or have already lifted - deferrals for blood donors who have lived in the UK or, more broadly, Europe, to reduce the threat of supply shortages. However, the high prevalence of silent infection according to abnormal PrP in lymphoid tissues (potentially 100 times higher than for clinical cases in the UK) remains a concern in assessing the potential iatrogenic risk associated with long-term silent carriers for a disease whose incubation periods can extend over decades. In the present study, after experimental intravenous contamination of cynomolgus macaques with v-CJD prions, a relevant model of the human disease, we observed a highly heterogeneous intra- and inter-individual distribution of apparent peripheral prion replication in lymphoid organs that appears to correspond largely to the prion load in blood, the highest levels of which are detectable by amplification-based detection assay. In addition, several primates have developed unexpected incomplete prion phenotypes that escape diagnosis by current conventional techniques and could be intravenously transmitted to mice in the absence of a functional immune system. The peculiar prion strains associated with these atypical phenotypes would involve peripheral mechanisms independent of the immune system, different from those of v-CJD. According to our observations, conventional lymphoid organ prevalence studies may underestimate the true extent of healthy v-CJD carriers, and blood transmission risk assessment should not be based on epidemiological data alone.

works.title: Modulation of Fe3+ homeostasis by African Swine Fever virus facilitates its efficient replication in Ornithodoros lahorensis and pigs
works.abstract: African swine fever virus (ASFV) can be transmitted through direct contact and, in specific ecological settings, by Ornithodoros spp. soft ticks. However, the cellular mechanisms that support ASFV replication in both porcine host and tick vector remain poorly understood. Iron is essential for cellular metabolism and viral replication, but excessive labile iron can induce oxidative stress and ferroptosis-like morphological changes in mitochondria. Whether and how ASFV exploits intracellular Fe3+ homeostasis to sustain its replication has not been fully defined. In this study, proteomic analysis of ASFV-infected PAM (pig) and OME/CTVM24 (derived from Ornithodoros moubata) cells revealed a marked reduction in ferritin/FTH1 abundance, suggesting that ASFV infection alters intracellular iron storage and availability. Further analyses showed that ASFV dynamically regulated labile Fe3+ levels during infection. At the early stage, ASFV promoted NCOA4-associated ferritin turnover, increased labile Fe3+ release, enhanced mitochondria-endoplasmic reticulum contact, and induced ferroptosis-like changes in mitochondrial morphology. At later stages, ASFV restrained excessive iron-associated damage, thereby maintaining an intracellular environment compatible with continued viral replication. Pharmacological depletion of labile iron with deferoxamine mesylate markedly suppressed ASFV replication in both porcine and tick-derived cells, indicating that controlled Fe3+ availability is required for efficient viral propagation. Mechanistically, the ASFV-encoded protein pA151R interacted with NCOA4 and promoted autophagic degradation of FTH1 in a manner dependent on its intact LC3-interacting region motif. pA151R also impaired mitochondrial outer membrane integrity and disrupted MDA5-MAVS/VISA signaling. Deletion of A151R impaired the ability of ASFV to modulate Fe3+ homeostasis and significantly reduced viral replication. ASFV infection increased serum iron levels in pigs and caused abnormal iron redistribution and depletion in splenic tissues in vivo. Similar iron depletion and transient ferroptosis-like morphological changes in mitochondria were observed in the salivary glands of ASFV-infected O. lahorensis. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that ASFV exploits Fe3+ homeostasis through a pA151R-NCOA4-FTH1-dependent mechanism to support replication in host and vector cells. This study provides new insights into ASFV metabolic regulation and identifies iron homeostasis and pA151R-mediated ferritinophagy as potential targets for strategies aimed at limiting ASFV replication and tick-associated transmission.

works.title: EPS-producing Leuconostoc as probiotics: biomedical potential and structure–function perspectives
works.abstract: With the increasing prevalence of diseases associated with gut dysbiosis, such as gastrointestinal diseases, immunological disorders, metabolic and cardiovascular diseases, and cancer, there is a growing need for effective strategies to restore the gut microbiota and promote overall health. In this context, underexplored lactic acid bacteria, particularly those capable of producing exopolysaccharides (EPSs), are gaining attention due to the diverse and pleiotropic health benefits of their EPSs. This narrative review provides an overview of the health-promoting properties of Leuconostoc species and their associated EPSs, with particular emphasis on the structure–function relationships underlying EPS bioactivity. Furthermore, it examines the mechanisms through which EPS-producing Leuconostoc strains may influence gut and systemic health and discusses their potential as next-generation microbiome-based interventions. Notably, most available evidence is derived from in vitro and other preclinical models, while clinical studies directly validating the efficacy and health benefits of Leuconostoc EPSs in humans remain limited.

works.title: Correction: Biocontrol potential of a rhizosphere-associated Bacillus amyloliquefaciens F2 isolate against Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cubense Tropical Race 4 in Pakistan

Evidence-gated integration of microbiome, metabolome, and host transcriptome data reveals a gap between reproducible signals and cross-layer mechanistic evidence in hepatocellular and colorectal cancer
works.abstract: Introduction Microbiome multi-omics studies frequently identify microbial, metabolic, and host transcriptional associations, but their reproducibility and support for connected biological mechanisms remain uncertain. We evaluated these relationships in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and colorectal cancer (CRC) using an eight-dimensional, non-compensatory evidence-gating framework. Methods Nine public HCC datasets spanning microbiome, metabolome, and host transcriptome profiles were analyzed alongside CRC microbial and metabolomic data and separate host transcriptomic datasets. Analyses included cross-cohort replication, participant-matched taxon–metabolite associations, host transcriptional responses, sensitivity testing, and independent evidence scoring. Complete mechanistic eligibility required support across all eight evidence dimensions. Results In HCC, 13 genera showed concordant directions and nominal significance across conventional leave-one-cohort-out analyses, but none met the adjusted external validation criterion. Six longitudinal plasma feature-window signals and 12 differential liver metabolites were identified without cross-specimen concordance under false discovery rate (FDR) correction. Three hepatic transcriptional programs replicated across independent bulk datasets, but none of the four HCC candidate families met all eight evidence requirements. In CRC, four bacterial species replicated in held-out disease-feature testing. Paired microbial and fecal metabolite profiles from 347 participants yielded 18 replicated taxon–metabolite associations, of which 10 met robustness criteria and eight retained support after joint-taxon adjustment. The Peptostreptococcus stomatis–glycocholate association replicated in held-out testing (adjusted residual r = 0.315, q = 0.00232) and remained significant after joint-taxon adjustment (β = 0.209, q = 0.0144) and unified-partition analysis with global Benjamini–Hochberg correction (held-out q = 0.0303). Reanalysis of glycocholic acid (GCA) treatment transcriptomic data identified increased SOX14, ZDHHC9, and CD274 expression, although the three-gene response score yielded an exact permutation P = 0.10. Independent assessments agreed on all 48 evidence ratings (quadratic-weighted κ = 1.000). Discussion Evidence gating distinguished reproducible molecular associations from complete cross-layer mechanistic support. The P. stomatis–glycocholate association, accompanied by complementary GCA-responsive host transcription, represents a candidate for further investigation rather than an established microbial–metabolite–host mechanism.

works.title: Increasing prevalence of a mupirocin- and fusidic acid-resistant MSSA CC121-t1994 clone in pediatric skin and soft tissue infections: 8-year longitudinal study at an Spanish Hospital
works.abstract: Introduction Skin and soft tissue infections (SSTI) in pediatric patients have increased in recent years, and mupirocin and fusidic acid are important therapeutic options. Materials and methods All 217 Staphylococcus aureus isolates recovered from pediatric SSTIs in a Spanish hospital during January 2018-october 2025 were characterized (one isolate/patient). The phenotypes and genotypes of antimicrobial resistance, virulence genes and genetic lineages were analyzed along three time periods (2018–2021, 2022–2023 and 2024–2025). Results Most of 217 isolates were methicillin-susceptible (MSSA, 91.2%), and these MSSA belonged to 14 clonal-complexes (CC), being CC121 (54.5%) the most prevalent followed by CC30 (11.6%) and CC45 (7.1%). Ten spa -types were found among MSSA-CC121 isolates, being t1994 predominant (75.0%), followed by t1077 and t272. Seventeen of the 19 MRSA isolates identified belonged to the lineages CC8, CC30, and CC5. Most of MSSA-CC121 isolates carried eta and/or etb (98/108, 90.7%), and this prevalence was even higher among CC121-t1994 isolates (93.8%). The tst gene was mainly detected among MSSA-CC30/CC22. The prevalence of MSSA-CC121 isolates increased during the 8-year study (21.6%/2018–2021, 50.6%/2022–2023, 65.2%/2024–2025), associated with an enrichment of spa -t1994 (9.8%/2018–2021, 59.6%/2024–2025), and a decrease in CC30 prevalence. High frequencies of mupirocin-resistant (MUP R , mostly mediated by mupA ) and fusidic-acid-resistant (FA R , mostly mediated by fusB ) were observed among S. aureus (43.8 and 30.9%, respectively), and resistance to both (MUP R -FA R ) was found in 29.5% of isolates, most of them MSSA-CC121 (95.3%). A significant increase in the rate of MUP R -FA R isolates was observed along the years, both among S. aureus (5.9%/2018–2021, 28.6%/2022–2023 and 43.8%/2024–2025) and CC121 isolates (27.3%/2018–2021, 53.8%/2022–2023 and 63.8%/2024–2025) ( p < 0.05). The prevalence of impetigo cases among the pediatric SSTIs increased along the years (2018–2021: 37.3%; 2022–2023: 68.8%; 2024–2025: 80.9%); in addition, a significant increase was observed in the prevalence of MSSA-CC121 and MSSA-CC121-MUP R -FA R in impetigo cases along the years ( p < 0.05). Conclusion a MUP R -FA R MSSA-CC121-t1994 clone, harboring mupA , fusB and exfoliatin genes, was increasingly detected among pediatric SSTIs in this hospital-based study, especially in impetigo cases, what deserves careful monitoring for its control.

works.title: Esophageal microecology: unraveling the mechanisms underlying esophageal cancer and precancerous lesions
works.abstract: Esophageal cancer is a common and lethal digestive malignancy worldwide. Despite advances in imaging and endoscopy, most patients are diagnosed at intermediate or advanced stages and have poor long-term outcomes. Perturbations of the oral, esophageal, and intestinal microbiota have emerged as potential risk factors for esophageal cancer and its precursors, although studies remain highly heterogeneous in populations, sampling methods, and analytical strategies. This review synthesises current evidence on the microecological features of the normal esophagus, with a primary focus on esophageal squamous intraepithelial neoplasia (ESIN)—synonymous with dysplasia—and esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC). Barrett’s esophagus (BE) and esophageal adenocarcinoma (EAC) are also examined selectively for comparative purposes to highlight distinct microenvironmental trajectories. We examine potential microbiota-mediated mechanisms, including chronic inflammation, immune modulation, metabolic alterations, genotoxicity, bacteria–fungus interactions, and bacteriophage-driven remodelling of host–microbe networks, and discuss translational opportunities to improve clinical outcomes.

works.title: Exploring the neighborhood of thermotolerant free-living amoebae in Costa Rican natural water reservoirs as a preliminary One Health approach in the field
works.abstract: Introduction Free-living amoebae (FLA) of the Vahlkampfiidae family are widely distributed in nature, occupying aquatic and terrestrial habitats. The group includes thermophilic amphizoic organisms such as Naegleria fowleri . This study aims to describe natural recreational freshwaters in terms of the presence of thermotolerant vahlkampfiids, sediment microbial communities and climatic/land use features. Methods Water samples were collected from 24 locations from Costa Rica. DNA was extracted from FLA cultivated at 42 °C and molecular identification using family and N. fowleri species-specific primers for conventional PCR was performed. DNA extractions of sediment samples were also performed for a microbial metabarcoding characterization approach through 16S rRNA V3-V4 region and 18S rRNA V4 region gene amplicons sequencing. A geographic information system was used to locate each sampling site in its respective climatic subregion and to establish a land use coverage buffer around it. Results and discussion Results revealed 20 positive locations for vahlkampfiids; the sites predominantly featured forest cover and were in climatic subregions with significant rainfall patterns. All locations were negative for N. fowleri ; however, identification by sequencing detected a predominance of Tetramitus spp., followed by Vahlkampfia sp. and Neovahlkampfia sp. Sediment metabarcoding showed mainly metazoans, microalgae and Proteobacteria in these benthic ecosystems. Even when N. fowleri was not found, our exploration showed that these aquatic environments of close human contact allow the presence of thermotolerant vahlkampfiids and might be surrounded by microbial communities of interest for future research regarding ecological interactions and public health risks.

works.title: The phageome in critical illness: bacteriophage–bacteria interactions, resistome dynamics, and pathogen domination in the intensive care unit
works.abstract: Critical illness disrupts microbial communities through antimicrobial exposure, altered nutrient supply, tissue injury, and loss of anatomical barriers. Bacterial profiling has linked these disturbances to pathogen domination and infection, but bacteria participate in ecosystems that also contain bacteriophages, eukaryotic viruses, and mobile genetic elements. This narrative review examines how the phageome may influence microbial ecological transitions during critical illness, including changes in colonization resistance, pathogen domination, and the potential progression to invasive infection. We integrate recent human observations with experimental evidence on phage predation, lysogeny, bacterial defense, spatial organization, and resistance-gene mobility. Longitudinal respiratory viromics and circulating phage DNA studies provide direct clinical entry points, whereas much of the mechanistic evidence originates from healthy volunteers, inflammatory disease cohorts, cultured communities, and animal models. These evidence levels support an ecological framework but do not establish a universal phage-mediated pathway to ICU infection. Phages can suppress susceptible pathogens, remove protective commensals, select resistant bacterial phenotypes, or support lysogen fitness. Their contribution to antimicrobial resistance extends beyond resistance genes encoded within phage genomes to transduction, phage–plasmid exchange, and indirect effects on conjugation and community composition. Interpretation requires separating viral detection from productive infection, bacterial DNA packaging from successful transfer, and relative abundance from absolute expansion. We propose a compartment-aware longitudinal research framework combining viral-particle and bulk metagenomics, bacterial strain resolution, functional validation, and prospectively adjudicated clinical events. The immediate clinical opportunity is to determine whether phage measurements add actionable information to bacterial surveillance; therapeutic manipulation remains a downstream application requiring ecological and clinical validation.

works.title: Antimicrobial peptide–drug conjugates: rational design, pharmacological evaluation, and translational perspectives
works.abstract: Antimicrobial peptide–drug conjugates (APDCs) combine peptide and antibiotic functions within a single covalent construct. APDCs share design features with antibody–drug conjugates, but the field lacks an integrated account of how such conjugates should be designed and evaluated. This review examines that process from scaffold selection to translational precedent. Design decisions are treated as medicinal chemistry: which antimicrobial peptide scaffold to start from and how to stabilize it, which payload to carry, whether the linker should be cleavable, conditionally stable, or non-cleavable, and whether engaging one or two targets yields a better antibacterial profile. Pharmacological evidence is then assessed for representative vancomycin, β-lactam, aminoglycoside, and fluoroquinolone conjugates, with experimentally demonstrated mechanisms distinguished from those that are indirectly inferred, computationally predicted, or hypothesized. In series reported through July 2026, conjugation produced large MIC reductions relative to inactive or resistant parent antibiotics, including in vancomycin-resistant enterococci, and in some cases restored activity against strains refractory to both parent molecules; comparisons with active standards of care were limited. By contrast, pharmacokinetic characterization is nearly absent, immunomodulatory and anti-biofilm mechanisms are only beginning to be dissected, in vivo efficacy has been reported for only seven APDC programs, and no dedicated toxicology study was identified. Two adjacent programs—the approved siderophore cephalosporin cefiderocol and the discontinued antibody–antibiotic conjugate DSTA4637S—serve as translational precedents, illustrating the manufacturing, safety, and regulatory hurdles an APDC must clear. Within these constraints, experimentally validated artificial-intelligence-assisted sequence design may support peptide modules for future APDCs, although our literature search did not identify an AI-designed APDC.

works.title: Gut microbial characteristics associated with pegylated interferon treatment response in chronic hepatitis B: insights into the gut–liver axis
works.abstract: Background Pegylated interferon (Peg-IFN) treatment response varies considerably among patients with chronic hepatitis B (CHB). The role of the gut microbiota in this heterogeneity remains unclear. This study aimed to characterize gut microbial features associated with Peg-IFN response and explore their potential relevance to the gut–liver axis. Methods A total of 64 patients with CHB who completed 24 weeks of Peg-IFN-based therapy were enrolled in this study. Fecal samples collected at week 24 were analyzed using 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Microbial characteristics and clinical factors associated with treatment response were evaluated, followed by development of an integrated classification model. Results Among the 64 patients, 38 were classified as responders and 26 as non-responders. Responders exhibited distinct gut microbial profiles, characterized by increased microbial richness ( p = 0.014), altered community composition ( p = 0.045), and different microbial interaction patterns. Dorea abundance was enriched in responders and independently associated with treatment response. Multivariable logistic regression identified lower baseline HBsAg levels (OR = 0.562, p = 0.048), higher platelet counts (OR = 1.020, p = 0.007), and increased Dorea abundance (OR = 3.876, p = 0.008) as independent factors associated with response. Restricted cubic spline analysis supported a significant association between Dorea abundance and response probability. The Virological–Host–Microbial (VHM) triad model integrating these factors demonstrated promising apparent discrimination (ROC-AUC = 0.790) and calibration in the development cohort. Conclusion Distinct gut microbial ecological patterns are associated with Peg-IFN treatment response in CHB, with Dorea representing a characteristic microbial feature. This study provides a multidimensional framework for understanding heterogeneity in interferon responsiveness and highlights the potential relevance of the gut–liver–immune axis.

works.title: Transitional ecosystem states in coastal waters undergoing changing oxygen conditions revealed by coupled geochemical and microbial dynamics
works.abstract: Background Coastal oxygen depletion is a major driver of changes in sediment biogeochemistry and microbial functioning. However, oxygen states vary over space and time, which results in temporal dynamics that are so far under explored. This study examined three sites with differing oxygen regimes across a year to investigate how temporal oxygen variability shapes surface sediment microbial communities and activity. Methods Coastal Baltic Sea surface sediments were sampled over one year at three sites with differing long-term oxygen regimes—one site that was predominantly oxic, one with predominantly low-oxygen conditions, and one intermediate site with fluctuating oxygen availability. Sediment biogeochemistry, 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing, and metatranscriptomic analyses were combined to assess temporal changes in microbial community composition and transcriptional activity. Results The results showed that long-term oxygen history was the primary factor structuring both microbial community composition and transcriptional profiles. The shallow site was characterized by mostly oxygenated conditions and exhibited relatively stable communities and transcriptional activity over time. The deep site was predominantly characterized by long-term low-oxygen conditions and was dominated by anaerobic metabolic patterns. In contrast, the intermediate site, that was exposed to more pronounced fluctuating oxygen conditions, showed the highest temporal variability in both community composition and RNA transcripts. This site also displayed stronger shifts in transcriptional activity over time, indicating a higher sensitivity of microbial processes to environmental variability compared to the other sites. Conclusion These results suggested that transitional oxygen habitats represented dynamic ecological states where microbial communities and functions rapidly responded to changing environmental conditions. Overall, oxygen availability strongly structured both microbial composition and activity in coastal sediments, with transitional habitats exhibiting enhanced temporal variability. These findings further indicated that environments experiencing fluctuating oxygen conditions may be particularly responsive to ongoing environmental change in coastal systems.

works.title: Harnessing waste-derived amendments for microbially mediated acid mine drainage remediation: from mechanisms to process optimization and machine learning
works.abstract: Acid mine drainage (AMD) remains a persistent environmental challenge, creating a need for treatment strategies that combine sustained contaminant control with resource-efficient use of residual materials. Waste-derived amendments may couple residue valorization with microbially mediated treatment of AMD, particularly mine-tailings leachate, but direct evidence combining variable waste-derived donors with heterogeneous collected leachate remains limited, and machine-learning (ML) models have rarely been validated across amendment batches, reactors, or sites. This review therefore evaluates amendment functions, microbial and geochemical mechanisms, operational constraints, and the role of ML in process development. A targeted narrative synthesis was conducted using publisher webpages, PubMed, and institutional repositories through 17 September 2026. Evidence was organized into four application settings: collected tailings-leachate treatment, source-zone tailings amendment, other real mine waters, and synthetic AMD; modeling studies were assessed separately for transferability. Representative studies show that performance is strongly endpoint-dependent. In 460-day field reactors containing organic substrates, sulfate removal was 26–35 mol% and Zn removal reached 88–95 mol%, whereas Mn removal was only 2–6 mol%. In a 172-day ethanol-fed reactor treating successive tailings leachates, sulfate removal reached 84.7 ± 6.9%, most metal removals approached 100%, and Mn removal was approximately 80%. A 17-run brewery-wastewater modeling study reported within-study R 2 values of 0.97 and 0.99, demonstrating predictive feasibility but not transferable or autonomous control. The review is limited by selective rather than exhaustive searching, incomplete access to some full texts, and heterogeneity in influent chemistry, treatment boundaries, and sampling periods, which precluded pooled analysis. Overall, waste-derived amendments can support sulfate reduction, alkalinity generation, biomass retention, and metal partitioning, but strong metal removal can coexist with incomplete sulfate conversion and element-specific limitations. Future progress requires continuous and field-scale validation, matched mass balances, disturbance testing, residual-stability assessment, and ML used as constrained decision support rather than as a substitute for mechanistic and prospective operating evidence.

works.title: Survival and genomic mutations of long-term Pseudomonas fluorescens cultures: an in vitro model to study persistence in food production environments
works.abstract: Background Microbial persistence in food production environments poses a significant challenge to food safety, as bacteria can survive cleaning and disinfection procedures by existing in dormant states and forming biofilms. Methods With the aim to investigate the long-term adaptive strategies three strains (CECT378, ps_20, and ps_77) belonging to the Pseudomonas fluorescens subgroup ( Pf ) were maintained in minimal medium for two years under nutrient starvation at 4 °C and 22 °C were characterized. Active cells (CFU), the PMAxx-derived genome-copy/CFU ratio, used as an indirect indicator of the presence of viable but non-culturable (VBNC) cells and persister cells were monitored across multiple time points. Whole-genome sequencing data from 330 clones recovered from cultures maintained at both temperatures were analyzed to investigate genomic adaptation during long-term survival. Results The strains maintained high cell densities (~10 7 –10 8 CFU/mL) throughout the experiment, with the active state predominating. The number of persister cells increased progressively over time, particularly at 4 °C, whereas the PMAxx-derived genome-copy/CFU ratio remained generally low, suggesting a limited potential contribution of VBNC cells. Whole-genome sequencing revealed strain-dependent mutation accumulation patterns,with dN/dS ratios below 1 in CECT378 and ps_20 and above 1 in ps_77. Convergent mutations were identified across strains in genes regulating biofilm formation, RNA polymerase subunits ( rpoS , rpoA ), two-component systems ( BarA/uvrY, cbrA ), and genes previously associated with the WS (wrinkly spreader) phenotype ( nlpD, PgaA, DGCs genes ). Conclusion The results suggested that transcriptional regulation could play a central role in the long-term survival of the species. Finally, biofilm adaptation may represent an important strategy for coping with stress and survival, with important implications for food safety management.

works.title: Fusobacterium nucleatum regulates SLC7A11, inhibits ferroptosis and leads to oxaliplatin resistance in colorectal cancer
works.abstract: Background Fusobacterium nucleatum ( F. nucleatum ), a pathogenic bacterium associated with colorectal cancer (CRC), has been increasingly linked to chemoresistance. While ferroptosis is recognized as a contributor to chemotherapy resistance mechanisms, the regulatory role of gut microbiota in this process remains poorly characterized. Methods To explore the potential relationship between gut microbiota dysbiosis and CRC recurrence, 16S rRNA sequencing was performed on CRC tissues, revealing a positive correlation between the high abundance of F. nucleatum in CRC tissue and tumor recurrence. Experimental validation confirmed F. nucleatum -mediated oxaliplatin (L-OHP) resistance both in vitro and in vivo . Analysis of the transcriptome of cells co-cultured with F. nucleatum identified an association between ferroptosis and F. nucleatum infection.
