Furthermore, in vitro analyses quantified malondialdehyde, ferrous iron, glutathione, and oxidized glutathione levels to assess potential ferroptosis modulation under L-OHP exposure. Results Mechanistically, F. nucleatum inhibits ferroptosis and promotes L-OHP resistance through the overexpression of SLC7A11. This effect is mediated by the TLR4/AP-1 signaling pathway, as confirmed by chromatin immunoprecipitation quantitative PCR (ChIP–qPCR) and dual-luciferase reporter assays, which showed enhanced binding of AP-1 c-Jun to the SLC7A11 promoter following F. nucleatum infection. Clinical data further supported the association between the TLR4/AP-1/SLC7A11 axis, F. nucleatum abundance in tumor tissue, and CRC recurrence. Conclusion These findings establish a direct role of F. nucleatum in L-OHP resistance through ferroptosis inhibition. Therapeutic targeting of F. nucleatum and ferroptosis pathways may thus offer novel strategies to mitigate chemotherapy resistance and improve the prognosis of CRC patients.

works.title: Microbial control of ocular homeostasis and disease: mechanisms, metabolites, and therapeutic opportunities
works.abstract: The relationship between microbiota and ocular disease is reshaping current views of eye health. Ocular homeostasis depends not only on local tissues but also on interactions among several systems. These systems include the ocular surface microbiota, gut microbiota, systemic immune and metabolic networks, the blood–eye barrier, and the neurovascular unit. Commensal microbial signals can preserve epithelial integrity, barrier immunity, wound repair, immune tolerance, vascular stability, and neuroprotection. Dysbiosis can convert this regulatory network into a source of ocular injury. This occurs through several mechanisms, such as lipopolysaccharide exposure, loss of short chain fatty acids, disturbed tryptophan, bile acid, and lipid metabolism, Th17 and Treg imbalance, complement activation, microglial reprogramming, and molecular mimicry. These regulatory interactions operate along an integrated, multi-compartment spatial network. Locally, the exposed ocular surface and contiguous periocular niches calibrate epithelial renewal and barrier immunity. Systemically, intestinal microbial communities regulate intraocular vascular integrity and neuroimmune tone through circulating metabolites, pathogen-associated molecular patterns, and immune cell trafficking. Low-biomass intraocular signals and the ocular virome provide additional layers of local immune governance. Disruption of this compartmentalized network characterizes ocular surface diseases, uveitis, diabetic retinopathy, age-related macular degeneration, glaucoma, and retinal degeneration. Therapeutic strategies are consequently shifting from empirical antimicrobial eradication toward targeted microbiota-directed interventions, including postbiotics, metabolite supplementation, and barrier-reinforcing platforms. Characterizing these host-microbial circuits may guide the development of therapies that restore ocular health by stabilizing local and systemic microenvironments.

works.title: A study on the sources of HIV-1 transmission in Haikou, China: insights from molecular genetics and field epidemiological investigations
works.abstract: Objective This study aimed to integrate molecular network analysis, Bayesian phylogenetic modeling, and field epidemiological investigation to systematically trace the sources of HIV-1 transmission in Haikou, China. Design A longitudinal molecular surveillance program was implemented between 2021 and 2024, combined with a cross-sectional field epidemiological investigation. Methods Subtype-specific local sequence databases were constructed from nationwide sequences. Molecular clusters containing both local and external sequences were subjected to phylogeographic analysis under a Bayesian relaxed molecular clock and a Skygrid model to infer transmission origins. Complementing the molecular analyses, field epidemiological investigations were carried out among a subset of participants to assess self-reported transmission sources. Results Among the 1,125 pol sequences, CRF01_AE (35.64%), CRF07_BC (38.58%), CRF65_cpx (7.20%), and CRF55_01B (4.53%) were the four most prevalent subtypes, with local clustering rates of 36.65%, 33.64%, 86.42%, and 54.90%, respectively. Phylogeographic analysis identified Guangdong as the primary origin of HIV-1 introductions into Haikou for all four subtypes, followed by Beijing (CRF01_AE_C1 and CRF65_cpx) and Shanghai (CRF07_BC). CRF01_AE showed bidirectional transmission between Haikou and Sanya, and between Haikou and Dongfang; CRF07_BC and CRF65_cpx both disseminated from Haikou to six other cities in Hainan. Field epidemiological investigations revealed that 52.33% (236/451) of participants had acquired HIV outside Haikou, with Guangdong being the primary source (16.95%, 40/236), followed by Sichuan (5.93%, 14/236). Within Hainan, Sanya accounted for the largest share (7.63%, 18/236). Conclusion By integrating molecular and epidemiological evidence, this study advances the tracing of HIV-1 transmission sources and underscores the critical need for cross-regional prevention strategies targeting mobile populations.

works.title: Protection against lethal pneumonic plague by intramuscular F1V vaccine incorporating a colloidal TLR4-TLR7 dual adjuvant
works.abstract: Yersinia pestis is a facultative intracellular bacterium that causes plague, which manifests in bubonic form and the more severe pneumonic and septicemic forms. There is no FDA-approved vaccine for plague, and those used in the past for human prophylaxis were suboptimal against aerosol infection or nonencapsulated strains. To provide broad protection against Y. pestis , further optimization of vaccine formulations is essential. In a lethal aerosol challenge model using nonencapsulated Y. pestis in BALB/c mice, we compared an existing benchmark vaccine to a similar formulation using novel TLR4-TLR7 dual adjuvant KUP101A in place of TLR9 adjuvant CpG 2006. In addition, we compared vaccination through the subcutaneous (SC) and intramuscular (IM) routes, and we compared vaccination using KUP101A with or without additional alum adjuvant. Two vaccine doses were given four weeks apart, and four weeks later mice were challenged via whole-body aerosol exposure. KUP101A compared favorably to CpG for conferring protection after Y. pestis challenge and led to significantly lower bacterial burden in tissues. This was observed despite similar humoral immunity and Th1/Th2 phenotype, and less evidence of splenic T cell memory than was seen with CpG. Alum was necessary for the protective effect of KUP101A, similarly to CpG. Finally, we saw evidence that IM vaccination was preferable to SC for inducing Th1 polarization, based on the ratio of serum IgG2a to IgG1 and splenocyte cytokine secretion. This study demonstrates that KUP101A is a promising adjuvant with a favorable safety profile for future Y. pestis vaccine development.

works.title: Research progress on the mechanisms of microbial degradation of antibiotics and attenuation of antibiotic resistance genes during composting
works.abstract: Antibiotics and their resistance genes (ARGs) commonly coexist in organic solid waste, posing significant ecological and public health risks. Composting is a crucial biological process for mitigating such composite pollution. This review elucidates the microbial mechanisms driving the simultaneous removal of antibiotics and ARGs in composting systems. Specifically, it details how parent antibiotic compounds are transformed through enzymatic degradation and co-metabolic pathways, thereby alleviating selection pressure on drug-resistant bacteria. Microbial strategies that interfere with the transmission and persistence of ARGs, including the inhibition of horizontal gene transfer and the degradation of extracellular DNA, are highlighted. Furthermore, this review introduces the core concept of “synergistic attenuation,” emphasizing the coupled relationship between antibiotic degradation and ARG suppression. It also summarizes the application of multi-omics techniques (e.g., metagenomics, metatranscriptomics, and metabolomics) in validating these complex mechanisms. Finally, it outlines future directions for enhancing this synergistic process through targeted regulation of microbial community structure and function, providing a theoretical foundation and innovative insights for optimizing composting as an efficient and low-risk organic waste treatment technology.

works.title: The mammalian archaeome: diversity, function and emerging roles in health and disease
The microbiome’s voyage beyond Earth
Hunt for the origins of an influenza pandemic
How marine particles shaped microbial evolution over Earth’s history
Dual-use virology research in the age of AI
works.abstract: We propose that dual-use research of concern policies should reflect emerging risks from recent technological innovations, including artificial intelligence, to ensure continued global biosafety, while acknowledging the wider societal benefits of genetic modification of viruses.

works.title: Flavonoid-mediated plant-microbiome interactions shape competitive outcomes between native and non-native mangroves
works.abstract: Understanding how non-native plants outcompete native species is a central question in ecology and critical for ecosystem management. Plant-microbiome interactions have been proposed to shape competitive outcomes and invasion success, yet such underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. This is particularly critical for globally important blue carbon ecosystems such as mangroves, where the non-native Sonneratia apetala is known to suppress the native Kandelia obovata . However, the mechanistic basis for this competitive suppression has not been resolved yet. Here we investigated interspecific competition between the S. apetala and K. obovata using multi-omics analyses (metagenomics, transcriptomics, and metabolomics) under controlled experiments. We found that co-cultivation with S. apetala reduced K. obovata dry biomass by 25.0% and downregulated flavonoid biosynthesis genes, accompanied by reduced levels of flavonoids in root exudates (e.g., catechin, baohuoside I, phloretin). Also, flavonoids were identified as key root exudates associated with the alteration of rhizosphere microbiomes, and their reduced exudation from K. obovata in the co-culture accompanied by decreased relative abundance of microbial groups (e.g., Coleofasciculaceae , Coraliomargaritaceae ) harboring genes involved in nitrogen fixation, phosphorus cycling, and cobalamin biosynthesis. Moreover, catechin (a representative flavonoid) amendment to plant-free sediments increased the abundance of microbial functional genes related to these processes, suggesting that catechin can alter microbial functional profiles under plant-free sediment conditions. Our results clarify how flavonoid-mediated plant-microbiome interactions shape competitive outcomes of non-native S. apetala and native K. obovata , offering a mechanistic insight for understanding biological invasions. This study provides perspectives for integrating mangrove-microbiome interactions into microbiome engineering in future mangrove reforestation and blue carbon management. Video Abstract

works.title: Modulation of the general stress response impacts protein expression, energy economy, and heterogeneity in virtually non-dividing yeast cultures
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Microbial cells adapt their physiology when growth is restricted by nutrient limitation, balancing survival with the capacity to produce proteins. Here, we investigated this adaptation in Saccharomyces cerevisiae by comparing retentostat cultures, in which specific growth rates reached below 0.001 h⁻¹, of a reference strain (ScNTi001) and a ∆ msn2 ∆ msn4 mutant (ScNTm001). We show that general stress-response transcription factors Msn2 and Msn4 are crucial for maintaining energy efficiency and for survival under this extreme calorie restriction. Their absence increased population heterogeneity and reduced viability, underscoring a role beyond merely stress resistance. To understand (heterologous) protein expression dynamics, we monitored how a stress-inducible promoter (P HSP12 ) and a constitutive promoter (P TEF1 ) impacted protein levels. The P HSP12 remained active at moderate to low growth rates, but expression sharply dropped below 0.001 h⁻¹, whereas the P TEF1 sustained protein expression, with activity linked to specific glucose uptake rates rather than growth rate. This decoupling revealed a trade-off: although P TEF1 -driven ymNeongreen-specific production rates were 70% higher in the absence of ∆ msn2 ∆ msn4 , overall product yields were 13% lower. IMPORTANCE This study demonstrates how Msn2 and Msn4 govern cellular robustness under extreme nutrient-limited conditions at near-zero growth rates. It also guides promoter selection strategies for growth-independent production processes. More broadly, this study shows that retentostats can be used as a valuable tool to dissect stress-response pathways, survival mechanisms, and growth-independent expression systems in microbial cell factories.

works.title: Retraction: Flaviviridae RdRp exploits NSUN2-driven m5C methylation to establish persistent infection
Dark CO2 fixation via the ethylmalonyl-CoA pathway establishes metabolic parity: A stoichiometric basis for compounding ecosystem shifts
works.abstract: A central challenge in microbial ecology, particularly in engineered systems, is understanding how competing guilds coexist and why communities deviate from expected stability. Whereas polyphosphate accumulation provides energy and redox buffering in many heterotrophs, how lineages lacking polyphosphate synthesis manage equivalent redox imbalances remains an overlooked question. Using an enhanced biological phosphorus removal system, we integrated quantitative stoichiometry with metaproteomics to resolve alternative metabolic strategies that underpin cellular homeostasis in heterotrophs. We show that glycogen-accumulating organisms (Ca. Competibacter GAO) achieve stoichiometric yield parity with polyphosphate-accumulating organisms (Ca. Dechloromonas PAO) through a parallel redox-buffering mechanism: heterotrophic CO2/HCO3- assimilation via the ethylmalonyl-CoA pathway. This CO2/HCO3- fixation couples structural carbon conservation with tight redox control, mitigating intracellular electron overflow and eliminating the long-assumed GAO bioenergetic inferiority. The energetic efficiency of GAOs is further fortified by fine-tuned metabolic wiring, featuring energy-efficient high-affinity acetate activation, ferredoxin-mediated biochemistry, and ATP-neutral polyhydroxyalkanoate (PHA) mobilization. Metabolic parity is established between the two guilds growing on acetate, yet minor formate co-feeding tilts the delicate PAO-GAO balance. Formate supplementation creates an asymmetric bioenergetic niche that grants per-cycle energy gains primarily to GAOs. Decoupled from hydraulic throughput, solids retention time control retains cells carrying accumulated intracellular inventory, translating per-cycle energetic edges into a multi-generational ratchet that drives a community shift from PAO-GAO co-dominance to GAO dominance. By exposing limitations of traditional single-substrate and single-cycle steady-state models, our findings reveal how inorganic resource management and generational metabolic compounding shape community assembly in biomass-retaining microbial ecosystems.

works.title: Free-living autotrophs drive a carbon fixation peak within the Orca Basin chemocline while heterotrophs dominate total activity from seawater to brine
works.abstract: Deep hypersaline anoxic basins (DHABs) are stratified, polyextreme environments found within enclosed and semi-enclosed seas worldwide. Here, we quantified microbial activity in Orca Basin, the largest known DHAB, to investigate carbon cycling across its steep chemical and salinity gradients. We measured total anabolic activity and dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) fixation as a function of metabolic lifestyle (autotroph or heterotroph) and spatial niche (free-living or particle-associated) using dual-isotope labeling experiments and single-cell analysis by nanoscale secondary ion mass spectrometry (nanoSIMS). Activity was detected within all ten depths investigated from seawater to hypersaline brine, including by most cells within the brine. DIC fixation and total anabolic activity peaked within the oxic-anoxic interface, notably separate from the peak in cell and particle density deeper in the halocline. Autotrophs drove the peak in DIC fixation, but heterotrophs drove that of total activity; autotrophs were more abundant than heterotrophs at this depth but on average smaller and slower growing. Particle-associated heterotrophs, but not autotrophs, were significantly more active than their free-living counterparts within the interface. Heterotrophic communities derived an average of 4% to 10% of their biomass from DIC across the vertical transect, contributing just 2% of total DIC fixation within the peak but the majority within overlying seawater. Metagenomic analysis of catabolically active, sorted cells indicated members of at least five phyla were active within the oxic-anoxic interface, including putatively autotrophic Thermoproteota. These data provide high-sensitivity microbial activity measurements in Orca Basin and highlight the widespread viability of the resident microbiome.

works.title: Temperature effects on life history strategies for rapid growth potential of leaf epiphytic bacteria
works.abstract: Phyllosphere bacteria, occupying both epiphytic and endophytic habitats, constitute a critical plant-atmosphere interface. However, their community assembly and life-history strategies (LHSs) in response to temperature increase remain poorly understood. Here, we compared leaf phyllosphere bacterial communities with those in other plant compartments across four representative plant species from an alpine meadow on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau. By combining observations along an elevational gradient with a controlled warming experiment, we found that temperature was closely associated with the deterministic assembly of leaf phyllosphere bacterial communities. Elevated temperature corresponded to shifts in taxonomic composition, diversity, assembly process, cross-compartment bacterial source, and co-occurrence network. Furthermore, elevated temperature was associated with a shift toward r-strategists in leaf phyllosphere bacterial LHSs, evidenced by higher ribosomal RNA operon (rrn) copy numbers for rapid growth potential and corroborated by genome assemblies of four warming-responsive epiphytic isolates and metagenomic sequencing. Based on 880 public 16S rRNA gene datasets from 45 locations on six continents, we identified a global increase in the rrn copy number in leaf epiphytic bacterial communities across diverse plant species, which was associated with elevated temperatures and enhanced diurnal fluctuation. Finally, we proposed a concept of four LHSs (growth, stress tolerance, competition, and resource acquisition) based on functional inference from 16S rRNA data, supported by the assembled epiphytic bacterial genomes and metagenomes. Collectively, our findings established a trait-based framework for understanding responses of leaf phyllosphere bacteria to future warming.

works.title: Farnesol keeps fungal spores asleep
Detoxification of host-relevant H 2 O 2 shapes Pseudomonas aeruginosa population gradients in flow
works.abstract: ABSTRACT During infection, bacterial populations need to overcome low levels of host-generated H 2 O 2 . However, experiments almost always use high H 2 O 2 levels that are rarely found in hosts. Here, we use microfluidics to investigate how host-relevant H 2 O 2 impacts populations of the human pathogen Pseudomonas aeruginosa PA14 in flow. Using long-channel microfluidic devices, we establish that cells at the front of a population remove H 2 O 2 and protect their downstream neighbors. Population-level protection is mediated by three OxyR-regulated scavenging systems (KatA, KatB, AhpCF), which are each sufficient to detoxify host-relevant H 2 O 2 . Mutants lacking all three systems are sensitive to H 2 O 2 , but can be cross-protected by resistant cells when co-cultured. Cross-protection is abolished in higher flow regimes, where H 2 O 2 is delivered faster than cells can remove it. Our results demonstrate how local detoxification provides global protection, which results in spatial gradients across bacterial populations in flow. Together, our findings highlight how biological, chemical, and physical factors collectively determine the fate of bacterial populations in host-relevant environments. IMPORTANCE Bacteria experience chemical and physical stresses during infection. For example, bacterial pathogens encounter low levels of host-generated H 2 O 2 in the bloodstream, urinary tract, and lungs. However, almost all laboratory experiments use much higher H 2 O 2 levels, which are uncommon in host environments. In this study, we used microfluidics to deliver host-relevant H 2 O 2 into populations of the human pathogen, Pseudomonas aeruginosa . We establish that P. aeruginosa uses three systems to detoxify H 2 O 2 , and strains lacking all three systems are highly sensitive. By co-culturing sensitive and resistant strains, we demonstrate how cells protect each other and form spatial gradients across mixed populations. Strikingly, we discover that cell–cell protection is lost in higher flow regimes, as flow-based delivery outpaces detoxification. Thus, our experiments reveal how host-relevant chemical and physical stressors combine to inhibit growth of bacterial populations.

works.title: Diversity and evolution of the ribovirian class Stelpaviricetes
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Metatranscriptome mining has dramatically expanded the known diversity of ribovirians at all taxonomic levels. We explored the class Stelpaviricetes in the phylum Pisuviricota that currently includes three orders and six recognized virus families: order Stellavirales with family Astroviridae infecting vertebrates; Patatavirales with families Potyviridae, the largest known family of plant ribovirians, and Potyliviridae; and Hypofuvirales consisting of three families of viruses associated largely with phytopathogenic fungi. Using an order-specific collection of Hidden Markov Model profiles for the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRP), the hallmark protein of ribovirians, we identified 103 putative families within Stelpaviricetes, most of which share an astrovirus-like genome architecture, encoding three protein domains: the RdRP, a chymotrypsin-like protease, and a single jellyroll capsid protein. The topology of the phylogenetic tree of the RdRP implies that the common ancestor of Stelpaviricetes had an astrovirus-like genome. The ancestor of the order Patatavirales acquired two additional domains, a papain-like protease and a superfamily 2 helicase, whereas the capsid protein was replaced with an unrelated one, forming filamentous capsids. The ancestor of Hypofuvirales also encoded a superfamily 2 helicase and a papain-like protease, but had lost the capsid protein. Hypofuvirales might have derived from Patatavirales or evolved independently from an astro-like ancestor. For the vast majority of Stelpaviricetes identified in metatranscriptomes, host assignment remains elusive. Nevertheless, analysis of endogenous virus elements and isolated viruses provides some clues suggesting that the common ancestor of Potyviridae and Potyliviridae had a fungal host, whereas the common ancestor of Stelpaviricetes might have been a protist virus. IMPORTANCE The enormous diversity of viruses on Earth is only now coming to light through extensive metagenome and metatranscriptome mining. Using vast databases of ribovirus genomes, we performed phylogenomic analysis of the class Stelpaviricetes , which includes the families Astroviridae and Potyviridae, the former comprising animal viruses and the latter comprising plant viruses. We identified more than 100 family-level groups of viruses, most of which have small, astrovirus-like genomes, likely resembling the common ancestor of Stelpaviricetes . In contrast, the putative common ancestor of Potyviridae and its sister family Potyliviridae exhibits higher genome complexity that apparently emerged in viruses of fungi. The most plausible scenario for the origin of Potyviridae involves horizontal transfer of a virus across kingdoms between plant-associated fungi and plants.

works.title: Structural insights into West Nile virus programmed ribosomal frameshifting reveal coordinated regulation by RNA, ribosome, and nascent peptide
works.abstract: Programmed -1 ribosomal frameshifting (-1 PRF) is essential for West Nile virus (WNV) gene expression and generates NS1', a protein implicated in viral replication and pathogenesis. However, the structural pathway by which translating ribosomes traverse the WNV frameshift signal remains poorly understood. Here, we combined cryo-electron microscopy, RNA structural modeling, molecular dynamics simulations, and functional analyses to investigate the mechanism of WNV -1 PRF. We resolved a pre-frameshift ribosomal complex together with four translocation intermediates, including a previously uncharacterized semi-rotated state in which the 40S subunit undergoes partial rotation while tRNAs remain in near-canonical A/A-P/P configurations. This intermediate is accompanied by remodeling of conserved peptidyl-transferase-center nucleotides, suggesting that active-site rearrangements can precede canonical tRNA movement during translocation. Structural modeling and simulations further suggest that the WNV frameshift-stimulatory RNA exists as a compact but conformationally heterogeneous ensemble capable of adopting multiple stable or metastable pseudoknot architectures. In addition, we identified direct interactions between the nascent viral peptide and the ribosomal exit tunnel, and disruption of the tunnel-occupying peptide reduced frameshifting efficiency. Together, our findings suggest that WNV frameshifting is governed not by a single stimulatory element but by the coordinated coupling of RNA dynamics, ribosome remodeling, and nascent-chain interactions.IMPORTANCEViruses often rely on a process called programmed ribosomal frameshifting to produce proteins important for infection. West Nile virus (WNV), a mosquito-borne pathogen that can cause severe neurological disease in humans, uses this strategy to generate NS1', a protein linked to viral replication and pathogenesis. However, how ribosomes are redirected into an alternative reading frame remains incompletely understood. Here, we provide structural insights into ribosome movement during translation of the WNV frameshift signal. Our findings also suggest that the viral RNA can adopt alternative conformations and that the emerging viral peptide may influence frameshifting efficiency. Together, these observations contribute to our understanding of how RNA structure, ribosomal dynamics, and nascent peptides may influence viral protein expression.

works.title: Unraveling the relationship between population composition and metabolite induction in high-precision cellulosic bacterial–fungal co-cultivations
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Co-cultures of filamentous microorganisms are a tool to unlock the biosynthetic machinery encoded in silent gene clusters. However, if bioactive compounds are to be produced biotechnologically, it is essential to understand the dynamics of microbial partnership. In this context, we have previously introduced a co-cultivation platform based on low-cost crystalline cellulose as a substrate. Here, the fungus Trichoderma reesei RUT-C30 degrades α-cellulose into soluble sugars to support the growth of the natural product-producing bacterium Streptomyces coelicolor A3(2), which is unable to utilize cellulose. This co-cultivation approach mimics a carbon-limited interaction scenario of natural habitats. We investigated how the population dynamics of both strains affect metabolite production by combining high-throughput online fluorescence monitoring with high-resolution liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS)-based metabolomics. We then determined the metabolic profile of the cultures and identified metabolites specifically induced during co-cultivation. The coupled analysis of population ratios and metabolomic data indicated that the highest number of induced metabolites compared to axenic cultures is observed in co-cultures with a balanced ratio of both strains. This analysis further led to deciphering a biotransformation of dimerumic acid, a hydroxamate siderophore produced by T. reesei , into the dehydroxylated derivatives eleutherazine B and talarazine A by S. coelicolor . Additionally, a small cluster of unique metabolites strongly induced in co-cultures was found to be structurally similar to steroidal lactones of the withanolide class, thus highlighting the potential for the discovery of natural products. Overall, the platform described combines natural product prospecting with a biotechnological production strategy that can be extended also to other co-cultures. IMPORTANCE This work provides a comprehensive analysis of population dynamics and metabolite production in a complex microbial co-culture. This approach integrates three key aspects. First, high-throughput online monitoring enables biomass tracking through fluorescence labeling in a system containing two filamentous microorganisms with distinct macro- and micromorphologies and a non-soluble fibrous substrate. Second, concomitant metabolomics analysis during co-cultivation settings helps to resolve metabolic interaction patterns. Interestingly, a metal-acquisition compound produced by the first microbe is chemically modified by the second, suggesting a competition strategy for an essential micronutrient. Third, from a biotechnological perspective, substrate solubilization resembles a fed-batch strategy that minimizes carbon catabolite repression during secondary metabolite production. Overall, this platform advances our understanding of microbial interactions and culture conditions that can be transferred to other culture platforms of relevance in bioprocess intensification.

works.title: Hydrogen production and fermentation in heliobacteria
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Heliobacteria are the only phototrophic members of the gram-positive bacteria. Heliomicrobium modesticaldum can grow chemotrophically in the dark using pyruvate as a carbon source. It can grow phototrophically only on acetate (plus CO 2 ). We found that dihydrogen production occurred only when fixing N 2 and increased ~5-fold upon replacing N 2 with argon. Introduction of genes encoding a [FeFe] hydrogenase and maturases ( hydAEFG ) from Acetivibrio thermocellus conferred the ability to produce H 2 at much higher levels. The modified cells made the most H 2 when grown chemotrophically, less when grown mixotrophically, and none when grown phototrophically, suggesting that only excess electrons were available for H 2 production. We tested several molecules as potential reduced fermentation products by this species. Only propanoate was observed, and its extracellular concentration could reach several millimolar. There was an inverse correlation between light intensity and propanoate production when the cells were grown on pyruvate, and phototrophic cultures produced no detectable propanoate. We conclude that propanoate is the major reduced fermentation product made by Hmb. modesticaldum, and we propose a pathway to produce it that is essentially a mini-cycle within the reductive TCA (rTCA) cycle, combining the first four reactions of the rTCA cycle with methylmalonyl-CoA mutase and epimerase, and methylmalonyl-CoA:pyruvate carboxytransferase. This pathway would, in effect, dispose of four reducing equivalents while driving the conversion of pyruvate to propanoate. The genes for the last six enzymes of this pathway seem to be part of an operon; the genes and potential operon are conserved in other heliobacteria, suggesting that this pathway exists in all or most heliobacteria. IMPORTANCE This study establishes that heliobacteria, the only phototrophic members of the Bacillota , produce propanoic acid as the reduced fermentation product when growing chemotrophically. The pathway used to make it resembles that of the Propionibacteria , except in the context of a mini-cycle within the reductive TCA (rTCA) cycle. This work confirms that the Heliomicrobium genus lacks a functional hydrogenase to make hydrogen as a way to dispose of excess electrons. Finally, it is shown that these organisms can be engineered to make dihydrogen as a reduced fermentation product if the genes for a clostridial hydrogenase and assembly proteins are expressed in Heliomicrobium modesticaldum .

works.title: Yellow fever virus infection triggers the assembly of compositionally unique and specialised stress granules
works.abstract: The phase separation of biomolecules into stress granules (SGs) allows the cell to tightly regulate translation activity in response to different stimuli, such as oxidative stress, starvation, or the recognition of non-cellular RNA. Recent reports suggest SGs induced during viral infection may act as a crossroad between the cellular stress response and the activation of the innate immune response. Here, we aimed to dissect the role of SGs in the context of yellow fever virus (YFV) infection. We found that YFV infection with both 17D vaccine and Asibi pathogenic strains resulted in translational shut-off and the formation of SGs at 48 hours post infection (hpi), although viral infection was already apparent at 24 hpi. This delay may be coupled to the ability of the YFV capsid to inhibit SG formation through an interaction with the SG scaffolding protein G3BP1. To elucidate the role of YFV-induced SGs during infection, we inhibited SG assembly using a small-molecule inhibitor as well as siRNA-mediated knockdown of SGs and found that while SG formation does not impact viral replication, silencing of SG scaffolding proteins is associated with increased expression of interferon-stimulated genes (ISG). Uncovering the proteome of YFV-induced SGs, our compositional analysis revealed a unique composition, distinct from NaAs-induced SGs, which displayed enrichment in mitochondrial proteins. Further functional analysis revealed that YFV infection is associated with mitochondrial damage and dysfunction, which coincides with formation of virus-induced SGs. Together, we propose that YFV-induced SGs may be involved not only in the modulation of cellular homeostasis but also in influencing mitochondrial functions.

works.title: Chandipura virus after recurrent outbreaks in India: Five questions that matter for preparedness
The underappreciated role for phase variation and quasi-clonality in microbial populations
works.abstract: Phase variation is a well-established phenomenon in some bacteria, where it generates heritable phenotypic variants within a population. These states, while reversible, are stable across generations, giving rise to quasi-clonal populations even when starting from a single bacterium. Underlying mechanisms include variation in short homopolymeric or heteropolymeric sequence repeats, DNA inversions mediated by site-specific recombination, reversible insertions and deletions, and switching between alternative methylation states. Although phase variation occurs in diverse bacteria, its contribution to phenotypic heterogeneity remains overlooked and use of the term is often absent in describing this phenomenon.

works.title: Suramin inspires next-generation broad-spectrum antiviral design targeting RdRps
works.abstract: Structural studies of diverse viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerases reveal that the broad-spectrum antiviral Suramin binds distinct sites while repeatedly exploiting conserved RNA-interacting and electrostatic features. This Pearl highlights common vulnerabilities within viral RNA polymerases and discusses how structural studies provide a framework for future antiviral design.

works.title: The contextual pathogenicity of Porphyromonas gingivalis
On the trail of novel bacteria: time to scale up the species description process
Antarctic intertidal sediments are overlooked hotspots of dimethyl sulfide production associated with Granulosicoccus-containing microbial communities
works.abstract: Dimethyl sulfide (DMS) is a volatile organosulfur compound that contributes to global climate regulation through its role in atmospheric aerosol formation. The Southern Ocean is an important source of DMS and represents a key region for marine sulfur cycling. However, previous studies have primarily focused on pelagic ecosystems, and the microbial drivers of DMS cycling in Antarctic coastal sediments remain poorly understood. Here, we integrated 16S and 18S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing, metagenomics, and DMSP-amendment incubation to characterize the DMS cycling in intertidal sediments of the climate-sensitive Fildes Peninsula. Our results revealed notable potential for DMS production via the DMSP cleavage pathway, in contrast to the demethylation-dominated pelagic ocean. Furthermore, the incubation experiments confirmed rapid DMS generation upon the addition of DMSP. Granulosicoccus , Ilumatobacter , and Cocleimonas were the potential drivers of DMS cycling, with genomic reconstruction demonstrating their roles in the biogeochemical cycles of sulfur and nitrogen. Our findings identify Antarctic intertidal sediments as potential hotspots of DMS production mediated by the DMSP cleavage pathway and Granulosicoccus -dominated microbial communities, necessitating their inclusion in polar biogeochemical models under climate change. Video Abstract

works.title: Viromic and metagenomic analyses reveal distribution and dissemination of antibiotic resistance genes in anaerobic digestion-composting systems: roles of quorum sensing and viruses
works.abstract: Under the “One Health” framework, untreated livestock waste serves as a critical vector for the cross-domain proliferation of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs). While integrated anaerobic digestion-composting systems are increasingly adopted for agricultural waste treatment, the dynamic succession of ARGs and the regulatory roles of quorum sensing (QS) and viral communities during the drastic environmental transitions remain critically unexplored. We applied comprehensive viromic and metagenomic analyses to track the dynamic fate of ARGs, ARB (antibiotic resistance bacteria), QS, and viral communities across a single campaign of full-scale anaerobic digestion-composting system treating cattle slurry. The relative abundance of total ARG (RPKG) was higher in cattle slurry digestate than in raw cattle slurry and lower in mature compost than in compost feedstock. The relative abundance of VFG-carrying contigs (RPKM) was also lower in mature compost than in compost feedstock. However, specific high-risk ARGs, notably aac(3)-VIIa and sul1 , exhibited extreme recalcitrance. At the maturation stage, we revealed that thermotolerant taxa, predominantly Bacillota and Actinomycetota, dominated the ultimate high-risk ARB. Crucially, the carriage of specific QS regulatory genes ( LuxR and DGC ) within ultimate high-risk ARB exhibited a highly significant positive correlation ( R 2 > 0.82, P < 0.001) with ARG and virulence factor gene (VFG) abundances. Furthermore, while lytic phages dominated the viral community, the thermophilic stage coincided with a marked decoupling of phage and ARB-host abundance trajectories, consistent with reduced viral abundance under thermal stress. Within this campaign, mean ARG abundance (RPKG) was higher in cattle slurry digestate than in raw cattle slurry. Mean ARG and VFG abundances (RPKG) were lower in mature compost than in compost feedstock. Nevertheless, aac(3)-VIIa , sul1 , and tet(M) , together with ARG-carrying MAGs affiliated with Bacillota and Actinomycetota, remained detectable in mature compost. QS ( luxR and DGC ) is associated mainly with persistence and potential horizontal gene transfer, whereas phages act chiefly as ecological predators and rarely carry ARGs, so that resistant-bacteria persistence coincided with weaker virus–host coupling at high temperature, rather than providing evidence for transduction. These observations suggest biologically targeted interventions (e.g., QS inhibitors or sequential phage inoculation) as candidate strategies whose feasibility and efficacy remain to be tested across different feedstocks, seasons, and full-scale operating conditions before any general management recommendation can be made. works.title: Raman spectra identify vancomycin-resistant phenotypes and their transcriptomic features in Staphylococcus aureus
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Staphylococcus aureus is a pathogenic bacterium that has been linked to multiple epidemics of novel antibiotic resistance. Vancomycin is the first-line antibiotic treatment for methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA) infections; however, various vancomycin-non-susceptible MRSA strains have emerged globally. Rapid assessment of the resistance levels and the underlying molecular profiles is crucial for preventing their spread and for counteracting resistance. Nevertheless, a broad resistance spectrum and diverse genetic alterations have hindered these efforts. Here, we demonstrated that vancomycin resistance levels of various MRSA strains can be determined using dimension-reduced Raman spectra obtained from single cells. Furthermore, transcriptome profiles of different strains can be predicted from these spectra using simple linear regression. This Raman-transcriptome correspondence enables mapping of transcriptomic components onto a dimension-reduced Raman space, allowing for characterization of gene groups associated with different phenotypes. Additionally, single-cell Raman spectroscopy has successfully identified a strain with higher phenotypic heterogeneity, which was subsequently validated by single-cell growth analysis. Overall, our results demonstrate the efficacy of Raman spectroscopy for identifying resistant phenotypes, their associated features for gene expression, and intrapopulation phenotypic heterogeneity. IMPORTANCE The spread of antibiotic-resistant bacteria threatens human health worldwide. Rapid identification of antibiotic resistance and molecular-level features of an infected pathogen is crucial for treating patients and counteracting the emergence and spread of new resistant bacteria. Here, we demonstrate that Raman spectra, measurable by exposing individual cells to a focused laser, can be used to infer the resistance phenotypes and global gene expression profiles of different Staphylococcus aureus strains. Furthermore, we present a method to visualize transcriptome components using the major axes of the dimension-reduced Raman space linked to important phenotypic features, such as resistance and virulence. This method identifies several gene sets related to crucial phenotypic features of pathogenic bacteria. Our results demonstrate a novel application of spectroscopy in microbiology by enabling the simultaneous identification of resistant and virulent phenotypes, as well as the underlying gene expression features.

works.title: The Story behind the Science: ATCC at 100 years
works.abstract: In 2025, ATCC celebrated its 100th anniversary, a longevity achieved by only a few organizations, and not too many individuals. During that century, ATCC grew from a small, donor-dependent collection of fewer than 200 microorganisms into the independent global biological resource center it is today. ATCC would not have been created and likely not have survived its early years without the involvement of ASM, the parent organization of ATCC. The scientists who founded ATCC, and those who followed, recognized the value of ATCC through its provision of reference standards as the essential tools and reagents required for the replication of experimental results. In this publication, we recognize ASM's key role in the formal establishment of ATCC in 1925 and its sustained support of ATCC's continuity. We begin with ATCC's founding and early development, followed by the struggle to establish and maintain ATCC's physical independence, and conclude with key aspects of ATCC's global activities.

works.title: HIV-1 subtype C: ecological fitness for efficient spread?
works.abstract: HIV-1 subtype C accounts for nearly half of global HIV infections and dominates in southern Africa, India, and parts of Asia. The global distribution and burden of subtype C may reflect founder effects, population size and structure, migration, transmission networks, epidemic history, and access to prevention and treatment, as well as efficient transmission fitness. The epidemiological success of clade C viruses seems at odds with conventional measurements of viral fitness. Several studies have reported that subtype C isolates exhibit reduced replication capacity compared to other clades of HIV-1 in activated peripheral blood mononuclear cells and blood-derived macrophages. These observations indicate that standard laboratory assays may not adequately capture the determinants of viral success in human populations. Here, we discuss the evidence that HIV-1 fitness may be ecological and dependent on the various changing cellular, anatomical, immunological, and epidemiological environments encountered during transmission and infection. Several characteristics of HIV-1 subtype C, including persistent CCR5 usage, CpG content, LTR promoter architecture, Tat function, and ongoing changes in regulatory and budding motifs, may influence transmission, replication, persistence, disease progression, and viral loads across distinct environments. Rather than representing a uniformly more or less fit lineage, subtype C may provide a model for understanding how ongoing adaptation to changing host environments may shape viral fitness and pandemic spread.

works.title: Metagenomic insights into the avian gut microbiome: novel viruses, antimicrobial resistance, and beyond
works.abstract: Birds play crucial roles in shaping ecosystems, and their gut microbiomes significantly influence host physiology and pathology. Understanding the composition, functions, and dynamics of avian gut microbiomes is therefore essential. Recent advances in metagenomic and metatranscriptomic sequencing have greatly increased our ability to characterize the avian gut microbiome. This review presents a systematic summary of the current knowledge regarding the composition of the avian gut microbiome as revealed through high-throughput sequencing technologies. It provides a statistical overview of the predominant bacterial and viral taxa present in the gut microbiomes of 195 bird species, revealing a persistent trend toward the discovery of novel viruses, and gives insight into the gene functions of these taxa. Interestingly, in terms of both antimicrobial resistance and multidrug resistance, wild birds harbor a greater diversity of resistance types than poultry. This review also presents a discussion of the relationships of avian life stages and the living conditions of birds with the gut microbiome and highlights practical applications of microbiome regulation in poultry production. Building on this foundation, future research priorities are outlined, such as the study of archaea, fungi, protists, and novel viruses, ways of improving methods to reduce costs and standardize protocols, and the development of more extensive metagenomic and metatranscriptomic data resources. Ultimately, these efforts could provide a holistic understanding of the avian gut microbiome.

works.title: Optimal regimens of praziquantel for schistosomiasis in young children
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Praziquantel (PZQ) is the drug of choice for control and treatment of schistosomiasis. Pharmacokinetic (PK) data for establishing a safe and effective PZQ dose in preschool-aged children are limited. We characterized PZQ pharmacokinetics in children aged 1–4 years with intestinal schistosomiasis. PZQ was administered at either 40 mg/kg or 80 mg/kg (split into two doses of 40 mg/kg, 3 h apart), and plasma concentrations were quantified. These data were pooled with pre-existing PK data from children aged 3–8 years, who received PZQ 40 mg/kg or 60 mg/kg. A population PK model was fitted to the pooled data, and individual drug exposure was estimated. Pharmacodynamic outcomes were egg reduction rate, and both parasitological and antigenic cure at 4 weeks post-treatment. The relationship between PZQ exposure and cure was established using regression analysis. Monte Carlo simulations were performed to assess the adequacy of weight-based PZQ dosing. A two-compartment model, with first-order absorption and elimination, best described PZQ disposition. Total body weight was allowed to influence clearance and the central compartment volume, with fixed allometric exponents 0.75 and 1, respectively. Simulations indicated that both weight-banded fixed-dose regimens and individual weight-based dosing achieved comparable drug exposures. The area under the concentration-time curve (AUC 0–24 ) of the total drug was a strong predictor of parasitological cure. PZQ 80 mg/kg achieved parasitological cure rates >85% but may still be insufficient for complete worm elimination, as demonstrated by the lower rate (69.5%) of antigen clearance. Further optimization of anti-schistosomiasis treatments may be required to achieve complete worm elimination in mass treatment programs. IMPORTANCE Schistosomiasis is a neglected tropical disease of significant global health concern, disproportionately affecting children in endemic areas. Praziquantel (PZQ) is the only drug currently recommended by the WHO, as a single 40 mg/kg dose for treatment of schistosomiasis. However, pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) data to support optimal dosing of PZQ for children <5 years are limited. In this study, we evaluated the PK/PD of PZQ, administered at 80 mg/kg (split into two doses of 40 mg/kg, 3 h apart), vs the standard 40 mg/kg regimen, in children aged 1–4 years. Our results indicate that PZQ exposure following 80 mg/kg achieves parasitological cure more effectively than the current standard 40 mg/kg single-dose regimen. In children with a heavy infection intensity, the 80 mg/kg dose may still be insufficient to achieve complete worm clearance. These results highlight the need for further optimization of PZQ regimens and the discovery and development of new antiparasitic agents.

works.title: The attachment rate of Vibrio anguillarum to microplastics strongly varies with strain identity, particle characteristics, and environmental conditions
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Microplastics (MPs), resulting from plastic objects and waste degradation, are increasingly abundant, particularly in marine environments. They exhibit a hydrophobic surface on which biofilms form easily. Metagenomic analyses of these biofilms have revealed that they often contain bacterial species potentially pathogenic to humans or animals. For this reason, MPs are suspected to present a risk to public health by acting as a vector for pathogenic bacterial species. To better understand this hazard, we studied different factors potentially affecting the bacterial attachment rate to MPs. Focusing on the fish pathogen Vibrio anguillarum , a collection of 16 GFP-labeled strains was assembled, including isolates from infected fish. Their attachment rates were measured using fluorescence microscopy on three types of MPs (milled polypropylene and polyethylene terephthalate particles, and commercially available polystyrene beads). A strong effect of the particle type was found, with higher attachment rates on milled particles, whose surface appeared qualitatively rougher based on visual examination of scanning electron microscopy images. Our results also revealed an intraspecific variation in attachment rate, highlighting the need for testing several strains of the same species to assess attachment rate and related hazards. Finally, it was observed that when a biofilm had formed by field incubation of the MPs, the differences in attachment rates between particle types were erased. The attachment of V. anguillarum depends on a combination of strain-related factors, particle characteristics, and environmental conditions, highlighting the need to combine microbiology, materials science, and environmental sciences to achieve a comprehensive risk assessment associated with MPs. IMPORTANCE Microplastics (MPs) are increasingly abundant, particularly in marine environments. They are suspected to present a risk to public health by acting as a vector for pathogenic bacterial species. Focusing on the fish pathogen Vibrio anguillarum , we measured the attachment rates of 16 strains on three types of microplastics (milled polypropylene and polyethylene terephthalate particles, and commercially available polystyrene beads). This study highlights a strong effect of the particle type, with higher attachment rates on irregular particles, as well as a strong intraspecific variation. In a second experiment, it was observed that when a natural marine biofilm had already formed on the microplastic particles, differences in attachment rates between particle types were erased. Our findings emphasize the importance of accounting for multiple factors when assessing the risks of MPs as carriers of pathogenic bacteria, with our study addressing the first step of the conceptual pathway linking attachment, persistence, transport, exposure, and ultimately infection.

works.title: An integrated cell culture–nanopore sequencing (ICC-NanoporeSeq) method for the simultaneous detection of multiple enterovirus types and quantification of infectious Enterovirus B
works.abstract: Enteroviruses (EVs) are ubiquitous contaminants of surface waters, where they can remain infectious for long periods of time. Most methods used for EV monitoring are unable to distinguish between infectious and non-infectious particles, or between EV types. Because different types exhibit both distinct environmental persistence and health implications, there is a need for type-resolved infectivity measurements. Here, we developed integrated cell culture-nanopore sequencing (ICC-NanoporeSeq), a method combining short-term cell culture amplification with nanopore sequencing of the VP1 gene. The ICC approach was adapted from a previously described ICC-reverse transcriptase quantitative PCR (ICC-RTqPCR) protocol, while the NanoporeSeq workflow was derived from a clinical EV typing protocol and optimized for environmentally circulating EV types. Using samples containing known concentrations of 10 EV types, the NanoporeSeq method accurately and reproducibly recovered the original proportions of all EV types after correction of biases. When applied to wastewater extracts, the method detected 45 EV types across five species. Furthermore, type-specific calibration curves generated with ICC-NanoporeSeq enabled quantification of the infectious concentrations of six EV types of the Enterovirus B species, allowing a simultaneous and type-resolved assessment of infectivity in mixed samples. Overall, ICC-NanoporeSeq provides a scalable approach for the parallel analysis of multiple EV types. Compared with the predecessor ICC-RTqPCR method, it eliminates the need for multiple type-specific PCR primers, and can therefore be readily expanded to include additional EV types.IMPORTANCECurrent methods used to detect enteroviruses (EVs) in environmental samples generally measure viral genome copies without determining whether viruses remain infectious, limiting their use in public health risk assessment or water quality monitoring. At the same time, available infectivity assays are often labor-intensive and cannot distinguish between different EV types. Here, we developed integrated cell culture-nanopore sequencing (ICC-NanoporeSeq), a method combining cell culture and nanopore sequencing to simultaneously quantify the infectious concentrations of multiple EV types in samples containing mixed EV populations. The method provides an efficient and scalable approach for studying EVs in complex environmental matrices. ICC-NanoporeSeq has potential applications in wastewater-based epidemiology, environmental surveillance, and disinfection studies, where understanding the persistence of different EV types simultaneously is crucial.

works.title: Cultivation of halophilic archaea in shallow subsurface Martian conditions has implications for extant life on Mars
works.abstract: ABSTRACT The present-day Martian surface is generally considered inhospitable to life because of low atmospheric pressure, intense surface radiation, global desiccation, and oxidizing chemistry, which has been increasing since the late Noachian. However, shallow Martian subsurface regions where mineralogy has shown groundwater movement may include localized hypersaline environments capable of retaining liquid water and supporting microbial metabolism. Haloferax volcanii , a model halophilic archaeon, has previously been shown to survive under low-pressure Martian conditions (24 mbar) and to grow anaerobically supported by the Mars-relevant oxyanions nitrate and perchlorate under high-salinity conditions. Here, we investigated whether H. volcanii could actively grow under a combination of environmental and chemical conditions relevant to potentially habitable shallow subsurface Martian lacustrine settings. Cultures were incubated for 160 days under anoxic, CO₂-enriched, low-pressure conditions (24 mbar) in hypersaline liquid media supplemented with nitrate or perchlorate. Growth was observed in all low-pressure treatments and was confirmed by increases in optical density and biological reduction of nitrate and perchlorate. Scanning electron microscopy revealed extensive biofilm formation in low-pressure cultures, and Raman spectroscopy demonstrated the persistence of carotenoid biosignatures after prolonged incubation under Martian conditions. Liquid loss remained below 4% across all treatments, indicating long-term stability of hypersaline brines throughout the experiment. These results demonstrate for the first time that a halophilic archaeon is capable of active growth and metabolism under a Mars-relevant combination of low pressure, high salinity, anoxia, and oxidizing chemistry, providing experimental support for the potential habitability of localized shallow subsurface Martian environments. IMPORTANCE The search for cellular life is a major objective of future Mars exploration. While many studies have examined whether microorganisms can survive under Martian conditions, far fewer have demonstrated active growth and metabolism. Here, we document Haloferax volcanii as the first halophilic archaeon capable of active growth under a defined combination of Mars-relevant low atmospheric pressure, high salinity, anoxia, and oxidizing chemical conditions. These findings expand the current understanding of the environmental limits of microbial growth and provide experimental evidence that localized brine environments in the shallow Martian subsurface could support active microbial metabolism if suitable organics and liquid water are present. These results are also relevant to planetary protection efforts, as they help constrain the potential for terrestrial halophilic microorganisms introduced during robotic or human exploration to persist and remain metabolically active in Martian environments. Furthermore, this study establishes a practical framework for cultivating halophilic microorganisms under low-pressure Martian conditions and may help guide future efforts to detect, cultivate, and characterize potential extant life on Mars.

works.title: A switch-rheostat circuit governs quorum sensing homeostasis in a phytopathogen
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Pseudomonas fuscovaginae , a wide-host-range plant pathogen of several cereal and grass species, possesses two canonical N -acyl homoserine lactone (AHL)-based quorum sensing (QS) systems called PfsI/R and PfvI/R, both of which are inactive under laboratory conditions but active in planta . The pfsI-pfsR intergenic region encodes RsaM, a putative protein that has since been hypothesized to act as a repressor switch of this QS circuit. In the present study, we demonstrate that the stringent repression exerted on the PfsI/R system depends entirely on the divergent promoter/intergenic pfsR-rsaM region rather than RsaM itself. Remarkably, this regulatory switch element stringently represses the expression of both the pfsR and rsaM genes. We further show for the first time that RsaM is endogenously expressed and functions as a negative regulator, modulating the PfsI/R circuit instead of preventing its activation. Taken together, our results evidence a unique two-tiered/hierarchical repression of a QS system, provided by a master repressor switch and a repressor modulator. IMPORTANCE Pseudomonas fuscovaginae is a globally occurring plant pathogen that employs N -acyl homoserine lactone (AHL)-based quorum sensing (QS) to regulate virulence. In this bacterium, QS signaling circuits display a rather unusual feature: the lack of activation at high cell densities under standard laboratory conditions. A hypothetical regulator named RsaM was previously linked to this phenomenon as a repressor switch acting on the PfsI/R AHL QS system in the absence of an unknown signal or stimulus. In this study, we show that a regulatory element within the pfsR - rsaM intergenic region acts as the primary switch of the PfsI/R QS system, independently of RsaM. Conversely, RsaM functions as a post-activation modulator that fine-tunes the QS response. This study advances our understanding of the regulatory configurations of unconventional QS systems by revealing a two-tier control mechanism in which a master regulatory switch governs circuit activation, while the previously uncharacterized protein RsaM controls signaling output once the system is engaged.

works.title: Correction for Lubin et al., “Characterization of chemotaxis in soybean symbiont Bradyrhizobium diazoefficiens ”
Harnessing phage defense systems to develop a Burkholderia bacterial host
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Heterologous production of metabolites and proteins requires the transfer of foreign DNA into a host. One common barrier to the genetic engineering of bacteria is their plethora of phage defense systems. Targeted deletion of defense system components can improve DNA transfer for downstream applications. We sought to improve the transformation efficiency of Burkholderia sp. FERM BP-3421, a β-proteobacterial host that has great potential for the high-titer production of bioactive small molecules. We investigated restriction-modification systems and the recently described Kiwa phage defense system. Through deletion of three restriction enzyme genes, transformation efficiency was improved nearly 7-fold. The electroporation protocol was also optimized with respect to temperature, cell density, and buffer composition, which resulted in an additional 40-fold improvement in transformation efficiency, reaching 1 × 10 6 CFU/µg plasmid DNA. Interestingly, a mimicry by methylation approach, where DNA is pre-methylated using two host DNA methyltransferases, outperformed the transformation efficiency obtained with restriction enzyme deletion mutants nearly 3-fold. Moreover, contrary to previous reports in Escherichia coli , deletion of the Kiwa system did not improve transformation efficiency into Burkholderia sp. FERM BP-3421. Understanding the impact of bacterial innate immune systems on genetic tractability is vital to improving non-model host strains to produce high-value molecules of interest. IMPORTANCE The ability to transfer DNA into bacteria is key to genetic engineering. However, bacteria have evolved immune defenses to recognize and protect themselves from foreign DNA, thwarting genetic manipulation. Here, we identified putative defense systems in a β-proteobacterial strain of interest and characterized their impact on DNA transfer. The defense systems studied belong to the well-known class of restriction-modification systems and to the recently described Kiwa system. Intriguingly, we observed higher DNA transfer efficiency by avoiding restriction-modification systems via pre-methylation rather than by restriction gene deletion. Future studies should investigate the underlying mechanism for this difference. Moreover, contrary to what was reported for γ-proteobacteria Escherichia coli , we showed that the Kiwa system does not impair DNA transfer into the β-proteobacteria Burkholderia sp. strain. There has been significant interest in the discovery of novel defense systems. Learning more about their complexity is important to enable genetic manipulation of previously intractable strains.

works.title: Novel electron transport powers archaeal methane metabolism across varied substrates and environments
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Methanogens are responsible for producing approximately one billion metric tons of methane each year within Earth’s anaerobic environments as a byproduct of their energy metabolism. They play a vital role in the global carbon cycle. There are three main pathways for methanogenesis: hydrogenotrophic, which uses H 2 and CO 2 to produce methane; methylotrophic, which utilizes methylated compounds like methanol and amines; and aceticlastic, which converts acetate into methane and CO 2 . Instead of substrate-level ATP production, methanogens conserve energy through a membrane-bound electron transport chain and flavin-based electron bifurcation (FBEB). Beyond the canonical modes of growth in methanogens, Methanosarcina acetivorans , a model acetotrophic methanogen, can conserve energy via direct interspecies electron transfer (DIET). Here, we review the metabolic pathways and electron transport processes involved in energy conservation during fermentative, respiratory, and DIET modes. Additionally, we discuss the role of FBEB in energy conservation in gut-associated Methanomassiliicoccus luminyensis . Finally, we discuss the potential roles of heterodisulfide reductase (Hdr) and the process of electron transfer during the reaction mechanism of electron-bifurcating HdrA2B2C2 complex in cytochrome-containing methanogens. Understanding the complex redox control mechanisms in these organisms has broader implications for sustainable energy and environmental management.

works.title: Sustainable 2-keto-L-gulonic acid biosynthesis via single-strain one-step fermentation
works.abstract: ABSTRACT L-ascorbic acid (vitamin C) is an essential antioxidant molecule that maintains normal physiological functions in humans. Currently, industrial production relies primarily on a three-strain, two-step fermentation process to produce 2-keto-L-gulonic acid (2-KLG), the direct precursor of vitamin C. 2-KLG is then converted to vitamin C through chemical lactonization. However, this process is limited by prolonged fermentation cycles, poor stability of the mixed-culture system, and complex process control. In recent years, engineered single-strain platforms capable of one-step 2-KLG biosynthesis have emerged as a promising strategy for more sustainable vitamin C production. Nevertheless, the efficiency of L-sorbose-to-2-KLG conversion in this system remains low, making it a major bottleneck to further improving 2-KLG production. This review summarizes recent advances on single-strain, one-step fermentation systems using Gluconobacter oxydans as the chassis strain. It focuses on strategies including genetic tool development, metabolic engineering, and key enzyme optimization. The review aims to provide a theoretical basis and technical reference for optimizing and industrializing green biomanufacturing systems for vitamin C.

works.title: Nitroxoline treatment of Balamuthia mandrillaris triggers genomic crisis, transcriptional collapse, and incomplete encystment via copper and iron chelation
works.abstract: Balamuthia mandrillaris is a free-living amoeba that can infect the central nervous system to cause granulomatous amebic encephalitis (GAE), a fatal disease with mortality rates up to 90%. GAE is typically treated with a six-drug regimen with limited efficacy and significant toxicity. Our lab previously identified nitroxoline, a quinolone antibiotic, as a promising therapeutic complement to the existing regimen, and in 2021 nitroxoline was first successfully used to treat a human patient. In this study, we elucidate nitroxoline’s mechanism of action using a combination of genomics, transcriptomics, chemical complementation, growth assays, and electron microscopy. In service of this goal, an annotated draft genome of B. mandrillaris strain CDC:V039 was generated using long read sequencing, yielding over 32,000 predicted protein coding sequences, the majority of which were present on telomere-to-telomere predicted chromosomal contigs. Leveraging this resource, comparative transcriptomics were used to characterize encystment responses to three different cellular stressors: nitroxoline, galactose, and hypoxia. Our findings reveal that nitroxoline-induced cysts undergo transcriptional collapse and genomic and structural destabilization via copper and iron chelation, and that preformed cysts are also disrupted by nitroxoline. These data provide insight into nitroxoline’s multifaceted impact on B. mandrillaris growth and cellular processes and advance our understanding of the transcriptional landscape associated with stress induced encystment. Our findings support the continued clinical study of nitroxoline as a complement to the existing regimen.

works.title: Unveiling the functional landscape of A-to-I RNA editing associated with Marek’s disease in chickens
works.abstract: Genetic improvement of disease resistance against viral infections represents a longstanding and formidable challenge in animal breeding. The antiviral innate immune response is highly regulated at the RNA level, especially through RNA modifications. Adenosine-to-Inosine (A-to-I) RNA editing modifies the mRNA sequence. Growing evidence shows that this type of RNA editing plays a key role in mediating cellular responses to viral infections and disease resistance. However, the role of RNA editing in cellular response to MD remains unclear. In this study, we examined A-to-I editing in CD4+ T cells during Marek's disease virus (MDV) infection. By comparing MD-resistant and susceptible chicken lines, we identified 642 A-to-I RNA editing events in CD4+ T cells, most of which were located within repeat elements, particularly in the CR1 family. We observed differences in RNA editing levels and counts between the two chicken lines with different infection statuses, indicating distinct editing patterns across genetic backgrounds and infection states. Additionally, ADAR (adenosine deaminases acting on RNA) expression was correlated with RNA editing frequency. We identified 21 RNA editing sites (RESs) associated with gene expression and 42, 14, and 38 RESs with predicted effects on amino acid sequences, alternative splicing, and miRNA-target binding, respectively. A comparative analysis revealed 131 group-specific RESs and 21 RESs shared across groups. Functional enrichment analysis of genes associated with group-specific RESs highlighted several terms related to MD resistance, including the MHC class I protein complex in non-infected MD-resistant birds. Significantly, we identified two L63-specific candidate RNA editing sites, chr6:26,600,122 in MXI1 and chr16:1,716,632 in MHCY57, which were predicted to affect gga-miR-1759-3p binding and amino acid sequence, respectively. Our findings reveal the landscape of A-to-I RNA editing in CD4 ⁺ T cells during MDV infection and provide new insights into its potential association with immune regulation and MD resistance.

works.title: Getting under your skin: The hidden dermal niche of trypanosomatid parasites
works.abstract: OverviewThe TriTryps—Trypanosoma brucei, Leishmania spp., and Trypanosoma cruzi—cause three major neglected diseases: Human African Trypanosomiasis (HAT), Leishmaniasis, and Chagas disease, respectively. A central challenge in the diagnosis and treatment of these diseases is their silent, often lifelong chronic phase. While our understanding of T. brucei and Leishmania has surged in recent years, knowledge gaps in T. cruzi research directly hinder our ability to reliably diagnose, treat, and monitor Chagas disease—which is endemic across the Americas and spreading globally.Most patients with Chagas disease show no symptoms for decades while the number of parasites in the blood (parasitaemia) drops to undetectable levels. While we know the parasite can sequester in heart and digestive tissues—leading to life-threatening complications in roughly one third of infected individuals—the full map of T. cruzi’s distribution in the host remains unclear, hampering diagnosis and treatment monitoring. If the parasite is not in the blood, how does its haematophagous (blood-feeding) insect vector continue to acquire and transmit infection? What other tissues might T. cruzi persist in during these silent decades?Recent breakthroughs in T. brucei and Leishmania suggest the answer is hiding in plain sight: the skin. Here, we evaluate the skin’s role as a critical parasite reservoir and hidden transmission interface, and propose a dermal-centric roadmap for future T. cruzi research. Shifting the paradigm from blood to skin could guide new avenues for the improved diagnosis, treatment and control of Chagas disease

works.title: A single-residue deletion in H9N2 hemagglutinin uncouples viral burden from disease severity
works.abstract: H9N2 avian influenza viruses are characterized by significant genetic diversity. Deletions within the hemagglutinin (HA) receptor-binding domain represent a notable, albeit rare, evolutionary trajectory. Here, we systematically characterized the multifaceted impact of a single-amino-acid deletion at residue 227 of HA (designated HAΔ227), a naturally occurring deletion within the 220-loop that overlaps a key antigenic epitope, using isogenic reverse genetics H9N2 viruses. Paradoxically, the HAΔ227 imposed a fitness cost and was associated with enhanced HA receptor-binding avidity, reduced apparent virion-associated NA activity, altered HA/NA functional balance, attenuated viral replication in vitro, and reduced respiratory shedding in vivo. Notably, despite this compromised replicative fitness, infection with the mutant virus was associated with an altered host immune response in chickens, characterized by elevated levels of interferon-γ (IFN-γ), interleukin-10 (IL-10), interleukin-1β (IL-1β), and monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1). These altered immune responses were associated with more severe pulmonary lesions, indicating a dissociation between disease severity and viral RNA load. Furthermore, the deletion increased the pH threshold for HA-mediated membrane fusion and substantially altered antigenic relationships. Collectively, our findings identify HA residue 227 as a functionally important site at which a single-residue deletion is associated with a phenotypic trade-off between replicative capacity and disease severity: reduced replicative fitness accompanied by altered inflammatory responses and greater tissue injury. This study highlights the potential phenotypic significance of a rare deletion in influenza virus HA and demonstrates that viral burden alone may not adequately predict disease severity.
