works.title: Global change reshapes marine microbial communities, functions and One Health outcomes
Engineering commensal Lachnospiraceae for programmable therapeutic delivery in the mouse gut
works.abstract: Engineered native gut bacteria could offer persistent, programmable therapeutic delivery in the gut, but many dominant taxa remain genetically intractable. Members of one such family of obligate anaerobic Clostridia, Lachnospiraceae, are prevalent in the human gut microbiome and produce metabolites linked to intestinal and metabolic health. Here we report a modular toolkit for engineering Lachnospiraceae, including constitutive and inducible expression, chromosomal integration and secretion systems. Applying this toolkit to gut native Coprococcus comes, we programmed the secretion of cytokine interleukin-22 (IL-22) in the mouse intestinal tract, where it induces epithelial defence transcriptional programmes. In a mouse model of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, IL-22-secreting C. comes improved glucose homeostasis, reduced systemic endotoxemia and attenuated hepatic steatosis. This work demonstrates that native Lachnospiraceae can be genetically programmed to modulate host metabolic and immune physiology. The toolkit provides a foundation for the development of Lachnospiraceae-derived engineered therapeutics and for dissecting causal relationships between commensal gene programmes and host physiology.

works.title: The microbial making and breaking of dimethylsulfoniopropionate and related compounds
Expanding arsenal of type III CRISPR-Cas antiviral defense
works.abstract: CRISPR-Cas systems are adaptive immune systems that protect prokaryotes from invading genetic elements through acquisition of foreign nucleic acid sequences and RNA-guided recognition of target molecules. Among the diverse CRISPR-Cas families, type III systems represent a highly complex and versatile branch that couples sequence-specific interference with nucleotide-based signaling and activation of diverse downstream immune responses. Recent discoveries have substantially expanded the functional diversity of type III CRISPR-Cas systems, revealing new subtypes, ancillary effectors, nucleotide second messengers, signal-degrading enzymes, and viral counter-defense strategies. Here, we summarize current mechanistic and structural insights into type III CRISPR-Cas biology, from adaptation and target recognition to immune signaling, ancillary effector-mediated responses, and defense regulation. We further discuss emerging biotechnological applications of type III systems and highlight key unanswered questions shaping future research in this rapidly evolving field.

works.title: Epigenetic and transcriptional control of sexual development in the multicellular Sordariomycete fungi
works.abstract: SUMMARY Many Sordariomycete fungi produce flask-shaped perithecia that encapsulate meiotic cells and facilitate dispersion of sexual spores. Perithecial development represents a striking example of complex multicellularity in fungi, requiring coordinated gene regulation through transcriptional, chromatin-based, and post-transcriptional mechanisms. This review summarizes recent work to dissect sexual development in several well-studied fungi: Neurospora crassa , Sordaria macrospora , Podospora anserina , and Fusarium graminearum . Studies with these fungi have uncovered interconnected regulatory mechanisms that coordinate fruiting body development. Transcription factor networks control differentiation of perithecial tissues and cell types. Chromatin regulators, such as histone chaperones, ATP-dependent chromatin remodelers, acetyltransferases, and Polycomb Repressive Complex 2, impact major developmental transitions. In addition, post-transcriptional mechanisms that operate during sexual development play critical regulatory roles. Recoding of the transcriptome by A-to-I mRNA editing is specific to perithecia and is essential for sexual development of N. crassa and F. graminearum . Finally, sex-specific genome defense pathways protect genome integrity and are essential for the completion of meiosis in some species. We summarize recent advances and highlight the remarkable regulatory complexity underlying fruiting body development in Sordariomycete fungi. In addition, we identify key open questions for future research.

works.title: More than the sum of its parts: reproductive addiction in the ecology and evolution of fungal-bacterial symbioses
works.abstract: SUMMARY Reproductive control exerted by endosymbionts over their hosts is an adaptation for maintaining host-symbiont associations across generations. This strategy is particularly well-characterized in endosymbiotic bacteria (EB) associated with arthropods, in which EB of disparate species have independently evolved diverse mechanisms to manipulate host reproduction, thereby ensuring their reliable transmission across host generations. Like arthropods, fungi in the phylum Mucoromycota commonly harbor ancient and highly coevolved EB that significantly affect fungal life histories, including reproduction. In particular, the symbiosis between the mucoromycete Rhizopus microsporus and its Mycetohabitans spp. endosymbionts is significantly contingent on reproductive addiction, as removal of the symbiont results in the loss or severe impairment of host asexual and sexual reproduction. Here, we synthesize the current knowledge on sexual reproduction in mucoromycete fungi and the Rhizopus microsporus–Mycetohabitans symbiosis. We highlight current gaps in the knowledge of mucoromycete reproduction as well as present novel hypotheses for studying these interactions based on the understanding of reproductive manipulation in arthropods.

works.title: RtmR is a membrane-embedded RRM family RNA-binding protein
works.abstract: ABSTRACT The animal symbiont Vibrio fischeri has served as a model organism for molecular processes underlying bacterial group behaviors, including quorum sensing, and biofilm development. Here, using a genetic approach to identify negative regulators of biofilm formation in V. fischeri , we identified a membrane-bound RNA-binding protein, RtmR (VF_2432), that acts as an inhibitor of the symbiosis polysaccharide (SYP) biofilm. Membrane localization of the protein seems to be required for protein stability or expression, as truncation of the transmembrane helices led to an inability to detect the protein. The conserved RNP1 and RNP2 motifs in RtmR’s cytoplasmic RNA recognition motif (RRM) domain are required for function, and we demonstrate binding to RNA substrates. Identification of RtmR RNA ligands was conducted with an individual-nucleotide resolution crosslinking and immunoprecipitation sequencing (iiCLIP-seq) approach that revealed a large interactome. One transcript identified was that of the biofilm regulatory histidine kinase RscS. We found that RtmR biofilm inhibition depends on RscS activity, and that RtmR negatively regulates levels of RscS. Overall, this work characterizes a novel type of bacterial RNA-binding protein. IMPORTANCE Bacterial RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) perform key functions to regulate stress responses and development. Bacterial RBPs, including the RNA chaperones Hfq and ProQ, the global regulator CsrA, and the cold shock proteins (Csps), have been extensively studied, although additional classes of RBPs have been predicted by bioinformatic methods, including those carrying an RNA recognition motif (RRM) domain. This work expands on recent studies of RRM domain proteins in bacteria to characterize a membrane-bound RRM protein that regulates bacterial biofilm development. Given our rapidly expanding knowledge regarding the role of RNA-binding proteins in bacterial molecular biology, this work contributes a new class of membrane-bound regulators with homologs in human pathogens and marine symbionts.

works.title: Phagocytosis of Acanthamoeba by macrophages and neutrophils and “kiss and run” evasion by Entamoeba histolytica
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Phagocytosis was discovered in the 19th century and is a cornerstone of innate immunity. Although amoebae species cause over 100 million cases of severe infections annually, one long-standing dogma remained unchallenged: that eukaryotic amoebae are too large to be phagocytosed. Here, we overturn this entrenched dogma and show that human macrophages and neutrophils efficiently phagocytose Acanthamoeba polyphaga and Vermamoeba vermiformis , in a phosphoinositide 3-kinase-dependent manner. In contrast, Entamoeba histolytica utilizes a “kiss and run” evasion strategy of phagocytosis. However, formalin-killed and UV-irradiated E. histolytica are efficiently phagocytosed. Macrophages respond to E. histolytica by formation of striking F-actin fibrillar projections, in contrast to the bona fide phagocytic cups that engulf killed E. histolytica , A. polyphaga , and V. vermiformis . Remarkably, neutrophils harboring phagocytosed amoebae are efferocytosed by macrophages. These findings redefine innate immunity to amoebae, the physical and biological limits of phagocytosis, and uncover divergent evolution among pathogenic amoebae to subvert phagocytosis. IMPORTANCE Eukaryotic amoebae have been presumed to be too large to be phagocytosed. We demonstrate that human macrophages and neutrophils can efficiently phagocytose diverse amoebae species, while Entamoeba histolytica evades phagocytosis, redefining innate immunity to amoebae and the physical limits of phagocytosis.

works.title: Monitoring single-cell metabolic phenotyping changes of Daqu microbiota during fermentation by Raman spectroscopy
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Monitoring microbial community dynamics during natural food fermentation is essential for stabilizing fermentation processes and improving product flavor profiles. This study employed single-cell Raman spectroscopy to monitor the metabolic change of Daqu microbiota during fermentation. First, we developed an operational phenotypic unit (OPU)-based clustering method to process Raman spectral data of a nine-member microbial community. The clustering was validated by sorting out representative single cells from different OPUs and performing 16S/ITS region sequencing. Second, single-cell Raman spectroscopy was applied to the mixed Daqu sample throughout fermentation, identifying 10 OPUs and 54 sub-OPUs. Single cells from different OPUs were sorted and sequenced to obtain taxonomic annotation, which were correlated with the Raman spectral characteristics of each OPU. The OPU-based Raman spectroscopy method was successfully used to monitor the single-cell metabolic phenotypes of Daqu microbiota during fermentation, and taxonomic annotations revealed the succession of microbial community structure. This study presents a novel approach for monitoring the dynamics of metabolic phenotypes within Daqu microbial communities, offering a data-driven decision-making approach for subsequent production operations in multi-species fermentation processes. IMPORTANCE Microbial communities play pivotal roles in diverse industrial processes, yet monitoring their metabolic dynamics remains challenging. Current omics approaches, including metagenomics, transcriptomics, and mass spectrometry-based metabolomics, fail to establish direct genotype-phenotype linkages at the single-cell level and often require destructive sampling. This study introduces operational phenotypic units (OPUs) as a novel framework to bridge this gap by integrating single-cell Raman spectroscopy with sequencing technologies. Our method enables non-destructive, rapid monitoring of metabolic phenotypes while preserving cells for downstream analysis. By applying this approach to solid-state Daqu fermentation, we demonstrate its capability to track microbial community succession and identify functionally distinct populations in real time. This data-driven strategy offers significant potential for optimizing multi-species fermentation processes across food, environmental, and biotechnological industries, providing a powerful tool for microbial community management and process control.

works.title: Antibiotic class shapes O-antigen-dependent phage outcomes in a clinical Pseudomonas aeruginosa isolate
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a high-priority opportunistic pathogen characterized by significant genetic plasticity and increasing multidrug resistance. Although phage–antibiotic combinations are increasingly explored to combat antimicrobial resistance, whether these interactions are synergistic or antagonistic and how different antibiotic classes influence phage replication and the subsequent development of resistance remain unclear. In this study, we examined combinations of the O-antigen-dependent phage phipa10 with amikacin (AMK), levofloxacin (LEV), or meropenem (MEM) against P. aeruginosa ZS-PA-35. At 24 h, the combinations showed antibiotic-dependent patterns of bacterial growth suppression. High concentrations of amikacin and meropenem reduced the extracellular yield of infectious phipa10. The highest tested levofloxacin concentration also reduced the recovered phage yield. Whole-genome sequencing of phage-resistant mutants showed that meropenem treatment drove large chromosomal deletions encompassing galU and hmgA , resulting in a characteristic brown pigmentation phenotype. LEV-selected isolates carried smaller deletions involving galU , whereas AMK-selected isolates shared a galU substitution. In a Galleria mellonella infection model, phipa10–antibiotic combinations improved host survival relative to either treatment alone, although the magnitude of the benefit varied across antibiotic classes. The meropenem combination yielded the highest observed survival proportion despite reduced phage yield in vitro . These results show that bacterial suppression, infectious phage yield, and resistance outcomes can diverge among the three tested antibiotic partners. IMPORTANCE Phage–antibiotic combinations may affect bacterial suppression, phage yield, and resistance-associated phenotypes differently. We compared three antibiotic partners in a single Pseudomonas aeruginosa –phage system. The observed growth, genetic, and larval survival outcomes varied across the tested treatments. Reduced phage yield did not preclude improved survival in the infection model. These observations support evaluating multiple outcomes when assessing a phage–antibiotic combination. Their broader relevance requires validation with additional isolates, phages, and antibiotics.

works.title: A heat-induced HagF-HrcA regulatory loop promotes chlamydial fitness and infectious progeny yield under stress
works.abstract: Bacterial survival under environmental stress requires precise regulation of protein homeostasis, yet how this is achieved in organisms with streamlined genomes remains incompletely understood. Here, we identify HagF as a previously unrecognized protein that antagonizes the conserved heat-inducible transcriptional repressor HrcA in Chlamydia. Using genetic and biochemical approaches, including overexpression and CRISPRi-mediated knockdown, we show that under non-stressed conditions, HrcA represses hagF along with its five known targets, including hrcA and four chaperone genes. Upon heat stress, HagF is induced and binds HrcA, attenuating its repressor activity. This negative feedback loop enhances chaperone gene induction, particularly from the hrcA-grpE-dnaK operon, and promotes infectious elementary body yield. Notably, HagF is conserved across members of the order Chlamydiales, highlighting a lineage-specific adaptation. Together, these findings define a regulatory circuit in which a specialized antagonist modulates a widely conserved repressor, enabling Chlamydia to couple heat-responsive gene expression with developmental progression and enhance fitness under restrictive conditions.

works.title: Modular design of Salmonella Typhimurium OMV-based nanovaccines for tunable dual-form polysaccharide antigen delivery
works.abstract: Bacterial diseases are primarily managed with antibiotics, but vaccination is widely acknowledged as the most efficacious strategy for their prevention. Bacterial polysaccharides serve as key protective antigens in hosts and are therefore consistently prioritized as targets for bacterial vaccine development. Polysaccharide-conjugated vaccines have emerged as a promising and effective approach to combat multidrug-resistant bacteria. In order to construct a vaccine carrier capable of delivering bacterial polysaccharides while inducing robust immune response, this study utilized outer membrane vesicles (OMVs) derived from Salmonella Typhimurium as the vaccine carrier instead of the traditional adjuvant components to enhance the immunogenicity of polysaccharide vaccine. S. Typhimurium was genetically engineered to enable the controlled synthesis of LPS and glycoprotein, which were encapsulated within OMVs as two distinct polysaccharide vaccine formulations. This engineered delivery system was used to deliver the O-antigen polysaccharide of Shigella flexneri 3a, and subsequent validation in a murine model further confirmed that its ability to elicit an effective in vivo immune response. The polysaccharide delivery carrier platform established in this study provides a foundation for the subsequent multi-form delivery of bacterial polysaccharides in next-generation biological vaccines.

works.title: DectiSomes as broad-spectrum antifungal drugs
works.abstract: are the primary causative agents for aspergillosis, candidiasis, cryptococcosis, and mucormycosis. They and their closest relatives are responsible for more than 94% of fungal disease-related deaths. All four fungal diseases may lead to meningitis, with mortality rates approaching 99%. They are among the WHO-designated priority fungal pathogens needing new and more effective treatments. In response to this therapeutic gap, we developed DectiSomes-drug-loaded liposomes targeted to fungal cells by host-pathogen receptors. Host-pathogen receptors have many advantages over antibodies as liposome-targeting proteins, including a lack of immunogenicity. Of the pathogen receptors we tested, Dectin-1 and Dectin-2 are the most effective targeting proteins against the fungal pathogens tested. Liposomes loaded with amphotericin B and coated with one of these pathogen receptors bind specifically and strongly to the four pathogens and kill them, reducing the effective dose of amphotericin B by more than an order of magnitude over the untargeted control. DectiSomes are also more effective in murine models of fungal infection. Furthermore, we developed small, malleable versions of DectiSomes with improved drug delivery to the brain and are more effective against cryptococcal meningitis, holding promise for treating all forms of fungal meningitis. Herein, we review our progress and discuss the potential of DectiSomes as a new and effective targeted delivery system for antifungal drugs. In addition, we discuss the challenges associated with fungal diseases and the roadblocks to antifungal drug development and medical mycology research.

works.title: Scaffold-level validation is needed for phage–host inference from metagenome-assembled genomes
works.abstract: Accurate phage-host prediction underpins ecological interpretation and experimental validation of uncultivated phages, yet most current approaches rely heavily on metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs). This reliance implicitly assumes that MAG-level quality metrics, such as completeness and contamination, ensure scaffold-level correctness. Here, we demonstrate that this assumption can be violated under particular challenging conditions. Tetranucleotide frequency (TNF) analyses reveal that CRISPR-associated regions often diverge compositionally from their host genomes, increasing the risk of misbinning, while experimentally validated phage-host genome pairs show consistent TNF separation between phages and their hosts, challenging compositional binning assumptions. Through controlled simulations, we further show that the incorporation of substantial amounts of TNF-matched, non-host phage sequences into high-quality MAGs does not substantially alter standard completeness and contamination estimates, rendering such errors largely undetectable. Together, these results expose a systematic and underappreciated source of bias in MAG-based phage-host inference and highlight the need for explicit scaffold-level validation beyond conventional genome-quality metrics. We further propose a practical scaffold-level validation framework that integrates structural linkage and taxonomic consistency to improve the reliability of phage-host inference from MAGs.

works.title: Deletion of the Envelope gene attenuates SARS-CoV-2 infection by altered spike localization and increased cell-to-cell transmission
works.abstract: Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) causes COVID-19, a highly transmissible acute respiratory infection that can result in severe pneumonia and death. Many details of SARS-CoV-2 infection are not fully understood, including the cell biology and host-virus interactions involved in coronavirus assembly and release, in which the Envelope (E) structural protein is instrumental. Deletion of E in other coronaviruses has been shown previously to either attenuate or abrogate infection. To determine the role of E in SARS-CoV-2 virus production and infectivity, we produced a reporter SARS-CoV-2 with or without the E gene deleted using a bacterial artificial chromosome. Replication of ΔE SARS-CoV-2 was attenuated in Vero E6 cells expressing human ACE2 and TMPRSS2 and in human epithelial cell lines. Electron and immunofluorescence microscopy and virology assays showed that ΔE SARS-CoV-2 increased cell surface expression of Spike (S) glycoprotein, leading to reduced S incorporation into ΔE SARS-CoV-2 particles and promotion of increased cell-to-cell transmission that evades neutralizing antibody inhibition. Trans-complementation of E partially rescued ΔE SARS-CoV-2 S incorporation and restored cell-free transmission. In addition to validating the role of E in retention of S in the ER-Golgi intermediate complex (ERGIC), our results showed that a lack of E led to reorganization of the ERGIC and Golgi during SARS-CoV-2 infection. Improved understanding of E in SARS-CoV-2 replication and host pathogenesis may help the development of novel therapeutics.IMPORTANCENon-Spike coronavirus structural proteins, including Envelope, are conserved, making them potential pan-coronavirus therapeutic targets. Many details about these proteins and their roles in viral replication and host pathogenesis are unknown. In this study, we showed that severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) replicates without Envelope but is attenuated and impaired in virus particle formation, with less Spike incorporated into virions and more Spike expressed on the cell surface compared to wild-type virus. SARS-CoV-2 lacking Envelope transmitted primarily via cell fusion and evaded neutralizing antibodies. In addition, the absence of Envelope resulted in the reorganization of the cell secretory compartment during SARS-CoV-2 infection. A better understanding of how Envelope influences SARS-CoV-2 replication could guide directed design of novel therapeutics for treatment of COVID-19 patients, as well as the potential for pan-coronavirus protection against future coronavirus outbreaks.

works.title: Interaction mechanisms of core dominant fungi during fermentation of Massa Medicata Fermentata: volatile compounds of Saccharomycopsis fibuligera inhibit the growth of Rhizopus oryzae
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Massa Medicata Fermentata (MMF) is a traditional fermented medicine whose quality is governed by complex microbial interactions. This study investigated the antagonistic effect of the core yeast Saccharomycopsis fibuligera against the filamentous fungus Rhizopus oryzae and its underlying mechanisms. In vitro co-culture assays demonstrated that S. fibuligera suppressed R. oryzae growth and amylase activity in a cell-density-dependent manner, with significant inhibition observed at cell densities of ≥1 × 10⁷ cells·mL⁻¹. The antagonism was driven by two putative pathways: direct spatial/nutritional competition and indirect suppression mediated by yeast-secreted volatile organic compounds (VOCs). HS-SPME-GC-MS analysis identified six major VOCs, primarily fatty acid ethyl esters and 2-phenylethanol, with the latter being the most abundant (0.5664 ± 0.0422 µg·g⁻¹ medium). Single-compound antifungal assays confirmed that isoamyl acetate, ethyl hexanoate, and 2-phenylethanol completely inhibited the growth of R. oryzae at elevated doses. Mechanistic investigations via SEM, PI staining, and biochemical assays revealed that these VOCs induce cell death by disrupting mycelial morphology, compromising membrane integrity, inhibiting ergosterol biosynthesis, and triggering lipid peroxidation. These findings elucidate a key antagonistic interaction between core functional fungi during MMF fermentation, providing a theoretical basis for targeted fermentation regulation and industrial standardization of this traditional herbal medicine. IMPORTANCE By revealing the cell-density-dependent dual-mode antagonism between S. fibuligera and R. oryzae , this study deepens our understanding of microbial interactions in traditional fermentation. The discovery of specific inhibitory VOCs and their membrane-disrupting mechanisms provides a theoretical basis for targeted process regulation. These insights are crucial for achieving precise fermentation control, which is essential for improving product consistency, reducing batch-to-batch variability, and advancing the traditional fermentation standardization of herbal medicines.

works.title: A Plasmodium knowlesi A1-H.1 transcriptome time course focusing on the late asexual blood stages
works.abstract: The zoonotic parasite Plasmodium knowlesi is closely related to Plasmodium vivax, the second leading cause of human malaria. P. knowlesi line A1-H.1 can be maintained in human erythrocytes and is an experimental model for P. vivax biology. We present the first transcriptome time course of the intraerythrocytic developmental cycle (IDC) of P. knowlesi A1-H.1 grown in human normocytes. Bulk RNA-sequencing was performed at five IDC stages using tightly synchronised cultures, enabling identification of constitutively expressed genes and stage-specific biomarkers, and investigation of temporal expression patterns of multigene families. Comparative analysis with P. vivax orthologues revealed strong genome-wide conservation of temporal expression. Analysis of invasion-associated genes and ApiAP2 transcription factors identified genes with conserved expression patterns for which P. knowlesi is likely a good model to study the P. vivax gene. To support comparative analyses, we developed an open-access interactive webtool to explore and visualise P. knowlesi - P. vivax - P. falciparum orthologue expression across the IDC (https://interactive.itg.be/app/pk-orthologue-expression-viewer). This time course dataset provides a reference transcriptome framework for P. knowlesi A1-H.1 and a resource for comparative Plasmodium biology. The interactive webtool facilitates rapid identification of candidate genes with conserved temporal expression, streamlining functional studies in which P. knowlesi A1-H.1 serves as a model for P. vivax.

works.title: One ring to rule: Cytokinesis in model and pathogenic fungi
Modulation of riboflavin biosynthesis enzymes in non-typhoidal Salmonella isolates differentially impacts human MAIT cell activation
works.abstract: Invasive non-typhoidal Salmonella (iNTS) sequence type 313 (ST313) isolates have emerged in sub-Saharan Africa, with a high incidence of multidrug resistance, enhanced intracellular persistence, increased dissemination and immune evasion. ST313 isolate D23580 was shown to avoid activation of mucosal-associated invariant T (MAIT) cells compared with a genetically similar, non-invasive Salmonella Typhimurium (S.Tm) 4/74 strain, but the mechanism remains unclear. Here, we studied immune responses to infection with typhoidal strains and ST313 isolates using comparative transcriptomic profiling of human peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs). MAIT cells responded to typhoidal strains but not to D23580. To uncover underlying mechanisms, we engineered an inducible CRISPRi system targeting riboflavin biosynthesis enzymes (rib), which process MAIT ligands, in D23580 and 4/74 strains. Several rib hypomorphs exhibited prolonged lag time in minimal media, which was more pronounced in D23580 than in 4/74. In PBMC infection, knockdown of lumazine synthase (RibH) and riboflavin synthase (RibE) resulted in contrasting MAIT cell activation phenotypes. RibH knockdown restored MAIT cell activation in D23580 but did not affect activation in 4/74. Conversely, RibE knockdown diminished MAIT cell activation by 4/74 but had no impact on MAIT cell activation by D23580. Metabolomic analysis revealed accumulation of the biosynthetic intermediate DMRL in RibE knockdown and a differential impact on riboflavin biosynthesis end products between D23580 and 4/74 RibH knockdown, suggesting altered pathway flux between the strains. Our results indicate RibH and RibE as pivotal nodes for strain-specific MAIT-activation during Salmonella infection of human PBMCs, illustrating teir central role in the complex interplay between bacterial metabolism and host immunity.

works.title: Pathogenicity and zoonotic potential of a novel pdm09-lineage H1N2 swine influenza A virus spatiotemporally linked to transboundary pig trade
works.abstract: International swine trade can disseminate influenza A viruses across borders, creating opportunities for reassortment with endemic swine viruses and the emergence of novel strains with zoonotic potential. Here, we characterize a novel H1N2 reassortant, A/swine/Korea/1030-3/2023 (1030-3), detected in South Korea and spatiotemporally associated with European swine lineages and international pig movement. 1030-3 harbors seven gene segments (PB2, PB1, PA, HA, NP, M and NS) closely related to a recent Danish zoonotic H1N1 virus of the 2009 pandemic (pdm09) lineage, and an N2 segment derived from an endemic Korean HxN2. In vitro assays demonstrated that 1030-3 preferentially bound human-type α2,6-linked sialic acid receptors and replicated efficiently in polarized human airway epithelial cells, although these properties were also observed in the endemic Korean H1N2 comparator 1027-1. In mice, 1030-3 caused moderate clinical signs and respiratory replication comparable to an early pdm09 reference strain NL09. In guinea pigs, 1030-3 transmitted to a subset of direct-contact animals but showed no detectable aerosol transmission under the conditions tested. In pigs, the natural host, 1030-3 replicated efficiently and transmitted to all direct-contact animals, with high respiratory shedding and a greater cumulative shedding burden in contact pigs than NL09. Contemporary human sera showed reduced neutralizing activity against 1030-3 relative to both human seasonal H1N1 and 1027-1, while antiserum against a recent H1N1 vaccine antigen also neutralized 1030-3 less efficiently. These findings identify a European-associated H1N2 swine influenza reassortant detected in South Korea that combines a distinct pdm09-derived genomic and antigenic background with efficient replication and transmission in pigs, α2,6-linked receptor preference, and reduced neutralization by human sera, underscoring the need for trade-aware surveillance of swIAVs and continued monitoring at the swine-human interface.

works.title: Predicting responses to prebiotic fibres: linking microbiota, function and clinical outcomes
Metabolic specialization in the gut microbiome of aquatic mammalian herbivores
works.abstract: Sirenians, such as manatees, are the only extant mammals fully adapted to aquatic herbivory. Through specialized hindgut fermentation, they play a role in modulating nutrient fluxes and carbon cycling across tropical coastal and riverine ecosystems. However, our understanding of their gut microbiome and its metabolic potential remains elusive. Here we present an ultradeep genomic atlas of the gut microbiome from 47 freshwater and marine manatees spanning distinct developmental stages, comprising 1,215 non-redundant prokaryotic metagenome-assembled genomes and their associated virome. The manatee microbiome encodes a multilayered enzymatic repertoire for plant cell wall deconstruction, including free enzymes, cellulosomes and CAZyme-enriched outer membrane vesicles, alongside diverse pathways for aromatic catabolism. Combining biochemical and structural approaches, we characterize a previously unrecognized enzymatic pathway involving epilactase, which enables a specific Bacillota species to exploit a carbohydrate inaccessible to most microbial life, defining a specialized biochemical strategy for nutrient niche partitioning. Together, these findings uncover the microbial and metabolic basis of aquatic mammalian herbivory.

works.title: Translational plant microbiome research takes root
Borrelia burgdorferi binds serum amyloid A and modulates subcutaneous adipose tissue immune signaling
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Following a tick bite, Borrelia burgdorferi spirochetes replicate in human skin and disseminate through tissues, including subcutaneous adipose tissue. Adipose is a complex organ containing both immune and non-immune cells that play a significant role in the immune response, yet little is known about adipose-specific immune signaling after B. burgdorferi infection. We investigated the landscape of immune signaling within adipose tissue-resident cells during B. burgdorferi infection in human tissue (skin and adipose tissue) ex vivo . Single-cell sequencing pathway analysis revealed upregulation of inflammatory pathways in skin, yet overall downregulation of immune pathways in adipose tissue cells during B. burgdorferi infection. Adipose-resident myeloid cells and adipose stem/progenitor cells (ASPCs) displayed an inflammatory profile characterized by the increased expression of IL-1β, TNF, and NFKB1. CellChat, a cellular communication comparative analysis, showed increased cell-to-cell communication across adipose-resident cell populations. ASPCs demonstrated the strongest outgoing signals, positioning them as key hubs of intercellular communication in adipose tissue. Interestingly, we observed adipose-specific downregulation of serum amyloid A (SAA), an inflammatory serum marker known to have antimicrobial properties and typically elevated in Lyme disease patients during acute infection. Therefore, we further evaluated the interaction between SAA and B. burgdorferi . Here, we show that human recombinant SAA protein directly binds B. burgdorferi spirochetes, reduces spirochete viability in a dose-dependent manner in vitro, and enhances phagocytosis. Taken together, these findings show that adipose tissue is a site of active immune signaling in the setting of infection and identify SAA as a host defense factor against B. burgdorferi . IMPORTANCE Borrelia burgdorferi is the bacterium that is transmitted by ticks and causes Lyme disease. These bacteria replicate in the skin to cause the localized skin rash erythema migrans, then disseminate to cause symptoms in other organs, including the joints and heart. Adipose tissue, or fat, is adjacent to skin, joints, and heart—all target organs of infection. In this study, we set out to understand how adipose tissue/fat plays a role in Lyme disease. We discovered that B. burgdorferi infection leads to an immune response in adipose tissue cells with specific downregulation of a gene called serum amyloid A (SAA). Our work shows that B. burgdorferi bacteria bind serum amyloid A (SAA), leading to decreased viability in vitro and enhanced uptake of B. burgdorferi by white blood cells. These findings highlight the dynamic role our fat can play during B. burgdorferi infection and can lead to the identification of new treatments for Lyme disease.

works.title: Structural characterization of a pseudaminic acid-modified lateral flagellar filament from Vibrio alginolyticus
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Bacterial flagellar filaments are often modified by glycans, but the structural basis and physiological significance of flagellin glycosylation remain poorly understood in many species. Vibrio alginolyticus produces lateral flagella for surface-associated motility in viscous environments, with LafA forming its filament as flagellin. A maf homolog encoding a putative flagellin glycosylation factor is located immediately downstream of lafA , suggesting that the lateral filament is glycosylated. To investigate this possibility, we purified the lateral flagellar filament from V. alginolyticus and determined the structure at 2.4 Å resolution by electron cryomicroscopy. Upon model building of LafA in the map, we identified additional densities connected to five serine residues, possibly corresponding to O-linked pseudaminic acid modifications. Mass spectrometric analyses identified these modifications as pseudaminic acid attached to Ser148, Ser173, Ser183, Ser189, and Ser197. Deletion of maf abolished lateral flagella formation and motility, and these defects were restored by complementation with maf . These results demonstrate that the Vibrio lateral flagellar filament is extensively modified by pseudaminic acid and that Maf is required for filament formation. Our findings provide the first structural insight into the glycosylation of the Vibrio lateral flagellar filament and establish a framework for understanding the role of flagellin glycosylation in surface-associated motility. IMPORTANCE A gene encoding a putative flagellin glycosylation factor (Maf) is located immediately downstream of lafA , the gene encoding lateral flagellin of Vibrio alginolyticus , suggesting that the lateral flagellar filament is glycosylated. Guided by this assumption, we determined the structure of the lateral flagellar filament by electron cryomicroscopy with mass spectrometry and identified five pseudaminic acid modifications on the filament surface. Genetic analyses further demonstrated that Maf is required for lateral flagellar formation and motility. These results provide the first structural characterization of a glycosylated Vibrio lateral flagellar filament and reveal a close link between flagellin glycosylation and motility organelle assembly.

works.title: Microbial metabolism of methotrexate produces a STAT3 signaling molecule that alleviates gut inflammation
works.abstract: Methotrexate (MTX) is a gold standard therapy for inflammatory diseases but has mixed therapeutic success in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). The gut microbiota impact MTX efficacy and toxicity by metabolizing MTX and altering its bioavailability, yet how inflammation alters this metabolism, and how the resulting metabolites act on the host, remain poorly understood. Here, we find that gut microbes, notably Clostridium asparagiforme, metabolize MTX via carboxypeptidase G2 (CPDG2) to produce deoxyaminopteroic acid (DAMPA). In intestinal epithelial cells, DAMPA preserves mitochondrial health through mitochondrial signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3) signaling and enhances mitophagy. DAMPA administration attenuates intestinal inflammation in vivo, and remodels colonic mitochondrial pathways. IBD mouse models show reduced microbial CPDG2 and DAMPA, while patients with IBD show reduced CPDG2 gene abundance and suppressed DAMPA-enriched mitochondrial pathways, potentially explaining MTX outcomes in IBD. Together, these findings reframe microbial MTX metabolism from passive drug detoxification to active regulation of host mitochondrial and inflammatory homeostasis.

works.title: Degradation of mucin O-glycans by a human gut symbiont requires a complex enzyme repertoire and promotes colonization
works.abstract: Summary Secreted mucins are the major component of the mucus layer that protects intestinal epithelial surfaces by blocking excessive interactions with the microbiota. Mucins are complex glycoproteins decorated with over 100 different O -glycans. Some bacteria can utilize mucins and excessive degradation has been associated with disruption of the mucus barrier and inflammation. Despite the importance of mucins, a detailed enzymatic pathway by which gut bacteria degrade colonic mucin O -glycans and the impact of this process on gut colonization are unknown. Here, we identified >100 genes that are expressed by the symbiont Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron during growth on different O -glycan substrates, revealing effects of glycan structure on gene expression. The characterization of 33 glycoside hydrolase enzymes revealed the pathway for colonic O -glycan degradation by this bacterium. In vivo competition experiments show that multiple exo-acting enzymes targeting mucin capping structures are central to gut colonization and may provide targets to inhibit bacterial mucin degradation.

Eco-evolutionary dynamics reshape microbial respiratory responses to warming
works.abstract: Earth System Models project a strong positive carbon-climate feedback from microbial respiration, the largest biotic carbon flux to the atmosphere. Yet experimental studies show that under sustained warming, the thermal sensitivity of microbial respiration often attenuates, through mechanisms that are debated and absent from models. I propose that attenuation is an emergent eco-evolutionary property: evolutionary temperature compensation lowers baseline respiratory rates within lineages; species sorting shifts biomass toward lineages with lower baseline rates; and species interactions reshape the aggregate response, all conditioned by substrate. The pace of these trait and compositional changes relative to warming determines how quickly attenuation develops. Embedding these dynamics in trait-based models could improve carbon-climate projections.

works.title: Machine learning methods to decipher the evolutionary dynamics of microbial pathogens
Synthetic microbial communities enable sustainable restoration of coal gangue-impacted soils by reprogramming nutrient cycling
works.abstract: Coal gangue disrupts microbial diversity and impairs nutrient cycling, constraining sustainable regional development. Traditional bioremediation relies on functional microbial traits, yet they often fail to colonize and perform in carbon-limited environments despite exogenous carbon inputs. We designed activity-oriented synthetic microbial communities (SynComs) to leverage exogenous carbon amendments and subsequently evaluated carbon use efficiency (CUE) as a community-level functional trait. High-activity SynComs were assembled from native and non-native strains based on their activity and metabolite interactions. The native-derived SynCom (SC3) enhances carbon and nitrogen cycling, whereas the non-native-derived SynCom (SC5) boosts diversity and phosphorus cycling (P < 0.05). These contrasts were associated with differences in strain functional contributions, community interactions, and carbon-source utilization. Metabolomics revealed greater functional microbial activation in SC5-conditioned biochar-derived metabolites than in glucose-derived metabolites. Multi-omics, single-cell Raman spectroscopy, and field studies confirmed the positive roles of SynComs in rhizosphere metabolism and nutrient cycling. Activity-driven SynComs approach was more efficient than single amendments, offering a potentially scalable strategy to restore carbon-limited tailing ecosystems and promote sustainability.

works.title: Environmental Drivers of Nontuberculous Mycobacteria in Tropical Freshwater Systems
works.abstract: Whilst microbial diversity still remains largely unexplored across environments and scales, microbial biogeography is shaped by edaphic and ecological drivers, and shifts in microbial community composition are frequently associated with host community structure and health. Nontuberculous mycobacteria represent a striking example of environmental microorganisms with opportunistic pathogenic potential. Unfortunately, understanding of their diversity and distribution in tropical freshwater environments remains limited, while such knowledge is crucial for predicting disease emergence and transmission. Here we aimed at (i) identifying microhabitat abiotic and biotic drivers influencing their diversity and distribution in French Guiana, (ii) comparing their diversity and distribution between French Guiana and Côte d'Ivoire, and (iii) examining co-occurrences between mycobacterial communities in different environmental contexts. By deploying an eDNA-based metabarcoding approach from tropical freshwater ecosystems, we suggest that their diversity and distribution are mainly driven by habitat type (urban vs. rural), sample type (water vs. sediment), and local abiotic factors such as phosphorus levels in sediments (with species-specific effects). Moreover, we found a stratified distribution of mycobacteria depending on sediment texture (fine silts vs. coarse sand) and depth. Overall, we suggest that their ecological interactions may occur at the microhabitat level rather than following clear biogeographic patterns.

works.title: Insight Into the Evolution of Symbiosis in the Cupriavidus Genus: Highly Conserved Symbiotic Island and a Patchy Phylogenetic Distribution
works.abstract: Currently, diversity and evolutionary studies on beta-rhizobia have primarily focused on Paraburkholderia, leaving the evolutionary history of symbiosis in the Cupriavidus genus largely unexplored. The present work provides an updated view of symbiotic Cupriavidus diversity and analyses the origin and evolution of their nitrogen-fixing capabilities. Using whole-genome phylogenetic reconstructions, we demonstrate that symbiotic Cupriavidus strains belong to five distinct evolutionary lineages, intermixed with non-symbiotic species. Comparative genomics revealed high synteny and sequence conservation within the symbiotic island across all lineages, suggesting a single ancestral acquisition of the nod-nif-fix clusters. However, in contrast, we observed very low sequence conservation among the (mega)plasmids carrying these genes. This finding definitively excludes the existence of a universal conserved replicon carrying the symbiotic genes within beta-rhizobia. Instead, our results reveal a mosaic evolutionary pattern where a highly conserved symbiotic island is mobilized across highly variable plasmid backbones. Ultimately, our findings highlight that the distribution of symbiotic traits in Cupriavidus has been shaped by a complex interplay of horizontal gene transfer, plasmid remodelling, and host-driven selective pressures, positioning South America as a key hotspot for beta-rhizobial biodiversity.

works.title: Long‐Term Acclimation and Membrane Lipid Remodelling Enable Anaerobic Oxidation of Methane at Low‐ pH by ‘ Ca . Methanoperedens vercellensis’
works.abstract: Anaerobic methanotrophic archaea are key members of the methane cycle, preventing emissions of the potent greenhouse gas into the atmosphere. Previous studies of freshwater anaerobic methanotrophs targeted their activity at circumneutral pH whereas molecular ecology studies detected anaerobic methane oxidizers in acidic environments such as peatlands. However, it remains unclear whether they can adapt to low pH and sustain an effective biological methane filter under acidic conditions. Here, we show that a granular enrichment culture of the freshwater methanotroph 'Ca. M. vercellensis' remains metabolically active down to pH 5.65 with appropriate acclimation time while it loses activity when experiencing immediate acid stress. Population-wide acclimation is required to support anaerobic methane oxidation at lower pH. Archaeal lipid analyses revealed an increased abundance of zwitterionic intact polar lipids over anionic lipids. This coincided with structural changes in biomass granules while methane oxidation rate and enrichment proportion of 'Ca. M. vercellensis' remained stable. These results demonstrate that 'Ca. M. vercellensis' remains metabolically active at lower pH values, despite increased maintenance energy requirements and the need for cytoplasmic pH homeostasis. Furthermore, they highlight that stress adaptations in slow-growing microorganisms requires long-term observation. Our findings provide new insights into methane cycling in acidic ecosystems.

works.title: The Broad Ecological Range of Salmonella enterica Serotype Typhimurium Is Associated With Genomic Diversification
works.abstract: Salmonella Typhimurium is a versatile foodborne pathogen with a broad ecological range, making it an ideal model to better understand pathogen adaptations that allow them to infect multiple hosts and persist across environments. Here, we analysed 595 genomes of S. Typhimurium representing three food animal sources (bovine, swine, and poultry) and one non-food animal source (wild birds). We found that S. Typhimurium from food animal sources generally had a more open pangenome and harboured more antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs). Notably, swine isolates exhibited the most open pangenome and the highest prevalence of ARGs, patterns that were associated with a greater presence of mobile genetic elements, particularly plasmids. Despite similar core genome sizes, S. Typhimurium from different sources displayed distinct patterns of positive selection in the core genome that varied in frequency and targeted functional categories. In contrast, although accessory genome sizes varied substantially across sources, the frequency of positive selection remained similar. Using machine learning, we identified source-predictive genetic variants, many of which are associated with stress-response functions. These findings suggest that gain and loss of accessory genes and positive selection acting on core genes support differential adaptation in S. Typhimurium, potentially contributing to its broad ecological range.

We characterized the taxonomic diversity of river microbial communities across diverse sites using high-throughput sequencing. Our findings demonstrate that environmental drivers—from seasonal cycles to farm-level inputs—predictably reshape the bacterial landscape, providing a framework for monitoring aquatic ecosystem dynamics.

works.title: Host Development and Environment Influence the Microbiomes of Aquatic Insects and Riparian Spiders
works.abstract: Larval aquatic insects harbour diverse microbiomes critical for physiology and development, yet the effects of metamorphosis combined with environmental exposures on this community remain unknown. Herein we examined bacterial microbiome composition and predicted function across larval and adult stages of three families of aquatic insects and riparian spider predators, collected upstream and downstream of wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) in Ontario, Canada. Insect host developmental stage was the primary driver of microbiome structure. Larval microbiomes were more diverse and showed higher abundances in pathways reflecting active feeding. Larval and adult populations of holometabolous insects shared few ASVs (3.8%-12.6% of the combined ASV pool), whereas a larger proportion was shared in hemimetabolous insects (23.4%). WWTP effluent exposures led to selective microbial filtering rather than broad community restructuring. Macroinvertebrate and spider microbiomes sampled downstream were characterized by higher abundances in bacterial taxa associated with wastewaters and increased xenobiotic degradation pathways. Such impacts on spider microbiomes provide evidence that ecological impacts of effluents cross the aquatic-terrestrial boundary. Lastly, a significant decrease of vertically transmitted endosymbionts (Rickettsiella, Wolbachia) was detected in aquatic insects, representing a pathway through which effluent pollution may affect host fitness without detectably altering overall microbiome diversity.

works.title: Targeted Mutagenesis Reveals Noncanonical Genetic Requirements for Carbon Monoxide Oxidation
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Carbon monoxide (CO) oxidation is a widespread microbial energy metabolism catalysed by MoCu CO dehydrogenase (CODH). Of the two phylogenetically distinct forms (form‐I and form‐II), only form‐I CODH is functionally verified. CODH activity requires maturation of the [CuSMoO 2 ] active site, linked in the carboxydotroph Afipia carboxidovorans OM5 to the genes coxDEF . CODH maturation remains untested outside of this system. Paraburkholderia terrae COX, a recently isolated carboxydovore, encodes both forms of CODH with a reduced and reorganised cox gene cluster. Using targeted mutagenesis, we identify rcoM , coxL , coxF , and coxG as essential for CO oxidation, whereas coxD, coxE , and mocA are non‐essential. Deletion of the accessory coxDEF genes produced distinct phenotypes compared to A. carboxidovorans OM5, revealing alternative routes for CODH maturation. Both coxL paralogs were deleted singly and in double knockouts, providing the first molecular evidence that form‐II CODH does not contribute to CO oxidation in vivo in these groups of bacteria. Together, these findings show that CODH maturation and function are not universally conserved and caution against inferring CO‐oxidising capacity solely from gene presence. Pb. terrae COX emerges as a genetically tractable model for elucidating the diversity and evolution of metalloenzyme assembly pathways in bacteria.

works.title: Functional Genomics of a Zinc‐Solubilising Kosakonia cowanii RL ‐16 and Its Application for Zinc Biofortification in Oryza sativa L.
works.abstract: Zinc (Zn) is assumed to be the most important micronutrient due to its involvement in different biochemical processes. The daily requirement of Zn for the human body, however, cannot be fulfilled by traditional staple crops such as rice due to its low availability to plants, especially in alkaline soils. The present study was carried out to investigate the potential of indigenous microbial flora, isolated from different agroecological zones, for Zn solubilization and combating Zn deficiency in rice. Out of a total of 135 isolates, RL-16, identified as Kosakonia cowanii, emerged as the most valuable resource for sustainable agricultural applications due to its incredible Zn solubilization potential and additional PGP characteristics. Gene mining of RL-16 revealed the footprints of solubilization of Zn and other nutrients. Under microcosmic conditions, zinc content was significantly improved for the treatment with RL-16 (134.7 mg/kg ± 0.6), compared to the control containing only an insoluble zinc source (107.7 mg/kg ± 1.6). Zinc translocation in seed (ZnSd) was enhanced by the application of RL-16 across both varieties, which was also confirmed by field evaluation. This study demonstrates the whole genome sequence analysis of Kosakonia cowanii and its potential role in Zn biofortification for more targeted and sustainable agricultural practices.

works.title: Microbial Syntrophy Drives Methanogenesis From Residual Hydrocarbons in Anaerobic Oil Sands Tailings
works.abstract: Anaerobic oil sands tailings can generate methane for decades as residual naphtha-range and petroleum hydrocarbons sustain microbial metabolism, but how microbial interactions link hydrocarbon turnover to methanogenesis remains poorly resolved. To characterize these microbial associations, we analyse two naphtha-amended anaerobic tailings incubation series using 16S rRNA gene relative abundance, hydrocarbon consumption, and methane production data within a cooperative game-theoretical framework. The abundance-informed Shapley analysis attributes system-level variation to bacterial-archaeal coalitions, highlighting key syntrophic partnerships. Several taxa show inferred contributions to methanogenesis that are disproportionate to their relative abundance, indicating that model-based attribution can differ from abundance ranking. Sensitivity analysis shows that the main methane-attribution patterns remain interpretable across alternative abundance-weighted coefficient formulations. These interaction patterns shift across incubation phases, showing that microbial control over hydrocarbon-dependent methanogenesis changes through time. When incorporated into stochastic forecasting, Shapley-derived reaction intensities improve predictive performance compared with reduced microbial and non-microbial benchmarks. Together, our results indicate that methane production in oil sands tailings can be interpreted through abundance-informed bacterial-archaeal coalition structure, providing a coalition-aware basis for interpreting and forecasting methanogenic hydrocarbon transformation.

works.title: Issue Information
Seasonal and Environmental Influences on Microbial Community Dynamics in the Dunk River Watershed, Prince Edward Island, Canada
works.abstract: Riverine ecosystems are crucial biogeochemical hubs, with their microbial communities playing a key role in nutrient cycling and overall ecosystem health. This study used shotgun metagenomic sequencing to characterize the seasonal and environmental drivers of taxonomic and functional microbial community structure (read depth between 1.91 and 30.44 bp) in four tributaries of the Dunk River watershed in Prince Edward Island (PEI), a landscape shaped by intensive agriculture and groundwater-dominated streamflow, where the seasonal and land-use impacts on the river's microbiome remain understudied. Although taxonomic composition showed no significant spatial variation among sampling sites, functional profiling identified subtle but distinct spatial signatures, primarily driven at the site with the least human impacts. Mass effects driven by above- or below-ground water dispersal pathways may override local selective pressures, resulting in a more uniform community structure across different locations. The study also identified significant correlations between certain rare microbial taxa and nutrient concentrations. This work provides critical baseline data on microbial ecology in PEI river systems, indicating that while temporal factors are the primary identifiable drivers among the measured variables, a substantial majority of the community variance remains unexplained, likely reflecting the inherent stochasticity of open riverine ecosystems.

works.title: Flagella‐Mediated Biofilm Formation and 3D Swarming Drive Virulence in the Honey Bee Pathogen Paenibacillus larvae
works.abstract: American foulbrood, a devastating bacterial disease affecting honey bee larvae, represents a major threat to apiculture worldwide. Its etiological agent, the Gram-positive, endospore-forming bacterium Paenibacillus larvae, has therefore been extensively studied to elucidate the molecular mechanisms underlying its pathogenicity and to identify key virulence determinants. In the present study, we identified the peritrichous flagella of P. larvae as a novel and important virulence factor of the genotype ERIC II. A flagella-deficient mutant was generated and shown to exhibit multiple defects in vitro associated with biofilm formation, including altered biofilm architecture, reduced adhesion, impaired floating capacity and loss of swarming motility. Survival assays using honey bee larvae, complemented by fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) analyses of infected larvae, further demonstrated the crucial contribution of flagella to virulence in vivo by mediating biofilm formation on the larval midgut epithelium as well as three-dimensional swarming during epithelial invasion.

works.title: The Association of Diet, Intestinal Microbial Starch Utilizers and Butyrate‐Producers in Early Life
works.abstract: During the first year of life, infant diet changes from liquid to solid food. Resistant starch is one of the first complex carbohydrates available to gut microbiota. With the overall goal to gain mechanistic understanding on the development of microbial starch utilization capacity and its impact on fermentation activity, we investigated the interplay of diet, starch utilizers Ruminococcus bromii and Bifidobacterium adolescentis and the butyrate producer Anaerobutyricum hallii using samples from the longitudinal CARE cohort, and in vitro. Infants started to consume resistant starch at 4 months. While less than one quarter of the infants harboured starch utilizers at 5 months, occurrence increased until the end of year one. In vitro, R. bromii and B. adolescentis degraded resistant starch but only R. bromii released reducing sugars. B. adolescentis formed acetate and lactate. In co-cultures, R. bromii with A. hallii produced more butyrate via reducing sugars than with lactate and acetate from B. adolescentis. At one year of age, infants that harboured both starch utilizer and A. hallii had higher faecal butyrate levels than those without these species. Our results suggest that differences in the mode of resistant starch degradation and cross-feeding contributed to functional redundancy and affected butyrate formation.

works.title: The Promise and Limitations of Metabolic Trait Prediction Across Diverse Bacteria
works.abstract: Metabolic traits mediate microbial interactions and underpin mechanistic models of community assembly. With the rapid expansion of genomic data and bioinformatic tools, it is widely assumed that metabolic traits such as substrate utilization can be reliably inferred from genomes alone. Here, we systematically evaluate this assumption by comparing genome-based predictions from four commonly used tools to high-throughput growth phenotypes of 186 marine bacteria. For simple substrates, prediction accuracy was limited and highly variable across taxa and substrates, with many strains predicted at or near chance levels. For three of four tools, most errors were false positives, indicating that apparent pathway completeness frequently fails to translate into growth under laboratory conditions. In contrast, genomic prediction of polysaccharide utilization based on carbohydrate-active enzyme content performed substantially better, suggesting that traits that depend on a few highly specific enzymes are easier to predict. While genome-based approaches can recover broad statistical patterns in metabolic strategies, their limited strain-level reliability constrains ecological inference and modelling. For the foreseeable future, large-scale experimental phenotypic characterization will remain an indispensable component of microbial ecology, both to reveal trait distributions and to ground-truth and improve genomic predictions.

works.title: Links Between Environmental Quality, Gut Microbiota, and Host Performance in Nutrient‐Impacted Springs
works.abstract: Microbial symbionts may enhance adaptation to environmental stress, yet their role in nutrient-enriched freshwater habitats remains unclear. We conducted a full-factorial laboratory experiment with least killifish, Heterandria formosa, manipulating water chemistry from four Florida springs and gut microbiota inoculations from conspecifics at those sites. Sequencing of 16S rRNA revealed that gut microbial richness was higher in fish reared in less nutrient-loaded waters, but inoculation treatments, if successful, did not produce significant shifts in composition. Gut communities consistently differed from ambient water, with enrichment of Pseudomonadota and Planctomycetota. Females grew more slowly in the most polluted water. In a parallel result, males displayed higher mass-specific metabolic rates in the most nutrient-loaded water. Reproductive output per female nearly doubled when experimental microbiota and water originated from the same site, despite stable microbial diversity, though parentage and inoculation success were not verified; therefore, these results should be interpreted cautiously. These results indicate that environmental quality shapes gut microbiota and host performance, and that matching microbial communities to habitat conditions can boost reproduction. Such interactions may contribute to freshwater fish resilience and merit integration into conservation strategies.

works.title: Divergent Responses of Bacterial and Microeukaryotic Diversity to Water‐Level Fluctuations in a Lake‐Floodplain System
works.abstract: Water-level fluctuations (WLF) are widely accepted as key drivers of aquatic species diversity in lake-floodplain systems, with diversity increasing as water levels rise. However, microorganisms may challenge this pattern that their richness does not necessarily increase with water levels. To resolve this inconsistency, we applied 16S and 18S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing to bacterial and microeukaryotic assemblages in Dongting Lake, China, during the low-water (LWP; January 2024) and high-water periods (HWP; August 2024). Microeukaryotic richness was higher during HWP than LWP (p < 0.01), whereas bacterial richness remained comparable (p = 0.96). Habitat-of-origin annotation indicated that terrestrial-derived microeukaryotes contributed to this increase (p = 0.02), whereas terrestrial bacterial inputs did not (p > 0.3), consistent with their divergent fates in the water column: soil microeukaryotes are more likely to persist after flooding than soil bacteria. Co-occurrence networks evidenced substantially stronger bacteria-microeukaryote associations at high water and partial least squares path modelling resolved a DOC-to-bacteria-to-microeukaryotes pathway activated only during the HWP. These signals suggest that enhanced hydrological connectivity promoted community coalescence, possibly through intensified trophic coupling, although this interpretation requires experimental verification. This study highlights that natural WLFs reshape microbial richness by intermittently reconnecting terrestrial and aquatic microbial species pools.

works.title: Mycoviruses in the Genomic Era: Ecological, Evolutionary and One Health Perspectives
works.abstract: Mycoviruses are widespread and ecologically significant components of the biosphere, acting as hidden modulators of fungal diversity, metabolism and symbiotic interactions. This review synthesizes historical and technological advances in mycovirus discovery within an integrative One Health framework linking human, animal, plant and environmental health. We trace the transition from early dsRNA-based detection and Sanger sequencing to modern metatranscriptomic, metagenomic and petabase-scale data-mining approaches that have dramatically expanded known mycovirome diversity, uncovering deeply divergent RNA virus lineages. We survey the major mycovirus families and their genomic architectures and compare the strengths and inherent biases of current discovery strategies. We critically assess evidence for horizontal viral transfer across kingdoms, distinguishing experimentally demonstrated cross-host replication from phylogenetic inference alone and review mycovirus roles in modulating fungal virulence in agricultural and clinical settings, explicitly separating robust findings from preliminary or speculative reports. Hypovirulence-based biocontrol of phytopathogenic fungi emerges as the only application currently supported by field-validated evidence, whereas mycovirus-based therapy for human fungal infection remains a long-term hypothesis rather than a near-term clinical strategy. We underscore the need to combine rigorous experimental and computational approaches to characterize mycovirome complexity and function and outline priority research directions for the coming decade.

works.title: Estuarine Biofilm Communities Adapt to Changing Conditions While Retaining Crucial Pollutant‐Combatting Functions
works.abstract: Industrialization has increased the influx of toxicants into intertidal and estuarine ecosystems. Intertidal sediments are exposed to heavy metals, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, pesticides, and other xenobiotics through effluents, shipping, spillages, battery disposal, and agricultural run-off. Pollutants accumulate in sediments, disrupting nutrient cycling and impairing primary productivity, thereby threatening coastal food webs. Sediment-bound biofilms or microphytobenthos are complex assemblages of microorganisms embedded in extracellular polymeric substances and play vital roles in biogeochemical cycling, sediment stabilization, and pollutant remediation. Their functional responses to contaminant exposure remain poorly understood, particularly in tropical estuaries. Biofilms from contaminated estuarine sediments were analysed using metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) and genome-scale metabolic models (GEMs) in a paired field-laboratory approach. Greater metabolic diversity of field biofilms indicated broader functional capacities to sustain pollutant exposure. Conserved genes linked to organic compound degradation and metal transport co-occurred across MAGs, suggesting integrated detoxification strategies. GEM-based simulations revealed metabolic cross-feeding underlying contaminant transformation. Culture conditions shaped microbial succession and ecological roles, yet core pollutant degradation and nutrient processing functions persisted, operated by dominant taxa. Microphytobenthic experimental studies rely on laboratory-cultured communities derived from field-collected samples. Contrasting community dynamics and altered metabolism due to 'bottle effect' are foundational for correctly interpreting laboratory-based experimental outcomes.

works.title: Widespread Microbial Suppression and Functional Shifts in Wastewater Treatment Microbiomes Under Climate Warming
works.abstract: Climate warming is expected to reshape microbial communities, yet its impacts on engineered microbial ecosystems remain poorly understood. Here, we developed a deep-learning framework to assess microbial responses to climate warming across global wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs). Under a +1.5°C warming perturbation, ~77% of analyzed microbial taxa showed predicted declines in relative abundance, accompanied by decreased weights in ~54% of reconstructed microbial associations. Keystone taxa were also predominantly predicted to decline, suggesting potential changes in community association structure under warming. From an exploratory ecological perspective, warming-associated increases in viral abundance may further contribute to microbial suppression through enhanced viral pressure on key taxa. Taxonomically inferred functional profiles suggested warming was also associated with broad shifts in ecological functional profiles, including potential impairments in nutrient cycling. Notably, increases in methanogenesis-associated taxa coupled with reduced methane oxidation suggested a potential imbalance in methane cycling. Together, these findings indicate that climate warming may substantially reshape the composition, interactions and ecological functioning of WWTP microbiomes. Our study provides a global assessment of climate-associated risks in engineered microbial ecosystems and offers a basis for developing climate-resilient wastewater management strategies.

works.title: Influence of Soluble and Mineral Sources of Cobalt on Methanogenesis and Growth in Methanosarcina barkeri Fusaro and Methanococcus maripaludis S2
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Cobalt (Co) is a required component of cofactors and coenzymes in all life and has a pronounced role in the one carbon metabolism of methanogens. However, methanogens often inhabit sulphidic environments where Co precipitates and is incorporated into low solubility mineral phases, such as pyrite (FeS 2 ). Here, we initially examined the influence of Co availability on the growth kinetics of (1) Methanosarcina barkeri with different methanogenesis substrates and (2) Methanococcus maripaludis with different sulphur sources. We then investigated Co acquisition from cobaltoan pyrite [(Co,Fe)S 2 ]. Co demand was highest in M. barkeri grown on methanol/acetate relative to hydrogen/carbon dioxide or methanol only and in M. maripaludis grown with sulphide relative to cysteine or cysteine/thiosulphate. Methanol/acetate‐grown M. barkeri and formate‐grown M. maripaludis grew with (Co,Fe)S 2 as well as with soluble sources of Co, Fe and S. Both strains required direct contact to reduce and solubilize Fe and S from (Co,Fe)S 2 . Further, M. barkeri grown with (Co,Fe)S 2 produced an equal amount of cobamides relative to cells provided with soluble Co, Fe, and S. These findings indicate that the availability of methanogenesis substrates and sulphur sources influence Co requirements for methanogens and that these organisms can acquire Co, Fe and S from (Co,Fe)S 2 .

works.title: Immobilized Epiphytic Bacteria Enhance Macrophyte Suppression of a Bloom‐Forming Cyanobacterium
works.abstract: Harmful cyanobacterial blooms are an increasing threat to freshwater ecosystems and water security worldwide. Biological control using macrophytes or algicidal bacteria is often studied separately despite natural co-occurrence. Here we show that the epiphytic bacterium Priestia megaterium strain BW, isolated from submerged macrophytes, exhibits strong algicidal activity and forms an enhanced suppression system with its host plant Vallisneria natans. Pre-colonization of BW on V. natans leaves achieves > 80% inhibition of Microcystis aeruginosa biomass within 5 days. When immobilized on a ceramic material carrier, BW rapidly suppresses algal photosynthetic efficiency within 48 h. Mechanistically, the algicidal effect follows a multi-pathway process involving early photosynthetic impairment, oxidative stress and subsequent cellular disintegration. Notably, the combined application of immobilized BW with V. natans produces stronger and faster suppression than either the bacterium or the plant alone. Our findings demonstrate that an epiphytic bacterium can retain potent algicidal activity outside its native biofilm and that its efficacy is markedly enhanced when re-integrated with the plant, providing direct evidence for plant-microbe synergistic control of cyanobacterial blooms.

works.title: Endophytic Success of Salmonella enterica and Escherichia coli in Plants via Root Uptake Is Governed by Stochasticity in Transpiration
works.abstract: Human foodborne pathogens can internalize into edible plant tissues through root uptake, yet the mechanisms governing this process remain poorly understood. Here, we developed a localized enrichment inoculation system that enables robust and reproducible investigation of bacterial internalization in plants. Using Arabidopsis thaliana and multiple microgreen species, we show that Salmonella enterica and Escherichia coli rapidly penetrate intact roots and translocate to shoots independent of bacterial motility, virulence, plant immunity or root tissue damage. Instead, internalization is strongly associated with plant transpiration activity. Transcriptomic and physiological analyses revealed that stochastic variation in photosynthesis and transpiration between genetically identical plants underlies highly heterogeneous contamination outcomes, producing near-bimodal distributions of bacterial load among individual plants. Suppression of transpiration through cooling or abscisic acid treatment significantly reduced pathogen internalization. These findings establish plant physiological stochasticity as a critical determinant of foodborne pathogen uptake and reveal new opportunities for mitigation strategies in agriculture.

works.title: Turning a Staphylococcus aureus virulence factor into an antibacterial therapy
Prokaryotes bridging the lipid divide
works.abstract: The fundamental biochemical and stereochemical difference in how cell membrane lipids are built between Archaea on one side, and Bacteria and Eukarya on the other is known as the lipid divide. It is often assumed to translate in the impossibility of combining membranes of both types. It was established early when little sampling of the biodiversity was available. Since then, exceptions have been revealed and accumulated. Here, we review those exceptions and complement them with a broad survey, revealing diverse bacteria with mixed membrane-lipid features. Together with liposome assays and synthetic-biology experiments, studies on these organisms suggest that the lipid divide can be bridged. We conclude by discussing the evolutionary implications for LUCA, the origin of the prokaryotic domains and eukaryogenesis.

works.title: Intestinal ROS triggers stress-induced dysbiosis by dismantling the hypoxic barrier
works.abstract: Stress consistently disrupts the vertebrate gut microbiome, leading to negative health outcomes. However, how systemic stress translates into reproducible microbial dysbiosis remains poorly understood. While current research primarily focuses on late-stage compositional shifts, the early biochemical signals and microenvironmental alterations that precede and initiate this structural breakdown represent a critical knowledge gap. Here we show that stress destabilizes the gut microbiome through a cascade initiated by intestinal reactive oxygen species (ROS). In zebrafish, stress rapidly elicits intestinal ROS accumulation in the distal intestine, emerging within hours and preceding any detectable changes in microbial composition. This early oxidative response does not immediately restructure the community but instead induces a functional collapse: anaerobic fermentation is selectively suppressed and short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) production sharply declines while community structure remains largely intact. The resulting SCFAs deficit weakens PPARγ-dependent epithelial metabolic programs, diminishes epithelial oxygen consumption, and erodes the physiological hypoxic barrier. Loss of this barrier re-engineers the luminal niche, enabling the relative enrichment of facultative pathobionts. Restoring epithelial bioenergetics or neutralizing intestinal ROS in zebrafish preserves hypoxia and prevents dysbiosis despite continued stress, identifying intestinal ROS as an early initiating signal of stress-induced dysbiosis. In restraint-stressed mice, the same ordered sequence—early ROS elevation, SCFAs decline, hypoxia loss, and the relative enrichment of facultative taxa—is likewise observed, supporting phenotypic and temporal conservation of this cascade. Our findings reveal that stress-induced dysbiosis is not a stochastic microbial drift, but a highly reproducible ecological cascade that is triggered by an early intestinal ROS burst in zebrafish and phenotypically conserved in mice. By shifting the paradigm from late-stage structural dysbiosis to the initial functional and microenvironmental collapse, we identify the maintenance of the intestinal hypoxic barrier as a critical therapeutic target for stress-related microbiome disorders. Video Abstract

works.title: Top-down mining of a lactobacilli-enriched gut niche in Tunchang pigs identifies a host-derived Limosilactobacillus reuteri strain with anti-colitis activity
works.abstract: The conventional ‘isolate-and-screen’ strategy for probiotic discovery often lacks ecological context, resulting in strains with uncertain safety profiles and unpredictable functional performance. Indigenous pig breeds, particularly those thriving under low-input husbandry conditions, represent underexplored ‘living libraries’ that offer host- and environment-shaped gut niches.
