Tunchang (TC) pigs, an indigenous breed from Hainan Province in southeastern China, provide a useful model for top-down, ecology-guided mining of host-derived probiotics from native gut niches. By combining cross-sectional age-gradient metagenomics with cross-breed comparisons, we defined a TC-pig gut niche with a lower overall burden of annotated VF/ARG features than that of Duroc × Landrace × Yorkshire (DLY) pigs. Notably, Limosilactobacillus reuteri was consistently detected within a lactobacilli-enriched core microbiota across developmental-stage groups and showed limited associations with annotated VF/ARG features at the community level. This niche was associated with higher relative levels of several host–microbe co-metabolites, including indoleacrylic acid and N-decanoylglycine. Guided by this framework, we isolated a TC pig-derived L. reuteri strain (TC-Lr) and a co-isolated Lactobacillus johnsonii strain (TC-Lj). Targeted profiling of cell-free culture supernatants revealed a distinct tryptophan-associated metabolic profile of these two isolates, with TC-Lr showing higher concentrations of indole-3-lactic acid and tryptophol than TC-Lj. In a mouse model of dextran sulphate sodium (DSS)-induced colitis, TC-Lr, but not TC-Lj, alleviated weight loss and disease activity, attenuated colon shortening and reduced inflammation-associated haematological alterations. TC-Lr also partially restored DSS-disrupted colonic metabolism, increasing adenosine while reducing creatinine and histamine levels. These findings support an ecology-guided, top-down framework for prioritising host-derived probiotics from indigenous livestock breeds. They further suggest that the TC pig gut, characterised by a lactobacilli-enriched community and a lower annotated VF/ARG burden at the community level, may serve as an ecological source for prioritising host-derived probiotic candidates. Video Abstract

works.title: Potent reaction hijacking inhibitors of Plasmodium falciparum asparagine tRNA synthetase
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Malaria remains one of the major threats to human health. Breakthrough drugs with high potency and low resistance risk are needed to combat the ever-increasing resistance to currently deployed antimalarials. Here, we explore a series of 4-aminoquinazoline-based sulfonamides (4AQS), with a synthetically accessible scaffold. Exemplars exhibit nanomolar potency against blood stage Plasmodium cultures, with up to 300-fold selectivity compared with a mammalian cell line. The compounds are active against transmissible stages of Plasmodium falciparum and refractory to resistance development. Targeted mass spectrometry reveals that the 4AQS compounds act as reaction hijacking inhibitors targeting P. falciparum aminoacyl tRNA synthetases (aaRSs). Subtle changes to the chemical structure switch the main target from cytoplasmic threonine tRNA synthetase ( Pf ThrRS) to cytoplasmic asparagine tRNA synthetase ( Pf AsnRS), a change that is associated with increased potency against P. falciparum . The target preference was confirmed by selective knockdown of different P. falciparum aaRSs and by tolerance selection in a mutator line. Consistent with aaRS targets, exemplar compounds activate the amino acid starvation response. Recombinant enzyme inhibition and thermal stabilization assays confirm the susceptibility of Pf AsnRS to reaction hijacking and show that human AsnRS is less susceptible. A molecular model of Asn-tRNA-bound Pf AsnRS reveals that a potent hijacker adopts a pose similar to adenosine 5′-monophosphate (AMP). An AlphaFold model of the native Pf AsnRS dimer helps explain the tolerance-conferring effect of a mutation at the dimer interface. IMPORTANCE Every year, at least 200 million new malaria infections are diagnosed, causing more than 600,000 deaths in Africa and Southeast Asia. Ever-increasing levels of resistance to current antimalarials are leading to an impending crisis. Breakthrough drugs with new modes of action are much needed. Here, we explore a series of inhibitors that hijack critical malaria parasite enzymes. The target enzymes catalyze the formation of a bond between the hijackers and an enzyme substrate, forming a tight-binding compound that disrupts the malaria parasite’s protein translation machinery. The hijacking inhibitors exhibit high-level potency against the disease-causing stage of the malaria parasite and are also active against transmissible stages. They exhibit up to 300-fold selectivity compared with a mammalian cell line, possess drug-like chemical attributes, and are easily synthesized. Importantly, the compounds are refractory to resistance development.

works.title: Pressure-induced membrane tension mechanically opens the germinant receptor GerA ion channel to trigger bacterial spore germination
works.abstract: ABSTRACT High pressure (HP) can trigger bacterial spore germination, acting either through germinant receptors (GRs) or the SpoVA channel. However, the mechanism by which HP activates these membrane-embedded proteins remains elusive. Here, using Bacillus subtilis , we demonstrate that the GerA GR is the primary target of moderate HP (50–300 MPa). Mutagenesis reveals that pore-lining residues within the GerA ion channel are essential for the pressure response, whereas canonical ligand-binding and intramembrane signaling residues are dispensable. We then propose a s tretch- t o- o pen (STO) model, in which HP differentially compresses the more compliant inner membrane (IM) relative to the rigid spore core, generating lateral membrane tension that promotes the opening of the GerA channel. In situ membrane tension measurements indicate HP-induced compression of IM phospholipids and elevated membrane tension. This tension-dependent gating is further supported by the pressure-dependent phenotypic rescue of GerA channel mutants. Consistently, HP increases IM permeability to water-soluble and membrane-impermeable agents (propidium iodide and formaldehyde), an effect potentiated by GerA, indicating concomitant opening of GerA by HP. Furthermore, modulating IM fluidity via heat activation or decoating altered membrane physical properties and delayed HP-induced germination, establishing the IM as the critical mechanical transducer. Additionally, computational modeling and calculations support faster compression of the IM than of the core under HP, rationalizing the source of tensile stress. Together, our findings establish a novel mechanism of HP-induced GerA activation via the STO model: HP compresses the IM, generates lateral tension, and promotes opening of the GerA ion channel to trigger bacterial spore germination. IMPORTANCE Bacterial spores are notoriously resilient, posing significant challenges to health and industry. While high pressure is known to trigger spore germination, the biophysical mechanism has remained elusive. Here, we provide evidence that high pressure mechanically activates the germinant receptor GerA via a “stretch-to-open” mechanism. Because the inner membrane is highly compressible compared to the rigid spore core, pressure induces membrane compression that generates lateral tension. This tension promotes opening of the GerA ion channel. Our study identifies the inner membrane as a critical mechanical transducer, addressing a long-standing question in spore biology and suggesting a distinct mechanosensory adaptation involved in spore revival.

works.title: An lncRNA containing tandem 66-nt repeats recruits PTBP1 to disrupt PB2-NP assembly and restrict influenza virus replication in vivo
works.abstract: Influenza virus replication relies on coordinated assembly of ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes in the nucleus, yet how host long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs) regulate this process remains poorly defined. Here, we identify the lncRNA AL645608.7 as a potent antiviral factor and show that its two splice variants restrict influenza replication. Mechanistically, AL645608.7 contains eight tandem 66-nt repeats that recruit the RNA-binding protein PTBP1, primarily through PTBP1's RRM3 domain. The AL645608.7-PTBP1 assembly then engages key viral RNP components-PB2 and NP-and functionally disrupts the PB2-NP interface, thereby suppressing viral RNA synthesis. Domain-mapping analyses further distinguish the regions responsible for PTBP1 recruitment from those involved in PB2 and NP engagement, demonstrating that distinct structural elements of AL645608.7 coordinate host-protein recruitment and viral RNP interference. Importantly, lipid nanoparticle delivery of AL645608.7 markedly reduces viral burden and improves disease outcomes in mice, providing a proof-of-concept nucleic-acid therapeutic strategy. Together, our findings reveal a repeat-programmed lncRNA mechanism that rewires a host RNA-binding protein to dismantle influenza RNP organization and support the therapeutic potential of lncRNA-based intervention against influenza virus infection. IMPORTANCE: This study identified that influenza virus infection significantly upregulated the long noncoding RNA (lncRNA) AL645608.7. Both of its transcripts, AL645608.7-v1 and AL645608.7-v2, exhibited antiviral activity against influenza virus. Mechanistically, AL645608.7 was shown to directly bind to the host protein PTBP1. Furthermore, the nuclear-localized AL645608.7 recruits PTBP1 via a 66-base repeat motif. Importantly, PTBP1 interacts with both the N- and C-terminal regions of the influenza virus polymerase subunit PB2 as well as the NP, thereby disrupting the NP-PB2 interaction. The AL645608.7-PTBP1 complex amplifies this inhibitory effect, ultimately impairing vRNA synthesis and blocking efficient viral replication. These findings offer novel insights into the functional role of noncoding RNAs in host-influenza virus interactions.

works.title: Putative conjugative transfer and persistence of carbapenem resistance gene bla OXA-72 from Acinetobacter pittii to Acinetobacter baumannii
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter (CRA) has been associated with increased morbidity and mortality in clinical settings. In this study, we explored the transfer potential of a mobilizable plasmid-harboring bla OXA-72 gene between Acinetobacter species originating from patients, municipal wastewater, and pig farm wastewater. PCR-based evidence suggested putative transfer of bla OXA-72 from Acinetobacter pittii to Acinetobacter baumannii . In this pair, the apparent frequency of PCR-marker-positive putative transconjugants varied depending on temperature and meropenem supplementation, with a higher frequency observed at 27°C than at 17°C and 37°C. Likewise, the presence of antibiotic pressure yielded a higher apparent conjugation frequency; however, this observation was limited to a single donor-recipient pair. Further, we revealed a phenotypic conversion in terms of meropenem susceptibility and a fitness cost in the putative transconjugants. While whole-genome sequencing did not conclusively verify the presence of bla OXA-72 or a fully resolved plasmid configuration, Oxford Nanopore read mapping consistently detected the chromosomal strA gene in all isolates. In contrast, only a limited number of reads aligned with the bla OXA-72 gene, traC , or the complete plasmid sequences. Comparative analyses further revealed variations in the composition of surface-associated factors and defense systems of the recipient strains, which could be considered as barriers to conjugation. Lastly, the persistence of PCR-detectable marker genes in putative transconjugants was variable and generally unstable over a 30-day period. Overall, these findings provide preliminary insights into the factors that may influence horizontal gene transfer and short-term maintenance of bla OXA-72 . IMPORTANCE Carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter (CRA) is a serious clinical concern linked to elevated morbidity and mortality. This study shed light on how the carbapenemase gene bla OXA-72 spreads in the environment via horizontal gene transfer. Using isolates of Acinetobacter pittii and Acinetobacter baumannii from municipal wastewater treatment plants, we show that PCR-based evidence of putative conjugative transfer of the bla OXA-72 gene depends on temperature and antibiotic exposure. The process also incurs fitness costs, and the transferred gene persists only briefly in recipient cells. These results emphasize the importance of environmental sources as reservoirs for antimicrobial resistance gene exchange. Additionally, variations in surface structures and defense systems may act as potential barriers to conjugation. Overall, the work improves our understanding of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) movement and supports the need for better integrated surveillance under a One Health approach.

works.title: Ligilactobacillus salivarius inhibits GII.4[P16] human norovirus replication in zebrafish larvae
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Human gut bacteria can modulate human norovirus (HuNoV) infection, underscoring the need to characterize virus-bacterium interactions. This study evaluated the effect of Ligilactobacillus salivarius on HuNoV GII.4[P16] replication using a zebrafish larva model. A GII.4[P16]-positive stool specimen was resuspended in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS), centrifuged, and the supernatant stored at −80°C. L. salivarius was grown overnight in de Man, Rogosa, and Sharpe broth, from which bacterial cells and cell-free supernatant (CFS) were collected. The overnight broth (OB), cells, and CFS were each mixed with virus suspension at a 1:1 ratio, and 3 nL were microinjected into 3-day post-fertilization larvae; controls received PBS with virus. Daily until 4 days post-infection (dpi), 2 samples of 10 pooled larvae were collected, and RNA was extracted and quantified by droplet digital PCR. Two-way analysis of variance showed that treatment and time significantly influenced viral RNA levels ( P < 0.001), with a marginal interaction ( P = 0.051) indicating consistent inhibitory trends across the study period. CFS-injected larvae showed replication comparable to controls ( P > 0.05), peaking at 5.31 log RNA copies/larva at 1 dpi, whereas cell-containing treatments (cells and OB) significantly reduced replication ( P < 0.01) throughout the 4-day period. An in vitro binding assay showed that 67% of the virus inoculum physically bound to L. salivarius . In a further comparison, both live and heat-killed bacteria reduced replication initially; live L. salivarius significantly inhibited replication at 3 dpi ( P < 0.05). These findings support the hypothesis that L. salivarius physically binds to HuNoV GII.4[P16] and inhibits viral replication, highlighting its potential as a probiotic intervention for HuNoV infection. IMPORTANCE Norovirus remains the leading cause of acute gastroenteritis worldwide, responsible for nearly 700 million cases and substantial economic burden annually, yet no vaccine or antiviral therapy currently exists. This study’s findings are significant because they identify a specific probiotic strain, Ligilactobacillus salivarius , capable of directly binding to and inhibiting replication of a clinically relevant norovirus genotype (GII.4[P16]), which is responsible for many recent outbreaks globally. By demonstrating that live bacterial cells—not just secreted metabolites—drive this antiviral effect, the study points toward a mechanistic, cell-mediated mode of action that could inform targeted probiotic formulations. The use of a zebrafish larva model also offers a valuable, scalable in vivo system for studying norovirus-microbiome interactions, addressing a major bottleneck in norovirus research caused by the lack of robust cell culture systems. Together, these findings advance understanding of bacterium-virus interactions and support further development of probiotic-based strategies for preventing or reducing norovirus infection severity.

works.title: High quality chromosomal genome assemblies of three human Plasmodium species directly from natural infections
works.abstract: Malaria, caused by mosquito-transmitted Plasmodium parasites, remains a major global health challenge. While P. falciparum accounts for most malaria deaths, the lesser-studied P. ovale spp. and P. malariae also contribute to disease burden across many endemic regions, typically causing milder but chronic infections. Here, we generated high quality, chromosome-level reference genomes for P. ovale wallikeri, P. malariae, and P. falciparum directly from blood samples taken from natural infections. Using PacBio Ultra-Low-Input HiFi long-read sequencing and Hi-C chromatin conformation capture, we overcome limitations posed by low parasite biomass and the absence of in vitro culture for P. ovale wallikeri and P. malariae. These high quality reference genomes resolve previously inaccessible subtelomeric regions that include expanded gene families likely involved in host-parasite interactions, and they enhance our understanding of parasite persistence, transmission, immune evasion and comparative evolutionary studies. This work provides a critical foundation for including these neglected species in global malaria elimination efforts.

works.title: Functional dissection of conserved RNAi pathways in antiviral immunity of several hemipteran insects
works.abstract: The small silencing RNA pathways are crucial post-transcriptional gene silencing mechanisms involved in antiviral defense, gene regulation, and transposon suppression. In insects, the three main pathways are the microRNA (miRNA), Piwi-interacting RNA (piRNA), and small interfering RNA (siRNA) pathways. While these pathways are well-studied in model insects like fruit flies and mosquitoes (Order: Diptera), their functions in non-model insects remain largely unexplored. In this study, we conducted a comprehensive functional screening of core RNAi-related genes in a hemipteran insect, the small brown planthopper (Laodelphax striatellus). Our results demonstrated that genes in the miRNA pathway (AGO1 and DCR1) and the piRNA pathway (Piwi and AGO3) are essential for the survival, development, and fecundity of L. striatellus, but they are not actively involved in the antiviral response. Unexpectedly, knocking down the key siRNA pathway gene DCR2 did not produce a detectable change in viral accumulation or the abundance of virus-derived small interfering RNAs. This finding suggests that substantial depletion of DCR2 does not detectably impair the measured antiviral siRNA responses in L. striatellus under our experimental conditions. A similar lack of detectable antiviral phenotypes following DCR2 knockdown was observed in three other representative hemipteran insects from different families/genera (Sogatella furcifera, Nilaparvata lugens, and Bemisia tabaci). Additionally, CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout of DCR2 resulted in embryonic lethality in homozygous mutant strains of L. striatellus, while heterozygous mutants showed significantly prolonged developmental duration. Functional RNAi-of-RNAi assays further demonstrated that DCR2 pre-knockdown did not detectably reduce silencing of a subsequently introduced dsRNA reporter in L. striatellus, and DCR2-heterozygous mutants with reduced DCR2 expression showed no change in viral accumulation. These results reveal an essential developmental role for DCR2 and indicate that partial DCR2 depletion does not measurably compromise antiviral immunity under the tested conditions. Collectively, our findings broaden our understanding of the organization and biological functions of small silencing RNA pathways in hemipteran insects.

works.title: Guardians of the blood: How Kupffer cells control systemic infection
SR-A1 cooperates with TLR4-NF-κB signaling to drive macrophage TGF-β1 expression and Treg induction during schistosome infection
works.abstract: Helminths induce regulatory T cells (Tregs) to establish chronic infections, promoting long-term persistence of both parasites and hosts. TGF-β1 is essential for Treg induction by initiating Foxp3 expression. Helminth infections are typically associated with high TGF-β1 levels, yet the mechanisms by which helminths drive its production are not fully understood. Here, we uncover a mechanism whereby the scavenger receptor class A1 (SR-A1) cooperates with TLR4 signaling to drive TGF-β1 production by macrophages. Mechanistically, schistosome egg antigens activate TLR4-p50 (NF-κB1) while concurrently engaging SR-A1 to upregulate c-Jun, thereby assembling c-Jun-p50 transcription complexes at the Tgfb1 promoter and enhancing TGF-β1 expression, subsequently inducing Tregs and mitigating liver immunopathology in Schistosoma japonicum-infected mice. Thus, we identify a previously unrecognized host-parasite interaction wherein SR-A1-TLR4 cooperation enables helminths to manipulate macrophage transcriptional programs for TGF-β1 expression and Treg induction, identifying a potential therapeutic target in the host for inflammatory helminthiasis.

works.title: Planetary-scale metagenomic analysis reveals CRISPR targeting dynamics across ecosystems
works.abstract: Interactions between microorganisms and their mobile genetic elements (MGEs), including viruses and plasmids, impact microbiome dynamics. CRISPR-Cas systems are important regulators of these host-MGE interactions, but a global understanding of the diversity, activity and roles of CRISPR spacers across Earth's biomes is still lacking. Here we develop a computational approach to search short-read data and collect 794 million CRISPR spacers across 367,609 public metagenomes, from which we identified 1.18 billion hits between 41 million spacers and 2.5 million viruses and plasmids. While spacers were highly variable across samples, those matching known viruses were more prevalent and conserved, consistent with a positive selection pressure associated with phage targeting. Among these, however, we find evidence suggestive of recurrent entry of phage genomes into non-host microbial cells, further blurring the line between CRISPR targeting and virus-host interactions. These results highlight key drivers of CRISPR targeting patterns likely to influence strain-level diversification and selection processes in microbiomes.

works.title: A human gut-associated picobirnavirus establishes the Picobirnaviridae as the third clade of RNA bacteriophages
works.abstract: Picobirnaviruses (PBVs) are commonly detected RNA viruses in human and animal guts and are associated with multiple human diseases. Although PBVs have been assumed to infect vertebrate hosts, there is neither direct evidence for this nor any culture system to propagate PBVs. Here we demonstrate that a PBV infects bacteria and is therefore an RNA phage. Two different PBVs from human faeces were propagated in germ-free mice after faecal microbiota transplantation, establishing a mouse model for PBV. One PBV could be cultured in vitro, in a community of anaerobic gut bacteria, and its growth could be inhibited by multiple antibiotics. RNA fluorescence in situ hybridization revealed PBV RNA within bacterial cells, and enrichment and sequencing of PBV RNA-containing cells identified a previously unidentified 'Candidatus Anaerotignum faecalis' as its host. Our findings define the family Picobirnaviridae as only the third clade of RNA phages in addition to leviviruses and cystoviruses.

works.title: Systemic exposure to typhoid toxin primes the murine vascular endothelium for intestinal perforation during Salmonella Typhi infection
Genomic analysis of early case samples from the 2025 Marburg virus outbreak in Ethiopia
works.abstract: In November 2025, Ethiopia reported its first outbreak of Marburg virus disease, with a case fatality rate of 64%. Here we report the analysis of seven near-complete Marburg virus genomes from seven early cases. The outbreak lineage belonged to the MARV.A.1 clade, which is closely related to genomes from historical human cases and bats. A high nucleotide identity across the seven genomes suggests human-to-human transmission after a zoonotic spillover event. These findings highlight the importance of genomic surveillance for outbreak detection, response and preparedness. Phylogenetic analysis of seven Marburg virus genomes from the 2025 outbreak in Ethiopia suggests human-to-human transmission after a spillover event.

works.title: Finding the Goldilocks zone: modulating glycoprotein cleavage and fusogenicity optimizes the efficacy of a candidate Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus vaccine
works.abstract: Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus (CCHFV) is the etiologic agent of a highly lethal hemorrhagic disease spread by ticks throughout Europe, the Middle East, Africa, and Asia, for which no FDA- or EMA-approved vaccines or therapeutics exist. A lack of fundamental understanding of the molecular mechanisms of CCHFV assembly, egress, and entry has challenged the development of medical countermeasures. Herein, we investigated the molecular basis of replicative efficacy of a highly protective recombinant vesicular stomatitis virus vaccine bearing the CCHFV glycoprotein complex (rVSV-GPC). We identified key amino acid residues associated with rVSV-GPC adaptation and showed that these could be transferred to a divergent CCHFV genetic background to afford a new vaccine vector with enhanced protective efficacy against heterologous viral challenge. We show that the key amino acid substitutions enhance rVSV-GPC infectivity via multiple distinct biochemical and cell-biological mechanisms. Our mechanistic studies provide the first evidence that SKI-1 cleavage at the GP38-Gn boundary modulates the pH threshold of CCHFV membrane fusion and points to a critical role for virion-associated GP38 and GP38-Gn interaction in regulating the pre-fusion conformation of the glycoprotein spike during virion biogenesis, egress, and cell entry. IMPORTANCE: Herein, we investigated the molecular basis of replicative efficacy of a highly protective rVSV-GPC vaccine candidate. We identified key amino acid residues associated with rVSV-GPC adaptation, including two novel residues, and showed that a minimal set of these could be transferred to a divergent CCHFV genetic background to afford a new vaccine vector with enhanced protective efficacy against heterologous viral challenge. Our work provides important new information to refine VSV-vectored CCHFV vaccines, to assess which critical GPC adaptations might benefit other vaccine modalities such as subunit and RNA, and to aid in the development of vaccines against divergent orthonairoviruses. Our findings also shed new light on the basic biology of CCHFV. We show that the key amino acid substitutions enhance rVSV-GPC infectivity via multiple, distinct biochemical and cell-biological mechanisms. Most notably, we provide the first evidence that SKI-1 cleavage at the GP38-Gn boundary modulates the pH threshold of viral membrane fusion. This points to an unanticipated role for virion-associated GP38 and GP38-Gn interaction in protecting and regulating the pre-fusion conformation of GPC during CCHFV biogenesis, egress, and cell entry.

works.title: Ablation of a maternal Cryptosporidium mRNA-binding protein results in sterile sporozoites
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Infection with Cryptosporidium is a leading cause of diarrheal disease and early childhood mortality. This apicomplexan parasite undergoes asexual and sexual replication within the same host, and recent studies have shown an intrinsic developmental program of obligate transition to male and female gametes and sex. While factors were identified that control male fate and development, how female gene expression is orchestrated remains largely unknown. Here, we use the Cryptosporidium Single Cell Atlas to discover an RNA-binding protein (F-RBP) as one of the earliest markers of female identity in C. parvum . Reporter parasites engineered based on this gene allowed us to calibrate transcriptional pseudotime against the real time of female development, revealing a significant window of transcriptional fate ambiguity. While F-RBP is an early transcript, the protein persists throughout female development and into the zygote. Conditional ablation of the F-RBP gene showed it to be dispensable for sex determination and early female development in vitro . However, the gene is essential in vivo, and its loss results in rapid cure. Cell biological experiments link this loss to the production of oocysts that release sporozoites incapable of host-cell invasion. F-RBP binds transcripts highly expressed in the female gamete, enriched for a sequence motif recognized by a Y-box protein family member, and forms mRNA-protein complexes in late females akin to processing or P bodies. We propose F-RBP’s essential role to be in the regulation of long-term homeostasis of maternally inherited RNA required for sporozoite infectivity. IMPORTANCE The parasite Cryptosporidium is responsible for millions of cases of severe diarrheal disease in young children, and the infection is both a consequence of and a risk factor for chronic malnutrition. There are no vaccines available, and a single approved treatment is largely ineffective. Infection relies on ingestion of the oocyst, an environmentally stable spore, which contains an invasive form of the parasite, the sporozoite. Oocysts and sporozoites are the products of parasite sex and the fusion of female and male Cryptosporidium parasites. Here, we report the critical role of an RNA-binding protein in female mRNA homeostasis. Maternal transcripts orchestrate the complex process of sexual replication and oocyst formation. Loss of the protein results in spores that fail to initiate the next round of the life cycle, and conditional ablation using a small-molecule trigger quickly cures infected animals, demonstrating the essential role of parasite sex in continued infection.

works.title: Targeted CPSF6 recoding reveals global fitness advantages of SPAD integration targeting and cell type-specific roles for capsid binding in HIV-1 DNA synthesis and nuclear import
works.abstract: ABSTRACT As part of the CFIm complex, CPSF6 regulates cellular gene expression via alternative polyadenylation. CPSF6 binds primate lentiviral capsids and has been implicated in HIV-1 reverse transcription, nuclear import, and integration targeting. However, interpretations of the role(s) of CPSF6 during HIV-1 replication are complicated by the transcriptional changes that occur when the protein is depleted from cells. To disentangle the role of CPSF6 in HIV-1 replication from alternative polyadenylation, we selectively recoded its capsid-binding phenylalanine-glycine motif to alanine-alanine in CD4-positive Jurkat T cells, CEM12D7 T cells, and THP-1 myeloid/macrophage cells using CRISPR/Cas9-based homology-directed repair. While large variations in single-round HIV-1 infection were observed among isolated T cell clones, en masse comparisons of recoded T cells to cloned control T cells failed to reveal any significant differences in infection levels. Consistent with an overall fitness advantage provided by DNA integration in speckle-associated domains, which was ablated by recoding across cell types, HIV-1 replicated more robustly in control T cell populations. Single-round infection, in addition to spreading replication, was reduced in recoded myeloid/macrophage cells, which correlated with reductions in reverse transcription, and more robust blocks to HIV-1 nuclear import. Recoded monocytes/macrophages, however, did not reveal any evidence for enhanced type I interferon production or sensing of HIV-1 nucleic acids. Altogether, we define endogenously recoded cell lines to uncouple capsid binding from CPSF6’s role in RNA metabolism, which highlights a global fitness advantage of targeted DNA integration and cell type-specific roles for CPSF6 in HIV-1 reverse transcription, nuclear import, and virus replication proficiency. IMPORTANCE HIV-1 usurps cellular factors to effectively replicate and avoid innate immune sensing. HIV-1 capsid binds CPSF6, but the consequences of this virus-host interaction on HIV-1 biology are necessarily complicated by the cellular role of CPSF6 in pre-RNA processing. By endogenously recoding CPSF6 to selectively disrupt capsid binding while preserving its RNA-processing activity, we demonstrate in two different T cell lines that CPSF6-mediated targeting of HIV-1 DNA integration into nuclear speckle-associated domains correlates with optimal viral replication. Recoded THP-1 myeloid/macrophage cells revealed additional single-round and multi-round infection defects, which correlated with reductions in reverse transcription and HIV-1 nuclear import. These defects, however, did not correlate with enhanced type I interferon production or detection of HIV-1 nucleic acids by known innate immune sensors. Our work clarifies diverse roles for the capsid-CPSF6 interaction in HIV-1 infection of T lymphocytic versus myeloid cell lines and provides novel cell reagents for future research studies.

works.title: Decoding microbial diversity in roots of rice plants under flooded conditions: influence of the host genotype, root compartment, and mycorrhizal association
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Rice is a vital staple for more than half of the world’s population, uniquely adapted to grow under flooded conditions. Our current understanding of root-associated microbiomes in rice plants under flooded conditions (anaerobic rice) is, however, limited. While rice plants are capable of establishing symbiotic associations with arbuscular mycorrhizal (AM) fungi, also under flooded conditions, little is known about the impact that mycorrhizal associations might have on the root microbiome. Here, we used metagenomic sequencing to characterize the root-associated microbiomes of cultivated rice grown under flooded conditions. The root endosphere and rhizosphere compartments were found to harbor distinct microbial communities, with bacterial taxa comprising approximately 95% of the total microbial community. At the phylum level, the root bacteriome was primarily composed of Pseudomonadota (Alphaproteobacteria, Betaproteobacteria, and Gammaproteobacteria), followed by Actinomycetota. The fungal microbiome was dominated by Ascomycota (Sordariomycetes, Eurotiomycetes, and Dothideomycetes) and Basidiomycota. Both root compartment and host genotype significantly influenced microbiome composition, with most genotype-specific recruitment occurring at the species level. These associations were further reshaped in plants pre-inoculated with the AM fungus Rhizophagus irregularis . Co-occurrence networks revealed a genotype-dependent effect in the complexity of microbial taxa in mycorrhizal rice plants. Key microbial species primarily involved in methane production and nutrient cycling (e.g., phosphate-solubilizing bacteria and nitrogen-cycling bacteria) residing in roots of flooded rice were identified. Functional analysis of gene abundance related to those microbial communities revealed compartmentalization, with nutrient-cycling bacteria being more prevalent at the endosphere. Overall, this study demonstrated that the rice genotype, root compartment, and mycorrhizal condition shape the root microbiome in rice plants, ultimately influencing holobiont dynamics in flooded rice fields. IMPORTANCE Plant roots harbor a large diversity of microorganisms that strongly influence plant health and improve stress tolerance. Among them, root colonization by arbuscular mycorrhizal (AM) fungi enhances mineral nutrition and mitigates environmental stress. Although most rice cultivated worldwide is grown under anaerobic conditions (flooded fields), investigation of microbial communities inhabiting root-associated compartments of flooded rice, including AM fungi, has received only little attention. Here, we demonstrated that the rice genotype, root compartment, and mycorrhizal condition markedly influence the microbiome in roots of rice plants in flooded conditions, thus illustrating the potential of the rice plant to shape its root-associated microbiome. Differential root-associated microbiomes of commercial rice varieties include microbes primarily associated with methane production and nutrient cycling. Elucidation of factors influencing root-associated microbiomes in flooded rice systems, including their association with AM fungi, offers practical guidance for exploiting root-associated microbial communities for sustainable rice cultivation while reducing reliance on agrochemicals.

works.title: A temperate phage acts as a symbiotic fitness enhancer for UPEC but surrenders to combination therapy through lysogeny suppression
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Temperate phages are increasingly recognized as key drivers of bacterial evolution. Here, we isolated a myoviral prophage, vB_EcoM_P899, from a clinical uropathogenic Escherichia coli (UPEC) isolate and characterized how lysogenization shapes host biology. Lysogenization significantly enhanced biofilm formation, swarming motility, oxidative stress resistance, and adhesion to macrophages (up to 100-fold) without altering antibiotic susceptibility or overall 72-h lethality in the Galleria mellonella larval infection model. Mechanistically, this is associated with upregulation of the fimbrial gene FimA and enhanced inducibility of the oxidative stress response genes KatE and OxyR under oxidative stress. Crucially, combining P899 with ciprofloxacin or kanamycin produced synergistic killing and suppressed new lysogen formation in an antibiotic-class-dependent manner. In contrast, ceftazidime, while synergistic, failed to prevent lysogeny. Our findings demonstrate that while prophage vB_EcoM_P899 promotes bacterial niche adaptation, its lysogenization frequency is significantly reduced under specific antibiotic pressure, facilitating clearance of the challenged UPEC population. This work provides a strong rationale for optimizing phage–antibiotic combination therapies to treat drug-resistant infections by simultaneously enhancing bacterial killing and limiting lysogenic survivors. IMPORTANCE This study reveals that lysogenization by a temperate phage can enhance the niche adaptation of uropathogenic Escherichia coli without increasing its virulence in the Galleria mellonella larval model or altering antibiotic resistance. Crucially, we demonstrate that combining this phage with select antibiotics (e.g., kanamycin and ciprofloxacin) not only kills the bacteria effectively but also actively suppresses the formation of new lysogens in an antibiotic-class-dependent manner. These findings uncover a novel role for temperate phages as symbiotic regulators within the host and provide direct experimental evidence for a phage–antibiotic combination strategy. This approach holds promise for combating chronic, recurrent urinary tract infections and offers a clinically viable pathway to address antibiotic tolerance in chronic, recurrent urinary tract infections.

works.title: Advancing NTM research with citizen science
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Nontuberculous mycobacteria (NTM) is a generic term for the >200 species of environmental mycobacteria . NTM are ubiquitous, but there is extensive variation in the distribution of individual species. In a recent article published in Applied and Environmental Microbiology , Wilsey et al. describe how community-based citizen science efforts helped map the distribution of NTM in Hawai’i (R. N. Wilsey, L.-H. Ding, S. N. Dawrs, C. K. Raulerson, et al., Appl Environ Microbiol 92:e00269-26, 2026, https://doi.org/10.1128/aem.00269-26 ). Mycobacterium chimaera , an opportunistic pathogen and the leading cause of NTM pulmonary disease in Hawai’i, was among the most common species isolated.

works.title: Phagocytosis of SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid- and RNA-containing immune complexes drives inflammatory cytokine production and endothelial dysfunction
works.abstract: The aberrant inflammation that characterizes severe COVID-19 is incompletely understood. Given the persistence of SARS-Cov-2 RNA and nucleocapsid protein (N) and the presence of anti-N antibody during the course of severe infection, we investigated the role of RNA-containing immune complexes (ICs) in driving inflammation. We found that ICs consisting of SARS-CoV-2 RNA, N, and anti-N IgG1 are internalized by primary human monocytes and stimulate inflammatory cytokines and chemokines in a manner dependent on Fcγ receptors and partially dependent on Toll-Like Receptor-(TLR)8. In addition, the inflammatory response induced in monocytes by RNA-containing ICs caused endothelial dysfunction in vascularized micro-organs. Using nasopharyngeal samples from SARS-CoV-2-infected individuals, SARS-CoV-2 RNA and N were captured by anti-N monoclonal antibody in the absence of lysing agents, indicating that SARS-CoV-2 RNA and N complexes are present outside of virions and cells. Finally, we found that during an early wave of COVID-19, higher anti-N IgG:IgM ratios were associated with more severe clinical outcomes, consistent with a role for inflammatory, IgG-mediated phagocytic clearance of nucleic acid-containing ICs in SARS-CoV-2 pathogenesis, perhaps mitigated by non-inflammatory, IgM-mediated clearance. We conclude that RNA-containing ICs may play a role in the pathogenesis of severe COVID-19. Since all pathogenic viruses encode nucleic acid-binding proteins such as N, and these proteins often elicit an antibody response, inflammatory clearance of nucleic acid-containing ICs may also contribute to disease severity in other viral infections.

works.title: Type III CI factors from wAlbB induce cytoplasmic incompatibility via a Host Modification mechanism
works.abstract: The widespread prevalence of the endosymbiotic bacterium Wolbachia among insect species relies on its ability to invade and manipulate host reproduction via several ways, among which cytoplasmic incompatibility (CI) is most studied. Two non-mutually exclusive models, the Host-Modification (HM) and the Toxin-Antidote (TA), have been proposed to explain the molecular basis of CI. Here, we investigate the CI-inducing activity of the Type III CI factors (cifs) from wAlbB, a strain currently being deployed to combat mosquito-borne diseases. This set of Cifs displays conserved subcellular localization dynamics in various insect cells. Both cifA and cifB are required for the induction of DNA damage in cultured cells, and transgenic Drosophila. Moreover, these cifs induce CI in Drosophila through the two-by-one manner, meaning cifA and cifB act together during spermatogenesis to induce CI, and maternal cifA can reverse the effect. Mechanistically, genetic, biochemical, cellular, and proteomic analyses reveal that this pair of cifs acts during the early stage of spermatogenesis but is dispensable in late-stage germline cells for CI induction. Collectively, our findings support the notion that wAlbB Type III cifs induce CI via a HM-based mechanism. Additional analyses suggest that different Wolbachia strains may employ distinct molecular mechanisms to induce CI.

works.title: Impact of ESKAPE pathogens on the One Health framework considering epidemiology and environmental occurrence
authors: Patrícia Alexandra Curado Quintas D Poeta
works.abstract: SUMMARYThe ESKAPE group of pathogens represents one of the most critical threats to global health due to their capacity to evade antimicrobial treatments. This review provides a structured synthesis of the literature addressing antimicrobial resistance mechanisms, epidemiological relevance, clinical impact, and emerging strategies for containment within a One Health framework. Relevant studies and surveillance reports were analyzed to characterize the global distribution and burden of these organisms across human, animal, and environmental settings. The evidence indicates that ESKAPE pathogens remain leading causes of healthcare-associated infections while increasingly being identified in non-clinical reservoirs, highlighting the interconnected nature of antimicrobial resistance. Recent findings point to sustained high morbidity and mortality associated with these pathogens, driven by the expansion of multidrug-resistant lineages, and the limited effectiveness of current therapeutic options. Key challenges identified include gaps in surveillance integration, the spread of resistance determinants across sectors, and variability in infection control practices. Addressing these issues requires coordinated strategies that integrate surveillance, antimicrobial stewardship, infection prevention, and the development of novel therapeutics within a comprehensive One Health approach.

works.title: Iron limitation reduces diatom carbon flow to bacteria through shifts in exometabolite consumption
works.abstract: Iron is required for photosynthesis and thus affects carbon fixation rates in widespread aquatic regions where availability is limited. Turnover of aquatic photosynthetically derived fixed carbon is largely constrained by bacterial activity, but it is unknown how algal iron limitation alters dissolved organic matter composition and subsequent processing through the microbial loop. We examined a bacterial community dependent on carbon from the diatom Phaeodactylum tricornutum to investigate how iron limitation alters bacterial carbon processing. By quantifying activity at single-cell-resolution with nanoSIMS, we found that iron limitation led to a 43% reduction in carbon-fixation but an 80% reduction in carbon transfer into bacterial biomass. Ultra-high-resolution exometabolomics revealed that iron limitation led to bacterial consumption of less labile compounds including aromatics, specific lipids, and nucleobases. A population of bacteria specific to the iron-deplete condition exhibited high anabolic activity yet low incorporation of newly fixed carbon, supporting a shift to consumption of compounds with longer residence times. From metagenome assembled genomes we identified candidate taxa and gene pathways responsible for this carbon processing shift. These results provide a mechanistic link between decreased carbon flow to bacteria under iron limitation and consumption of less labile exometabolites responsible for this decreased flow. This has implications for predicting organic matter composition and turnover in iron deplete surface oceans and manipulating algal-bacterial interactions in engineered systems.

works.title: Listeria monocytogenes favors the vacuolar compartment during ex vivo human placental infections
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Listeria monocytogenes poses a serious concern during pregnancy, as these microbes can cross the placental barrier to infect the developing fetus. The pathogen’s intracellular lifecycle has been well characterized in cultured cells, where the internalized bacteria escape short-lived Listeria -containing vacuoles (LCVs), replicate in the cytoplasm, and recruit host actin to generate comet tails that enable their intra- and inter-cellular movement. Whether these events occur during intact human placental infections remains unknown. Through ex vivo placental infections, we characterized the spatiotemporal progression of L. monocytogenes in a physiologically relevant system. We found that the actin-rich structures, which are hallmarks of cultured cell infections, were essentially absent (<1% of L. monocytogenes were associated with actin-rich structures). Instead, the bacteria remained predominantly restricted within LCVs, where they also replicated. Quantitative histological and immunofluorescence analyses showed that 39% of wild-type L. monocytogenes remained within Rab5-positive vacuoles and 44% in Lamp1-positive vacuoles, whereas only 1%–4% were observed in cultured placental cells. Most vacuoles lacked the vATPase and cathepsin B, indicating that placental LCV vacuoles were non-acidified, non-degradative endosomal niches. These results closely phenocopied infections using Δ hly-L. monocytogenes , which do not generate listeriolysin O (LLO), a bacterial toxin crucial for LCV escape. Together, our findings reveal that L. monocytogenes primarily reside within LCVs during ex vivo human placental infections, contrasting the classical in vitro models and emphasizing the importance of studying bacterial pathogenesis in intact human tissues. IMPORTANCE L. monocytogenes infection during pregnancy can result in miscarriage, stillbirth, or severe neonatal disease because the bacterium can cross the placental barrier. Current understanding of L. monocytogenes pathogenesis is largely based on cultured cell models, where bacteria rapidly escape vacuoles, replicate in the cytoplasm, and spread using host actin. By examining infections in intact ex vivo human placental tissue, we show that this paradigm does not accurately reflect a placental infection. Instead, L. monocytogenes remains predominantly within vacuoles that may support bacterial replication, while actin-based motility is rare. Our work provides new insight into placental listeriosis and highlights the importance of studying host-pathogen interactions in physiologically relevant models.

works.title: A putative GtrB-like glycosyltransferase modulates cation-dependent BCP8-2 phage infection and cell surface structure in Bacillus cereus
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Bacillus cereus is a foodborne pathogen of growing concern due to its persistence and antimicrobial resistance. To identify host determinants influencing susceptibility to phage BCP8-2, a mini-Tn 10 transposon mutant library of B. cereus ATCC 14579 was constructed and screened for altered phage susceptibility. A mutant (BC2012) showing partial resistance carried an insertion in BC_RS27090 (previously BC_5432 ), encoding a putative GtrB-like bactoprenol glycosyltransferase. Complementation restored phage sensitivity, confirming its functional involvement. The mutant showed a slight reduction in efficiency of plating, whereas, adsorption assay revealed significantly reduced phage binding and infectivity, particularly under cation-rich conditions. Furthermore, adsorption kinetics and one-step growth curve in mutant supported that gtrB mutation affects initial adsorption. Microscopy showed altered surface morphology with thinner, smoother cell walls. These data indicate that gtrB affects surface properties essential for cation-dependent phage adsorption and infection and provide a foundation for future studies on the role of surface glycosylation and ionic interactions in Gram-positive phage biology. IMPORTANCE Pathogenic Bacillus cereus is resilient across diverse environments and produces diverse toxins linked to foodborne outbreaks. Bacteriophages provide an effective strategy to control B. cereus ; however, molecular targets of phage–host interaction are poorly understood, limiting the effective phage-based control. The current study addresses this gap by identifying a putative bactoprenol glycosyltransferase (GtrB), a viral factor in phage BCP8-2 susceptibility. Data obtained highlight a partial reduction of phage infection in the gtrB mutant, demonstrating that GtrB-like glycosyltransferase significantly contributes to BCP8-2 phage infection and adsorption. Our findings provide significant insights into advancing phage therapy, antibiotic resistance, and B. cereus biocontrol in food and clinical settings.

works.title: Controlled human infection with Plasmodium falciparum-infected mosquito bites elicits antibodies against mosquito salivary protein SG1L3
works.abstract: Human malaria infections begin with the injection of Plasmodium sporozoites via mosquito saliva. Whole sporozoite immunizations have been used as a model to study immune responses to malaria parasites, having culminated in circumsporozoite protein (CSP)-targeting vaccines and monoclonal antibodies (mAbs). However, antibody responses targeting non-CSP antigens on the sporozoite surface remain poorly characterized. Here, we isolated single B cells from a human volunteer immunized by Plasmodium falciparum-infected mosquito bites, who had acquired non-CSP-specific antibodies that recognize sporozoites. We identified two mAbs that recognize the surface of P. falciparum sporozoites, but do not bind to CSP. Using immunoprecipitation followed by mass-spectrometry, we found that the target of these mAbs is not a P. falciparum protein but the mosquito salivary protein SG1L3. We observed that recombinant SG1L3 binds to P. falciparum sporozoites. However, the SG1L3-specific mAbs and SG1L3-specific polyclonal antibodies from this volunteer, as well as polyclonal antibodies raised against recombinant SG1L3 in rabbits, fail to block liver stage infection in vitro, making this an unlikely target for functional antibodies. We observed that inhabitants from an area with intense Anopheles exposure in Burkina Faso can have antibodies against SG1L3, and that antibody titers increase with age. In conclusion, we identified the first human mAbs against a mosquito saliva protein that binds to the surface of sporozoites. Future work should assess whether naturally acquired antibodies against this protein may be used as a serological marker of mosquito exposure.

works.title: MUCOR-ADVANCE: Uniting multidisciplinary science to defeat a deadly fungus
Defective viral genomes of porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome virus type 2: Generation, characterization and interference effects on viral replication
works.abstract: Porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome virus type 2 (PRRSV-2) is a major swine pathogen that causes substantial economic losses worldwide. Defective viral genomes (DVGs) are important regulators of viral replication, persistence, and evolution in many RNA viruses. However, the characteristics and functions of DVGs generated during PRRSV-2 infection remain unknown. Here, we systematically analyzed publicly available high-throughput sequencing datasets and characterized DVGs generated during both in vitro and in vivo PRRSV-2 infection. We found that PRRSV-2 preferentially generates large deletion DVGs, particularly in porcine alveolar macrophages (PAMs), and that DVG formation is associated with microhomology sequences, RNA secondary structure and AU-rich sequences. Break positions were enriched in the GP5/M genomic region, whereas rejoin positions clustered predominantly within the nsp1/nsp2 genomic region of the PRRSV-2 genome. Notably, the deletion events within the same gene were highly enriched in the nsp2 region, where multiple naturally occurring nsp2 deletion sites overlapped with DVG junction sites. These findings suggest that DVG-associated recombination may contribute to the formation of PRRSV-2 nsp2 deletion variants. Functionally, PRRSV-2-derived DVGs exhibited potent broad-spectrum antiviral activity against multiple prevalent PRRSV-2 lineage strains and PRRSV-1. Overall, our findings provide the first systematic characterization of PRRSV-2 DVGs, reveal a potential evolutionary link between DVGs and nsp2 deletion variants, and highlight the antiviral potential of PRRSV-2 DVGs.

works.title: Magic pathways: the genes and enzymes of psilocybin biosynthesis
works.abstract: SUMMARY Species of several mushroom genera, among them Psilocybe and Inocybe , biosynthesize psilocybin, the prodrug to the powerful psychotropic and perception-altering analog, psilocin. While “magic” mushrooms are popular as recreational drugs, advanced clinical trials have shown that psilocybin is a valuable future (and, in some countries, available) medication against depression and anxiety. In this review article, we focus on the metabolic processes leading to psilocybin in the fungal cell and present the biosynthetic enzymes, their structures, and the reactions catalyzed. Remarkably, mushrooms have evolved psilocybin biosynthesis twice independently, involving genes and enzymes that are only distantly related or unrelated altogether. We also present routes on how this iconic natural product can be made biocatalytically in vitro or in heterologous hosts in vivo . Despite substantial progress in psilocybin research over the past decade, we present unsolved questions that remain for the current and the next generation of researchers.

works.title: Spatial recovery and persistence of Pseudomonas chlororaphis M71 and Trichoderma atroviride SC1 in grapevine following stem injection
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Establishing biocontrol agents (BCAs) within grapevine tissues could provide a means of protecting internal plant compartments, but little is known about their spatial and temporal fate after vascular delivery or whether the graft union constrains their distribution. We compared the internal recovery of two biologically contrasting BCAs, the bacterium Pseudomonas chlororaphis M71 and the filamentous fungus Trichoderma atroviride SC1, following controlled stem injection into rooted and grafted grapevine plants. A xylem-mobile dye was used as a reference for immediate passive fluid transport, while viable microbial recovery was assessed over time and complemented by quantitative isolation and microscopy. At 48 h, the dye generally showed broader longitudinal distribution than either of the microorganisms. The two microorganisms displayed markedly different patterns. M71 persisted for up to 56 days, but remained predominantly associated with tissues close to the injection site. In contrast, SC1 was recovered from a broader range of tissues, including roots, and remained detectable for up to 56 days. In grafted plants, both microorganisms were recovered on both sides of the graft union, indicating that the graft interface was not an absolute barrier, although recovery depended on microbial identity and inoculation position. Green fluorescent protein-labeled M71 cells and SC1 hyphae were observed within xylem vessels, confirming internal localization and, for SC1, vegetative development after injection. These results show that, and how, both microbial biology and grafted-plant architecture influence the internal fate of injected BCAs in grapevine. IMPORTANCE Beneficial microorganisms established inside grapevine tissues could potentially protect from infections regarding internal tissues, but little is known about how such microorganisms distribute and persist inside grapevine after injection into the plant tissues. This study shows that two biocontrol agents (BCAs) with contrasting biological characteristics follow markedly different spatial and temporal patterns. Pseudomonas chlororaphis M71 persisted mainly near the site of introduction, whereas Trichoderma atroviride SC1 was recovered from a broader range of tissues and developed hyphae within xylem vessels. Importantly, the graft union was not an absolute barrier to microbial recovery. These findings provide a framework for selecting where and when BCAs should be introduced during grapevine propagation and highlight that vascular access, persistence, and broad within-plant establishment are distinct properties that should be considered when developing endophytic biocontrol strategies.

works.title: Combined application of Pseudomonas chlororaphis strains and zinc suppresses Alternaria alternata leaf spot in chili pepper
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Chili pepper ( Capsicum annuum L.) is a vital vegetable crop susceptible to yield loss from Alternaria alternata (Fr.), Keissl., which causes leaf spot/blight and fruit rot. Harnessing beneficial rhizobacteria offers an eco-friendly strategy to enhance plant resilience to biotic stressors. In vitro screening identified Pseudomonas chlororaphis strains viz., P. chlororaphis subsp. aurantiaca (ARS-38) and P. chlororaphis subsp. chlororaphis (RP-4) as potent antifungal strains, inhibiting A. alternata growth by 62% and 64%, respectively. In a zinc (Zn)-amended medium, their antifungal activity increased further, reducing fungal growth by 70% with individual strains and 93% when combined. Microscopy revealed fungal growth inhibition linked to conidia and conidiophore disintegration. In planta under open-field pot conditions, A. alternata infection resulted in 100% disease incidence (DI) and altered histochemical, photosynthetic, and enzyme responses. Treatment with ARS-38 + RP-4 in Zn-amended soil enhanced plant resistance by increasing lignin and phenolic accumulation and reducing enzyme activities, resulting in a 96% reduction in DI. Zinc supplementation improved plant health and enhanced disease suppression when combined with the bacterial strains. Combining rhizobacteria with Zn (2 mg/kg) emerges as a promising strategy to mitigate Alternaria leaf spot disease and enhance biostress tolerance in chili plants. IMPORTANCE Biological control offers a sustainable approach for reducing fungal diseases while limiting reliance on chemical fungicides. This study shows that two Pseudomonas chlororaphis strains, ARS-38 and RP-4, combined with low-level zinc supplementation, strongly suppress Alternaria alternata , an important chili pepper pathogen. The combined treatment reduced fungal growth in vitro and substantially decreased disease development in plants while improving structural, physiological, and biochemical responses associated with plant health. The findings demonstrate the potential value of integrating beneficial rhizobacteria with micronutrient supplementation for sustainable disease management and provide a basis for further development of microbial–micronutrient strategies for crop protection.

works.title: Anaerobic microorganisms alter heavy oil chemistry by oxygenation and sulfurization
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Microbial transformation of heavy oil under anoxic conditions involves complex changes in hydrocarbon and heteroatom-containing molecular compositions. However, the molecular-level evolution of sulfur-containing compounds and their relationship to hydrocarbon transformation remain insufficiently resolved. In this study, long-term anaerobic microcosms containing heavy oil from Pitch Lake, Trinidad and Tobago, were analyzed using Fourier transform ion cyclotron resonance mass spectrometry (FT-ICR MS) and microbial community profiling to evaluate temporal changes in molecular compositions and microbiota structure over 945 days of incubation. FT-ICR MS detected 4,499 molecular formulas dominated by CHO-, CHNO-, CHOS-, and CHNOS-class formulas. Pronounced compositional shifts occurred during incubation, with sulfur-containing molecular formulas becoming increasingly abundant and resulting in a marked increase in CHOS-class formulas over time. Intensity-weighted elemental formulas showed increasing oxygen and sulfur abundances, while the average m / z increased from 344 at day 93 to 366 at day 945, corresponding to an approximately 6.4% increase in the intensity-weighted average molecular mass. Multivariate analyses revealed distinct temporal clustering of samples and parallel shifts in microbial community composition, depicting a greater contribution of anaerobic and sulfur-associated taxa. Correlation analyses further showed associations between microbial community shifts and increasing abundances of oxidized sulfur-containing compounds, particularly CHSO 3 - and CHSO 4 -class formulas. These findings indicate substantial reorganization of the heteroatom-containing molecular pool during anoxic incubation and highlight the potential roles of microbial and sulfur-related processes in the transformation of heavy oil under anoxic conditions. IMPORTANCE Heavy oil reservoirs contain complex mixtures of hydrocarbons and heteroatom-containing compounds that undergo transformation under anoxic conditions. Characterizing the molecular-level changes occurring during these transformations is important for understanding hydrocarbon biodegradation, the persistence of recalcitrant compounds, and the formation and fate of organic sulfur species in oil reservoirs. Using Fourier transform ion cyclotron resonance mass spectrometry (FT-ICR MS) and microbial community analyses, this study reveals that long-term anaerobic incubation drives enrichment of CHOS-class formulas, reduced microbial diversity, and shifts toward anaerobic, sulfur-associated taxa. These findings demonstrate that microbial and sulfur-driven processes play a key role in reorganizing oil chemistry and suggest that co-metabolic activity contributes to the accumulation of partially transformed sulfur-containing compounds. By directly linking changes in microbial community composition with ultrahigh-resolution molecular characterization, this work provides important new insights into the microbial and chemical mechanisms controlling heavy oil transformation and sulfur metabolism in subsurface oil reservoirs.

works.title: AspA activity orchestrates a growth-stress survival trade-off in Yersinia pestis via metabolic reprogramming
works.abstract: ABSTRACT The aspA gene of Yersinia pestis exhibits a pronounced polymorphism at codon 363, with the dominant TTG allele encoding an inactive aspartate ammonia-lyase (AspA) while the GTG allele encoding an active enzyme. We previously demonstrated that this polymorphism drives an environment-dependent fitness trade-off, yet the underlying mechanism remains unclear. To address this, we first characterized the phenotypic differences between the two strains and revealed a clear growth-stress survival trade-off: the GTG (AspA-active) strain grew faster and produced more ATP, whereas the TTG (AspA-inactive) strain, despite slower growth, exhibited superior survival under nutrient limitation with oxidative, anaerobic, or hyperosmotic stress. Exogenous aspartate reversed the GTG strain’s disadvantages under anaerobic or cold stress. To dissect the metabolic basis, we performed 13 C-labeled metabolic flux analysis on these two strains. The GTG strain rapidly converted aspartate to fumarate via AspA, fueling the TCA cycle and boosting ATP production. In contrast, the TTG strain displayed stalled aspartate utilization and accumulated amino acids and lipids. Supplementation with TCA cycle intermediates (fumarate, succinate, or malate) partially rescued TTG growth, confirming that reduced TCA flux limits its proliferation. Collectively, AspA activity orchestrates a growth-stress survival trade-off through metabolic reprogramming, underlying the antagonistic pleiotropy of Y. pestis in aspartate-available or stressful environments. The “metabolic congestion” strategy of the TTG strain enhances survival under multiple stresses relevant to the flea gut, and it is plausible that this metabolic reprogramming may contribute to transmission and provide a selective advantage under flea-borne conditions. IMPORTANCE The plague bacterium Yersinia pestis encounters oxidative, anaerobic, and hyperosmotic stresses—conditions relevant to its flea gut environment during transmission. This study reveals that a single, naturally occurring polymorphism in the aspA gene shifts the bacterium’s metabolism from a growth-focused mode to a “metabolic congestion” state that enhances survival under these stresses in vitro . Our work provides a mechanistic framework for understanding how metabolic reprogramming could influence adaptation to vector-like conditions, offering a plausible basis for the environment-dependent fitness trade-offs that may shape transmission dynamics.

works.title: Acetate scavenging and aromatic funneling of lignocellulose-derived carbon in the denitrifier Pseudomonas veronii
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Lignocellulose degradation and denitrification frequently co-occur in soils and sediments with fluctuating or limited O 2 availability, yet the ability of facultative denitrifiers to couple aromatic carbon turnover to nitrate respiration remains poorly understood. Here, we characterized a novel isolate, Pseudomonas veronii strain B19, for its genetic potential and physiological performance during growth on hemicellulose- and lignin-derived substrates under oxic and denitrifying conditions. Genome analysis revealed extensive aromatic catabolic pathways, including a complete β-ketoadipate route funneling lignin-derived compounds to central metabolism. Despite lacking classical endo-xylanases, the strain grew on acetylated xylan, with faster denitrification kinetics than on glucose. Proteomic and electron flow analyses indicate that xylan utilization proceeds via deacetylation and acetate assimilation through acetyl-CoA. Notably, the carbon source governed the denitrification regulatory phenotype: glucose elicited bet hedging and transient nitrite accumulation at the oxic–anoxic transition, whereas xylan-derived acetate supported a seamless transition to denitrification. On alkali-solubilized lignin, the strain utilized soluble monoaromatic compounds under both oxic and denitrifying conditions. Oxic metabolism proceeded through strong induction of O 2 -dependent mono- and dioxygenases, enabling extensive aromatic catabolism, whereas under denitrifying conditions, conversion was only partial, with vanillate accumulation and electron-limited but stoichiometrically efficient nitrate reduction at minimal N 2 O formation. Together, these findings demonstrate that B19 links lignocellulose-derived carbon turnover to denitrification under limited O 2 , prioritizing electron flux over carbon yield. Its preference for soluble, low-molecular-weight lignin fractions and converging catabolic pathways indicate a role in downstream turnover of already-depolymerized lignin-derived aromatics, consistent with biological funneling and relevant to lignin valorization. IMPORTANCE Denitrification and the breakdown of plant-derived carbon are central to nitrogen and carbon cycling in soils and sediments, yet how these processes intersect when oxygen is scarce is poorly understood. Most denitrifiers are thought to rely on simple carbon sources, while the breakdown of polymeric lignin is considered oxygen-dependent. Here, we show that the facultative anaerobe Pseudomonas veronii B19 couples the turnover of acetylated hemicellulose and soluble, low-molecular-weight lignin-derived aromatics to denitrification, sustaining respiration under oxygen limitation by prioritizing electron flux over carbon yield. Notably, the carbon source itself dictated the organism’s denitrification behavior, switching it between distinct regulatory strategies. By resolving these mechanisms in a single isolate, this work clarifies how facultative denitrifiers may process depolymerized plant carbon and shape nitrogen gas emissions in oxygen-limited environments, and identifies traits relevant to the downstream microbial valorization of lignin-derived aromatics.

works.title: A cryptic lactate cycle in CO fermentation by Clostridium ljungdahlii
works.abstract: ABSTRACT The valorization of C1 gases presents a route toward the utilization of industrial waste gases as resources. Acetogens such as Clostridium ljungdahlii serve as promising microbial cell factories for light-independent carbon fixation and high-value compound production, yet their efficiency is often limited by energy constraints and poorly understood metabolic pathways. Here, we investigated lactate metabolism in C. ljungdahlii during carbon monoxide (CO) fermentation via growth and product profiling, 13 C-labeling, gene knockouts, and transcriptomics. Although lactate cannot serve as the sole source of carbon and energy for C. ljungdahlii ’s growth, we found that lactate can be co-fermented with CO into acetate. 13 C-tracing further revealed concurrent lactate production and oxidation during CO fermentation, with the unlabeled lactate fraction increasing from 1.0% (day 2) to 5.0% (day 6), indicating the existence of an active lactate cycle. Genetic and transcriptional analyses showed that lactate production and oxidation were catalyzed by two distinct lactate dehydrogenases: LdhA (CLJU_RS15865) and the electron-bifurcating Ldh/EtfAB_1 complex (CLJU_RS10590–CLJU_RS10600), respectively. Disruption of the lactate cycle, particularly in the Ldh/EtfAB_1 mutant, improved energy metabolism and triggered intracellular metabolic rearrangements. This mutant produced approximately 10-fold more lactate and shifted the acetate/ethanol ratio from 3.7:1 to 2.1:1, accompanied by upregulation of the AOR (aldehyde:ferredoxin oxidoreductase)-mediated ethanol production pathway. Subsequent ldhA overexpression further elevated lactate titer to ~2.5 mM, confirming the potential for lactate production from CO. The results imply that the cryptic lactate cycle dissipates energy but aids in intracellular redox balancing during CO fermentation. These findings provide new insights into the metabolic engineering of acetogens to produce target compounds, such as lactate and ethanol. IMPORTANCE Acetogens possess a natural carbon fixation pathway, the Wood-Ljungdahl pathway, enabling them to fix CO or CO2 to produce acetate. Among various acetogens, Clostridium ljungdahlii exhibits strong tolerance to CO and thus holds great application potential for the resource utilization of syngas. However, the physiological and metabolic mechanisms underlying its autotrophic fermentation remain incompletely understood, which imposes limitations on metabolic engineering efforts. In this study, we systematically investigated lactate metabolism in C. ljungdahlii and revealed the existence of a cryptic lactate cycle during CO fermentation. By characterizing this cycle’s operation and its impacts on energy metabolism and carbon distribution, we elucidated its potential physiological functions. These findings not only expand our understanding of the physiological and metabolic behaviors of acetogens during autotrophic fermentation but also provide theoretical guidance for the future metabolic engineering of lactate, ethanol, and other compounds.

works.title: Development of improved host-vector system for enhanced production of santalene isoforms in Azospirillum brasilense
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Azospirillum brasilense is a non-photosynthetic bacterium that possesses the ability to produce carotenoids, in which squalene is a critical intermediate of the carotenoid biosynthetic pathway. Farnesyl pyrophosphate (FPP) serves as a precursor for the production of sesquiterpenoids; hence, its availability is a major bottleneck in the microbial biosynthesis of several major plant sesquiterpenes. We improved the utility of A. brasilense Cd for the heterologous production of sesquiterpenes by enhancing intracellular availability of FPP and disrupted the chromosomal hpnC gene to block the squalene biosynthetic pathway to decrease a competing sink for FPP, along with the introduction of the heterologous Escherichia coli ispA gene, together with additional copies of the native A. brasilense dxps and crtE genes. These genetic manipulations, along with the expression of codon-harmonized santalene synthase from Santalum album, enabled an increase in the production of α -santalene by 50-fold, α-exo -bergamotene by 20-fold, and β -santalene by 10-fold in A. brasilense Cd. Additionally, we developed a fructose-inducible santalene synthase expression system, which may be more efficient and economical than the isopropyl β-D-1-thiogalactopyranoside-inducible system. Finally, by cloning and expressing genes encoding cytochrome P450 monooxygenase and its cognate NADPH-cytochrome P450 reductase, we have shown the potential of A. brasilense to produce santalols, the most desired ingredient of sandalwood oil. IMPORTANCE Sandalwood oil is among the most valuable natural fragrances and is also known for its diverse biological activities. The biosynthesis of santalene, a major constituent of sandalwood oil, originates from the universal precursors isopentenyl diphosphate (IPP) and dimethylallyl diphosphate (DMAPP) via the MEP pathway. This pathway is naturally present in Azospirillum brasilense , a plant growth-promoting rhizobacterium, making it a suitable host for the heterologous production of sesquiterpenes. This study has shown the possibility of using A. brasilense as a promising host-vector system for enhancing the production of santalene isomers by several fold. It has also shown the superiority of a fructose-inducible system over the isopropyl β-D-1-thiogalactopyranoside-inducible system for the industrial production of high-value secondary metabolites in this bacterium.

works.title: Oxidation of Fe(II) by nitrate-reducing Fe(II)-oxidizers enriched from Fe(III)-rich microbial mats of an extreme acidic river (Río Tinto, Spain)
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Nitrate-reducing Fe(II)-oxidizing (NRFeOx) microorganisms have been detected in the subsurface of the Iberian Pyrite Belt (Spain), where the Río Tinto originates. However, it is not known whether NRFeOx microorganisms are present in the Fe(III)-rich microbial mats that developed within the surface waters where the river originates, and the geochemical conditions progressively shift from circumneutral to highly acidic. Moreover, it is not known what the main (microbial) Fe(II) oxidation pathway is under in situ pH conditions. To answer these questions, we (i) analyzed the in situ bacterial community and Fe mineralogy of the Fe(III)-rich microbial mats, (ii) set up NRFeOx enrichment cultures (either with NO 3 − /Fe 2+ aq or acetate/NO 3 − /Fe 2+ aq ), and (iii) evaluated denitrification and Fe(II) oxidation capabilities of the NRFeOx enrichments under in situ pH conditions. We found that the microbial mat was composed mainly of poorly crystalline minerals, such as ferrihydrite and schwertmannite, with the microaerophilic Fe(II)-oxidizing genus Gallionella (18.3% ± 4.9% DNA-based and 10.8% ± 1.9% RNA-based relative 16S rRNA [gene] abundances) being the main bacteria present and active. NRFeOx was only observed in the enrichment culture amended with acetate/NO 3 − /Fe 2+ aq , where Rhodoblastus (between 73.1% and 91.0% DNA-based) was the main enriched genus. The production of nitrite in the Rhodoblastus-dominated culture suggested that chemodenitrification, i.e., the abiotic oxidation of Fe(II) by nitrite, was the main Fe(II) oxidation pathway at pH between 6.2 and 7. However, under more acidic conditions (pH 5.8), nitrate reduction still occurred without Fe(II) oxidation. Overall, this study suggests that NRFeOx microorganisms present in the Río Tinto microbial mats may couple NO 3 − reduction to Fe(II) oxidation in anoxic circumneutral microniches where nitrate and organic carbon are also available. IMPORTANCE The potential role of nitrate-reducing Fe(II)-oxidizing (NRFeOx) microorganisms in subsurface pyrite weathering and the formation of acid mine drainage environments, such as the Río Tinto river, is still poorly understood. By focusing on Fe(III)-rich microbial mats formed at the interface between anoxic Fe(II)-rich groundwater and oxic conditions, this study addresses how NRFeOx microorganisms contribute to nitrogen, iron, and carbon cycling in this acidic environment. Moreover, identifying and enriching NRFeOx microorganisms adapted to low pH can deepen our understanding of their metabolic versatility and resilience. These insights extend beyond characterizing the origin of Río Tinto by informing models of acidic rock drainage generation, guiding bioremediation strategies for the simultaneous removal of nitrate and heavy metals from contaminated waters, and providing analogs for potential microbial life in iron-rich, anoxic extraterrestrial environments such as early Mars.

works.title: From CBASS and Thoeris to Panoptes: Phage sponges and the inversion of bacterial immunity
MARK3 promotes host antiviral defense by driving GEF-H1–mediated TBK1 activation
