works.abstract: Innate immunity constitutes the body's first line of defense against pathogenic challenge, serving not only as a physical and cellular bulwark that rapidly curbs microbial proliferation but also as the essential rheostat that orchestrates downstream adaptive immune responses. Here, we identified MARK3, a serine/threonine protein kinase of the conserved MARK family, as a crucial regulator of innate antiviral immunity that promotes type I interferon (IFN-I) production in a kinase-dependent manner. Using both in vitro and in vivo models, we demonstrate that MARK3 exerts broad-spectrum antiviral activity via a signaling axis involving GEF-H1 and TBK1. Mechanistically, MARK3 directly interacts with GEF-H1 and phosphorylates it at Ser645. This phosphorylation event potentiates the activation of TBK1, leading to enhanced IRF3 phosphorylation. Activated IRF3 then translocates to the nucleus, where it triggers potent IFN-I induction and the downstream expression of interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs). Our study establishes MARK3 as an important antiviral kinase and defines the MARK3-GEF-H1-TBK1 axis as a novel signaling pathway driving interferon-mediated antiviral defense.

works.title: Author Correction: Phage therapy: from basic biology to clinical application
Lack of ancestral SARS-CoV-2 imprinting promotes Omicron sublineage BA.3.2.2 infection in children
works.abstract: The ongoing SARS-CoV-2 evolution is constrained by population-level immune imprinting. Recent genomic surveillance revealed an unexpected demographic shift with the Omicron sublineage BA.3.2.2 being predominant in paediatric populations globally. Here we show that this paediatric susceptibility arises from the absence of immune imprinting against ancestral SARS-CoV-2 Wuhan strain. Serological analyses reveal a failure to neutralize BA.3.2.2 in young children with no ancestral strain exposure. Single-B-cell sequencing analyses demonstrate that BA.3.2.2 evades Omicron-specific Class 1/4 neutralizing antibodies that target the ACE2-binding site, encoded by immunoglobulin heavy-chain variable (IGHV) germline genes IGHV2-5 and IGHV5-51, which dominate in weakly imprinted individuals. BA.3.2.2 remains susceptible to broadly cross-reactive Class 1 antibodies, encoded by IGHV3-53/66, typically enriched in adults with strong Wuhan-strain imprinting, such as mRNA vaccine recipients. Together, these findings show that classic immune imprinting provides superior protection against a highly divergent variant, explaining the age-biased transmission of BA.3.2.2, and informing future paediatric vaccination strategies. Predominance of the Omicron sublineage BA.3.2.2 in paediatric cohorts results from the absence of vaccine-induced immune imprinting to the ancestral SARS-CoV-2 Wuhan strain, resulting in distinct patterns of immunoglobulin heavy-chain variable region usage in children and adults.

works.title: Bacterial steroid hormones shape coral immunity during heat stress
Structure, function, and evolution of topoisomerase modulatory proteins in bacteria
works.abstract: SUMMARY DNA topoisomerases are essential for maintaining the integrity and functionality of the genome. By homeostatically controlling the genome topology in bacteria, these enzymes influence essential cellular processes such as gene expression, replication, recombination, and chromosome segregation. Although DNA topoisomerases were initially considered to act as stand-alone enzymes, they are now being recognized as integral components of dynamic protein complexes that perform diverse functions in vivo . The discovery of several proteinaceous modulators of DNA topoisomerases has expanded the understanding of their functional versatility. These are encoded either by the bacterial chromosome or extrachromosomal elements like plasmids and bacteriophages. Chromosomally encoded modulators are engaged in fine-tuning topoisomerase activity, enabling them to carry out specialized cellular functions beyond their canonical enzymatic roles. Crucially, they prevent genomic instability that may arise from dysregulated topoisomerase activity. By altering DNA topology, modulatory proteins can influence transcriptional bursting, leading to epigenetic heterogeneity within the bacterial populations, crucial for bacterial stress adaptation. In contrast, topoisomerase interacting proteins encoded by plasmids and phages have dedicated roles in facilitating plasmid maintenance and phage propagation by suppressing host defenses and promoting horizontal gene transfer. We present a comprehensive analysis of the topoisomerase modulatory proteins discovered so far, offering insights into the mechanisms by which DNA topology and homeostasis are maintained within the intracellular environment. We project the potential of topoisomerase modulator-based drug design as a promising strategy for combating multidrug-resistant bacterial pathogens.

works.title: Systems-level orchestration of oxygenic photosynthesis and nitrogen fixation in cyanobacteria
works.abstract: SUMMARYDiazotrophic cyanobacteria represent a unique group of prokaryotes that are capable of performing two physiologically conflicting processes: oxygen-generating photosynthesis and oxygen-sensitive nitrogen fixation. Adaptive evolution over millions of years has culminated in two complex, divergent strategies-spatial and temporal separation-that allow extant cyanobacteria to reconcile these antagonistic pathways. While the long-studied spatial separation strategy utilized by most filamentous strains is well understood at the molecular level, the temporal separation mechanisms in unicellular and non-heterocystous filamentous cyanobacteria remain an expanding but under-reviewed area of research. This review focuses on the orchestration of photosynthesis and nitrogen fixation in cyanobacteria, with an emphasis on temporal separation. We discuss molecular mechanisms driving the synchronization of carbon and nitrogen fixation in filamentous cyanobacteria, highlighting recent findings that elucidate the complex regulatory networks involved in maintaining an optimal C/N balance. In contrast, for unicellular cyanobacteria, where regulatory mechanisms are less defined, we synthesize various discoveries that challenge the prevailing view that these prokaryotes are metabolically disadvantaged by strict diurnal constraints. We review studies that indicate the metabolic plasticity of these strains, potentially conferred by effective oxygen-protective mechanisms, including a robust circadian clock that regulates intracellular oxygen levels. This plasticity allows adaptation to diverse diurnal conditions, preferentially segregating the incompatible processes into opposite phases while also accommodating both processes under light when daylength conditions are suboptimal. Such metabolic flexibility likely predisposes these prokaryotes to be naturally selected for nitrogen-fixing symbioses with eukaryotes and eventually, as recently demonstrated, to evolve into a nitrogen-fixing organelle.

works.title: Ecological and evolutionary dynamics of chlamydiae endosymbionts in social amoeba host communities
works.abstract: Endosymbiotic interactions have played fundamental roles in shaping the evolution of complex eukaryotes. However, how ecological processes shape endosymbioses that are still segregating in host populations have been less described. Here, we characterize the ecological and evolutionary dynamics of chlamydiae bacterial endosymbionts in dictyostelid social amoeba host communities. Our survey of over 1400 host isolates from across a 1200 km range revealed 41 unique chlamydiae haplotypes across 11 different host species, the prevalence of which significantly varied across host species and sampling locations. Patterns of chlamydiae phylogenetic divergence were not associated with geographic dissimilarity but were associated with patterns of host diversification, suggesting a shared evolutionary history and co-dispersal between some symbiont and host lineages. However, relatively few symbiont haplotypes showed both significant host specificity and high prevalence, indicating that most associations are not ecologically meaningful. Nonetheless, our laboratory passaging experiments showed that naturally occurring chlamydiae infections can be vertically transmitted across host generations. Finally, we found overall chlamydiae haplotype diversity was negatively associated with prevalence across host populations, mirroring the classic tension between selection and the influx of neutral variation due to ecological drift and stochastic environmental acquisition. To formalize this observation, we developed a stochastic differential equation model incorporating vertical and environmental symbiont transmission, as well as ecological selection and drift. This model recapitulated the observed diversity-prevalence relationship, and is consistent with a scenario in which most chlamydiae haplotypes are ecologically neutral and stochastically acquired, whereas relatively few are vertically transmitted and selectively relevant within their host populations.

works.title: Comprehensive sequence analysis reveals the vast β-lactam resistome
works.abstract: Most antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) evolved in environmental microbes long before humanity's antibiotic breakthrough, and widespread antibiotic use accelerated the dissemination of ARGs among clinical pathogens. Although environmental ARG classes, such as β-lactamases, are widely discussed, their presence and distribution remain underexplored, with existing studies often lacking the scalability and taxonomic resolution required for comprehensive analysis. In this study, we present a comprehensive map of the β-lactamase resistome using an integrated bioinformatics and experimental workflow. We identify a vast reservoir of putative β-lactamase sequences spanning all four β-lactamase classes—more than 12-fold the number listed in current ARG databases. We generated a β-lactamase taxonomy-environment map by identifying ~ 108,000 putative β-lactamases across diverse bacterial phyla and environmental ecosystems. Notably, the relative frequency of putative β-lactamases was only ~3.9-fold lower than that of the essential recA gene across diverse environmental ecosystems, with signals of relative enrichment observed in wastewater and plant-associated samples. The enrichment in plant-associated and wastewater samples suggests that these environments may represent important reservoirs of putative β-lactamases. We identify taxonomic and environmental contexts that may represent candidate reservoirs of close homologs of clinically relevant β-lactamases, extending beyond wastewater to plant-associated, terrestrial, and aquatic settings. Overall, we present a comprehensive workflow and reusable mapping tool to identify and classify the β-lactamase resistome, revealing its diversity, distribution, and a largely unexplored reservoir with potential for mobilization into clinical pathogens. Video Abstract

works.title: Decoding the metagenome of the precious red coral: discovery of a new spirochete lineage and carotenoid-producing bacteria
works.abstract: Abstract The precious red coral Corallium rubrum is an ecologically and economically iconic Mediterranean octocoral, yet the diversity and functions of its microbiome remain a “blackbox” at the genomic scale. Here, we present a genome-resolved metagenomic analysis of C. rubrum , reconstructing 25 high-quality metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs), including 16 from wild colonies and 9 additional ones from a laboratory colony, to gain insight into the functional potential of its microbiome. Our phylogenomic analysis of the two dominant Spirochaetota symbionts reveals that one of the two symbionts represents a potential novel, previously undescribed lineage, which appears to be exclusively associated with octocoral species. Functional profiling indicates that these Spirochaetota exhibit different metabolic pathways, and are adapted to the symbiotic life, probably representing mutualistic partners for C. rubrum . Their genomes encode biosynthetic pathways of a wide range of essential amino acids and vitamins, and the capacity to ferment sugars to acetate, potentially supplementing host dietary deficiencies. We also identified an interesting symbiont, affiliated with the Qipengyuania genus, that possesses the genomic potential for the biosynthesis of the carotenoid canthaxanthin, one of the main pigments involved in the red color of C. rubrum . The other MAGs encode a wide range of metabolic pathways, especially those linked to nitrogen and sulfur transformations. Our findings suggest potential metabolic interactions between the red coral host and its microbiome. This study offers detailed taxonomic and functional characterization of newly identified octocoral symbionts, establishing a foundation for future investigations into octocoral symbiotic relationships.

works.title: A σ B -dependent sRNA provides a repressor function to the general stress response in Clostridioides difficile
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Clostridioides difficile is an anaerobic, gram-positive gastrointestinal pathogen that poses a significant health threat worldwide. A recent RIL-seq characterization of the Hfq-mediated RNA-RNA interactome revealed that small regulatory RNAs (sRNAs) are key post-transcriptional regulators of virulence-related processes in C. difficile , including the initiation of sporulation. In the model Proteobacteria species E. coli and S. enterica , sRNAs often function as non-coding elements in vital stress responses mediated by alternative sigma factors, acting as repressors within these regulatory networks. However, whether this principle is broadly conserved across bacterial phyla remains largely unexplored. Here, we demonstrate that the Hfq-dependent sRNA SrsA is part of the regulatory network of the alternative sigma factor σ B , which governs the general stress response in Firmicutes. Consequently, SrsA is highly expressed during the transition from exponential to stationary phase and under infection-related stress conditions, such as oxidative stress. We show that SrsA represses a highly conserved small protein family that regulates sporulation and three genes in the methyl-fixing branch of the Wood-Ljungdahl pathway (WLP). Infection of mice further revealed that SrsA contributes to disease severity and bacterial recovery from antibiotic treatment in an acute and relapse mouse model of C. difficile infection. In summary, our data suggest that integrating SrsA into the σ B regulon helps coordinate sporulation and vital metabolic pathways of C. difficile in response to infection-relevant stress conditions. IMPORTANCE The central role of sRNAs as non-coding arms of stress responses represents a paradigm of sRNA function in Gammaproteobacteria. However, it remains unclear how broadly this regulatory principle is conserved across the bacterial tree of life. In our study, we identified the sRNA SrsA as a non-coding regulator involved in the sigma B-mediated stress response to nutrient limitation and radical stress in the intestinal pathogen Clostridioides difficile . We demonstrate that SrsA suppresses the production of a conserved family of spore regulators and of enzymes of the Wood-Ljungdahl pathway, establishing a role in regulating sporulation and gut colonization. Our work provides novel insights into the regulation of the Wood-Ljungdahl pathway, which is usually associated with autotrophic bacteria, and highlights the metabolic flexibility this anaerobic gut pathogen has evolved to survive in a nutrient-limited and inflamed gut environment.

works.title: RasGAP and Crk bind Anaplasma phagocytophilum effector AteA at tyrosine-phosphorylated EPLYA motifs
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Host cell signaling networks play critical roles in responding to bacterial infections. Intracellular pathogens manipulate these signals to establish a replicative niche in the host cell. Vector-borne rickettsial pathogens, such as Anaplasma phagocytophilum , encounter the dual challenge of interfacing with cell signaling in both the mammalian host and the tick vector Ixodes scapularis . A central feature that enables A. phagocytophilum survival in both mammals and ticks is the t ype 4 s ecretion s ystem (T4SS), which secretes effector proteins into the host cell to manipulate biological processes. Only a few A. phagocytophilum T4SS effectors have been experimentally tested, primarily in mammalian cells. While AteA has been identified as the first T4SS effector known to be essential for A. phagocytophilum survival in the tick, its molecular targets in the tick remained unknown. Here, we investigated AteA interactions with tick cell proteins and a possible mechanism of AteA activation. AteA contains multiple EPIYA-like short linear motifs with the consensus sequence EPLYA. Other known bacterial EPIYA motif effectors, including AnkA from A. phagocytophilum , target mammalian phosphotyrosine signaling proteins. We found that AteA is tyrosine-phosphorylated at EPLYA motifs by the non-receptor tyrosine kinases Src and Abl in eukaryotic cells and during tick infection. Protein pull-down assays revealed that Ixodes SH2 domain-containing proteins, RasGAP and Crk, preferentially interact with phosphorylated AteA EPLYA motifs. RasGAP and Crk have interconnected roles in cell signaling, suggesting that A. phagocytophilum targets these pathways during infection of the arthropod vector. IMPORTANCE Tick-borne diseases are on the rise globally, linked to changes in climate, land use, and human-animal interactions. Interrupting vector-borne transmission requires understanding how the vector and pathogens interact. Recent studies have shown ticks detect and respond to pathogens through cellular immune and stress signaling pathways. We previously demonstrated that the tick-borne bacterium Anaplasma phagocytophilum encodes a tick-specific secreted effector, AteA, that is essential for the pathogen’s survival in the tick. Here, we showed that AteA is phosphorylated by tick cell kinases, which promotes binding to host cell SH2 domain-containing proteins that are integral to cellular signaling networks. Understanding how these interactions affect signaling pathways in the tick will be essential if interventions targeting the vector are to be developed.

works.title: Nest ecology-associated impacts of wastewater on wild bee microbiomes
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Anthropogenic pollution affects environments differently depending on proximity to the pollution source, exposure route, and species ecology. Thus, understanding an organism’s ecological role and exposure route to contaminants is central to assessing pollution impact. Treated municipal wastewater releases contaminants into waterways and alters microbial communities. Plants absorb contaminants and expose animals through foraging and nest-building activities. Nesting ecology differences of ground and wood cavity-nesting bees offer insight into niche-specific susceptibility to pollution. We compared gut microbiomes of directly exposed soil-nesting Halictus ligatus and indirectly exposed wood-nesting Ceratina spp. upstream and downstream of wastewater. We collected bees, flowers, and soil and analyzed their bacterial microbiomes using 16S rRNA sequencing. The effect from wastewater explained a much larger proportion of the variance in the ground-nesting H. ligatus microbiome than wood cavity-nesting Ceratina adults, Ceratina larvae, and pollen provisions. Conversely, soil and flower microbiomes remained stable, indicating higher stability. These findings suggest that wastewater exposure leads to strong host-associated microbiome disruption, with ground-nesting bees most affected. IMPORTANCE Because contaminants bind strongly to soil, ground-nesting bees near wastewater are likely most impacted, while wood cavity-nesting bees are likely less impacted since plant uptake of contaminants is species dependent. These results suggest that exposure routes drive contaminant susceptibility, with bee-associated microbes most vulnerable. Because bees are important pollinators and biodiversity contributors, these disruptions point to broader ecological risks in increasingly contaminated landscapes.

works.title: Mechanistic insights into atmospheric and room-temperature plasma (ARTP)-induced genomic alterations and phenotypic evolution in Saccharomyces cerevisiae
works.abstract: as a model, we performed a comprehensive characterization of the mutational landscape and DNA repair pathways elicited by ARTP. Under high-lethality conditions (~99% mortality), ARTP treatment induced a substantial mutational burden, with SNVs and InDels rates increasing 25.2- and 36.7-fold relative to untreated controls, respectively. These mutations exhibited a pronounced bias toward C-T/G-A and A-T/T-A substitutions and InDels within AT-rich regions. Remarkably, the frequency of loss of heterozygosity (LOH) surged 57.4-fold, suggesting a potent capacity for inducing DNA breaks. Through sectored colony assays, we demonstrate that ARTP primarily inflicts pre-replicative double-strand breaks (DSBs), with reciprocal crossovers serving as the predominant driver of terminal LOH. The distribution and pattern of LOH were also altered in ARTP-treated cells. Mechanistically, our study establishes that the translesion synthesis polymerases Rev1 and Pol ζ are indispensable for converting ARTP-induced lesions-likely pyrimidine dimers-into fixed point mutations. In contrast, Rad30 facilitates high-fidelity bypass across these dimers. The base excision repair pathway appears largely dispensable for the processing of these lesions. In contrast, the nucleotide excision repair pathway plays a predominant role in mitigating ARTP-induced mutations. Finally, the strategic application of iterative ARTP mutagenesis facilitated the rapid evolution of acetate-tolerant strains. Our findings provide fundamental insights into the molecular signatures of ARTP mutagenesis, offering a framework for its optimized application in directed evolution. IMPORTANCE: While ARTP is a cornerstone of non-thermal mutagenesis in industrial biotechnology, its genetic impact has long been treated as a "black box." This study provides a high-resolution molecular dissection of ARTP-induced genomic alterations using a diploid yeast model. We demonstrate that ARTP is not merely a source of point mutations but a potent catalyst for pre-replicative double-strand breaks and extensive mitotic recombination. By elucidating the pivotal roles of specific DNA repair pathways in mutation fixation, we transition ARTP from a purely empirical screening tool to a mechanistically grounded platform for directed evolution. Furthermore, we demonstrate the practical utility of this platform by evolving acetate-tolerant strains and identifying the underlying genetic drivers of their resilience.

works.title: Rapid detection of the oak wilt pathogen ( Bretziella fagacearum ) using loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP)
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Oak wilt, caused by Bretziella fagacearum , is a destructive disease of Quercus species. Symptoms consist of leaf scorch, dieback, defoliation, vascular discoloration, and eventual death. Prompt diagnosis is crucial for timely management that involves laborious and expensive practices such as sanitation, cutting of infected trees, and proactive tree removal to create a buffer zone, root trenching, and/or fungicide injections. Due to these resource-intensive management tactics, laboratory test accuracy and speed are paramount. Diagnoses of oak wilt currently rely on culturing, nested PCR, or qPCR, but all these methods have limitations, ranging from ambiguous results to high barriers to application. We developed a rapid, robust, and sensitive loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) diagnostic test using primers and probes that target a section of the internal transcribed spacer region of the rDNA of the oak wilt pathogen , B. fagacearum . This assay can detect B. fagacearum from pure isolates and environmental samples, including branch sapwood, leaf petioles, nitidulid sap beetle vectors, and degraded fungal mats. The LAMP assay developed here is sensitive to a detection limit as low as 1 pg/μL and can detect the pathogen in under 20 min. This real-time LAMP-based diagnostic test is thoroughly validated to specifically detect the oak wilt pathogen, B. fagacearum , and is demonstrated to detect the fungus from a variety of routinely collected sample types. Our rapid molecular detection protocol can provide a useful tool for diagnostic labs, forest health practitioners, and researchers studying oak wilt. IMPORTANCE Oak wilt is a deadly disease of oaks that represents a growing threat to natural and planted forests throughout eastern North America. To enhance the speed and accuracy of molecular diagnostics for this disease, we designed a molecular test using l oop-mediated isothermal amp lification (LAMP) to reliably and rapidly detect the oak wilt pathogen, Bretziella fagacearum . To optimize the practicality of this assay in real-world conditions, we developed a rigorous validation process that incorporated the known breadth of genetic diversity of the oak wilt pathogen, sample tissue range, and a panel of non-target fungi to assess the potential for false positives. The novel assay is demonstrated to be highly specific and can detect B. fagacearum from host sapwood, leaf petioles, and nitidulid sap beetles, serving as a versatile new tool for forest health surveillance. Our approach also represents a thorough framework for researchers interested in the development of rapid molecular methods for the detection of forest microbes more broadly.

works.title: Evidence for holocentric centromeres in the early branching apicomplexan parasite Cryptosporidium parvum
works.abstract: During its asexual cycle, Cryptosporidium parvum (C. parvum) amplifies through three rounds of nuclear division before undergoing cytokinesis to form infectious merozoites. However, chromosome organization and segregation during nuclear division remain poorly studied. Here, we visualized H3-histones, including the centromeric histone H3 (CENH3), telomeres, and centrosomes during mitosis. Nuclear division was accompanied by centrosome duplication and elongated microtubules that spanned the dividing nuclei. Surprisingly, C. parvum centromeres detected by CENH3 showed diffuse staining throughout nuclear division and overlapped with telomeres in the apical nucleus. Analysis of centromeres based on CENH3 capture and DNA sequencing revealed numerous distinct binding sites scattered across all eight chromosomes, including both coding regions and intergenic regions, which were typified by GA rich repeat sequences. The unique holocentric chromosome structure of C. parvum is unlike the single regional centromeres found in related apicomplexans, suggesting it arose independently from other known examples in plants, insects and worms.

works.title: Type I interferon signaling promotes early innate control of Borrelia burgdorferi infection
works.abstract: Borrelia burgdorferi , the causative agent of Lyme disease, elicits a robust type I interferon (IFN-I) response that has been strongly associated with chronic inflammatory manifestations such as Lyme arthritis. Although IFN-I is known to be induced early during infection, its functional role in the initial stages of B. burgdorferi infection remains unclear. Here, we identify a protective role for IFN-I signaling in the early control of B. burgdorferi . At 5 days post-challenge, mice lacking the type I interferon receptor (IFNAR1) exhibited markedly elevated spirochetal burdens at the site of inoculation, indicating that IFN-I signaling contributes to restricting early bacterial expansion. By 10 days post-challenge, IFNAR1 deficiency resulted in significantly increased bacterial loads in the skin and a trend toward higher loads in heart tissues, while joint burdens remained unaffected. Mechanistically, IFN-I signaling enhanced macrophage uptake of B. burgdorferi , phagosomal processing, and intracellular killing, while also modulating inflammatory cytokine responses and promoting macrophage recruitment to the inoculation site. Conversely, pharmacological activation of IFN-I signaling augmented macrophage antimicrobial function and improved bacterial clearance. Together, these findings establish IFN-I as a key component of early host defense against B. burgdorferi and reveal a time-dependent role for IFN-I signaling in Lyme disease pathogenesis, with protective functions during early infection that contrast with its pathogenic effects at later stages.

works.title: The Trichomonas vaginalis pseudocyst is a viable cell stage with a distinct transcriptome and an intact membrane
works.abstract: Trichomonas vaginalis is the causative agent of trichomoniasis, the most common non-viral sexually transmitted infection (STI). Despite its prevalence, low levels of public knowledge and research funding and the absence of T. vaginalis screening or control programs have led to its categorization as a “neglected” STI. Unlike other STIs in the USA, prevalence increases with age, peaking among individuals in their 40s. Both a motile trophozoite stage and a non-motile pseudocyst state have been described for the parasite, although it was long debated whether the latter is a quiescent stage or a degenerate form on its way to cell death. Here we characterize the T. vaginalis pseudocyst by flow cytometry, membrane integrity assays, transcriptomics, and reversion studies. Pseudocysts were induced by culturing trophozoites in acidic media or in iron depleted media, with a variety of resulting survival rates. Flow cytometry studies showed that pseudocysts have intact cell membranes and express phosphatidylserine on their cell surface. Fluorescence-activated cell sorting studies also identified distinct sub-populations of parasites, revealing the importance of using pure live pseudocyst cultures in reversion studies. Pseudocysts were transcriptionally active for several days and had consistent subsets of genes with increased expression compared to trophozoites, although decreased transcription of genes involved in metabolism. Comparative transcriptomics of pseudocysts and trophozoites of two T. vaginalis strains revealed distinct cell states. Combined, our results provide evidence that the pseudocyst cell state is a stress-induced stage of T. vaginalis that can remain viable for days, with implications for a role in persistent infections.

works.title: Newly developed monoclonal antibodies for marmoset immunosuppression enable KSHV lytic replication and salivary shedding: A promising model for KSHV pathogenesis studies
works.abstract: Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV) is the causative agent of Kaposi sarcoma, a malignancy that primarily affects immunocompromised individuals, and is also linked to multiple other diseases. Progress in understanding KSHV pathogenesis and developing effective vaccines or therapies has been severely limited by the lack of a reliable in vivo model that recapitulates infection, persistence, and disease. Previous work suggested that the common marmoset (Callithrix jacchus), a small New World primate, can support KSHV infection and pathogenesis, but the reproducibility and utility of this model has not been rigorously established. Here, we sought to validate the common marmoset as a non-human primate model for KSHV studies by evaluating viral infection under both immunocompetent and immunosuppressed conditions. We first tested the use of intravenous and oral tacrolimus-based immunosuppression, confirming infection in challenged marmosets but also encountering tacrolimus dosing inconsistencies and toxicity. To overcome these limitations, we developed and validated a targeted immunosuppression approach using two novel mouse-marmoset chimeric monoclonal antibodies, anti-CD4 [TAWA] and anti-CD8 [OCHO], to selectively deplete T cell subsets. Altogether, we demonstrated across four independent experiments that KSHV can establish systemic infection in both immunocompetent and immunosuppressed conditions marmosets, evidenced by viremia in peripheral blood mononuclear cells, detectable seroconversion, and tissue persistence. The chimeric antibodies mediated efficient, subset‑specific depletion of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells and enabled a quantifiable, well‑tolerated immunosuppressive regimen. Moreover, we showed for the first time that monoclonal antibody-treated marmosets exhibit KSHV shedding in saliva and lytic replication, indicating that infection in this model is not merely latent but supports a full, human‑like replication cycle. Together these findings validate the common marmoset as a susceptible and translationally relevant non-human primate for studying KSHV infection and introduce a practical immunosuppressive tool for dissecting viral pathogenesis and immunity in vivo, providing a platform for testing vaccine and therapeutics.

works.title: Rebuilding the gut: Decoding enteric pathogenesis using next-generation human in vitro models
works.abstract: Traditional in vitro and in vivo models often fail to replicate the complex physiology of the human gastrointestinal (GI) tract, and consequently, do not fully capture how this environment influences the infective strategies employed by enteric pathogens. Here, we evaluate air-liquid interface (ALI) cultures and gut-on-a-chip (GoC) microfluidic systems as next-generation in vitro models (NGIMs) that recreate critical features of the human GI mucosal surface, including the mucus layer, crypt-villus architecture, and biomechanical forces that modulate enteric pathogenesis. We review their application towards bacterial, fungal, viral, and parasitic infections, highlighting novel mechanisms that were previously undetected using traditional models. Comparing the two approaches, we outline how ALI excels for studies involving mucus and for cost-effective implementation, whereas GoC systems uniquely capture peristalsis and luminal flow, revealing dynamic pathogen-host interactions. Notably, both platforms enable complex co-culturing, allowing pathogen-host-commensal dynamics to be studied in a reductionist manner. Lastly, we discuss how future efforts aimed at better mimicking the human GI tract could incorporate stromal, immune, and enteric nervous system components, while also improving accessibility and standardization. Taken together, both ALI and GoC systems offer significant opportunities to provide new insights into infection biology, while also serving as effective preclinical platforms for precision medicine and the evaluation of next-generation antimicrobial therapies.

works.title: L-Histidine resensitizes multidrug-resistant bacteria to carbapenems by inhibiting New Delhi metallo-β-lactamase activity
works.abstract: Plasmid-mediated New Delhi metallo-β-lactamase (NDM)-producing Gram-negative pathogens have severely undermined the clinical utility of carbapenems, the last-resort antibiotics for multidrug-resistant infections. Given the limited pipeline of novel antibiotics, there is an urgent need for more effective anti-infective strategies. Through untargeted metabolomics and functional screening, we find that L-histidine (L-His), a key downregulated metabolite in NDM-positive bacteria, remarkably restores carbapenem susceptibility. Mechanistically, L‑His acts through two complementary pathways: (i) direct competitive inhibition of NDM enzymatic activity via zinc chelation at the active site, and (ii) upregulation of the nickel ion transport gene cluster nikABCDE, which increases intracellular Ni2+ accumulation and further suppresses NDM function through non‑competitive inhibition. Overexpression of nikA potentiates the bactericidal activity of meropenem, whereas deletion of nikAB attenuates the synergistic effect of L‑His and meropenem. In a murine peritonitis‑sepsis model, co‑administration of L‑His with meropenem significantly improves survival and reduces bacterial burden, with a favorable safety profile. Collectively, our findings reveal L‑His as a multi‑mechanistic metabolic adjuvant that combines direct enzyme inhibition with disruption of metal homeostasis, positioning it as a promising therapeutic strategy against NDM‑positive carbapenem‑resistant infections.

works.title: Vaccinia virus growth factor induces divergent signaling programs and biological outcomes from cellular epidermal growth factor
works.abstract: Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) signaling is a major pathway that controls cellular growth, survival, proliferation, and differentiation. Viruses often hijack this pathway to create a favorable environment to support their replication. Vaccinia virus (the prototype member of poxviridae) encodes its own viral growth factor (VGF). VGF is a secreted viral polypeptide with sequence and structural homology to the cellular EGF, which binds to and activates EGFR signaling. Studies from our lab and others have shown that VGF promotes metabolic reprogramming, cell motility, virulence, and spread during VACV infection. However, it remains unclear whether VGF fully mimics EGF signaling or selectively rewires downstream pathways to meet the specific demands of viral replication. To address this question, we used quantitative global phosphoproteomics to systematically compare signaling programs induced by EGF and VGF in primary human foreskin fibroblasts. By analyzing global phosphorylation patterns, kinase activity inference, and motif enrichment, we found that although both peptides engage the same EGFR receptor, EGF and VGF induce distinct downstream phosphorylation and bias downstream kinase activities. Transcriptomic analysis provided a complementary view of the cellular responses to the ligand treatment. Moreover, we found that VGF is more effective at promoting VACV plaque formation than EGF, thereby providing functional support to the VGF-biased EGFR signaling nodes important for viral spread. These findings highlight differences in how viral and cellular growth factors activate EGFR signaling and position poxviral growth factors as powerful tools for examining the fundamental principles of cellular signaling.

works.title: Hydrophobic remodeling of the SARS-CoV-2 RBD large loop attenuates ACE2 engagement and viral fitness
works.abstract: The SARS-CoV-2 Omicron subvariant JN.4 harbors a unique A475V substitution within the receptor binding domain (RBD) but exhibits limited expansion compared to its parallel descendant JN.1. Here, we investigate how hydrophobic remodeling within RBD large loop (residues 475-490) modulates receptor engagement and spike function. Cryo-electron microscopy reveals that A475V induces local remodeling of the receptor-binding motif (RBM) and alters the RBD-ACE2 interaction geometry. Local refinement revealed that the bulky valine substitution disrupts the local interaction network surrounding residue 475, resulting in a 3.5-fold reduction in ACE2-binding affinity compared with BA.2.86. In contrast to the L455S substitution in JN.1, which primarily alters the receptor-binding interface, A475V within the flexible large loop influences both local loop conformation and global spike conformational properties. Systematic mutagenesis identifies A475 and F486 as functionally constrained hydrophobic residues that preserve the structural framework of ACE2 engagement despite extensive sequence variation within the surrounding loop. Together with molecular dynamics simulations and functional assays, our findings establish the RBD 475-490 large loop as a structurally plastic yet functionally constrained element that balances receptor recognition, conformational stability, and antigenic diversification. These results provide a mechanistic framework for understanding region-specific evolutionary constraints that shape SARS-CoV-2 RBD adaptation.

works.title: Comparative S-acyl-proteomics reveals post-translational modulation of fungal purine metabolism for Verticillium wilt
works.abstract: Verticillium wilt, caused by the fungus Verticillium dahliae, is a devastating plant disease leading to severe global agricultural losses. Although the interaction between V. dahliae and host plants has been extensively investigated, the role of metabolic regulation in fungal development and pathogenicity remains poorly understood. Fatty acids serve as metabolic substrates for S-acylation, a post-translational modification that modulates protein properties and functions, yet this process has not been characterized in V. dahliae. Here, our systematic analysis revealed that the protein S-acyltransferase VdERF2 is essential for the development and pathogenicity of V. dahliae. Through comparative S-acyl-proteomic analyses, we found that VdERF2-dependent S-acylation is significantly enriched in metabolic pathways, especially purine metabolism. Among the identified substrates, VdHIUH, an enzyme involved in converting uric acid to allantoin in purine metabolism, requires S-acylation for its full function in fungal development and virulence. VdERF2-mediated S-acylation enhances the activity of VdHIUH, thereby reducing uric acid accumulation. Furthermore, allantoin reduces reactive oxygen species elevated by the VdHIUH S-acylation defect, partially alleviating the fungal developmental impairment. Collectively, our findings reveal a critical mechanism by which S-acylation modulates purine metabolism in V. dahliae, providing new insights into the molecular basis of fungal pathogenicity and offering potential targets for improving crop resistance to Verticillium wilt.

works.title: Removal of VirD2 from a synthetic T-DNA complex of Agrobacterium by the host DNA repair protein TDP2
works.abstract: During plant genetic transformation, Agrobacterium transfers to its host cell a single-stranded segment of DNA (T-DNA), as a covalent complex with the virulence protein VirD2, which is ultimately integrated into the plant genome. The covalently bound VirD2 molecule is an obstacle to the ligation of the T-DNA 5'-end to host genomic DNA; therefore, VirD2 must be cleaved from the VirD2-T-DNA complex (T-complex) before the integration is completed. An interesting idea was raised that TDP2 (tyrosine phosphodiesterase 2), a protein known to resolve protein-DNA adducts, could represent a pathway for VirD2 removal from the T-complex; however, this function has not been proven directly. Here, we developed a simple technique to generate fluorescently labeled VirD2-ssDNA complexes in vitro and explored the DNA substrate requirements for the VirD2-mediated formation of these complexes, establishing a tractable experimental system for studying VirD2 removal from synthetic T-complexes. Using this system, we demonstrated that TDP2, from mammalian or plant origin, can specifically cleave VirD2 from these synthetic T-complexes; this activity was Mg2+-dependent and required a conserved C-terminal histidine residue of TDP2. Our results strongly support the hypothesis that plant TDP2 can remove VirD2 from the T-DNA before its integration into the plant genome.

works.title: S-layers as functional armours: structure, function and variability in Clostridioides difficile
works.abstract: Surface layers (S-layers) are paracrystalline protein lattices that serve as molecular exoskeletons and environmental interfaces across diverse bacteria and archaea. Despite their widespread occurrence, S-layers remain comparatively understudied. The available models do not fully represent the structural and physiological diversity of S-layers, and fragmented methodologies limit comprehensive functional comparisons and detailed characterisation. Recently determined high-resolution structural details for multiple variants of Clostridioides difficile S-layer provide a uniquely rich model system with functional links to antimicrobial resistance, phage recognition and immune evasion. In this review, we present C. difficile S-layers as extremely diverse, adaptable and multifunctional structures. We (i) summarise known S-layer roles in C. difficile infection; (ii) present a comprehensive comparison of their extremely diverse structures, including unique features and topological differences in lattice assemblies; (iii) propose quantitative metrics for comparative, structural analysis of these S-layers; (iv) outline S-layer pore size thresholds for the diffusion of metabolites essential for C. difficile growth; and (v) explore possible mechanisms underlying S-layer function and highlight the key outstanding questions.

works.title: RNA viruses as drivers of rapid diatom succession within a single bloom event
works.abstract: Diatoms frequently dominate seasonal phytoplankton blooms and contribute ~40% of marine primary production. Viruses drive phytoplankton mortality and bloom collapse, yet how viruses regulate diatom bloom dynamics is not well resolved. Here, using quantitative metatranscriptomics, we tracked temporal patterns of diatoms and associated viruses at near-daily resolution during the spring bloom in the Gulf of Aqaba, Red Sea. We captured distinct phases and rapid restructuring within both the diatom community and cell-associated virosphere. Diatom transcriptional profiling indicated activation of stress and death pathways prior to taxon-specific demise. RNA viruses emerged as dominant players within the bloom, with fluctuations of putative diatom-infecting RNA viruses across intracellular and extracellular fractions revealing sequential waves of active virus infection that were consistent with virus-mediated diatom mortality. Correlation and codon usage analyses further implicated specific diatom taxa as putative hosts for the identified RNA viruses. Rather than a uniform 'boom and bust', the spring diatom bloom comprised a mosaic of overlapping successional waves of diatom and viral taxa unfolding on daily timescales. These findings support RNA viruses as drivers of diatom turnover, advancing our understanding of how viruses temporally structure diverse diatom assemblages and the biogeochemical trajectory of diatom blooms in marine systems.

works.title: Animal markets are associated with elevated viral diversity and virus–host connectivity across wildlife–farm interfaces
works.abstract: Animal markets represent important interfaces among wildlife, farmed animals, and humans, yet their role in shaping viral diversity, community structure, and cross-host viral sharing remains incompletely understood. We performed metatranscriptomic analysis of 279 samples collected across wild, farm, and market-associated settings in Guangdong Province, China, with the animal-derived samples encompassing 15 host orders. We identified 106 vertebrate-associated viral lineages represented by 259 viral strains, including 19 putative novel viruses representing 13 putative viral lineages. Viral diversity and viral community composition differed significantly among ecological settings, with market-associated samples generally showing higher viral richness and distinct virome structures than wild and farm samples. The higher viral richness observed in market-associated samples remained evident in sensitivity analyses addressing pooled sampling, host composition, and unequal sampling effort. Viral sharing was observed across wild, farm, and market-associated settings, with market-associated host groups showing particularly extensive virus–host connectivity. Network analyses further indicated greater viral connectivity in market-associated settings, with host groups showing higher degree and betweenness centrality and more extensive virus–host associations. In addition, 38 viral sequences representing 13 viral lineages had documented pathogenic relevance based on reported disease associations in humans or other vertebrate hosts. Zoonotic relevance varied among viral lineages and depended on lineage-, subtype-, or genotype-specific evidence, highlighting the importance of distinguishing disease-associated viruses from those with demonstrated zoonotic potential. Animal markets were associated with greater viral diversity, distinct viral community composition, and broader patterns of viral sharing and connectivity, supporting their role as ecological interfaces linking wildlife and farm systems. However, shared detections do not establish the direction or frequency of viral movement, and temporal heterogeneity remains an important consideration. These findings highlight the value of integrated One Health surveillance across wildlife trade and agricultural systems, together with lineage-specific assessment of viruses with potential human-health relevance. Video Abstract

works.title: Questioning the role of antibody-dependent enhancement in severe dengue
FibriLysins disrupt Staphylococcus aureus biofilms and abscess communities
works.abstract: The rise of antibiotic resistance, particularly among pathogens such as methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, necessitates innovative antibacterial strategies. Here we introduce FibriLysins, a class of engineered enzymes combining staphylokinase and endolysin, which dismantle fibrin-encapsulated multicellular staphylococcal communities, including biofilms and staphylococcal abscess communities (SACs). We characterized diverse staphylokinases, developing a library of 27 FibriLysins, with a 78% positive hit rate. The lead variant, FL-028, has significant antibacterial activity against prevalent clinical S. aureus isolates. In vitro, FL-028 reduced bacterial counts in SACs by 3.4 log and in biofilms by 2.3 log. In vivo, FL-028 exhibits superior efficacy in a mouse model of bone fracture-related infection, outperforming vancomycin by 1 log and eliminating SAC presence in tissues. FL-028 shows no adverse effects on bone healing, as confirmed by histological examination, mechanical testing and micro-computed tomography analyses. These preclinical findings highlight the potential of FibriLysins as a robust and safe therapeutic approach against difficult-to-treat staphylococcal infections.

works.title: Ecological Kinetics and Evolutionary Dynamics of Antibiotic Resistance in Complex Environments
works.abstract: Antibiotic-resistant bacteria are common in natural environments, including the microbiota of animal and human hosts. The local physical, chemical, and biological conditions of environmental patches and matrices vary both qualitatively and quantitatively. Often, these conditions are found as gradients, creating intersections that can either facilitate or inhibit the spread and evolution of antibiotic resistance (AbR). Ecological kinetics (EcoK) describes how combinations of these conditions influence the abundance and transmission of antibiotic-resistant populations, as well as the mobile genetic elements that carry resistance genes. Evolutionary dynamics (EvoD) concerns the effects of environmental conditions on genetic variation, the expression of resistance traits, and the evolvability of host bacteria, ultimately contributing to the emergence and selection of AbR. This review examines the influence of numerous environmental conditions on EcoK and EvoD. This field remains poorly understood, and further research is essential to identify high-risk areas where surveillance for the emergence and spread of AbR should be implemented.

works.title: Biophysics of Microbial Locomotion
works.abstract: -the work of Galileo Galilei marked the beginning of the quantitative study of motion for scope-observable entities. Extending this physics-based perspective to the microscope-observable microbial world has uncovered principles of motion that diverge sharply from our everyday intuition, revealing physics as being essential to understanding microbial motility. In this review, we explore the fundamental physical principles that enable and constrain the motility strategies evolved by diverse microorganisms, with a focus on prokaryotes, to enable propulsion in fluids and along surfaces. We examine how microbial motility functions in complex, heterogeneous environments, and we provide a brief evolutionary perspective on microbial motility by highlighting its costs and benefits. In summary, we show how including a physical approach in the study of microbial motility both unveils general solutions and specific adaptations and enables a better understanding of a world for which our intuition is not trained.

works.title: Mg2+, ATP, and the Control of Bacterial Metabolism
works.abstract: In all living cells, chemical reactions known as metabolism generate energy and building blocks for cellular structures. Metabolism produces and consumes ATP, the major currency of cellular energy. Because approximately 85% of ATP is bound to Mg 2+ , bacteria reduce their ATP concentration when cytoplasmic Mg 2+ availability drops below a certain threshold. This reduction in ATP concentration reshapes metabolism and gene transcription as well as protein synthesis, solubility, and turnover. This article reviews how ATP acts both directly and via ATP-derived signaling molecules, such as 3′,5′-cyclic AMP (cAMP), bis-(3′,5′)-cyclic dimeric-AMP (c-di-AMP), diadenosine tetraphosphate (Ap 4 A), and guanosine-3′,5′-tetra- and pentaphosphate [(p)ppGpp], which direct adaptations to stresses bacteria experience in their natural environments. It also discusses how Mg 2+ -responsive regulatory systems supersede canonical control of metabolism and protein homeostasis by governing ATP amounts and how this bacterial response slows growth, modifies cell envelope structures, and favors survival.

works.title: Computational Peptide Design: Emerging Concepts in Antibiotics, Immunity, and Evolution
works.abstract: Peptides are among the smallest functional biomolecules. Learning to systematically design their activity would revolutionize biology and medicine. Yet achieving this goal remains an open challenge. Recent advances in machine learning enable the discovery and design of peptides at scale, not only yielding new antibiotic agents effective against priority pathogens but also revealing unexpected roles for peptides in host immunity. In this review, we survey how artificial intelligence (AI) methods can be used to mine genomes, proteomes, and even ancient sequence data to uncover "encrypted" peptide antibiotics across the tree of life and over evolutionary time. We highlight emerging approaches for activity prediction, structure-activity modeling, sequence optimization, and de novo peptide generation, and we discuss workflows that tightly couple in silico design with high-throughput experimental validation. We further introduce the concept of "encrypted immunity," in which ordinary proteins encode latent antimicrobial fragments, and we outline translational opportunities as well as remaining challenges on the path to bringing AI-designed peptides to the clinic.

works.title: Biomolecular Condensates in Bacteria
works.abstract: Bacteria use membraneless compartments, or biomolecular condensates, to organize cellular processes in space and time. These condensates assemble and function within a highly constrained physical landscape shaped by a crowded cytoplasm, structured nucleoid, membrane surfaces, and distinct polar zones. In this review, we examine condensates involved in genome maintenance, RNA metabolism, cell division, signaling, and metabolic regulation, focusing on how cellular microenvironments and physiological state shape when and where these condensates form, which molecules they recruit, and the material states they adopt. In turn, condensates can concentrate molecules for biochemical reactions, sequester them for storage or protection, release or redistribute them as conditions change, and position them at specific cellular sites. Disentangling the contribution of the condensed state from that of the underlying molecular interactions will be essential for determining how condensates regulate bacterial physiology.

works.title: Next-generation probiotics: beyond lactic acid bacteria to untapped taxa and engineered strains for better health
works.abstract: In this perspective, we discuss the evolving landscape of next-generation probiotics (NGPs), challenging the ambiguity of the term and proposing a framework for unifying the concepts associated with the field. We highlight the potential of novel candidates, including lactic acid bacteria and other commensal microorganisms from untapped taxa and genetically engineered strains, while examining their applications for human health. Rather than defining NGPs as a distinct category, we propose using the term to describe microbial-based health-promoting products in development, particularly where novelty relates to the organism, mechanism, engineering strategy, formulation, or targeted function. We address their safety concerns and regulatory challenges, while clarifying the divergence between therapeutic and dietary supplement pathways. We argue that as these products become more fully characterized and their safety, efficacy, intended use, and regulatory pathway are established, more specific terminology may take precedence, including the long-accepted probiotic category once efficacy and safety are established, or the live biotherapeutic products category if they are specifically developed for therapeutic applications. We suggest that the future of the 'beneficial microbes for health' field depends on striking a balance between the benefits of innovation and the necessity of rigorous safety and efficacy considerations.

works.title: Amino acid availability influences Staphylococcus aureus interaction with the nasal microbiota in a strain- and community-specific manner
works.abstract: BACKGROUND: Only some individuals carry Staphylococcus aureus in the nose, predisposing them to endogenous infections. While microbial cooperation and competition are known to shape environmental and intestinal microbial communities, their impact on pathogen colonization within the nasal microbiome is largely unknown. RESULTS: Using a newly curated nasal strain collection and systematic pairwise interaction analysis, we investigated competitive and collaborative traits between diverse S. aureus strains and nasal communities. Our experiments revealed that nasal species strongly modulate S. aureus growth in a strain- and community-specific manner both in vitro and in gnotobiotic mice. Nutrient-dependent interactions emerged as key drivers. In one example, we found that tyrosine provided by synthetic communities supported proliferation of an auxotrophic S. aureus strain. Screening of a large collection of S. aureus strains identified tyrosine dependency in 8% of strains, with colonization impaired in the absence of supportive communities, indicating broader relevance of this interaction. CONCLUSIONS: Our findings reveal distinct metabolic adaptations that enable S. aureus to exploit specific features of resident nasal communities, highlighting complex interspecies networks that influence colonization in the human nose. These insights may inform microbiome-editing strategies to displace S. aureus from the nasal niche. Video Abstract.

works.title: Theft of host transferrin receptor-1 by Toxoplasma gondii is required for infection
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Host nutrient acquisition is essential for apicomplexan parasite infection, yet mechanisms underpinning this are not defined. We discovered the genome of Toxoplasma gondii lacks conserved genes for iron transport and storage and these host cell proteins, including the transferrin receptor 1, transferrin, ferritin heart/heavy and liver/light chains, and clathrin light chain, are robustly taken up by tachyzoites. Acquisition of these host cell proteins was conserved across host cell species and parasite virulence types. Increased trafficking of host cell transferrin receptor 1 to endolysosomes boosted tachyzoite acquisition of host proteins and growth rate. Bradyzoites possessed little capacity to acquire host cell proteins, consistent with the cyst wall representing a barrier to host cell protein cargo. This study provides insight into essential functions associated with parasite theft of host iron acquisition and storage proteins. IMPORTANCE Host nutrient theft is a dogmatic principle of parasitism. The paradigm that Toxoplasma gondii avoids association with host proteins, seemingly abstaining from them as a nutritional stream and for immune system avoidance, is changing. Many host proteins are enriched at the parasitophorous vacuole, but that barrier may be breached since exogenous proteins expressed by host cells transverse to T. gondii bodies. Our work presented here provides in vivo context to this new view because several host iron homeostatic proteins are acquired and retained within the parasite to support infection. These findings not only shed light on how T. gondii could acquire iron but also reveal new host-parasite interactions of theft and integration of host proteins by pathogens.

works.title: The cell wall integrity pathway kinase Mpk1 regulates extracellular vesicle production and apoptotic-like vesicle release in Cryptococcus neoformans
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are important mediators of fungal physiology and host interactions, yet the mechanisms governing their production remain poorly understood. In Cryptococcus neoformans , EV production is tightly regulated by environmental conditions, suggesting the existence of dedicated signaling pathways. Here, we screened a kinase deletion library to identify regulators of EV production and found that the cell wall integrity (CWI) pathway acts as a major negative regulator of EV production. Deletion of the CWI kinases MPK1 , MKK2 , or BCK1 increased EV release. Unexpectedly, the size of EVs produced by CWI mutants differed markedly from wild type. Accordingly, cryo-electron microscopy revealed the accumulation of larger vesicles with altered size distributions in the mpk1 Δ mutant. These EVs lacked the characteristic mannoprotein-based fibrillar surface decoration observed on most wild-type vesicles, exhibited reduced association with capsular polysaccharide, and contained substantially less protein. Quantitative proteomic analysis demonstrated extensive remodeling of the EV proteome, with depletion of glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI)-anchored proteins, and enrichment of ribosomal proteins and histones. Finally, mpk1 Δ EVs displayed several hallmarks of mammalian apoptotic EVs, including phosphatidylserine exposure, and were produced under conditions associated with reduced cell viability. Together, these findings identify the CWI pathway as a central regulator of fungal EV production and provide evidence that C. neoformans produces distinct EV populations through genetically regulated pathways. Our results provide evidence for an apoptotic-like EV population in fungi and reveal an unexpected link between cell wall integrity signaling, cell death, and EV diversity. IMPORTANCE Fungal extracellular vesicles (EVs) contribute to virulence, antifungal resistance, and host-pathogen interactions, yet the mechanisms governing their production remain poorly understood. Here, we identify the cell wall integrity signaling pathway as a major regulator of EV production in the human fungal pathogen Cryptococcus neoformans . We further show that disruption of one of the major kinases of this pathway induces the production of a distinct population of EVs with structural and molecular features resembling mammalian apoptotic EVs. These findings demonstrate that fungi produce multiple EV populations through genetically regulated pathways rather than a single constitutive mechanism. By establishing the existence of apoptotic-like EVs in fungi, our work provides new insight into fungal EV production and lays the foundation for investigating how different EV populations contribute to fungal physiology, pathogenesis, and antifungal resistance.

works.title: mGem: Antibiotic tolerance across the growth-rate continuum in chronic human infections
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Antibiotic failure is frequently attributed to genetic resistance, yet many chronic infections persist despite clinical isolates remaining susceptible to antibiotics. Antibiotic tolerance offers an alternative explanation, but is commonly interpreted through persisters, dormancy, and growth arrest. We argue this theory is incomplete. In vitro studies consistently demonstrate that growth rate strongly influences antibiotic susceptibility, while bacteria in chronic human infections occupy a broad continuum of growth states. However, experimental models of tolerance largely examine rapidly growing or growth-arrested bacteria and rarely encompass the substantially slower growth rates found in chronic infection. We propose that tolerance can emerge from stochastic growth-rate heterogeneity within clonal populations without requiring transition into dormancy. Thus, understanding tolerance requires defining how antibiotic survival changes across the growth-rate continuum. Further studies directly examining antibiotic tolerance at slow growth rates representative of chronic infection are needed to understand tolerance during human infection.

works.title: The core interaction network of transcription elongation factors is broadly maintained across diverse bacteria
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Bacterial transcription elongation has been investigated most thoroughly for the model bacterium Escherichia coli. The E. coli elongation factor NusG associates through its N-terminal domain with the transcription elongation complex (TEC), while its C-terminal domain forms mutually exclusive interactions with either ribosomal protein S10 or Rho termination factor. The E. coli NusG:S10 complex bridges the TEC with a pioneering ribosome for coupling of transcription and translation. NusG also participates in antitermination complexes (ATC) that inhibit Rho-dependent termination and increase transcription of rRNA operons. A characteristic sequence in the nascent rrn RNA, called boxA , loads E. coli NusB:S10 onto the NusG-bound TEC, leading to the formation of the rrn ATC. However, these findings may not extend to all bacteria. Rho-dependent termination is less important in gram-positive bacteria, including some that do not encode Rho, and transcription and translation remain uncoupled in Bacillus subtilis and many other gram-positive bacteria. It is therefore unclear whether the interaction network for E. coli elongation factors is conserved in these organisms. We identified boxA -like sequences upstream of 16S and 23S genes in Bacillus species and found that they associate directly with NusB. We also found that B. subtilis S10 associates with both NusB and NusG, and that Rho can also associate with NusG. Bioinformatic analyses revealed conservation of interaction interface residues across multiple phyla. Together, these data demonstrate that the core interaction network of bacterial elongation factors is broadly conserved across diverse bacteria, despite differences in how these interactions function in individual species. IMPORTANCE Escherichia coli is known to use several key elongation factors that promote direct coupling of transcription with translation. These factors also trigger the formation of an antitermination complex that protects the synthesis of ribosomal RNA and CRISPR transcripts from interference by the Rho termination factor. However, Bacillus subtilis is not thought to couple transcription with translation. It is also not known whether B. subtilis needs to suppress Rho, given that its Rho is dispensable. Therefore, we purified B. subtilis elongation factors and mapped their interaction network. Surprisingly, we find that the B. subtilis elongation factors form complexes that closely resemble E. coli counterparts, despite the significant mechanistic differences in how these bacteria control transcription elongation.

works.title: Lineage II Escherichia coli O157:H7: genomes, prophages, colicins, and the absence of detectable Stx2
works.abstract: ABSTRACT The genomes of three lineage II strains of E. coli O157:H7 (FRIK2069, FRIK2455, and FRIK2533) with different pulsed-field gel electrophoresis patterns were sequenced, assembled, and compared. The genomes were closely related, with overall synteny, with the exception of a 302 kbp inversion in FRIK2069. FRIK2533 lacked pO157, which may account for its limited isolation. FRIK2455 was the dominant strain isolated over several years and was selected for comparison with lineage I (Sakai) and lineage I/II (EC4115) strains. Distinct polymorphisms were identified in prophages and MGEs among the three lineages. All lineages contained stx1 prophages and the locus of enterocyte effacement. The stx2a prophage was present in Sakai and EC4115, while the stx2c prophage was found in EC4115 and FRIK2455. Eleven geographically disparate LII strains from the United States were tested for functional phage and Stx2. Three of the 11 LII strains underwent delayed lysis after 24 h post-mitomycin C treatment. stx2 transcription was observed in two of the three lytic strains, but Stx2 was not detected in the lytic or non-lytic LII strains by Western blot. The supernatant of lysates from eight lineage II strains inhibited growth of the phage host ( E. coli strain MG1655) due to the production of a colicin (D, B, or M). These findings add to the body of evidence that LII EHEC do not produce functional phage or a detectable level of Stx2. Additionally, colicin production and pO157 may be key characteristics to the persistence of EHEC strains in the bovine host and farm environment. IMPORTANCE Escherichia coli O157:H7 is a human pathogen that is phylogenetically separated into three lineages. Strains belonging to lineages I and I/II are isolated from both clinical and bovine samples, whereas lineage II strains are only isolated from bovine and environments they occupy. This study sequenced, assembled, and compared the genomes of three lineage II strains. The genomes were closely related and syntenic, with differences in plasmid content and a chromosomal inversion. Comparison of the genome from FRIK2455 (lineage II strain) with the genomes of lineage I and I/II strains found distinct polymorphisms in prophages and mobile genetic elements. None of the lineage II strains examined produced functional phage or Stx2, but eight strains produced a colicin. Results from this study support previous reports that lineage II strains do not produce a detectable level of Stx2. Additionally, colicin production and pO157 may contribute to the persistence of EHEC in bovine.

works.title: Plasmid-mediated copper resistance in Xanthomonas euvesicatoria pv. perforans : determination of plasmid copy number and stability
works.abstract: ABSTRACT The management of bacterial spot of tomato is challenged by the widespread occurrence of copper resistance among its causal pathogens. In Xanthomonas euvesicatoria pv. perforans , a major causal agent, copper resistance is conferred by cop genes organized in an operon located on either the chromosome or plasmid. In the United States, copper resistance is predominantly chromosomally encoded. Plasmid-borne resistance is limited to a few phylogenetic groups but is prevalent in other bacterial spot pathogens. We hypothesized that plasmid-encoded copper resistance genes exhibit higher expression than chromosomally encoded genes but may be unstable in the absence of selective pressure for resistance. To test this hypothesis, we examined how the chromosomal versus plasmid-borne cop operon influences gene copy number and expression, as well as plasmid stability. Relative to strains with only chromosomal resistance, strains carrying plasmid-encoded resistance exhibited an increased copy number of copB , a key gene in the operon, while strains carrying both chromosomal and plasmid-encoded resistance showed an even greater increase in gene copy number. Correspondingly, copB expression was elevated in both groups. During in vitro growth without copper, partial or complete plasmid loss occurred in a subset of strains, and genome sequencing of colonies with reduced plasmid size revealed transposase-mediated plasmid rearrangements. These findings demonstrate that plasmid-borne copper resistance increases gene copy number and expression of copper resistance genes but can be unstable without copper selection in some strain backgrounds, highlighting the role of mobile genetic elements in shaping Xanthomonas euvesicatoria pv. perforans adaptation to changing copper environments. IMPORTANCE Plasmids are key players in the dissemination of antimicrobial resistance. Although copper resistance is widespread among Xanthomonas euvesicatoria pv. perforans strains, copper-based bactericides remain at the forefront of disease management. We previously demonstrated that distinct genetic elements, including plasmid- and chromosomally encoded genomic islands, contribute to the acquisition of copper resistance and the occurrence of multicopy resistance in X. euvesicatoria pv. perforans . Here, we show that the localization of copper resistance genes on a plasmid, chromosome, or both influences gene copy number and expression of copper resistance genes. Furthermore, rearrangements between co-resident plasmids affect plasmid stability, leading to the loss of copper resistance in X. euvesicatoria pv. perforans . These findings highlight how plasmid dynamics can shape bacterial evolvability and adaptation to selective environments.

works.title: Dual activities of lysis and capsule degradation enable the bacteriophage protein Lys33795 to effectively disrupt Streptococcus suis biofilms
works.abstract: Streptococcus suis (S. suis) is an encapsulated zoonotic pathogen that can form recalcitrant biofilms. Bacteriophage-derived endolysins and depolymerases represent promising antibiofilm agents, but currently, no report has described protein which displays both of lytic and capsule degradation activities simultaneously. Here, we mined the porcine gut virome and identified Lys33795, a dual-activity antibacterial protein that degrades both capsule and peptidoglycan of S. suis. Lys33795 consists of an N-terminal GH25_muramidase domain and a C-terminal cell wall binding domain (CBD). However, translational reinitiation at an internal start codon (M217) in the Lys33795 sequence generates an additional CBD that may assembles with the full-length protein to form an oligomeric complex. Interestingly, the GH25 muramidase truncation fragment of Lys33795 not only retains its classical function as a peptidoglycan hydrolase for degrading bacterial cell walls but also exhibits degradation activity towards capsule. This discovery contrasts sharply with the traditional functional understanding of the GH25 family. In addition, the CBD alone has a stable dimer and, as a nonstandard depolymerase without any classical polysaccharide-degrading catalytic domains, retains its degradation activity against S. suis capsule. We elucidated the molecular mechanism of Lys33795 exhibiting dual activity by combining mutagenesis, lysis, and capsule degradation activity assays. In addition, the results of in vitro and in vivo experiments showed that Lys33795 can effectively prevent and clear S. suis biofilms, and is more effective than single active mutants, and has a enhance effect when used in combination with antibiotics. This study describes the first multimeric bacteriophage protein with dual activities of lysis and capsule degradation against S. suis, encoded by a single gene. These findings provide valuable insights for designing potent antibacterial proteins targeting encapsulated pathogens.

works.title: HIV-1 cell-to-cell infection of macrophages escapes restriction by the BST-2 host cell factor independently of the Vpu counteracting viral protein
works.abstract: As HIV-1 target cells, macrophages can be infected by cell-to-cell virus transfer from infected T cells through cell-cell fusion leading to the formation of virus-productive multinucleated giant cells (MGCs). We recently demonstrated that this route of infection escaped host cell restriction acting on the early steps of the viral life cycle. Here, we investigated whether restriction factors acting on late steps of HIV-1 replication were also bypassed in virus cell-to-cell infection of macrophages. We focused on the impact of the interferon(IFN)-induced factor BST-2/tetherin acting on virus release, a process counteracted by the Vpu viral protein. We show that deletion of Vpu did not significantly affect HIV-1 cell-to-cell infection of IFN-stimulated macrophages, and virus assembly in virus containing compartments was not affected in MGCs. Accordingly, depletion of BST-2 in IFN-stimulated macrophages had no impact on virus cell-to-cell transfer, formation of MGCs and virus production. However, cell-to-cell infection of macrophages was still sensitive to the nelfinavir protease inhibitor, whereas we previously showed that this route of infection was resistant to antiviral drugs acting on early steps of virus replication. Our results show that HIV-1 cell-to-cell infection of macrophages escapes restriction factors acting on both early and late steps of the virus life cycle, but displays resistance to antiviral drugs specifically acting on the early steps of virus replication.

works.title: Correction: Targeted lysosomal activation in bladder epithelium enhances clearance of intracellular uropathogenic Escherichia coli
works.abstract: [This corrects the article DOI: 10.1371/journal.ppat.1014448.].

works.title: Rapid and convergent evolution of Wolbachia genomes in mosquito cell culture
works.abstract: Wolbachia are widespread bacterial symbionts of arthropods that manipulate host reproduction and can confer fitness benefits, such as protection against viral pathogens. Their self-spreading ability coupled with their antiviral effect has been harnessed in health programmes to curb the transmission of dengue virus by Aedes mosquitoes. In this context, a better understanding of evolutionary dynamics over short timescales is critical to inform and improve the efficacy of Wolbachia-based disease control interventions. Moreover, experimental evolution of Wolbachia may provide a powerful approach for generating novel symbiont strains with improved properties for disease control. Here we generated new mosquito cell lines by introducing five Wolbachia strains from Drosophila into the symbiont-free Aedes albopictus Aa23 cell line. Following transinfection, long-read whole-genome sequencing revealed multiple mutations, including structural changes, some of them being associated with major shifts in bacterial density. Signs of convergent evolution, an excess of non-synonymous mutations and comparisons with previous studies, indicate that Wolbachia evolution in cell culture is predominantly driven by selection and occurs faster than in insect hosts. Altogether, our study demonstrates that cell culture is a valuable tool to investigate short-term symbiont evolution, explore the genetic basis of bacterial density regulation and generate higher-density symbiont strains suitable for disease control.

works.title: A toxic friendship drives gut dysmotility
Steroid hormones produced by coral-associated Endozoicomonas influence coral immune response during thermal stress
works.abstract: The coral microbiome is believed to play a crucial role in sustaining corals and enabling adaptation to perturbations.
