A ubiquitous group of coral-associated bacteria, known as Endozoicomonas, are hypothesized to provide essential metabolites to corals, although detailed dynamics of the interactions between host and microbe are poorly understood. Here multi-omics and laboratory validation experiments reveal that Endozoicomonas encodes genes for the metabolism of coral-derived testosterone and converts ubiquitous cholesterol into testosterone and progesterone, both important steroids that accumulate within the coral holobiont during thermal stress. Field sampling along a natural temperature gradient showed general suppression of coral steroid hormones under thermal stress and during white syndrome manifestation. Provision of testosterone or progesterone to corals during laboratory thermal stress induced transcriptional reprogramming of the coral innate immune response, suggesting microbial involvement in host immune modulation. These findings highlight a previously unrecognized potential mechanism of microbial contribution to coral resilience. Multi-omics and laboratory experiments reveal that a coral-associated bacterium can produce testosterone and progesterone; these two hormones alter the coral host’s innate immune responses during thermal stress.

works.title: Human astroviruses: molecular virology
works.abstract: SUMMARYHuman astroviruses (HAstVs) are important etiologic agents of pediatric gastroenteritis and are increasingly recognized as pathogens associated with extraintestinal disease, including encephalitis and meningitis, particularly in immunocompromised individuals. Despite their clinical relevance, widespread prevalence, and expanding genetic diversity, no approved vaccines or antiviral therapies are available. Progress toward effective interventions requires a comprehensive understanding of HAstV molecular biology, including mechanisms of cell entry, viral replication, and immune recognition. In this review, we summarize current knowledge of HAstV epidemiology, clinical manifestations, evolution, and taxonomy, emphasizing recent advances in molecular and structural virology. We examine the HAstV replication cycle, including emerging insights into receptor usage, double-membrane vesicle biogenesis, protease-driven maturation, the capsid's membrane-lytic activity, and virion uncoating. Recent advances in determining high-resolution structures of the capsid core and spike of classical and non-classical HAstVs are highlighted, providing a framework for understanding virion assembly, maturation, and antibody neutralization. These molecular and structural insights highlight conserved and clade-specific vulnerabilities, refine current models of HAstV biology, and identify key molecular determinants that may serve as targets for antiviral development and vaccine design. We also outline critical unresolved questions that define priorities for future research.

works.title: TriLock-FISH enables in situ discrimination of influenza cRNA and mRNA for single-cell analysis of viral replication and transcription
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Influenza A virus produces three RNA species—viral RNA (vRNA), complementary RNA (cRNA), and messenger RNA (mRNA)—whose synthesis and trafficking are spatially compartmentalized. However, the high sequence similarity between cRNA and mRNA hinders their distinction in situ , limiting understanding of the spatial organization of the viral replication-transcription dynamics. Here, triple-lock fluorescence in situ hybridization (TriLock-FISH) was developed to distinguish vRNA, cRNA, and mRNA in situ with high specificity. TriLock-FISH enabled a genome-wide, time-resolved single-cell atlas of RNA abundance and localization, revealing marked cell-to-cell variation in RNA abundance but relatively conserved spatial organization. cRNA was found to be predominantly nuclear, with a small but reproducible cytoplasmic fraction. Application to infected mouse lung tissue demonstrated simultaneous spatial detection of all viral RNA species. This approach provides a highly specific framework for single-cell analysis of RNA virus replication and transcription. IMPORTANCE Influenza virus relies on three closely related RNA molecules for replication and gene expression, yet distinguishing them inside infected cells has remained technically challenging. This limitation has hindered understanding of viral replication in space and time. We developed triple-lock fluorescence in situ hybridization, which enables simultaneous visualization of all three viral RNA species across all eight influenza genome segments in infected cells and tissues. Single-cell analysis revealed striking heterogeneity in viral RNA abundance across infected cells, whereas intracellular RNA localization patterns remained relatively conserved. Complementary RNA, a replication intermediate long thought to be strictly nuclear, was also detected at low levels in the cytoplasm. These findings provide new insight into influenza virus replication and establish a broadly applicable tool for studying RNA virus biology.

works.title: The lumpy skin disease virus protein LSDV003 regulates MHC-I trafficking and surface expression
works.abstract: Lumpy skin disease (LSD) is a severe transboundary disease of cattle caused by lumpy skin disease virus (LSDV), which is highly transmissible and responsible for substantial economic losses worldwide. Although cellular immune responses are critical for controlling poxvirus infections, the viral strategies used by LSDV to evade cytotoxic T-cell immunity remain poorly understood. In this study, we demonstrate that LSDV infection markedly downregulates major histocompatibility complex class I (MHC-I) surface expression in host cells. Screening of LSDV-encoded proteins identified LSDV003 as a key viral factor responsible for MHC-I downregulation. Mechanistically, LSDV003 interacts with both the MHC-I heavy chain and β2-microglobulin and mediates endoplasmic reticulum (ER) retention of MHC-I via a C-terminal HNEL motif, thereby preventing its transport to the cell surface. Mutational analyses demonstrated that disruption of the HNEL motif impaired the ability of LSDV003 to alter MHC-I localization and surface expression. Furthermore, an LSDV003-deficient virus exhibited a markedly reduced capacity to suppress MHC-I surface expression. Collectively, these findings identify LSDV003 as a viral regulator of MHC-I trafficking and reveal a mechanism by which LSDV modulates host immune recognition.IMPORTANCELumpy skin disease is a highly contagious viral disease of cattle that has spread rapidly across Afro-Eurasia and causes major economic losses. However, the mechanisms used by lumpy skin disease virus to evade host immune defenses remain incompletely understood. In this study, we identify a previously unrecognized lumpy skin disease virus protein, LSDV003, that reduces the surface expression of major histocompatibility complex class I molecules in infected cells. We found that LSDV003 prevents these molecules from leaving the endoplasmic reticulum by using a C-terminal retention motif, thereby altering their normal intracellular trafficking. An LSDV003-deficient virus showed a reduced ability to suppress major histocompatibility complex class I surface expression during infection. These findings reveal an important immune evasion strategy used by lumpy skin disease virus and highlight LSDV003 as a potential target for improved vaccines and antiviral approaches to control this economically important disease.

works.title: Atypical E3 ligase HOIL1 promotes MDA5 signaling and ester-linked ubiquitination of LGP2
works.abstract: The RIG-I-like receptors, RIG-I and MDA5, are innate sensors of RNA virus infections that are critical for mounting a robust antiviral immune response. Heme-oxidized IRP2 ligase 1 (HOIL1), a component of the linear ubiquitin chain assembly complex (LUBAC), is essential for interferon induction in response to viruses sensed by MDA5, but not viruses sensed by RIG-I; however, the underlying mechanism remains unclear. LUBAC contains two atypical E3 ubiquitin ligases, HOIL1 and HOIP. While HOIP generates "linear" polyubiquitin chains, HOIL1 catalyzes ester-linked ubiquitination of serine and threonine residues and glucosaccharides. Here, we show that HOIL1 E3 ligase activity is critical for MDA5-dependent interferon induction, whereas HOIP E3 ligase activity plays a minor role. Mechanistically, HOIL1 E3 ligase activity was required for MDA5 translocation to mitochondrion-associated membranes and the formation of MAVS aggregates. We further identified LGP2, a positive regulator of MDA5 oligomerization, as a HOIL1-interacting protein and substrate for ester-linked ubiquitination. In mice, loss of HOIL1 or its E3 ligase activity markedly impaired early interferon responses following infection with viruses sensed by MDA5. While HOIL1 deficiency resulted in increased viral burden and reduced survival, loss of HOIL1 ligase activity alone did not, indicating that HOIL1 exerts additional functions during antiviral immunity. Collectively, these findings establish ester-linked ubiquitination by HOIL1 as a critical mechanism regulating MDA5 signaling.IMPORTANCEThe rapid and robust production of interferon is critical for controlling viral infections. Cytoplasmic RNA sensors, RIG-I and MDA5, detect infection with distinct groups of viruses, leading to the transcriptional induction of interferon. However, inappropriate production of interferon triggered by aberrant MDA5 activation by cellular RNAs causes severe inflammatory disorders. Here, we report that the ubiquitin ligase activity of heme-oxidized IRP2 ligase 1 (HOIL1) is critical for the production of interferon in response to viruses that are sensed by MDA5 in cells and mice. We identify the third RIG-I-like receptor, LGP2, as a substrate for ester-linked ubiquitination by HOIL1, and show that, like LGP2, HOIL1 ubiquitin ligase activity is required for the efficient oligomerization of MDA5 and the initiation of downstream signaling leading to the induction of interferon. These findings reveal a new regulator of MDA5-driven interferon production and identify a potential therapeutic target for MDA5-mediated inflammatory diseases.

works.title: Electron transfer to nitrogenase in Paenibacillus polymyxa
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Nitrogenase requires low-potential electrons to reduce N 2 to produce ammonia. The direct electron donors to nitrogenase are reduced ferredoxin (Fd) and flavodoxin (Fld). The enzymes that reduce Fd or Fld for N 2 fixation mainly include pyruvate-flavodoxin (ferredoxin) oxidoreductase (PFOR), ferredoxin-NADP + reductase (FNR), R hodobacter n itrogen f ixation protein complex (Rnf), and bifurcating electron transfer flavoprotein complex (Fix). Paenibacillus polymyxa is a model for studies of nitrogen fixation, but the pathways of electron transport to nitrogenase are unknown. In this study, we characterized the electron transport pathway to nitrogenase in P. polymyxa . Deletion analysis showed that among 15 genes encoding Fds, Fld, and Fd-/Fld-reducing enzymes, only cbiW gene and pfoAB operon decreased nitrogenase activity (31% and 37% relative to wild type, respectively). Triple deletion of cbiW and pfoAB led to a reduction of nitrogenase activity by 61%. Elemental analysis and ultraviolet-visible absorption spectroscopy revealed that the purified Fd protein encoded by cbiW is a [2Fe-2S] Fd. The purified Fd protein was able to substitute for Klebsiella NifF (Fld) to transfer electrons from pyruvate to Klebsiella nitrogenase in vitro. The pfoAB operon encodes PFOR, which is composed of two subunits. Klebsiella oxytoca NifJ (PFOR) was able to support nitrogen fixation in the Δ pfoAB mutant. These findings suggest that [2Fe-2S] Fd encoded by cbiW and PFOR encoded by the pfoAB operon constitute an electron transport pathway to Paenibacillus nitrogenase. IMPORTANCE Gram-positive and facultatively anaerobic Paenibacillus polymyxa is a model diazotroph whose nif (nitrogen fixation) genes encoding nitrogenase have been used for engineering yeast and plants. However, the pathway of electron transfer to Paenibacillus nitrogenase is unknown. In this study, we demonstrate that Fd encoded by cbiW and PFOR encoded by the pfoAB operon constitute an electron transport pathway to Paenibacillus nitrogenase. Fd encoded by cbiW is a [2Fe-2S] Fd, and PFOR encoded by the pfoAB operon is a heterodimer. In contrast, in many gram-negative diazotrophs, [4Fe-4S] Fds are widely used as electron donors to nitrogenase, and PFORs (NifJs) are homodimers. These results suggest that there may be some differences in the mechanisms of electron transfer to nitrogenase between gram-negative and gram-positive bacteria. The identified electron transport components in P. polymyxa will have great potential for use in engineering eukaryotes.

works.title: Chemical diversity analysis identifies inhibitory compounds in the secretomes of citrus-associated Bacillus spp. to the Huanglongbing pathogen, “ Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus,” and citrus root pathogens
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Huanglongbing (HLB) is a devastating and incurable citrus disease associated with the gram-negative, phloem-limited, and unculturable bacterium “ Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus” ( C Las), transmitted by the psyllid Diaphorina citri . Our goal was to identify high-performing microbial candidates from a previously established citrus-associated microbial collection for the management of HLB and associated root pathogens. Candidate selection was based on bioactivity, genomic, and metabolomic profiles. Eighteen Bacillus isolates were screened for antagonistic activity against Liberibacter crescens , C Las, and citrus-associated Phytophthora and Fusarium spp. Phylogenetic analysis grouped the isolates into four species groups: Bacillus velezensis , B. subtilis , B. pumilus , and B. cereus . Among these, B. velezensis exhibited the strongest and broadest inhibitory activity, followed by B. subtilis . This enhanced antagonistic potential is likely associated with the greater number and diversity of biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) identified. Notably, C Las-inhibitory isolates included B. velezensis (CB0021 and CB0909) and B. altitudinis (CB0086). Bacilysin and surfactin BGCs were conserved across all C Las-inhibitory isolates, suggesting a potential role in C Las suppression. Accordingly, surfactins were detected in bioactive fractions of B. velezensis (CB0027 and CB0909) and B. subtilis (CB0893), supporting their likely contribution to bioactivity and inhibiting L. crescens growth in vitro , highlighting their potential as candidate compounds for C Las management. Overall, this study underscores the importance of microbial discovery, screening, and characterization as an effective strategy for identifying sustainable solutions to manage HLB. IMPORTANCE Huanglongbing (HLB) is a severe disease of citrus that has altered the citrus landscape worldwide and currently has no cure. It is caused by the bacterium “ Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus” ( C Las) and transmitted by the psyllid Diaphorina citri . Currently, the most effective control strategy for this disease relies on trunk injection of antibiotics oxytetracycline and streptomycin, and there is a need to find alternative solutions to complement or replace chemical control. Here, we aimed to select high-performing candidates from our previously established citrus-associated microbial collection to manage HLB and root-associated pathogens. We screened 18 Bacillus isolates for antagonistic activity against Liberibacter crescens , C Las, and citrus-associated Phytophthora and Fusarium spp., and we generated their genomic and metabolomic profiles. Our research centers on selecting microbial candidates for their bioactivity and antimicrobial metabolite production, aiming to develop effective plant-protective bioinoculants for mitigation of HLB.

works.title: Multi-Dot/Icm effector mutants reveal distinct host responses in Legionella infected macrophages
works.abstract: Legionella pneumophila is the causative agent of Legionnaires' disease, an accidental and severe form of pneumonia. The replication of L. pneumophila within alveolar macrophages requires the Dot/Icm type IV secretion system that translocates more than 330 bacterial effector proteins into the infected host cell. Many Dot/Icm effectors possess eukaryotic-like domains and manipulate host processes by functional mimicry. However, only a minority of effectors have been fully characterized. Redundancy among effector protein activities and host targets has complicated functional characterization of individual effector proteins. To explore the collective impact of Dot/Icm effectors on host cell processes, we created a library of 14 L. pneumophila genomic mutant strains lacking effector-rich regions (a total of 85 effector genes deleted) and used the multi-deletion mutants to interrogate host-pathogen interactions. While none of the mutants exhibited a defect in intracellular replication in THP-1 macrophages, several were attenuated in amoebae, including a mutant lacking a predicted amino acid transporter. In THP-1 cells, we observed that wild-type L. pneumophila 130b triggered a strong inflammatory and cellular stress transcriptional response in macrophages, whereas six mutants displayed reduced interferon signalling and one mutant displayed a marked decrease in the global expression of host heat shock response (HSR) genes. Through the creation of further sub-deletions, we found that the Dot/Icm effector kinase LegK4 was responsible for induction of the host HSR via the canonical transcription factor heat shock factor 1 (HSF1). Infection of THP-1 macrophages deficient in HSF1 revealed a potential role for the host HSR in the early stages of L. pneumophila infection. Together, these results reinforce the utility of multi-gene deletions to identify Dot/Icm effector phenotypes and the importance of the host HSR to L. pneumophila infection.

works.title: Aridity shifts plant–microorganism relationships
Pseudomonas turns protection into pathology
The Pathomycosphere: A Spatially Defined Framework in Pathogen Ecology
works.abstract: Fungal pathogens have historically been studied as autonomous agents, as self-contained units independent of their associated microbiota, with disease outcomes attributed to fungal virulence factors acting on susceptible hosts. However, many pathogenic fungi harbor bacterial associates that influence their ecology, persistence and virulence. The pathobiome concept addressed this limitation by framing disease as an outcome of multi-kingdom interactions. Yet most pathobiome studies rely on correlative analyses of microbial abundances with pathogens, lacking spatial resolution to identify which microorganisms physically interact with pathogenic structures. Conversely, the hyphosphere provides micrometer-scale spatial resolution but has been investigated predominantly in non-pathogenic fungi. Here, we propose the pathomycosphere as a spatially defined and experimentally tractable subset of the pathobiome: a hypha-associated microbial assemblage in which physical association with the pathogenic member, prolonged or transient has a consequence for the pathogen's biology, with pathogenicity residing in the fungus, an associated microorganism or their interaction. This framework bridges the pathobiome and hyphosphere concepts by anchoring disease-associated microbial interactions to hyphal interface, where mechanistic investigation becomes feasible. Pathomycosphere provides operational tractability to explore microbial partnerships contributing to pathogenesis, and positions fungal-associated bacterial consortia as important components of pathogen biology with relevance to disease ecology beyond agricultural systems.

works.title: Multilayered network analysis reveals the centrality of newly discovered Nucleocytoviricota in wastewater treatment plant communities
works.abstract: Viruses of the phylum Nucleocytoviricota are remarkable entities due to their exceptionally large genomes and complex gene repertoires, which blur the lines between viral and cellular life. Previous research has leveraged computational approaches to map their extensive diversity. Experimental work has, in parallel, begun to elucidate their intricate interactions with hosts, bacterial symbionts, co-infecting virophages, and other mobile genetic elements.Although unlikely to replicate all simultaneously within the same host cell, the convergence of these entities within a single environment creates a dense hub of potential interactions that calls for a holistic, topology-based analysis. Here, we recovered high-quality genomes of 61 Nucleocytoviruses, 15 virophages and 14 polinton-like viruses from deeply sequenced metagenomes of 23 Danish wastewater treatment plants, and integrated them into a multilayered interaction network together with microbial contigs. This network recovered putative interactions across multiple levels, including Nucleocytoviruses co-occurring with hyperparasitic elements, associations with abundant activated sludge bacteria, and read-level signals of integration events. We show that the giants among viruses act as centrality-inducing entities, elevating others into highly central positions within the community and therefore are key players shaping the microbial community structure, ecology and evolution in wastewater treatment plants.

works.title: Mitochondrial heteroplasmy as a transitional state in the evolution of fungicide resistance
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) can exist in homoplasmic or heteroplasmic states, but the dynamics and stability of heteroplasmy remain poorly understood in fungal plant pathogens. Because a key fungicide target (cytochrome b ) is encoded in the mitochondrial genome, understanding these mtDNA dynamics is crucial for predicting resistance development and evolution in agricultural pathosystems. In Zymoseptoria tritici, mutations G143A and Y132C in the quinone outside inhibitor-binding site of the cytochrome b subunit confer a high level of resistance to the fungicides pyraclostrobin and metyltetraprole, respectively. Under fungicide selection, these mutations were observed to coexist only transiently. Using experimental evolution and single-cell analysis, we demonstrate the presence of a temporarily heteroplasmic state in which both G143A and Y132C alleles coexist within individual cells at variable ratios. Allele predominance within the heteroplasmic populations shifted rapidly in response to fungicide pressure, resulting in a mitochondrial mutation switch that ultimately led to either G143A or Y132C homoplasmy. This finding provides evidence that transient heteroplasmy represents a critical intermediate phase during the transition between resistance genotypes in Z. tritici . To our knowledge, this is the first single-cell demonstration of mitochondrial heteroplasmy in a pathogenic fungus, offering new insights into mitochondrial genome dynamics that shape adaptive responses to fungicides. IMPORTANCE Mitochondrial genomes in fungal pathogens are generally considered to be genetically uniform. However, our work shows that mitochondrial heteroplasmy can form a transient and unstable state that enables switching between resistance-associated haplotypes under changing selective pressures. Using single-cell analysis, we demonstrate that individual cells harbor varying proportions of resistance alleles, which can rapidly shift depending on fungicide exposure. These findings provide new insight into how mitochondrial genome dynamics contribute to microbial adaptation and highlight a previously underappreciated mechanism that may influence the emergence and development of antifungal resistance.

works.title: Competition-dominated microbial interactions and adaptive mutations enhance synthetic denitrifying community functions
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Understanding how interspecific interactions shape ecosystem functioning is a fundamental and longstanding question in ecology, especially along an evolutionary trajectory. Here, we used experimental evolution to evaluate how microbial interactions and adaptive mutations shaped community-level functions in synthetic denitrifying communities (SDCs) along a species richness gradient (one, two, and six species). Our results showed that competitive microbial interactions were observed and significantly ( P < 0.05) enhanced denitrification rates in the six-species SDCs during experimental evolution. Genome and metagenome re-sequencing analysis revealed the highest fixed non-synonymous and frameshift mutations within the six-species SDCs, among genes involved in nutrient transport, DNA repair, and secretion pathways. AlphaFold2 protein structure prediction, molecular docking, and Evo 2 host fitness prediction indicated that the fixed mutations could improve host strain fitness, and partial least squares path modeling (PLS-PM) further revealed that interspecific competition accelerated adaptive mutations, thereby reinforcing community-level functions, indicating potential Red Queen dynamics. This study offers novel insights into our understanding of eco-evolutionary mechanisms linking species richness, microbial interactions, adaptive mutations, and community functions, with important implications for active nitrogen removal and greenhouse gas mitigation in diverse ecosystems. IMPORTANCE Microbial diversity is widely recognized as a key driver of ecosystem functioning, yet how species interactions shape ecosystem functions through evolutionary processes remains poorly understood. Using synthetic denitrifying communities with different levels of species richness, we show that interspecific competition can accelerate adaptive mutations and enhance community-level denitrification over evolutionary timescales. Communities with higher species richness accumulated more adaptive mutations, particularly in genes associated with nutrient transport, DNA repair, and secretion systems, ultimately improving microbial fitness and denitrification performance. Our findings provide direct experimental evidence that microbial competition can promote functional adaptation, consistent with the Red Queen hypothesis. This study advances our understanding of the eco-evolutionary mechanisms linking species richness, microbial interactions, adaptive evolution, and ecosystem functioning.

works.title: Wildlife-associated ecosystems in Algeria harbor internationally distributed ESBL-producing clones and plasmids, including a CTX-M-15 Klebsiella pneumoniae ST17 lineage associated with a conserved IncFIB(K) resistance plasmid
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Expanded-spectrum cephalosporin-resistant Enterobacterales (ESC-R-E) have disseminated beyond clinical settings, but their occurrence and genomic epidemiology in wildlife remain poorly characterized, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. ESC-R may result from the production of extended-spectrum β-lactamases (ESBLs) or AmpC-type cephalosporinases. We investigated the prevalence, resistance mechanisms, and population structure of ESC-R-E in free-ranging wildlife, captive wild animals, and zoo workers in Algeria. Between October 2021 and June 2023, 1,899 fecal samples were collected across six Algerian provinces. ESC-R-E isolates were recovered by selective culture and characterized by antimicrobial susceptibility testing, and whole-genome sequencing. Overall, 73 ESC-R-E isolates (3.9%) were identified, including seven OXA-48-like carbapenemase co-producers (0.4%). Carriage was significantly higher in captive animals (13.5%) than in free-ranging wildlife (1.6%) or zoo workers (7.7%). Among the 66 ESBL-producing isolates analyzed, CTX-M enzymes predominated ( n = 61), particularly CTX-M-15 ( n = 53). Klebsiella pneumoniae was the predominant species ( n = 33), with ST17 accounting for 27/33 isolates. Closely related CTX-M-15-producing ST17 isolates were recovered from captive animals, free-ranging wildlife, and a zoo worker and carried an IncFIB(K) plasmid harboring bla CTX-M-15 within a multidrug resistance region closely related to globally disseminated plasmids. Globally disseminated high-risk Escherichia coli clones were also detected, namely ST167, ST361, ST410, and a persistent ST38 lineage in Algerian wildlife since 2016. These findings demonstrate the circulation of high-risk Enterobacterales lineages and mobile resistance plasmids in Algerian wildlife-associated ecosystems and highlight the need for integrated One Health surveillance of antimicrobial resistance at the human-animal-environment interface. IMPORTANCE Wildlife is increasingly recognized as a potential reservoir and sentinel for antimicrobial resistance, yet genomic data from low- and middle-income countries remain scarce. This study provides one of the largest genomic investigations of expanded-spectrum cephalosporin-resistant Enterobacterales in wildlife from North Africa. We demonstrate that internationally disseminated high-risk Klebsiella pneumoniae and Escherichia coli lineages, together with globally distributed CTX-M-15-carrying plasmids, are circulating among captive animals, free-ranging wildlife, and humans in zoological environments. The recovery of closely related K. pneumoniae ST17 isolates from different host species highlights the potential for antimicrobial resistance dissemination across the human-animal-environment interface. These findings extend the known ecological range of clinically important resistant Enterobacterales beyond healthcare settings and identify wildlife-associated ecosystems as part of the broader antimicrobial resistance network. Our study underscores the value of integrating wildlife into One Health surveillance programs to better understand and mitigate the environmental spread of antimicrobial resistance.

works.title: Antidepressant desvenlafaxine identified in wastewater promotes transformation and antibiotic resistance risk in Acinetobacter baylyi ADP1 via metabolic adaptations
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) are known reservoirs of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs). Non-antibiotic compounds, such as antidepressants, may further promote ARG acquisition through horizontal gene transfer (HGT). Desvenlafaxine, a serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (SNRI) listed on the EU Surface Water Watch List, is among the most frequently detected antidepressants in WWTP effluents, yet its role in HGT has not been examined. Here, we detected desvenlafaxine at the highest concentrations among four antidepressants monitored across three municipal WWTPs in western New York. Using Acinetobacter baylyi ADP1 as a model recipient in natural transformation assays ( n = 6), we found that desvenlafaxine significantly increased transformation frequency at 10 mg/L (1.74 ± 0.33-fold) and 50 mg/L (1.49 ± 0.19-fold; P adj < 0.05). Effects occurred without induction of reactive oxygen species or loss of membrane integrity, consistent with its very low toxicity (IC 20 ~1,300 mg/L). Instead, desvenlafaxine induced dose-dependent increases in membrane fluidity and shifts to less negative zeta potentials, suggesting that electrostatic interactions between its cationic amine group and the negatively charged membrane reduce surface repulsion and facilitate plasmid proximity during uptake. Non-targeted proteomics revealed a biphasic response: at 10 mg/L, competence-associated proteins (PilB, ComM) were upregulated, and STRING analysis identified networks linked to membrane transport, transcriptional regulation, and envelope remodeling, while no connected network was recovered at 50 mg/L. Electron microscopy confirmed higher pilus frequency at both doses. Together, these findings reveal a non-oxidative, envelope-mediated route by which a widely detected antidepressant increases bacterial competence. IMPORTANCE The spread of antibiotic resistance poses a serious and escalating threat to human health worldwide. While antibiotic use is widely recognized as a key driver, non-antibiotic pharmaceuticals released into the environment through wastewater have received far less attention. Antidepressants are among the most frequently detected drugs in treated wastewater effluents, yet their potential to promote antibiotic resistance transfer in bacteria remains poorly understood. This study demonstrates that desvenlafaxine, one of the most abundant antidepressants found in municipal wastewater, can increase the uptake of antibiotic resistance genes in an environmental bacterium at concentrations above those currently measured in effluent, and identifies the bacterial cell-surface changes that enable this without cytotoxicity.

works.title: Urea reshuffles soil microbial balance
Quinone-trapping filaments enhance respiratory capacity
works.abstract: Cells expand respiratory capacity by adding internal membranes or forming cristae. A new study by Kropp and colleagues shows that the Gram-positive bacterium Bacillus subtilis instead builds hollow protein filaments that sequester and transport quinones, extending the cell's respiratory capacity without adding membranes. This strategy, widespread across Bacillota, reveals an alternative route to bioenergetic expansion.

works.title: Nanoscale pesticide delivery suppresses pathogens and enriches beneficial microbiomes for safer crop protection
works.abstract: Nanocarrier-based pesticide delivery platforms substantially boost agrochemical utilization efficiency, yet their cascading ecological repercussions for rhizosphere and soil microbial ecology remain insufficiently understood. Here, a star polycation (SPc) nanocarrier was employed to construct a matrine nano-formulation (MT@SPc) with typical nano-pesticide characteristics. MT@SPc and commercial matrine formulation (MT SL) were employed as representative systems to further evaluate their impacts on rhizosphere and soil microbial ecosystems. Compared with MT SL, MT@SPc reshaped rhizosphere microbial communities by suppressing phytopathogens and promoting the enrichment of beneficial bacteria. Further validation using four representative bacterial isolates obtained from soil demonstrated that MT@SPc significantly inhibited the growth of the phytopathogen Pectobacterium carotovorum, whereas enriched beneficial bacteria exhibited lower susceptibility to MT@SPc. Multi-scale mechanistic analyses revealed that MT@SPc could interact with bacterial cell surfaces through physicochemical interactions, resulting in pronounced surface deformation and structural damage in P. carotovorum. Multi-omics analyses associated with physiological and biochemical assays further demonstrated that MT@SPc disrupted cell wall and membrane integrity, leading to ionic imbalance, metabolite leakage and oxidative stress. However, beneficial bacteria maintained higher stability, and their enrichment was associated with microbial community shifts following pathogen suppression. Overall, this study reveals that nano-pesticides drive rhizosphere community restructuring through differential microbial responses, providing mechanistic insights into nano-pesticide-microbiome interactions in complex ecological systems.

works.title: Contrasting edaphic and land-use signatures of microbial phosphorus mobilisation and accumulation genes
works.abstract: Phosphorus (P) is an essential nutrient that constrains productivity across many terrestrial ecosystems. Soil microorganisms regulate P transformation through distinct functional strategies, yet how these strategies vary with land use and environmental conditions across chronically P-impoverished landscapes remains poorly understood. Here, we combined 268 soil metagenomes from natural, pasture, and cropland systems across Australia with genome-resolved analyses of 1,077 metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs). Results revealed contrasting genomic distributions among P-cycling strategies. P accumulation genes were widely distributed across bacterial phylogeny, whereas mineralization gene and solubilisation gene were concentrated within specific lineages. Land-use-associated differences were most evident in the relative abundances of mineralisation and solubilisation genes, whereas accumulation genes showed comparatively little variation. Soil properties were stronger predictors of relative P-cycling gene abundance than climatic variables. Among these variables, soil pH was the strongest predictor of both the combined relative abundance of P-cycling genes and mineralisation genes, whereas accumulation genes were negatively associated with the mineral-associated organic carbon fraction. Continental predictions further suggested higher combined relative P-cycling gene abundance in wetter south-western and coastal eastern regions. These analyses reveal contrasting microbial P-cycling gene strategies across Australian soils and provide a genome-resolved framework for understanding their phylogenetic distributions and environmental associations at the continental scale.

works.title: mGem: Innate immune sensing of HIV-1 transcription in myeloid cells—a tale of two transcription start sites
works.abstract: Suppressive antiretroviral therapy (ART) in people with HIV (PWH) arrests progression to AIDS and onward viral transmission. However, viral transcription from integrated HIV-1 proviruses persists on treatment and is linked to markers of chronic immune activation, contributing to the accelerated development of comorbidities in PWH. Of particular interest are persistent responses in long-lived tissue-resident myeloid cells, which direct tissue-level inflammatory processes through cytokine secretion and interactions with other immune cell populations. Here, we review recent findings on viral nucleic acid sensing events in HIV-infected myeloid cells to shed light on possible mechanisms of persistent inflammation resulting from chronic HIV-1 transcription in myeloid cells in PWH.

works.title: Host-like temperature unlocks glucose uptake and metabolism in pathogenic Leptospira
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Pathogenic Leptospira transitions between environmental reservoirs and mammalian hosts, exposing the bacterium to distinct temperature conditions. Although Leptospira is generally considered to rely primarily on long-chain fatty acids for growth and to have limited capacity to use glucose, whether host-like temperature alters glucose-associated metabolic capacity remains unclear. Here, we used transcriptome-integrated genome-scale metabolic modeling to examine temperature-dependent metabolic states in pathogenic Leptospira . Models contextualized with transcriptomic data from cultures at 37°C predicted increased flux through glucose transport, glucose phosphorylation, and downstream glucose-associated reactions than it did at 29–30°C. Similar temperature-dependent predictions were obtained for another pathogenic Leptospira species under in vitro conditions. Consistent with these findings, analysis of leptospires cultivated intraperitoneally in dialysis membrane chambers also predicted enhanced glucose uptake and metabolism under host-temperature conditions. In vitro validation experiments showed increased bacterial uptake or accumulation of a fluorescent glucose analog, elevated expression of candidate glucose transporter genes, and glucose-dependent enhancement of bacterial growth at 37°C. Treatment with a glucose degradation pathway inhibitor, 2-deoxy- d -glucose, further supported a contribution of glucose-associated processes to proliferation at 37°C. Together, these findings indicate that pathogenic Leptospira displays condition-dependent glucose uptake and glucose-associated metabolic activity that become apparent at host-like temperature, as opposed to being glucose-incompetent at environmental-like temperature. This prediction-driven framework refines the conventional view of Leptospira carbon metabolism and provides a basis for future studies of glucose-associated metabolic capacity during mammalian infection. IMPORTANCE Environmental reservoirs play a central role in the transmission of many bacterial pathogens, yet the metabolic mechanisms that enable adaptation to both environmental and host-associated niches remain largely unknown. Using a prediction-driven framework that combines contextualized genome-scale metabolic modeling with multi-omics analyses and experimental validation, we discovered that pathogenic Leptospira activates glucose uptake and metabolism only under host-like conditions. This finding resolves a long-standing misconception arising from studies performed under conventional laboratory conditions and fundamentally revises our understanding of Leptospira physiology. More importantly, our study establishes an integrative systems biology strategy for uncovering condition-dependent metabolic traits that would be difficult to identify experimentally alone, with broad applicability to diverse environmentally transmitted pathogens.

works.title: Cross-linking mass spectrometry guided structure prediction of disordered Encephalitozoon hellem proteins
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Microsporidia such as Encephalitozoon hellem are obligate intracellular human parasites that remain genetically intractable, limiting the functional characterization of their proteomes. Experimental structural studies are challenging, as many proteins in microsporidia comprise a large percentage of disordered regions. Computational structural studies based on homology-based modeling and the use of deep-learning algorithms for microsporidian proteins also remain limited because most have little to no sequence similarity to proteins with solved structures. To address these limitations, we developed an approach that incorporates cross-linking mass spectrometry (XL-MS) data into structure prediction. XL-MS data provide upper-bound distance constraints that can be incorporated into protein deep-learning-based modeling and subsequent docking. Using this approach, we generated a model of two interacting E. hellem spore wall proteins, spore wall protein 1B (Swp1b) and endospore protein 1 (EnP1), which have no clear homologs outside of microsporidia and contain several disordered regions. These proteins are abundant spore wall proteins of microsporidia and previously were not known to interact with one another. The resulting model not only is consistent with the experimental cross-links used to generate the model but was also subsequently confirmed by independently generated XL-MS data. The described AlphaLink-Modeller framework for structure prediction is particularly well suited to proteins with limited homology and/or substantial flexible regions, given that they adopt a defined structural state within a biological context, thereby extending integrative modeling approaches to previously inaccessible targets. IMPORTANCE In this article, we demonstrate an improved method for the prediction of the structure of protein complexes with no clear homologs and a considerable number of disordered regions. This is significant because these types of proteins are critical to understanding the biology of organisms, yet model generation of these classes has been inaccessible. The method incorporates experimental data obtained from cross-linking mass spectrometry (XL-MS) into the modeling process, providing a method to integrate such experimental data into computational modeling of the structure of proteins and protein interactions. For this paper, we have used this method for predicting the structure of two highly abundant Encephalitozoon hellem proteins in the spore wall that are important for host cell infection due to this pathogen of humans and other vertebrates.

works.title: Whole-genome analysis uncovers four novel Streptomyces species linked to sweet potato soil rot in China
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Sweet potato soil rot, caused by pathogenic Streptomyces , is an emerging threat to sweet potato production in China. However, the diversity and pathogenic mechanisms of the associated species remain poorly understood. In this study, symptomatic storage roots exhibiting typical pox-like lesions were collected from major production regions in Henan and Guangdong provinces. A total of 225 actinomycete strains were isolated using optimized methods, and six highly pathogenic strains were identified through tuber slice, hydroponic, and pot inoculation assays. Morphological, physiological, whole-genome sequencing, and phylogenetic analyses revealed considerable diversity among these pathogenic isolates. Average nucleotide identity (ANI) analysis showed that strain (ST10) was closely related to Streptomyces albogriseolus , whereas the remaining strains displayed substantial genomic divergence, indicating diverse taxonomic affiliations. Comparative genomic analysis identified a conserved core genome together with extensive strain-specific gene content, reflecting both functional conservation and adaptive evolution. Phylogenomic analysis placed several isolates close to S. ipomoeae , and others within distinct pathogenic lineages. Notably, none of the six strains possessed the canonical thaxtomin biosynthetic gene cluster, suggesting that pathogenicity is mediated by alternative virulence mechanisms. Instead, conserved gene clusters associated with siderophores and stress-related metabolites were identified, indicating potential roles in host colonization and ecological adaptation. These findings expand our understanding of the genomic diversity and potential pathogenic mechanisms of sweet potato-associated Streptomyces and provide a valuable foundation for disease management and resistance breeding. IMPORTANCE Herein, we established an optimized isolation method yielding 225 actinomycete strains and a rapid pipeline for pathogenic identification of sweet potato-associated Streptomyces . Six isolates were confirmed as causal agents of sweet potato soil rot, including four novel species. Complete genome sequences of five strains provide a fundamental resource for elucidating pathogenesis mechanisms and advancing taxonomic and evolutionary studies of the genus. The absence of canonical thaxtomin biosynthetic genes across all pathogenic strains, combined with the presence of conserved siderophore and stress-related metabolite clusters, demonstrates that these pathogens utilize alternative virulence mechanisms distinct from well-characterized Streptomyces plant pathogens. Comparative genomics reveals a conserved core genome alongside strain-specific gene content, reflecting functional conservation and adaptive evolution. These genomic resources and experimental validations establish a foundational framework for understanding pathogen diversity, enabling accurate diagnosis of emerging strains and directly informing resistance breeding programs by identifying genetic targets for screening sweet potato germplasm.

works.title: Local temperature and humidity are associated with proportion of antimicrobial-resistant Escherichia coli isolates in farm environments: considerations for on-farm surveillance
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Evidence suggests that increased local temperatures are associated with higher prevalence of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in environmental bacteria. This observational cohort study investigates associations between local climate and the proportion of antimicrobial-resistant Escherichia coli isolated from 2,766 farm environment samples from 53 English dairy farms. A non-linear Bayesian model that accounts for decreased test sensitivity at low E. coli abundance was used to estimate the proportion of antimicrobial-resistant E. coli from colony count data. A 20°C increase in local temperature was associated with a 5.0-fold increase in the proportion of streptomycin-resistant E. coli (95% credible interval [CI]: 1.03–33.0; absolute increase: 0.2%, 95% CI: 2.3 × 10 −3 %–1.2%). Weaker evidence suggested that increased temperatures were associated with increased proportions of tetracycline-resistant E. coli . Increasing relative humidity was associated with an increase in the proportion of amoxicillin-, streptomycin-, and tetracycline-resistant E. coli . A 32% increase in relative humidity (from 60% to 92%) was associated with a 4.7-fold increase in the proportion of amoxicillin-resistant E. coli (median; 95% CI: 1.4–15.7; absolute increase: 1.3%, 95% CI: 0.2%–3.5%). For amoxicillin and streptomycin, a synergistic effect where increasing both temperature and humidity was associated with increased proportions of antimicrobial-resistant E. coli was observed, with weak evidence of this effect observed for tetracycline. These findings highlight the importance of considering weather conditions, sample characteristics, and seasonality in livestock AMR surveillance. Associations between local weather conditions and the proportion of livestock E. coli exhibiting AMR suggest that climate change may influence the burden of One Health AMR. IMPORTANCE Understanding how environmental conditions are associated with variability in antimicrobial resistance (AMR) prevalence is critical for developing robust livestock AMR surveillance and anticipating the potential effects of climate change. The non-linear Bayesian modeling approach developed here adjusts for Escherichia coli abundance-associated variability in test sensitivity, enabling the influence of risk factors associated with the proportion of antimicrobial-resistant E. coli within samples to be more accurately estimated. Applying this approach to 2,766 fecal samples from 53 dairy farms in Southwest England indicated that the proportion of antimicrobial-resistant E. coli generally increased under warmer and wetter conditions. These findings suggest that environmental conditions can influence the prevalence of antimicrobial-resistant E. coli in dairy farm environments and demonstrate the importance of accounting for weather-related variability in livestock AMR surveillance. Adjusting for these associations in livestock AMR surveillance could improve the accuracy of modeling AMR trends and strengthen the assessment of climate-associated AMR risks.

SIV reservoir depletion and clearance from neonatal macaques following transient CCR5 depletion
works.abstract: Antiretroviral therapy (ART) suppresses viraemia in people with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), but HIV provirus persists indefinitely in CD4-expressing cells. Cells containing active provirus express viral proteins and have been successfully targeted using broadly neutralizing antibodies (bnAbs). In contrast, cells containing latent provirus cannot be specifically targeted without latency reactivation. Meaningful depletion of the latent HIV or simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV) reservoirs has not been demonstrated except with cytotoxic conditioning for bone-marrow transplantation. Here we show that both the active and latent SIV reservoirs can be eliminated from infant macaques via profound but transient depletion of cells that express CCR5 using a single shot of CCR5/CD3 bispecific antibody. Neonatal rhesus macaques were infected with SIVmac251, then treated with ART beginning at 1 week after infection, followed by treatment with either a CCR5/CD3-bispecific or a CD4-specific antibody, both of which depleted target cells and accelerated the decline in plasma viraemia. Upon ART cessation, while rebound occurred quickly in all animals treated with ART alone, most animals treated with CCR5/CD3 bispecific antibody remained aviraemic for >3 months. Several remained aviraemic to the end of follow-up and efforts to detect replication-competent virus were unsuccessful. Our results show that bispecific antibody treatment achieves meaningful depletion of the replication-competent SIV reservoir and supports the possibility that clinically meaningful depletion of the HIV reservoir might be achievable for recently infected individuals.

works.title: Disentangling microbiota-dependent and -independent impacts of antibiotics on host physiology
works.abstract: Antibiotics are believed to affect host physiology by altering the gut microbiota. However, it remains unclear which effects of antibiotics are microbiota dependent and which are microbiota independent. Here we present a resource encompassing host and microbiota responses to antibiotic treatment and a computational tool with which to analyse them. Metagenomic and transcriptomic analyses of conventional and germ-free mice revealed that antibiotic administration routes and their combinations affect host and microbiota responses. We developed CompoRes—a computational tool that distinguishes the microbiota-independent impact of antibiotic-induced perturbations, revealing that antibiotics directly impact host physiology. We found that diurnal expression of major histocompatibility complex class II in the mouse colon is controlled by glucose via feeding. This pattern was lost during antibiotic treatment as vancomycin altered feeding behaviour in a microbiota-independent and evolutionarily conserved manner. Together, our study establishes a direct, non-microbial pathway by which antibiotics reshape host immunity and circadian physiology. Using a computational tool called CompoRes, the authors show that antibiotics can alter feeding behaviour, immunity and circadian regulation, revealing a non-microbial pathway by which antibiotic treatment reshapes host physiology.

works.title: IgG coating of Lactobacillus crispatus is associated with cervicovaginal immune homeostasis and reduced preterm birth rates, identifying S-layer proteins as candidate antibody targets
works.abstract: Abstract Background Maternal host immune system responses to cervicovaginal microbiota influence the risk of microbial-driven spontaneous preterm birth (sPTB). Immunoglobulins are present in cervicovaginal fluid (CVF). There are decreased IgG concentrations in women with CST I compared to CST IV, but their role in sPTB is unclear. Here, we investigate immunoglobulin coating of vaginal bacteria in 100 women at high-risk of sPTB (48 sPTB vs 53 term). Results Lactobacillus -dominated communities, especially L. crispatus -dominated, had higher proportions of IgG coating than high diversity, Lactobacillus -depleted communities. There was a positive correlation between IgG and IgG2 coating, indicating IgG2 was the main bound subclass. The percentage of bacterial coating by IgG and IgG2 was higher in women who delivered at term compared to preterm, and IgG coating negatively correlated with concentrations of CVF pro-inflammatory immune mediators. IgG and IgG2 both bound to L. crispatus surface layer proteins (SLPs), identifying SLPs as potential targets of antibody binding associated with immune homeostasis and term birth. Conclusions Our results reveal an association between vaginal bacterial antibody coating and mucosal microbe-immune homeostasis with reduced cervicovaginal inflammation and term birth. These represent a potential component of host-microbe interactions associated with pregnancy outcome.

works.title: A novel mycovirus identified in clinical isolates of Cryptococcus neoformans
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Mycoviruses are widespread throughout the fungal kingdom and are known to infect diverse fungal taxa, including fungal species that are important plant and human pathogens. Although many mycoviruses have been found to have minimal effects on their host, several viruses have been found to modulate fungal physiology, and, as a result, impact fungal virulence. Screens for mycoviruses in clinically relevant fungi have identified numerous mycoviruses within several important human pathogens, but mycoviruses remain uncharacterized in the clinically relevant human pathogen Cryptococcus neoformans. C. neoformans is an opportunistic encapsulated yeast responsible for life-threatening cryptococcal meningitis, a leading cause of mortality among immunocompromised individuals, particularly those with HIV/AIDS. We performed a search for viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRP) signatures in publicly available C. neoformans transcriptomic data. This search identified Totiviridae viral genomes within six clinical isolates of C. neoformans from Botswana. All six isolates originated from the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) of HIV-positive individuals with cryptococcal meningitis. Reverse transcription PCR (RT-PCR) independently validated the continued presence of the virus in three of these clinical isolates. Subsequent analysis of the viral genome identified two genotypes of a single species of Totivirus. This new species possesses canonical features of the Totiviridae family, including a slippery heptamer and a predicted RNA pseudoknot structure involved in programmed −1 ribosomal frameshifting for RdRP expression. Taken together, these results provide evidence of a mycovirus capable of infecting C. neoformans . IMPORTANCE We report the identification of a mycovirus capable of infecting Cryptococcus neoformans . While mycoviruses inhabit diverse fungal taxa, they have previously remained uncharacterized in this clinically significant fungal pathogen. The identification of the mycoviruses within C. neoformans isolated from the cerebrospinal fluid of individuals with cryptococcal meningitis places emphasis on the potential role of mycoviruses in the pathogenesis of C. neoformans .

works.title: Seasonal and evolutionary patterns of planktonic Hikarchaeia reveal ecological niches of marine rare biosphere constituents
works.abstract: Members of Marine Group IV, now termed Hikarchaeia, hold an important transitional evolutionary position among Archaea but remain uncultivated, and their ecology remains uncharacterized. Over a 5-year period, we performed monthly profile sampling in the North Atlantic Subtropical Gyre and sequenced V4 16S rRNA gene amplicons, while also collecting additional size-fractionated and metagenomic samples. Hikarchaeal relative abundance annually peaked at ~1% of prokaryotic amplicons. Their relative abundances were significantly higher after deep winter mixing when thermal stratification isolated exported dissolved organic matter in the twilight zone (TZ), the boundary region between the epipelagic and mesopelagic. A diminutive 1.17 Mbp complete hikarchaeal genome was recovered by sequencing and co-assembling diel TZ metagenomes from 200 m during summer, where their relative abundances were highest. Phylogenomic reconstruction incorporating our new metagenome-assembled genome (MAG) and public MAGs established five clades. Clades I and III were in subtropical and tropical environments, with vertical partitioning: Clade I dominated the TZ, and Clade III detection initiated in the lower mesopelagic and extended into the bathypelagic. Clade V is polar-associated. Data sparsity makes Clade II and IV distributions unclear. All Hikarchaeia recovered thus far appear to be free-living aerobes capable of heterotrophy. Unlike MGI, MGII, and MGIII Archaea, and most marine pelagic bacteria, the Hikarchaeia encode bacterioruberin biosynthesis, except deep Clade III. Hikarchaeia also have nitrile hydratases alongside enzymes for carbon monoxide oxidation and menaquinone biosynthesis, suggesting previously unrecognized roles in nitrogen and carbon cycling. Collectively, our studies reveal niche partitioning of evolutionarily distinct uncultivated Hikarchaeia clades and patterning within the rare biosphere.IMPORTANCEThe ocean and its vertical water-column structure are changing with planetary warming; yet, there are many enigmatic microbes, especially those that inhabit the deep ocean. Here, we illuminate a group of uncultivated Archaea that were discovered over two decades ago but still lack clear distributions and habitat preferences. With the first complete hikarchaeal genome now in hand, we identified distinct lineages within the Hikarchaeia that occupy different marine niches. Strong reoccurring seasonal patterns were observed that closely followed the annual cycle of temperature-driven ocean stratification. Given rapid natural and anthropogenic perturbations at hand, establishing baselines for these Archaea is critical for improving our understanding and modeling of marine microbiomes and their biogeochemical functions.

works.title: Ecophysiology of the cosmopolitan nitrite-oxidising genus Candidatus Nitromaricola
works.abstract: The majority of marine nitrite-oxidising bacteria (NOB) belong to three uncultured genera within the Nitrospinaceae family and thus the ecophysiology of these main nitrate producing microorganisms in the ocean remains poorly resolved. Here, we report on the environmental characterization of one of these genera, which we name Candidatus Nitromaricola. A single species within this genus, Candidatus Nitromaricola pontica, comprises >95% of the nitrite-oxidising community in the permanently stratified Black Sea. This provided a unique opportunity to study this globally abundant genus in situ, across pronounced environmental gradients of oxygen and inorganic nitrogen concentrations. We show that Ca. Nitromaricola pontica is capable of oxidising nitrite at similar rates in both oxic and apparently anoxic waters, although it had a higher abundance in the more oxygenated waters of the Black Sea. The genome of Ca. Nitromaricola pontica indicates that like other NOB, it is a chemolithoautotroph, oxidising nitrite, and fixing inorganic carbon. However, Ca. Nitromaricola pontica and other members of the Ca. Nitromaricola genus lack canonical high affinity terminal oxidases found in some other NOB genera. Single-cell analyses confirmed active autotrophic growth and showed that ammonium and urea, rather than nitrite, were the main nitrogen sources for biomass production. Our findings identify Ca. Nitromaricola as a globally abundant marine NOB and highlight its cosmopolitan lifestyle.

works.title: Longitudinal strain-level metagenomics reveals reciprocal Lactobacillus dynamics and outcome-associated protein variants during IVF treatment
works.abstract: The vaginal microbiome influences reproductive outcomes, yet strain-level dynamics during assisted reproductive treatment remain unexplored. Existing studies rely on species-level resolution that cannot distinguish within-species functional heterogeneity, leaving mechanistic questions unanswered. We conducted longitudinal shotgun metagenomic sequencing of vaginal samples from 41 women undergoing IVF/ICSI treatment across six timepoints (pre-stimulation baseline through pregnancy testing; 186 samples total). Strain-level analysis using inStrain revealed that Lactobacillus crispatus genomic stability and Lactobacillus iners adaptive flexibility both associate with pregnancy success, representing a reciprocal dynamic pattern. Functional protein analysis identified two outcome-associated targets: Inerolysin, a cholesterol-dependent cytolysin from L. iners , and L-lactate dehydrogenase (L-LDH) from L. crispatus . Structural modeling suggested that the Success-specific Inerolysin S429P mutation is predicted to disrupt cholesterol-binding, potentially attenuating cytolytic activity, while the L-LDH P169L mutation may enhance catalytic efficiency. Four orthogonal computational methods (FoldX thermodynamic calculation, ESM-1v evolutionary scoring, ConSurf conservation analysis, and 10 ns molecular dynamics simulation) provided convergent computational evidence supporting these structural interpretations. Critically, these protective variants were enriched at baseline (T1) rather than arising during treatment, indicating that pre-existing strain genetics predispose to differential responses under hormonal stress. A baseline 18-SNV prediction panel achieved an internal cross-validation AUC of 0.945 and an external validation AUC of 0.784 in an independent cohort ( n = 69) sequenced on a multiplex amplicon PCR platform. These findings reveal strain-level functional variants as candidate mechanistic determinants of reproductive success and potential biomarkers for personalized risk assessment in ART. The reciprocal dynamics of L. crispatus stability and L. iners adaptive flexibility, together with the dual-protein mutation pattern, suggest targets for strain-specific probiotic interventions. All computational predictions require experimental validation through biochemical and functional assays. Video Abstract

works.title: Acetate modulates host physiology and bacterial energetics to improve antibiotic efficacy during obesity-associated infection
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Antibiotic efficacy is conventionally attributed to the susceptibility of the infecting pathogen. However, obese patients experience disproportionately poor infection outcomes despite receiving antibiotics to which pathogens remain genetically susceptible. These observations suggest that host-associated factors can influence treatment outcomes independently of the bacterial genotype, although the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. Using a mechanistic comparison of diet-induced obese and healthy mice infected with Acinetobacter baumannii , we demonstrate that the effect of antibiotics is not solely a property of the pathogen but can be governed by a gut microbiota-derived metabolite acting on both host immunity and bacterial physiology. We identify obesity-associated acetate depletion as a key driver of antibiotic treatment failure, linking gut microbial metabolism to antibiotic activity during infection. We observed that this depletion impaired innate immune activation, reducing cytokine responses and neutrophil-mediated bacterial clearance. Under these conditions, A. baumannii displayed enhanced tolerance to bactericidal antibiotics, particularly tobramycin. Given these findings, we investigated whether acetate could be leveraged therapeutically to restore antibiotic efficacy. We observed that oral acetate supplementation remodeled the dysbiotic microbiome, whereas systemic acetate restored innate immune competence and neutrophil-mediated bacterial clearance. Most importantly, acetate reversed antibiotic tolerance and restored aminoglycoside killing by directly sensitizing host-induced tolerant bacterial populations. Mechanistically, acetate directly reprogrammed bacterial physiology to enhance aminoglycoside-mediated killing. Combined acetate-tobramycin treatment resulted in eradication of tolerant populations and markedly improved bacterial clearance in vivo . Our findings establish a mechanistic link between host metabolic state and antibiotic efficacy and identify acetate as a therapeutic intervention for obesity-associated gram-negative infections. IMPORTANCE Antibiotic treatment failure in obese patients remains poorly understood and therapeutically unaddressed. This study reveals that host metabolic state can control antibiotic response through a gut microbiota-derived metabolite that acts on both host defense and bacterial physiology. We identify obesity-driven depletion of microbiota-derived acetate as a previously unrecognized determinant of antibiotic failure, operating independently of bacterial resistance. By simultaneously restoring gut microbial balance, rescuing impaired innate immunity, and directly sensitizing pathogens to aminoglycoside killing through bacterial membrane alteration, acetate supplementation addresses the host-pathogen-microbiome axis through a single intervention. Given its established clinical safety, acetate represents a compelling combination therapy alongside aminoglycosides in obesity-associated gram-negative infections in a population for which host-directed treatment strategies are currently limited.

works.title: Transmission of lactic acid bacteria: a case study of the human vaginal microbiome
works.abstract: Lactic acid bacteria (LAB) are among the microorganisms to which humans are most frequently exposed, largely via consumption of fermented foods and probiotics and through interpersonal contact. Such continued exposure to LAB does not necessarily result in stable engraftment, raising fundamental questions about which factors mediate successful LAB transmission and niche specialization across human-associated microbiomes. Here, we rethink transmission of LAB across the human life course, spanning food-associated, within-host, and interindividual routes, highlighting that LAB transfer can occur across multiple contexts, but long-term engraftment depends less on exposure and more on host-mediated selection. As a paradigmatic case study, we present the human adult vaginal microbiome, a low-diversity environment generally dominated by strains of specific Lactobacillus species. These strains display clear signatures of niche specialization in the vaginal environment, making them taxonomically and functionally distinct from other LAB, and illustrating how host-mediated selection rather than exposure alone determines which LAB persist. This proposed conceptual framework, combined with the experimental and computational tractability of LAB, enables a better understanding of LAB engraftment in the human host, contributing to improved design and strain-level efficacy assessment of microbiome-based interventions, including probiotics, live biotherapeutic products, and microbiota transplants.

works.title: Exploring the biogeographical patterns and driving mechanisms of microbial communities in four microhabitats of Zostera japonica beds
works.abstract: Understanding the spatial distribution patterns and driving mechanisms of plant-associated microbial communities across multiple scales is essential for uncovering the generation and maintenance of microbial diversity under plant influence. However, large-scale evidence on the biogeographical patterns of seagrass-associated microbes remains scarce. Here, we sequenced microbial communities in four microhabitats (seawater, phyllosphere, rhizosphere, and sediment) of Zostera japonica beds in China, generating 480 amplicon sequencing datasets and 40 metagenomes. Subsequent analysis explored the structure and functional potential of microbial communities in these microhabitats. The microbial community exhibits significant spatial distribution patterns, characterized by latitudinal distribution patterns and distance decay relationships. While the null model results suggest a dominance of random processes in the construction of microbial communities in Zostera japonica beds, NST analysis reveals a transition from stochasticity to determinism in the assembly of rhizosphere bacterial communities with increasing latitude. Response ratio and GAM analysis further demonstrate differential responses of bacterial and fungal communities to environmental factors, indicating selective regulation of microbial groups by specific environmental drivers in different microhabitats. Functional analysis reveals that key genes involved in nitrogen and sulfur metabolism (such as nirS , norBC , cysNDCH , and cysJI ) display latitudinal gradient changes and microhabitat-specific differences in annotated microbes. For example, the cysC gene found in northern sampling points is sourced from Actinomycetota, Bacteridota, and Cyanobacteriota, while in southern sampling points, it primarily comes from Campylobacterota and Pseudomonadota, highlighting the functional adaptability of microbes to environmental heterogeneity. As the first systematic investigation into the biogeographic patterns of microbial communities associated with marine macrophytes, this study not only elucidates the multi-scale distribution patterns of Zostera japonica bed microbiomes but also establishes a theoretical framework for the dual regulation of microbial communities by latitude and microhabitat. The discoveries provide new insights into further investigating the interactions between microbes and seagrasses, as well as the potential for biogeochemical cycling. They contribute to understanding the adaptive strategies of seagrass ecosystems under different environmental pressures and how microbial communities respond to these stressors. This information is crucial for assessing the health of seagrass beds, predicting their response to environmental changes, and formulating effective conservation and management measures based on scientific evidence. Video Abstract

works.title: Diversity of dirammox microorganisms
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Our knowledge of the nitrogen cycle has been advanced by the discovery of anammox bacteria, ammonia-oxidizing archaea, and comammox bacteria, along with their high diversity. Direct ammonia oxidation (dirammox), a recently discovered heterotrophic nitrification pathway, converts ammonium and organic nitrogen directly to N 2 through the DnfABC multienzyme system, further expanding our understanding of the nitrogen cycle. However, the taxonomic distribution, prevalence, and nitrogen metabolic potential of microorganisms encoding dirammox genes remain poorly understood. Here, large-scale genome mining identified complete dnfABC gene clusters in 690 genomes representing 3 phyla and 26 genera. The dnfABC cluster showed a striking bimodal prevalence: it was nearly ubiquitous in Alcaligenes , Delftia , and Microvirgula but occurred sporadically in most other genera. These microorganisms were recovered from diverse environments, particularly organic nitrogen-rich habitats. Comparative analyses of DnfABC phylogeny, gene cluster organization, GC content, and flanking mobile genetic elements indicate that the dnfABC cluster is conserved within several core genera, whereas its sporadic distribution in other lineages suggests that horizontal gene transfer may have contributed to its dissemination. The dnfABC cluster co-occurs with genes associated with assimilatory nitrate/nitrite reduction to ammonium, dissimilatory nitrate/nitrite reduction to ammonium, denitrification, and/or nitrogen fixation, but not with marker genes for nitrification or anammox, indicating diverse nitrogen metabolic potential among potential dirammox microorganisms. Functional assays further showed that diverse dnfABC clusters consistently conferred ammonium- and glutamine-oxidizing activities in Escherichia coli , despite exhibiting low activities in their native hosts. These results suggest that dirammox is a broadly distributed, metabolically flexible, and tightly regulated pathway and may represent an overlooked route of nitrogen transformation in organic-rich habitats. IMPORTANCE Nitrogen is essential for all life, and our understanding of the nitrogen cycle has advanced substantially with the discovery of anammox bacteria, ammonia-oxidizing archaea, and comammox bacteria, which exhibit remarkable taxonomic and metabolic diversity. This study suggests that the recently discovered dirammox pathway may be more widespread in nature than previously recognized. Potential dirammox microorganisms exhibit broad phylogenetic and ecological distributions, high genomic diversity, and notable metabolic versatility. Functional assays indicate that dirammox activity is tightly regulated in native hosts, suggesting that its ecological role depends on specific environmental conditions. Unlike canonical nitrification and anammox, dirammox operates under conditions where other nitrogen transformations are limited, highlighting an important route of nitrogen loss in organic-rich habitats. These findings highlight the previously overlooked potential role of dirammox in nitrogen cycling, expand our understanding of microbial contributions to the global nitrogen cycle, and provide a foundation for future ecological and environmental research.
